docs.title: 4.1.8. Multiple Classes in a Single File
docs.text:
For a short example, a package containing multiple files is unnecessarily large. As in the previous chapter, we will therefore write a single file—[Classes01.kt], for example—which contains the function [main], possibly other functions, and the classes the program needs. Each file is placed in a package named after it ([classes01]), which allows each program in the project to have its own [Person] class: the class [Person] in the file [Classes01.kt] has the full name [classes01.Person]; the class in the file [Classes02.kt] has the full name [classes02.Person], and so on. It is executed using the command [gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes01.Classes01Kt].

It is important to understand how the compiler processes such a file. The classes in the file are ordinary, high-level classes, exactly as if they were written in their own file; the high-level functions, including [main], are grouped into a class named after the file, [Classes01Kt]. Compiling the file demonstrates this:

> kotlinc src/main/kotlin/classes01/Classes01.kt -d classes
> ls classes/classes01
Classes01Kt.class
Person.class

This has a consequence that distinguishes Kotlin from Java. In Java, the classes in a compact source file are nested within an implicit class and share their private members with the [main] method in the file. In Kotlin, there is no enclosing class: a member [private] of a class remains inaccessible to the function [main], even if it is written in the same file. The short examples in this chapter will therefore show the same compilation errors as the program [persons].

docs.title: 4.1.9. Another way to initialize: overloading
docs.text:
Let’s continue with the class [Person] and add a second method, [initialize], to it. The program [Classes01.kt] is as follows:

// overloading of the initialize method
package classes01

fun main() {
    val p1 = Person()
    p1.initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30)
    p1.identify()
    val p2 = Person()
    p2.initialize(p1)
    p2.identify()
}

// the Person class is declared after the main function
class Person {
    // private properties
    private var firstName = ""
    private var lastName = ""
    private var age = 0

    // initialization from three values
    fun initialize(p: String, n: String, age: Int) {
        firstName = p
        lastName = n
        this.age = age
    }

    // initialization from another person
    fun initialize(p: Person) {
        firstName = p.firstName
        lastName = p.lastName
        age = p.age
    }

    // identity of the person
    fun identify() {
        println("[$firstName, $lastName, $age]")
    }
}
  • line 2: the program package;
  • lines 4–10: the main program;
  • line 14: the class [Person] is declared after the function [main]. In Kotlin, the order of declarations in a file does not matter;
  • lines 21–24: the [initialize] method from the previous paragraph;
  • lines 28–31: a second method, [initialize].

We now have two methods named [initialize]: this is valid as long as they accept different parameters (in number or type). The method [initialize] is said to be overloaded. The compiler chooses which method to call based on the actual parameters: [p1.initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] (line 6) calls the first one, and [p2.initialize(p1)] (line 9) calls the second one. The return type alone is not sufficient to distinguish between two methods: two methods with the same name and the same parameters that differ only in their return type would be rejected. We’ll see that in Kotlin, default parameter values often eliminate the need to write multiple versions of the same method.

The parameter of the second method is a reference ([p]) to a person. The properties of the person ([p]) are then assigned to the current object ([this]). Note that the method [initialize] has direct access to the properties of the object [p] even though they are private (lines 29–31). This is always true: a method of a [C] class has access to the private members of all objects of the same [C] class.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes01.Classes01Kt
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

docs.title: 4.1.10. Constructors of the Person class
docs.text:
A constructor is a function called when an object is created. It is generally used to initialize the object. It can accept parameters but does not return a value. If a class [C] has a constructor that accepts n parameters, creating an object of that class is written as [val obj = C(arg1, arg2, ... argn)].

When a class [C] has one or more constructors, one of these constructors must be used to create an object of that class. If a class [C] does not declare any constructors, it has a default constructor with no parameters that does nothing. The object’s properties then retain their initial values. This is what happened in the previous programs, where we wrote [Person()].

Kotlin distinguishes between two types of constructors:

  • the primary constructor, at most one per class, declared in the class header immediately after the class name: [class Person(firstName: String, lastName: String, age: Int)];
  • secondary constructors, declared in the body of the class using the keyword [constructor]. When a class has a primary constructor, every secondary constructor must call it, either directly or through another secondary constructor.

The program [Classes02.kt] provides three constructors for the class [Person]:

// constructors of the Person class
package classes02

fun main() {
    val p1 = Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)
    p1.identify()
    val p2 = Person(p1)
    p2.identify()
    val p3 = Person()
    p3.identify()
}

// the primary constructor is declared in the class header:
// its parameters preceded by val (or var) are also properties of the class
class Person(private val firstName: String, private val lastName: String, private val age: Int) {
    // secondary copy constructor: it calls the primary constructor
    constructor(p: Person) : this(p.firstName, p.lastName, p.age)

    // secondary constructor without parameters: it also calls the primary constructor
    constructor() : this("?", "?", 0)

    // identity of the person
    fun identify() {
        println("[$firstName, $lastName, $age]")
    }
}
  • Line 15: the primary constructor. Its three parameters are preceded by [private val]: this is a shorthand notation that declares both a constructor parameter and a private, read-only property with the same name, initialized with the parameter’s value. The class has no other properties: these are declared in the header;
  • Line 17: the secondary copy constructor. The notation [: this(p.firstName, p.lastName, p.age)] calls the constructor of the same class that accepts three parameters: [String], [String], and [Int]—in this case, the primary constructor. This is referred to as chained constructors. As a result, the initialization code is written only once. This constructor has no body: it has nothing else to do;
  • line 20: the secondary constructor with no parameters, also chained to the primary constructor. Since the class has declared a primary constructor with parameters, it no longer has a default constructor: if we want to be able to write [Person()], we must declare it;
  • Lines 4–10: The three constructors are used.

The abbreviated notation in line 15 is equivalent to the following, longer notation, where the parameters of the primary constructor—excluding *[val]*—are simply parameters used to initialize properties declared in the body of the class:

class Person(firstName: String, lastName: String, age: Int) {
    // properties initialized with the parameters of the primary constructor
    private val firstName: String = firstName
    private val lastName: String = lastName
    private val age: Int = age
    ...
}

This is much shorter than the Java version, where you must declare the fields and then initialize them one by one in the constructor ([this.firstName = firstName;]…). The primary constructor has no body: the statements to be executed when the object is constructed are placed in [init] blocks, which we’ll cover a little later. We’ll also see that, thanks to default parameter values, Kotlin often doesn’t need secondary constructors: [class Person(..., private val age: Int = 0)] allows you to write both [Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] and [Person("Jean", "Dupont")].

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes02.Classes02Kt
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[?, ?, 0]

docs.title: 4.1.11. Object References
docs.text:
We use the [Person] class from the previous program, omitting its parameterless constructor but including the [initialize(String, String, Int)] method from the beginning of the chapter. Its properties are therefore declared using [var] rather than [val]. The test program becomes the following [Classes03.kt]:

// object references
package classes03

fun main() {
    // p1
    val p1 = Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)
    print("p1="); p1.identify()
    // p2 references the same object as p1
    val p2 = p1
    print("p2="); p2.identify()
    // p3 references an object that is a copy of the object referenced by p1
    val p3 = Person(p1)
    print("p3="); p3.identify()
    // we change the state of the object referenced by p1
    p1.initialize("Micheline", "Benoît", 67)
    print("p1="); p1.identify()
    // since p2 = p1, the object referenced by p2 has changed state
    print("p2="); p2.identify()
    // p3 does not reference the same object as p1: the object referenced by p3 has not changed
    print("p3="); p3.identify()
    // are p1 and p2 the same reference? and p1 and p3?
    println("p1 === p2 : ${p1 === p2}, p1 === p3 : ${p1 === p3}")
}

class Person(private var firstName: String, private var lastName: String, private var age: Int) {
    // secondary copy constructor
    constructor(p: Person) : this(p.firstName, p.lastName, p.age)

    // initialization
    fun initialize(p: String, n: String, age: Int) {
        firstName = p
        lastName = n
        this.age = age
    }

    // identity of the person
    fun identify() {
        println("[$firstName, $lastName, $age]")
    }
}

The function [print] (lines 7, 10, …) writes its parameter without starting a new line. The two statements on these lines are separated by a semicolon, which is only necessary in Kotlin to write multiple statements on a single line. Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes03.Classes03Kt
p1=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p2=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p3=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p1=[Micheline, Benoît, 67]
p2=[Micheline, Benoît, 67]
p3=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p1 === p2 : true, p1 === p3 : false

When the variable [p1] is declared by [val p1 = Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] (line 6), [p1] references the object [Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] but is not the object itself. In C, this would be referred to as a pointer—that is, the address of the created object. If [p1] were declared as [var p1: Person? = ...] and we then wrote [p1 = null], it wouldn’t be the object [Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] that would be modified, but rather the reference [p1] that would change its value. The object would be “lost” if it were not referenced by any other variable: the memory it occupies would later be reclaimed by the Java virtual machine’s garbage collector, which executes Kotlin programs just like Java programs.

When we write [val p2 = p1] (line 9), we initialize the reference [p2]: it “points” to the same object (it refers to the same object) as the reference [p1]. Thus, if you modify the object “pointed to” (or referenced) by [p1], you also modify the one referenced by [p2] (lines 4–5 of the results). Note that [p1] and [p2] are declared alongside [val]: the keyword prohibits changing the reference contained in the variable, not modifying the referenced object, which is what the call to [p1.initialize(...)] does (line 15).

When you enter [val p3 = Person(p1)] (line 12), a new object, [Person], is created. This new object will be referenced by [p3]. If you modify the object referenced by [p1], it does not affect the object referenced by [p3] (line 6 of the results).

Finally, on line 22, the operator [===], applied to two object references, indicates whether they refer to the same object: [p1] and [p2] refer to the same object, while [p1] and [p3] refer to two different objects, although they have the same content (line 7 of the results). This is the [] operator in Java. In Kotlin, the [] operator compares the contents of the objects by calling their [equals] method: we’ll see later how to define it. For a class that does not define [equals], as in this case, [p1 == p3] still compares the references and evaluates to [false].

docs.title: 4.1.12. Passing Object Reference Parameters
docs.text:
In the previous chapter, we saw that Kotlin, like Java, passes function parameters by value: the function receives a copy of the actual parameter’s value. Let’s see what this means when the parameter is an object reference. To do this, we’ll use the class [StringBuilder] (the class of JDK, which Kotlin uses directly). A [String] object cannot be modified: an operation like [s.uppercase()] returns a new [String] object. A [StringBuilder] object, on the other hand, is a mutable string: its [append] method appends characters to the string without creating a new object.

In Java, the example assigned a new object to the parameter [sbf1] of the called function. This is not possible in Kotlin: a function parameter is read-only, just like a variable [val]. The compiler rejects the statement [sbf1 = StringBuilder("test1*****")]:

Classes04.kt:5:5: error: 'val' cannot be reassigned.
    sbf1 = StringBuilder("test1*****")
    ^^^^

The program [Classes04.kt] therefore copies the parameter [sbf1] into a modifiable local variable:

// passing parameters of object reference type
package classes04

fun main() {
    val sb0 = StringBuilder("test0")
    val sb1 = StringBuilder("test1")
    println("In calling function before the call: sb0=$sb0, sb1=$sb1")
    val sb2 = changeStringBuilder(sb0, sb1)
    println("In calling function after the call: sb0=$sb0, sb1=$sb1, sb2=$sb2")
}

// the called function
fun changeStringBuilder(sbf0: StringBuilder, sbf1: StringBuilder): StringBuilder {
    println("Start of called function: sbf0=$sbf0, sbf1=$sbf1")
    // we modify the object referenced by sbf0
    sbf0.append("*****")
    // a parameter is read-only: sbf1 = StringBuilder(...) would be rejected.
    // The local variable sbl first references the same object as sbf1, then a new object
    var sbl = sbf1
    sbl = StringBuilder("test1*****")
    // a new object is returned to the caller
    val sbf2 = StringBuilder("test2*****")
    println("End of called function: sbf0=$sbf0, sbf1=$sbf1, sbl=$sbl, sbf2=$sbf2")
    return sbf2
}
  • Lines 5–6: two references, [sb0] and [sb1], to objects of type [StringBuilder];
  • line 8: these are passed to the function [changeStringBuilder], whose result—a third reference—is assigned to [sb2];
  • lines 13–24: a high-level function, which has the formal parameters [sbf0] and [sbf1]. When the function starts, [sbf0] and [sb0] are two distinct references that point to the same object: the reference [sb0] was copied into [sbf0] (references are passed by value). The same applies to [sbf1] and [sb1];
  • lines 19–20: the local variable [sbl] first receives the reference [sbf1], then the reference to a new object. This is what the Java program did with the parameter [sbf1] itself.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes04.Classes04Kt
In calling function before the call: sb0=test0, sb1=test1
Start of called function: sbf0=test0, sbf1=test1
End of called function: sbf0=test0*****, sbf1=test1, sbl=test1*****, sbf2=test2*****
In calling function after the call: sb0=test0*****, sb1=test1, sb2=test2*****

Explanations:

  • [sb0] and [sbf0] are two distinct references to the same object. This object was modified via [sbf0] (line 16). This modification is visible via [sb0] (line 4 of the results);
  • [sb1], [sbf1], and, initially, [sbl] are three distinct references to the same object. [sbl] is assigned a new value and now points to a new object (line 20). This does not change the value of [sbf1] or that of [sb1], which continue to point to the original, unmodified object (lines 3 and 4 of the results);
  • a Kotlin function cannot, therefore, change the value of a variable belonging to the caller. To pass a new object to the caller, it returns it as a result (lines 22 and 24). When there are multiple results, they are grouped into an object: a pair ([Pair]), as seen in the previous chapter, or a data class (see below).

Remember that a function can modify the object referenced by a parameter, but not the caller’s variable that contains the reference. Like Java, and unlike C#, Kotlin does not pass parameters by reference; it goes a step further than Java by prohibiting any assignment to a parameter, which prevents confusion between the parameter and the caller’s variable.

docs.title: 4.1.13. Temporary Objects
docs.text:
In an expression, you can explicitly call an object’s constructor: the object is created, but there is no variable to access it later (to modify it, for example). This temporary object is created for the purpose of evaluating the expression and is then discarded. The memory space it occupied will later be automatically reclaimed by the garbage collector, whose role is to reclaim memory space occupied by objects that are no longer referenced by the program’s data.

Consider the following program, [Classes05.kt], where the constructors of the [Person] class display a message. This is an opportunity to introduce the initialization block [init]:

// temporary objects
package classes05

fun main() {
    Person(Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)).identify()
}

class Person(private val firstName: String, private val lastName: String, private val age: Int) {
    // the init block is executed by the primary constructor
    init {
        println("Constructor Person(String, String, Int)")
    }

    // the secondary constructor first calls the primary constructor, then executes its body
    constructor(p: Person) : this(p.firstName, p.lastName, p.age) {
        println("Constructor Person(Person)")
    }

    // identity of the person
    fun identify() {
        println("[$firstName, $lastName, $age]")
    }
}
  • line 5: the object [Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] is constructed and then passed to the copy constructor, which constructs a second object; the method [identify] is then called on that object. Neither of the two objects is referenced by a variable;
  • lines 9–11: Since the primary constructor has no body, the statements to be executed when the object is constructed are placed in a [init] block. A class can have multiple [init] blocks: these are executed, along with the initializations of the properties declared in the class body, in the order in which they are written. They are part of the primary constructor and have access to its parameters;
  • lines 15–16: A secondary constructor may have a body. It is executed after the constructor called by [: this(...)]—in this case, the primary constructor with its [init] blocks.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes05.Classes05Kt
Constructor Person(String, String, Int)
Constructor Person(String, String, Int)
Constructor Person(Person)
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

The results show the sequential construction of the two temporary objects. The first is constructed by the primary constructor (line 1 of the results). The second is constructed by the secondary constructor, which begins by calling the primary constructor—hence the execution of the [init] block (line 2)—and then executes its own body (line 3). In Java, the copy constructor in the example was not chained to the primary constructor and displayed only its own message; in Kotlin, as long as a class has a primary constructor, every object passes through it: the [init] blocks are always executed.

docs.title: 4.1.14. Properties: Getter and Setter Methods
docs.text:
In Java, the convention is to declare private fields and provide access to their values through public methods: getters, such as [getAge()], and setters, such as [setAge(int)]. These methods are written by hand (or generated by the development environment), and the user of the class writes [p.setAge(p.getAge() + 1)]. Kotlin, like C#, has properties: a public property is data that the user reads and writes using dot notation, like a field, but which is actually read and written through a getter and a setter. The compiler generates them. The program [Classes06.kt] demonstrates this:

// properties instead of getters and setters
package classes06

fun main() {
    val p = Person("Jean", "Michelin", 34)
    // reading the properties: implicit call of their getter
    println("p=(${p.firstName},${p.lastName},${p.age})")
    // writing a property: implicit call of its setter
    p.age = 56
    println("p=(${p.firstName},${p.lastName},${p.age})")
}

// three public read-write properties
class Person(var firstName: String, var lastName: String, var age: Int)
  • line 14: the class *[Person]* fits on a single line. The three parameters of the primary constructor are preceded by *[var]*: these are three public properties (default visibility), which are both readable and writable. Since the class has no body, the curly braces are omitted;
  • line 7: reading the properties [p.firstName], [p.lastName], and [p.age]. Each read operation is a call to the property’s accessor;
  • Line 9: Writing the property [age], that is, calling its setter.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes06.Classes06Kt
p=(Jean,Michelin,34)
p=(Jean,Michelin,56)

The [javap] tool from JDK, which displays the contents of a [.class] file, shows what the Kotlin compiler generated for the [Person] class (the [-p] option also displays private members):

> javap -p -cp build/classes/kotlin/main classes06.Person
Compiled from "Classes06.kt"
public final class classes06.Person {
  private java.lang.String firstName;
  private java.lang.String lastName;
  private int age;
  public classes06.Person(java.lang.String, java.lang.String, int);
  public final java.lang.String getFirstName();
  public final void setFirstName(java.lang.String);
  public final java.lang.String getLastName();
  public final void setLastName(java.lang.String);
  public final int getAge();
  public final void setAge(int);
}

Each property resulted in a private field (lines 3–5), a public getter, and a public setter (lines 7–12), which follow the naming convention established in the early days of Java, namely “JavaBeans”: the getter for the property [age] is named [getAge], and its setter is [setAge]; a boolean property whose name begins with [is]—such as [isActive]—has a getter with the same name, [isActive], and a setter named [setActive]. This is important: many Java libraries (such as Jackson for JSON and Hibernate for databases, which we’ll use later) rely on this convention to locate an object’s data; they can find the data for Kotlin objects without any difficulty. Conversely, a Kotlin program that uses a Java class writes [p.age] to call [p.getAge()], and [p.age = 56] to call [p.setAge(56)]. We also note that the class and its methods are [final]: we’ll see with inheritance that in Kotlin, classes and methods are final by default.

The notation [p.age = 56] resembles the assignment of a public field. The difference is significant: because it uses a setter, we can—without changing anything in the code written by the class’s users—later assign a setter to the property that controls the values it receives. This is the subject of the following section. In Kotlin, therefore, we never write accessors or setters in the Java style: we declare properties.

docs.title: 4.1.15. Setters That Validate Received Values
docs.text:
The advantage of setters over public fields is the ability to control the values assigned to the fields: a setter can validate the received value and throw an exception if it is invalid. Kotlin allows you to provide a property with a custom getter ([get]) and a custom setter ([set]). Consider the program [Classes07.kt]:

// setters that check the validity of the values received
package classes07

fun main() {
    val p = Person("Jean", "Michelin", 34)
    println("p=(${p.firstName},${p.lastName},${p.age})")
    p.age = 56
    println("p=(${p.firstName},${p.lastName},${p.age})")
    try {
        p.age = -4
    } catch (ex: IllegalArgumentException) {
        println(ex.message)
    }
    // constructor without parameters then assignment of the properties
    val p2 = Person()
    p2.age = 7
    p2.firstName = "Arthur"
    p2.lastName = "Martin"
    println("p2=(${p2.firstName},${p2.lastName},${p2.age})")
    try {
        val p3 = Person()
        p3.firstName = "Paul"
        p3.lastName = " "
    } catch (ex: IllegalArgumentException) {
        println(ex.message)
    }
    // the constructor also checks the values received
    try {
        val p4 = Person("", "Durand", 20)
        println("p4=(${p4.firstName},${p4.lastName},${p4.age})")
    } catch (ex: IllegalArgumentException) {
        println(ex.message)
    }
}

// the class has a primary constructor without parameters
class Person() {
    // properties with a custom setter (set)
    var firstName = ""
        set(value) {
            // valid first name?
            require(value.isNotBlank()) { "invalid first name ($value)" }
            // field designates the backing field that stores the value of the property
            field = value
        }

    var lastName = ""
        set(value) {
            // valid last name?
            require(value.isNotBlank()) { "invalid last name ($value)" }
            field = value
        }

    var age = 0
        set(value) {
            // valid age?
            require(value >= 0) { "invalid age ($value)" }
            field = value
        }

    // secondary constructor: it goes through the setters to benefit from their checks
    constructor(firstName: String, lastName: String, age: Int) : this() {
        this.firstName = firstName
        this.lastName = lastName
        this.age = age
    }
}

The three properties have a custom setter that validates the received value:

  • lines 39–44: the property [firstName]. Its declaration is followed, on the subsequent lines, by the definition of its setter, [set(value) { ... }]. The parameter [value] is the value assigned to the property (the name [value] is conventional, as in C#); its type is that of the property. The property has no custom accessor: it retains the generated accessor, which returns the stored value;
  • Line 42: The function [require(condition) { message }], discussed in the previous chapter, throws a [IllegalArgumentException] exception—the exception designed to signal an invalid parameter—if the condition is false. The message, calculated by the lambda expression within curly braces, is constructed only in this case. The function [isNotBlank] returns [true] if the string contains at least one character other than a space. There is no need to test the value [null] as in Java: the property is of type [String], not [String?], and the compiler prohibits assigning [null] to it;
  • Line 44: In a getter or setter, the keyword [field] refers to the field that stores the property’s value (known as the “backing field”). Do not write [firstName = value]: this would be a call to the setter itself, which would call itself indefinitely;
  • lines 47–58: The properties [lastName] and [age] are constructed using the same pattern;
  • line 37: the class has a primary constructor with no parameters. The initial values of the properties ([""] and 0) are assigned directly to the fields, without going through the setters;
  • Lines 62–65: A secondary constructor that initializes the object using the setters. This allows it to take advantage of the checks performed by the setters, which are written only once. Here, [this.firstName = firstName] is the call to the setter for the property [firstName] with the value of the parameter [firstName].

Why not write [class Person(firstName: String, lastName: String, age: Int)] with properties initialized by [var age = age]? Because initializing a property at its declaration directly affects the field without calling the setter: an age of -4 would be accepted without an error. To verify the values received by the primary constructor, we write the checks in a [init] block, or, as shown here, we pass the values through the setters.

In Java, setters called by the constructor had to be declared as [final]: otherwise, a derived class could have redefined them, and the parent class’s constructor would have called the new version even before the derived class’s constructor was executed. In Kotlin, classes and their members are final by default: this precaution is unnecessary.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes07.Classes07Kt
p=(Jean,Michelin,34)
p=(Jean,Michelin,56)
invalid age (-4)
p2=(Arthur,Martin,7)
invalid last name ( )
invalid first name ()

Line 3 of the results shows that the assignment [p.age = -4] (line 10) was rejected by the setter: [ex.message] is the exception message. Lines 15–18: An object is created using the parameterless constructor and then initialized by its setters. Lines 21–23: The name containing a space is rejected (line 5 of the results). Lines 29–30: The three-parameter constructor rejects an empty first name (line 6 of the results).

Java does not have object initializers—a syntax that would allow multiple properties to be set within the object creation expression itself. Neither does Kotlin, but it offers two equivalent solutions: named and default-valued constructor parameters, and the [apply] function. We’ll cover them in the next two paragraphs.

docs.title: 4.1.16. Read-Only Properties and Optional Parameters
docs.text:
A property declared with [val] must be assigned a value exactly once—at the time of its declaration, in the primary constructor, or within a [init] block—and cannot be modified thereafter. The compiler enforces this. This is equivalent to the [final] field in Java: the property has only a getter, no setter. The [Classes08.kt] program illustrates several cases, as well as default parameters and named arguments:

// read-only properties, private setter, computed property,
// mandatory and optional parameters, named arguments
package classes08

fun main() {
    val p = Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30, "Angers")
    println(p.identity)
    // the first name is read / write
    p.firstName = "Jacques"
    // the age can only be modified inside the class
    p.growOlder()
    println(p.identity)
    // the following lines are rejected by the compiler
    // p.lastName = "Durand" // lastName is a val property
    // p.age = 40            // the setter of age is private
    // p.identity = "?"      // identity is a val (computed) property

    // a mandatory parameter and an optional parameter
    val c1 = Contact("jean.dupont@example.com")
    println("Contact : ${c1.email}, ${c1.phone}")
    // named arguments, in any order
    val c2 = Contact(phone = "02 41 00 00 00", email = "paul.martin@example.com")
    println("Contact : ${c2.email}, ${c2.phone}")
    // Contact(null) is rejected by the compiler; an empty email is rejected at runtime
    try {
        val c3 = Contact(" ")
        println("Contact : ${c3.email}")
    } catch (ex: IllegalArgumentException) {
        println("Error: ${ex.message}")
    }
}

class Person(var firstName: String, val lastName: String, age: Int, val city: String) {
    // the age can be read by everyone, but its setter is private
    var age = age
        private set

    // a computed property: it has no backing field, its getter computes its value
    val identity: String
        get() = "[$firstName, $lastName, $age, $city]"

    // the age is only modified by the methods of the class
    fun growOlder() {
        age++
    }
}

// the email is mandatory, the phone optional: its parameter has a default value
class Contact(val email: String, val phone: String = "unknown") {
    // check executed when the object is constructed
    init {
        require(email.isNotBlank()) { "the email is mandatory" }
    }
}
  • line 33: the first name is a [var] property, which is read-write; the last name and city are [val] properties, which are read-only. The constructor assigns a value to them, which cannot be changed afterward. The parameter [age], without [val] or [var], is simply a constructor parameter;
  • lines 35–36: The property [age] is initialized with the parameter [age]. It is readable by everyone, but its setter is private ([private set]): it can only be modified by the class’s methods, such as [growOlder] (lines 43–44). The setter retains its default behavior: it does not require a body;
  • lines 39–40: a computed property. It has a custom accessor, [get() = ...], which calculates its value each time it is read based on the other properties; it has no field to store a value. To the user of the class, nothing distinguishes it from another property: [p.identity] (line 7). This is equivalent to the [getIdentity()] method in the Java version;
  • lines 14–16: three statements that the compiler rejects, for the reasons given in the comments. If we uncomment them, the compiler reports the following (we have also uncommented the [Contact(null)] statement mentioned on line 24):
Classes08.kt:14:7: error: 'val' cannot be reassigned.
    p.lastName = "Durand" // lastName is a val property
      ^^^^^^^^
Classes08.kt:15:7: error: cannot access 'age': it is private in 'classes08.Person'.
    p.age = 40            // the setter of age is private
      ^^^
Classes08.kt:16:7: error: 'val' cannot be reassigned.
    p.identity = "?"      // identity is a val (computed) property
      ^^^^^^^^
Classes08.kt:24:13: error: null cannot be a value of a non-null type 'String'.
    Contact(null)
            ^^^^
  • line 49: the class [Contact] has a required property, email, and an optional property, phone. The optional nature of the phone property is expressed by a default value for the constructor’s parameter [phone]: [val phone: String = "unknown"]. If the argument is omitted, as in line 19, the parameter takes this value. In Java, which does not have optional parameters, a second constructor—chained to the first—was required; in Kotlin, a single constructor suffices. Default values are used in the same way for the parameters of any function;
  • line 22: the arguments are named: [phone = "02 41 00 00 00"]. They can then be provided in any order, and the call is more readable when multiple parameters have the same type. Named arguments also allow you to omit only one optional parameter among several: with [f(a: Int = 0, b: Int = 0)], you can write [f(b = 5)];
  • Lines 51–52: The mandatory nature of the email is first expressed by the parameter type: [String] does not accept the value [null], and the call [Contact(null)] is rejected at compile time (last error above). In Java, this had to be checked at runtime ([Objects.requireNonNull]). The next step is to reject an empty email address: this is the role of the block [init], which is executed when the object is constructed. On line 26, an email address consisting of a single space is rejected.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes08.Classes08Kt
[Jean, Dupont, 30, Angers]
[Jacques, Dupont, 31, Angers]
Contact : jean.dupont@example.com, unknown
Contact : paul.martin@example.com, 02 41 00 00 00
Error: the email is mandatory

Note how short the declarations are: the [Person] class, which took up about fifty lines in Java with its getters, setters, and validation, takes up only about fifteen lines in Kotlin.

docs.title: 4.1.17. The apply and also functions instead of fluid mutators
docs.text:
In Java, when an object has many optional fields, the number of constructors increases and setter calls become longer. A common technique is to have each setter return the current object ([this]): the calls can then be chained together—this is referred to as “chained” methods: [new Person().setFirstName("jean").setLastName("Dupont").setAge(30)]. In Kotlin, default parameters and named arguments make this technique much less useful. And when you want to set multiple properties of an object immediately after its creation, the standard library provides “scope functions” that can be used with any object, including [apply] and [also]. The program [Classes09.kt] illustrates these and, in passing, introduces the properties [lateinit]:

// instead of "fluent" setters: the scope functions apply and also
// a lateinit property
package classes09

fun main() {
    // apply executes the block with the object as current object (this), then returns the object
    val p = Person().apply {
        firstName = "  jean "
        lastName = "Dupont"
        age = 30
    }
    println(p.identity)
    try {
        p.lastName = ""
    } catch (ex: IllegalArgumentException) {
        println(ex.message)
    }
    try {
        p.age = -4
    } catch (ex: IllegalArgumentException) {
        println(ex.message)
    }
    println(p.identity)
    // also executes the block with the object as parameter (it), then returns the object
    val p2 = Person().apply { firstName = "Arthur"; lastName = "Martin"; age = 7 }
        .also { println("Creation of ${it.identity}") }
    // reading a lateinit property that has not yet received a value
    try {
        println(p2.city)
    } catch (ex: UninitializedPropertyAccessException) {
        println(ex.message)
    }
    p2.city = "Angers"
    println("${p2.identity} lives in ${p2.city}")
}

class Person {
    // properties checked by their setter
    var firstName = ""
        set(value) {
            field = validate(value, "first name")
        }

    var lastName = ""
        set(value) {
            field = validate(value, "last name")
        }

    var age = 0
        set(value) {
            require(value >= 0) { "invalid age ($value)" }
            field = value
        }

    // a property without an initial value: it will receive its value later
    lateinit var city: String

    // identity: the type of the property is inferred from its getter
    val identity get() = "[$firstName, $lastName, $age]"
}

// checking a mandatory string: it is returned without its leading and trailing spaces
// (private top-level function: it is only visible in this file)
private fun validate(value: String, label: String): String {
    require(value.isNotBlank()) { "invalid $label ($value)" }
    return value.trim()
}
  • lines 7–10: [obj.apply { ... }] executes the block between curly braces with [obj] as the current object: within the block, [firstName = " jean "] refers to [this.firstName = " jean "], where [this] is the new person. Then [apply] returns the object itself, which is assigned to [p]. The assignment acts as an object initializer; each assignment goes through the property setter and thus its validations;
  • lines 39–46: the setters for the first name and last name assign the value returned by the function [validate] to the field;
  • lines 64–66: The validations for the first name and last name, which are identical, are factored into the function [validate]. It does not use any properties of a person: we have made it a high-level function, declared as [private], and therefore visible only in the file [Classes09.kt]. In Java, this would have had to be implemented as a private static method of the class. The function [trim] removes the leading and trailing spaces from the string;
  • line 59: the type of the computed property [identity], [String], is inferred from its accessor expression;
  • Lines 25–26: [obj.also { ... }] executes the block by passing it the object as a parameter, referred to as [it], and then returns the object. It is used for a secondary action—such as a progress display, as shown here—without interrupting the call chain. Here, [apply] returns the person, [also] displays it and then returns it in turn, and it is assigned to [p2]. Line 25: The three assignments in the [apply] block are written on a single line, separated by semicolons;
  • Line 56: A property of a type other than [null] must, in principle, be assigned a value upon creation. The keyword [lateinit] (“late initialization”) waives this requirement: the property [city] will be assigned its value later (line 33). If it is accessed before then, a [UninitializedPropertyAccessException] exception is thrown (lines 29–31). [lateinit] applies only to a property [var] of an object type that is not [null] ([String], but not [Int] or [String?]) and without custom accessors or mutators. It is used when the value is provided after the object is constructed, for example by a dependency injection framework such as Spring (Chapter 6) or by an initialization method in a test. Within the class, the expression [::city.isInitialized] indicates whether the property has been assigned a value.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes09.Classes09Kt
[jean, Dupont, 30]
invalid last name ()
invalid age (-4)
[jean, Dupont, 30]
Creation of [Arthur, Martin, 7]
lateinit property city has not been initialized
[Arthur, Martin, 7] lives in Angers

The first name "jean," which was entered with spaces around it (line 8), was stored without them (line 1 of the results). Invalid modification attempts were rejected, and the person was not changed (lines 2–4 of the results). Line 6 of the results is the message for exception [UninitializedPropertyAccessException].

There are three other scope functions: [let], seen in the previous chapter with the values [null], [run], and [with]. They differ in how the block refers to the object ([this] or [it]) and in what they return (the object or the result of the block):

FunctionObject in the blockResultTypical Use[apply][this]The objectConfigure a newly created object[also][it]The objectFollow-up action (monitoring, verification) in a sequence[let][it]The result of the blockProcess a non-[null] value: [x?.let { ... }][run][this]The result of the blockCalculate a value from an object[with][this]The result of the block[with(obj) { ... }]: Multiple calls on the same object

To build complex objects, Java often uses the “Builder” design pattern: an auxiliary class, equipped with fluent methods, collects values and then constructs the final object. In Kotlin, a constructor with named parameters and default values replaces this pattern in most cases.

docs.title: 4.1.18. Class members: the companion object
docs.text:
Suppose we want to count the number of [Person] objects created in an application. We could manage a counter ourselves, but we risk overlooking temporary objects that are created here and there. It seems safer to include a statement in the constructor of the [Person] class that increments a counter. This counter cannot be an ordinary property, since each object has its own properties: it is a property of the class itself, not of a particular instance of that class.

Java declares such a member using the keyword [static]. Kotlin does not have a [static] keyword: class members are declared in a companion object ([companion object { ... }]), a single object attached to the class and declared within the class body. Its members are used with the class name: [Person.nbPersons], [Person.unknown()]. Here is an example, [Classes10.kt]:

// class members: the companion object; a singleton object (object)
package classes10

fun main() {
    val p1 = Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)
    val p2 = Person(p1)
    Person(p1)
    Log.write("Number of persons created: ${Person.nbPersons}")
    // a class method
    val p3 = Person.unknown()
    p3.identify()
    p2.identify()
    Log.write("Number of persons created: ${Person.nbPersons}")
}

class Person(private val firstName: String, private val lastName: String, private val age: Int) {
    // secondary copy constructor
    constructor(p: Person) : this(p.firstName, p.lastName, p.age)

    // the init block is part of the primary constructor: every construction increments the counter
    init {
        nbPersons++
    }

    // identity of the person
    fun identify() {
        println("[$firstName, $lastName, $age]")
    }

    // the companion object: its members are those of the class itself
    companion object {
        // class property: readable by all, modifiable only by the Person class
        var nbPersons = 0L
            private set

        // class method
        fun unknown() = Person("?", "?", 0)
    }
}

// a singleton object: the Log class and its single instance are declared together
object Log {
    // the state of the object: the number of the last message written
    private var number = 0

    fun write(message: String) {
        number++
        println("[$number] $message")
    }
}
  • lines 31–37: the companion object for the class [Person];
  • lines 33–34: the class property [nbPersons], initialized to 0 (of type [Long] due to the suffix [L]). It is readable by everyone ([Person.nbPersons], line 8), but its setter is private: only the class [Person] can modify it. There is no need to define, as in Java, a private field and a static accessor method [getNbPersons()];
  • line 37: a class method. It is called using the class name: [Person.unknown()] (line 10). A method of the companion object does not have a current [Person] object: it cannot directly use a person’s properties. A method that creates and returns an object of its class, such as this one, is called a “factory”;
  • lines 21–22: the block [init] increments the counter. It is part of the primary constructor, and the copy constructor—which is chained to the primary constructor—therefore also executes it.

The last element of the program is a singleton object, [Log], declared using the keyword [object] (lines 42–48):

  • A declaration such as [object Log { ... }] declares both a class and its single instance, which is created automatically when it is first used. There is no constructor: no other [Log] object can be created. The object is referenced by its name: [Log.write(...)];
  • an object has a state—in this case, the number of the last message written—which is preserved from one call to the next;
  • A companion object is a special case of a singleton object: one that is attached to a class.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes10.Classes10Kt
[1] Number of persons created: 3
[?, ?, 0]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[2] Number of persons created: 4

The program correctly counted the temporary object created on line 7. The log numbered its two messages. Compilation produces a class for the companion object, [Person$Companion], alongside the classes [Person], [Log], and [Classes10Kt]; a method of the companion object is thus, for JVM, an instance method of the [Person.Companion] object. To allow a Java program to call it as a static method ([Person.unknown()] rather than [Person.Companion.unknown()]), it is annotated with [@JvmStatic].

From the beginning, we’ve been using functions that, in Java, would be static methods: [println], [readln]… In Kotlin, these are top-level functions, declared outside of any class. This is the Kotlin way of writing what Java calls a utility class, such as the class [Math]: a file containing high-level functions (the standard library provides [kotlin.math.sqrt] and [kotlin.math.PI]), or, if you want to group functions under a single name, a [object]. The companion object is reserved for items that are truly specific to the class: factories, constants, and counters.

docs.title: 4.1.19. An array of people
docs.text:
An object is a piece of data like any other, and as such, multiple objects can be grouped into an array [Classes11.kt]:

// an array of persons
package classes11

fun main() {
    // an array of 3 references, all initialized to null
    val friends = arrayOfNulls<Person>(3)
    friends[0] = Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)
    friends[1] = Person("Sylvie", "Vartan", 52)
    friends[2] = Person("Neil", "Armstrong", 66)
    // display: the elements are of type Person?
    for (friend in friends) {
        friend?.identify()
    }
}

class Person(private val firstName: String, private val lastName: String, private val age: Int) {
    // identity of the person
    fun identify() {
        println("[$firstName, $lastName, $age]")
    }
}
  • Line 6: creates an array of 3 elements. The function [arrayOfNulls<Person>(3)] initializes these elements with the value [null], meaning they do not reference any objects: the array type is therefore [Array<Person?>], an array of references that can hold the value [null]. Colloquially, we refer to this as an “array of objects,” even though it is merely an array of object references. The creation of the array—which is itself an object—does not create any objects of the same type as its elements; this must be done subsequently;
  • lines 7–9: creation of the 3 objects of type [Person];
  • lines 11–12: display the contents of the array [friends]. The variable [friend] is of type [Person?]: the compiler requires the safe call [friend?.identify()], which does nothing if [friend] is equal to [null].

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes11.Classes11Kt
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Sylvie, Vartan, 52]
[Neil, Armstrong, 66]

The element type [Person?] indicates that an array created empty in Java contains [null]. This is avoided in Kotlin by creating the array with its elements, as shown in the following paragraph.

docs.title: 4.1.20. Type Inference and Array Initialization
docs.text:
The program [Classes12.kt] demonstrates the syntax that simplifies the creation of objects and arrays:

// type inference and array initialization
package classes12

fun main() {
    // the type of the variable is inferred from the expression that initializes it
    val p1 = Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)
    val p2 = Person()
    p2.firstName = "Arthur"
    p2.lastName = "Martin"
    p2.age = 7
    // an array created and initialized by a list of values
    val friends = arrayOf(
        p1,
        p2,
        Person("Sylvie", "Vartan", 52),
        Person("Neil", "Armstrong", 66),
    )
    for (friend in friends) {
        println(friend.identity)
    }
    // an array created on the fly, passed as a parameter
    display(arrayOf(Person("Pauline", "Leduc", 12), p1))
    // an array whose elements are computed by a lambda from their index
    val children = Array(3) { i -> Person("Child${i + 1}", "Martin", i + 2) }
    display(children)
}

// a function that receives an array of persons
fun display(persons: Array<Person>) {
    for (p in persons) {
        println("Display : ${p.identity}")
    }
}

// all properties have a default value: Person() is possible
class Person(var firstName: String = "", var lastName: String = "", var age: Int = 0) {
    // identity
    val identity get() = "[$firstName, $lastName, $age]"
}
  • Line 6: The type of the variable, [Person], is inferred from the expression that initializes it. The variable is nonetheless typed: [p1] can only refer to a person. This has been the standard notation in Kotlin since the beginning of the course; the Java equivalent is the keyword [var]. Kotlin goes a step further than Java: type inference also applies to properties ([identity], line 38) and to the return type of functions whose body is an expression;
  • line 36: all properties have a default value. The primary constructor can therefore be called without arguments, [Person()] (line 7), and the person is then assigned its properties (lines 8–10). There is no need to declare a parameterless constructor;
  • Lines 12–16: An array created and populated by the function [arrayOf(...)], which receives the values of the elements. The size of the array is the number of values; its type, [Array<Person>], is derived from the type of the values: the elements cannot be of type [null]. A trailing comma (line 16) is allowed in an argument list, as in any parameter list: it makes it easier to add an element;
  • line 18: the loop variable [friend] is of type [Person]: no safe call this time;
  • line 22: an array created on the fly, passed as a parameter. This is called an anonymous array: it is not referenced by any variable in the function [main]. Unlike in Java, there is no difference in syntax depending on whether the array is created in a declaration or elsewhere;
  • line 24: the constructor [Array(size) { i -> ... }] creates an array in which each element is calculated by the lambda based on its index [i];
  • lines 29–31: a high-level function that takes an array of people.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes12.Classes12Kt
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Arthur, Martin, 7]
[Sylvie, Vartan, 52]
[Neil, Armstrong, 66]
Display : [Pauline, Leduc, 12]
Display : [Jean, Dupont, 30]
Display : [Child1, Martin, 2]
Display : [Child2, Martin, 3]
Display : [Child3, Martin, 4]

We will make little use of arrays of objects: the next chapter introduces lists ([List], [MutableList]), which are more flexible ([listOf(p1, p2)] is written as [arrayOf(p1, p2)]).

docs.title: 4.2.1. Overview
docs.text:
Here we discuss the concept of inheritance. The purpose of inheritance is to “customize” an existing class so that it meets our needs. Suppose we want to create a class [Teacher]: a teacher is a specific type of person. They have attributes that other people do not have: the subject they teach, for example. But they also have the attributes common to all people: first name, last name, and age. A teacher is therefore a full member of the class [Person] but has additional attributes. Rather than creating a class [Teacher] from scratch, we prefer to build upon the existing class [Person] and adapt it to the specific characteristics of teachers. This is made possible by the concept of inheritance.

To indicate that the class [Teacher] inherits from the class [Person], we write [class Teacher(...) : Person(...)]: the name of the parent class follows the colon, as in C#, whereas Java writes [extends Person].

[Person] is called the parent class (or base class, or superclass), and [Teacher] is called the derived class (or child class, or subclass). A [Teacher] object has all the characteristics of a [Person] object: it has the same properties and methods. These properties and methods of the parent class are not repeated in the definition of the child class; we simply specify the properties and methods added by the child class. A Kotlin class can inherit from only one parent class.

An important difference from Java: in Kotlin, a class is final by default, meaning it cannot be inherited from. To allow derivation, the parent class must be declared [open] (“open”). This is a deliberate choice by the language designers: a class must be designed to be derived from, and the person writing it must state this explicitly.

The examples in this paragraph are two multi-file programs, located in the packages [inheritance1] and [inheritance2]. In the [inheritance1] package, the [Person] class is defined as follows in [Person.kt]:

package inheritance1

// open: the Person class can have derived classes
open class Person(firstName: String, lastName: String, age: Int) {
    // properties checked by their setter
    var firstName = ""
        set(value) {
            field = validate(value, "first name")
        }

    var lastName = ""
        set(value) {
            field = validate(value, "last name")
        }

    var age = 0
        set(value) {
            require(value >= 0) { "invalid age ($value)" }
            field = value
        }

    // identity of the person
    val identity get() = "[$firstName, $lastName, $age]"

    // construction: initialization through the setters, counting, trace
    init {
        this.firstName = firstName
        this.lastName = lastName
        this.age = age
        nbPersons++
        println("Constructor Person(String, String, Int)")
    }

    companion object {
        // number of persons created
        var nbPersons = 0L
            private set
    }
}

// checking a mandatory string
private fun validate(value: String, label: String): String {
    require(value.isNotBlank()) { "invalid $label ($value)" }
    return value
}
  • line 4: the class is open ([open]): subclasses can be derived from it. The primary constructor has three parameters, which are not properties (no [val] or [var]);
  • lines 6–19: three properties whose setters verify the received value (see program [Classes07.kt]). The checks for the first name and last name, which are identical, are factored into the private function [validate] (lines 42–44), as in the program [Classes09.kt];
  • line 23: the method [identify] from the first examples has been replaced by the calculated property [identity], which returns the person’s identity instead of displaying it;
  • Lines 26–31: The primary constructor’s block [init] initializes the object using property setters, increments the person counter, and displays a follow-up message. It is placed after the property declarations: property initializations and the [init] blocks are executed in the order in which they are written, and a property must have been initialized (here with [""] or 0) before it can be used;
  • lines 34–37: the person counter from the section on the companion object.

We create a class [Teacher] that inherits from the class [Person] [Teacher.kt]:

package inheritance1

// the Teacher class derives from the Person class:
// its primary constructor passes three of its parameters to the constructor of the parent class
class Teacher(firstName: String, lastName: String, age: Int, var section: Int) :
    Person(firstName, lastName, age) {

    // trace
    init {
        println("Constructor Teacher(String, String, Int, Int)")
    }
}

The class [Teacher] adds to the properties and methods of the class [Person]:

  • lines 5–6: The class [Teacher] derives from the class [Person]. The header is written on two lines to fit on the page;
  • line 5: a property [section], declared in the primary constructor ([var section: Int]), which is the number of the section to which the teacher belongs within the faculty (roughly one section per subject). The property is read-write: it replaces the getter and setter of the Java version;
  • Lines 9–10: a [init] block that displays a progress message.

docs.title: 4.2.2. Creating a Teacher Object
docs.text:
A child class does not inherit constructors from its parent class. It must define its own constructors. The header for the [Teacher] class is as follows:

class Teacher(firstName: String, lastName: String, age: Int, var section: Int) :
    Person(firstName, lastName, age) {

The primary constructor receives four parameters ([firstName], [lastName], [age], [section]) and passes three ([firstName], [lastName], [age]) to its parent class—in this case, the class [Person]—using the syntax [: Person(firstName, lastName, age)] (line 2). We know that this class has a constructor, [Person(String, String, Int)], which will allow us to create a person using the passed parameters. Once the construction of the [Person] portion is complete (initializations and [init] blocks of the [Person] class), the construction of the [Teacher] object continues with the initialization of its [section] property and the execution of its own [init] blocks. The notation [: Person(firstName, lastName, age)] corresponds to the [super(firstName, lastName, age);] statement in the Java constructor; if the derived class does not have a primary constructor, each of its secondary constructors calls the parent class’s constructor via [constructor(...) : super(...)].

In summary, the constructor of a derived class:

  • passes to its parent class the parameters that the parent class needs to construct itself;
  • uses the remaining parameters to initialize its own properties.

It might have been preferable to directly initialize the properties [firstName], [lastName], and [age] directly in the [Teacher] class, using statements like [this.firstName = firstName]. This is possible here because these properties are public and mutable, but it would be a poor solution, and it would be impossible if they were private: the private members of the [Person] class are accessible only to methods of the [Person] class. All other objects, including objects of derived classes as in this case, must access them through public (or protected, such as [protected]) members. Most importantly, the [Person] part of the object must in any case be instantiated by a constructor of the [Person] class. If you write [: Person()] without arguments, the compiler reports that the parameters for the parent class’s constructor are missing:

Teacher.kt:6:5: error: no value passed for parameter 'firstName'.
    Person() {
    ^^^^^^
Teacher.kt:6:5: error: no value passed for parameter 'lastName'.
    Person() {
    ^^^^^^
Teacher.kt:6:5: error: no value passed for parameter 'age'.
    Person() {
    ^^^^^^

Using the parent class’s constructor is therefore the correct solution, and it is the standard approach: when creating a child object, you first call the parent object’s constructor and then complete the initializations specific to the child object ([section] in our example).

Finally, if you omit the keyword [open] before the class [Person], the derivation is rejected:

Teacher.kt:6:5: error: this type is final, so it cannot be extended.
    Person(firstName, lastName, age) {
    ^^^^^^

docs.title: 4.2.3. Inherited Methods
docs.text:
The class [Teacher] does not define a property named [identity]. The expression [e.identity], where [e] is a teacher, therefore refers to the property [identity] inherited from the class [Person]: it is public and, by inheritance, becomes a public property of the class [Teacher]. The same applies to methods. The test program [Main.kt] from the package [inheritance1] is as follows:

package inheritance1

fun main() {
    // a teacher
    val e = Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61)
    // the identity property inherited from the Person class
    println(e.identity)
    // the section property specific to the Teacher class
    println("section=${e.section}")
    // a person
    val p = Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)
    // the display function receives a Person or an object of a derived class
    display(e)
    display(p)
    // the toString method inherited from the Any class
    println(e.toString())
    println(p.toString())
    println("Number of persons created: ${Person.nbPersons}")
}

// displays the identity of p
fun display(p: Person) {
    println(p.identity)
}
  • line 5: creation of a teacher;
  • line 7: display of the teacher’s identity, obtained via the [identity] property inherited from the [Person] class;
  • line 9: the property [section], specific to the class [Teacher];
  • lines 13–14: call to the function [display] (lines 22–23) with a teacher and then a person. We’ll return to this in the next paragraph;
  • lines 16–17: call to the [toString] method on both objects. We’ll also come back to this.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=inheritance1.MainKt
Constructor Person(String, String, Int)
Constructor Teacher(String, String, Int, Int)
[Lucile, Dumas, 56]
section=61
Constructor Person(String, String, Int)
[Lucile, Dumas, 56]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
inheritance1.Teacher@2f0e140b
inheritance1.Person@7440e464
Number of persons created: 2

We can see that:

  • an object [Person] (line 1 of the results) was constructed before the object [Teacher] (line 2);
  • [e.identity] provided the identity of the teacher’s [Person] part, without its section (line 3);
  • the person counter also counts the teacher (line 10): a teacher is a person.

To obtain a teacher’s complete identity, the class [Teacher] must define its own property [identity]. This is what the package [inheritance2] does.

docs.title: 4.2.4. Polymorphism
docs.text:
Consider a class hierarchy: C0 ← C1 ← C2 ← … ← Cn, where Ci ← Cj indicates that class Cj is derived from class Ci. This implies that class Cj has all the characteristics of class Ci plus additional ones. Let Oi be objects of type Ci. It is valid to write [Oi = Oj] with j > i. Indeed, by inheritance, class Cj has all the characteristics of class Ci plus additional ones. Therefore, an object Oj of type Cj contains an object of type Ci. The operation [Oi = Oj] causes the variable Oi, of type Ci, to reference the object Oj: only the members defined in class Ci can be accessed through it.

The fact that a variable Oi of class Ci can actually reference not only an object of class Ci but any object derived from class Ci is called polymorphism: the ability of a variable to reference different types of objects.

Let’s take an example and consider the function [display] from the previous program:

fun display(p: Person) {
    println(p.identity)
}

We can pass it either a *[Person] or a *[Teacher]: In the latter case, the formal parameter [p], which is of type [Person], receives a value of type [Teacher]. Since the type [Teacher] is derived from the type [Person], this is valid. The expression [p.identity] used here the property [identity] of the class [Person], the only one that exists in the program: for the teacher (line 6 of the results), we only obtain the identity of its “Person” part .” Let’s see what happens when the class [Teacher] has its own property [identity].

docs.title: 4.2.5. Method Redefinition and Dynamic Binding
docs.text:
In package [inheritance2], class [Person] is the same as the one in package [inheritance1], with two changes:

    // identity of the person: open, it can be overridden in a derived class
    open val identity get() = "[$firstName, $lastName, $age]"

    // overriding the toString method of the Any class
    override fun toString() = identity
  • Line 2: The property [identity] is declared as [open]: it can be overridden in a derived class. In Kotlin, methods and properties are final by default, just like classes: only the members [open] of a class [open] can be overridden;
  • lines 4–5: an override of the [toString] method, discussed in the following paragraph.

In the [Teacher] class, the [identity] property is redefined as follows:

package inheritance2

// a Kotlin class is final by default: the Teacher class cannot be derived from
class Teacher(firstName: String, lastName: String, age: Int, var section: Int) :
    Person(firstName, lastName, age) {

    // trace
    init {
        println("Constructor Teacher(String, String, Int, Int)")
    }

    // the identity property overrides that of the parent class
    override val identity get() = "Teacher[${super.identity},$section]"
}
  • Line 13: The property [identity] overrides the property of the parent class; it has the same name and the same type. It uses the property [identity] from its parent class, designated as [super.identity], to retrieve the “Person” portion, then supplements it with the section specific to the class [Teacher]. A method is redefined in the same way: same name, same parameters, same return type, and the keyword [override];
  • Line 13: The keyword [override] is required. It serves the same purpose as the [@Override] annotation in Java, which is optional: if the property did not redefine anything (e.g., a typo in the name or a different type), the compiler would report the error instead of silently creating a new member. Conversely, a redefinition without *[override]* is rejected:
Teacher.kt:13:9: error: 'identity' hides member of supertype 'Person' and needs an 'override' modifier.
    val identity get() = "Teacher[${super.identity},$section]"
        ^^^^^^^^
  • and if the [identity] property of the [Person] class is not declared as [open], the redefinition is rejected:
Teacher.kt:13:5: error: 'identity' in 'Person' is final and cannot be overridden.
    override val identity get() = "Teacher[${super.identity},$section]"
    ^^^^^^^^
  • Line 3: The class [Teacher] is not declared as [open]: it is final, as we’ll explain a little later.

Consider a [Teacher] object [E]. This object contains a [Person] object:

The property [identity] is defined in both the class [Teacher] and its parent class [Person]. The version used by [p.identity] is determined at runtime, based on the actual type of the object referenced by [p], rather than at compile time based on the declared type of the variable. This is known as dynamic binding. To execute [o.m()], the virtual machine searches for a method named [m] in the following order:

  • in the class of the [o] object;
  • in its parent class, if it has one;
  • in the parent class of its parent class, if it exists;
  • and so on.

The same applies to a property, where reading the property involves calling its accessor, which is a method. Inheritance therefore allows you to redefine members in the child class that have the same signature as those in the parent class. This is what allows you to adapt the child class to its own needs. The program [Main.kt] from the package [inheritance2] is as follows:

package inheritance2

fun main() {
    // a teacher
    val e = Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61)
    display(e)
    // a person
    val p = Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)
    display(p)
    // seen as a Person, the teacher remains a teacher
    val pe: Person = e
    println(pe.identity)
    println((e as Person).identity)
    // println(Any?) displays the result of the toString method of the object
    println(e)
    println(p)
    // an array of persons of different types
    val persons = arrayOf(p, e)
    for (person in persons) {
        println("${person::class.simpleName} : $person")
    }
}

// displays the identity of p
fun display(p: Person) {
    println(p.identity)
}

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=inheritance2.MainKt
Constructor Person(String, String, Int)
Constructor Teacher(String, String, Int, Int)
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
Constructor Person(String, String, Int)
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
Person : [Jean, Dupont, 30]
Teacher : Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]

This time, in row 3 of the results, the [display] function correctly displayed the teacher's full identity. Lines 11–13 of the program show that, when viewed through a variable of type [Person] or converted to [Person] by the operator [as] (the equivalent of the Java operator [(Person)]), the teacher remains a teacher: it is still the property [identity] of the class [Teacher] that is used (lines 6–7 of the results). The conversion changes the type of the reference, not that of the object.

In this regard, Kotlin is closer to C# than to Java. In C#, a method can only be overridden if it is declared virtual ([virtual]), and the override is indicated by [override]; in Kotlin, [open] serves the same purpose as [virtual]. In Java, on the other hand, all methods are overridable by default, except those declared as [final]. In all cases, once the method is overridden, the binding is dynamic.

docs.title: 4.2.6. The Any class and the toString method
docs.text:
The [Any] class is the “parent” class of all Kotlin classes. Thus, when you write [class Person], you are implicitly writing [class Person : Any()]. It corresponds to the Java class [java.lang.Object]: at runtime, for JVM, it is actually [Object].

The class *[Any] defines three methods, all of which are *[open], and from which all objects inherit:

  • [toString(): String]: returns a textual representation of the object. By default, this is the object’s full class name, followed by the character [@] and a hash code written in hexadecimal;
  • [equals(other: Any?): Boolean]: indicates whether the object is “equal” to the object [other]. By default, it is only equal to itself: the method compares references, just like the [===] operator. This is the method called by the [==] operator;
  • [hashCode(): Int]: returns a hash code for the object, used by dictionaries and sets (next chapter). The methods [equals] and [hashCode] are discussed later.

The [getClass()] method of the Java class [Object] is not a method of [Any]: In Kotlin, the expression [obj::class] returns the Kotlin description of the object’s actual class (of type [KClass]), whose property [simpleName] is the class name; [obj::class.java], or [obj.javaClass], returns the Java description ([Class]).

It was the method [toString] of the class [Any] that was used by the calls [e.toString()] and [p.toString()] from the package [inheritance1]: [inheritance1.Teacher@2f0e140b] and [inheritance1.Person@7440e464] (lines 8–9 of the results; the numbers vary from one execution to another). Although we did not redefine the [toString] method in the [Person] and [Teacher] classes, the [toString] method in the [Any] class was able to display the object’s actual class name.

In the [inheritance2] package, the [Person] class redefines the [toString] method: [override fun toString() = identity]. The keyword [override] is also required here. Let’s return to the program [Main.kt] in the package [inheritance2]:

    // println(Any?) displays the result of the toString method of the object
    println(e)
    println(p)
    // an array of persons of different types
    val persons = arrayOf(p, e)
    for (person in persons) {
        println("${person::class.simpleName} : $person")
    }

On line 2, the function [println(message: Any?)] accepts a parameter of type [Any?]; therefore, since [Any] is the superclass of all classes, any object—in this case, a [Teacher]—can be passed. It prints the result of the object’s [toString] method to the console. Since the binding is dynamic, the [toString] method of the actual object is used—in this case, the one inherited from the [Person] class. This method returns [identity], a redefined property: for the teacher [e], it is therefore the property [identity] of the class [Teacher] that is used, as shown in line 8 of the results. It is therefore unnecessary to redefine [toString] in the class [Teacher].

The same mechanism applies to string templates: in ["... : $person"] (line 7), the object [person] is converted to a string by its method [toString]. The loop on line 6 iterates over an array of references to [Person], which actually point to objects of different types: [person::class.simpleName] returns the actual class name of each object (lines 10–11 of the results).

docs.title: 4.2.7. Final, open, and sealed classes
docs.text:
The class [Teacher] in the package [inheritance2] is declared as [class Teacher(...) : Person(...)], without the keyword [open]: it is final. The declaration [class TeacherResearcher(...) : Teacher(...)] would be rejected by the compiler with the message already encountered: [this type is final, so it cannot be extended]. In Java, it’s the opposite: a class is open by default, and you make it final using the keyword [final]. Kotlin’s approach prevents accidental subclassing of a class that was not intended to be subclassed. The same applies to members: a method or property can only be overridden if it is declared as [open]. A member that overrides another ([override]) is itself overridable in subsequent derived classes, unless it is declared as [final override].

Between a class open to all derivations and a final class, Kotlin offers—as Java has since version 17—an intermediate option: the sealed class ([sealed]), for which all direct derived classes are known at compile time. The program [Classes13.kt] illustrates this:

// final classes, open classes and sealed classes
package classes13

fun main() {
    val persons = arrayOf(
        Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 61),
        Student("Paul", "Martin", "computer science"),
        Adjunct("Marc", "Petit"),
        Consultant("Lise", "Morel", "Airbus"),
    )
    for (p in persons) {
        println("${p::class.simpleName} : ${p.identity}")
    }
    // when on a sealed class: the compiler knows that all cases are handled
    for (p in persons) {
        println("${p.firstName} is ${description(p)}")
    }
    // the allowed direct subclasses of the sealed class Person
    println("Person is sealed: ${Person::class.java.isSealed}")
    for (c in Person::class.java.permittedSubclasses) {
        println("allowed subclass: ${c.simpleName}")
    }
}

// a when expression without an else branch
fun description(p: Person): String = when (p) {
    is Teacher -> "a teacher in section ${p.section}"
    is Student -> "a student in ${p.major}"
    is Adjunct -> "an adjunct"
}

// a sealed class: its direct derived classes are all known at compile time
sealed class Person(val firstName: String, val lastName: String) {
    open val identity get() = "[$firstName, $lastName]"
}

// a derived class is final by default
class Teacher(firstName: String, lastName: String, val section: Int) : Person(firstName, lastName) {
    override val identity get() = "${super.identity}, section $section"
}

class Student(firstName: String, lastName: String, val major: String) : Person(firstName, lastName) {
    override val identity get() = "${super.identity}, major $major"
}

// open: the hierarchy is open again from this class
open class Adjunct(firstName: String, lastName: String) : Person(firstName, lastName)

// a class derived from Adjunct: allowed, since Adjunct is open
class Consultant(firstName: String, lastName: String, val company: String) : Adjunct(firstName, lastName) {
    override val identity get() = "${super.identity}, company $company"
}
  • line 33: the class [Person] is sealed. Its direct subclasses must be declared in the same package and module as it (in any file within that package). Unlike in Java, there is no list of allowed classes ([permits]): it includes all classes in the package that are its direct subclasses, in this case [Teacher], [Student], and [Adjunct]. A sealed class is implicitly abstract (see below: you cannot create objects of this class, only of its derived classes) and its constructor is protected: it is intended only for derived classes;
  • line 34: the property [identity] is open: derived classes can redefine it;
  • Lines 38–43: The classes [Teacher] and [Student] are final by default. In Java, a class derived from a sealed class must be declared as [final], [sealed], or [non-sealed]; in Kotlin, the default rule suffices;
  • Line 47: The class [Adjunct] is open ([open]): it reopens the hierarchy, allowing any class to derive from it. This is equivalent to Java’s [non-sealed]. A third option is to declare it as [sealed] itself. The class has no body: there is nothing to add to the [Person] class;
  • line 50: the class [Consultant] derives from [Adjunct], which is allowed;
  • lines 5–9: The array type, [Array<Person>], is inferred by the compiler: it is the most specific common type among the four objects;
  • lines 26–29: the expression [when], seen in the previous chapter, tests the type of the person here using the operator [is]. In each branch, the compiler knows that [p] is of the type being tested: [p.section] is accepted in the [is Teacher] branch without explicit conversion. This is “smart casting,” which is explained in more detail at the end of the chapter. Most importantly, the expression [when] has no branch [else]: since the class [Person] is sealed, the compiler knows that every person is a [Teacher], a [Student], or a [Adjunct], and that all three cases are handled. A consultant is an adjunct: they are handled by the third branch;
  • lines 19–21: the Java description of the class ([Person::class.java]) indicates whether it is sealed ([isSealed]) and lists its permitted direct subclasses ([permittedSubclasses]). For a sealed class, the Kotlin compiler produces the same information as the Java compiler: for JVM, the class [Person] is a sealed Java class.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes13.Classes13Kt
Teacher : [Lucile, Dumas], section 61
