The value of an instance is a random number between 0 and 99 (line 61), provided by a random number generator in the class [kotlin.random.Random] shared by all instances: it is stored in the class’s companion object (line 68), which serves the same purpose as the static field in the Java version. This generator is initialized with a fixed “seed”: it therefore always produces the same sequence of numbers, making the results reproducible. This is not the same algorithm as that of the [java.util.Random] class: the resulting sequence is therefore not the same as that of the Java version. If reproducibility is not required, the default generator [Random.Default] (for example, [Random.nextInt(100)]) is used; or, for security purposes, the class [java.security.SecureRandom];
  • lines 73–77: The class [StringValue] also implements the interface [IValue]: the value of an instance is the length of the character string passed to the constructor, calculated by the property accessor;
  • lines 15–19: Pairs of objects of type [RandomValue] are sorted. The function [repeat(5) { ... }] executes the block five times;
  • lines 22–25: A pair of objects of type [StringValue] is sorted;
  • line 26: if this line is uncommented, the compiler reports that the type [Int] is invalid.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes19.Classes19Kt
pi=(1,2)
pn=(a,null)
Before --> (67,8)   After --> (8,67)
Before --> (73,41)   After --> (41,73)
Before --> (28,53)   After --> (28,53)
Before --> (26,93)   After --> (26,93)
Before --> (31,39)   After --> (31,39)
Before --> (xxxxxxxxxxxxxx,xx)
After --> (xx,xxxxxxxxxxxxxx)

Here are the errors encountered during compilation once line 26 is uncommented:

Classes19.kt:26:5: error: cannot infer type for type parameter 'T'. Specify it explicitly.
Classes19.kt:26:11: error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Pair<Int>', but 'Pair<uninferred T (of fun <T : IValue> order)>' was expected.

The compiler attempted to infer the type [T]: the pair constraint requires [T] = [Int], and the bound constraint requires that [T] implements [IValue]; since the two constraints are incompatible, it cannot find a type [T] (“uninferred T”). If you specify the type yourself—[order<Int>(pi)]—the message is more straightforward: [type argument is not within its bounds: type parameter 'T (of fun <T : IValue> order)' must be subtype of 'IValue', but actual: 'Int'].

docs.title: 4.8.3. Generic Interfaces: Comparable<T> and Comparator<T>
docs.text:
To illustrate the concept of a generic interface, we’ll sort a list of people according to different criteria. For this purpose, Kotlin provides functions for mutable lists (and arrays) that sort the collection in place, and functions for all collections that return a new, sorted list without modifying the original. We’ll use several of them:

  • [list.sort()] sorts the list according to the natural order of its elements: These elements must implement the [Comparable<T>] interface, whose sole method, [operator fun compareTo(other: T): Int], compares the current object to the [other] object. This is the Java interface [java.lang.Comparable], as seen from Kotlin;
  • [list.sortWith(comparator)] sorts the list according to the order defined by a comparator object, which implements the [Comparator<T>] interface (an alias for [java.util.Comparator]), whose method [fun compare(a: T, b: T): Int] compares two objects;
  • [list.sortedWith(comparator)], [list.sortedBy { ... }], and [list.sortedByDescending { ... }] return a new sorted list.

The methods [compareTo] and [compare] follow the same rule: they return a positive number if x > y, 0 if x == y, and a negative number if x < y. It is up to the developer to define the meaning of the operators <, ==, and >. For example, if [p1] and [p2] are two [Person] objects, we can say that p1 > p2 if the name of [p1] comes after the name of [p2] in alphabetical order. This will result in an ascending sort based on the people’s names. If we want to sort by age, we’ll say that p1 > p2 if the age of [p1] is greater than the age of [p2]. To sort in descending order, simply reverse the signs of the results.

We now know enough to sort a list of people. The program [Classes20.kt] is as follows:

package classes20

import java.text.Collator
import java.util.Locale

// the generic interfaces Comparable<T> and Comparator<T>: sorting a list of persons
fun main() {
    val persons = mutableListOf(
        Person("claude", "pollon", 25),
        Person("valentine", "germain", 35),
        Person("paul", "germain", 32),
    )
    // display
    display("List to sort", persons)
    // sort according to the natural order of persons (Comparable): the age
    persons.sort()
    display("List after sorting by age", persons)
    // sort by last name and first name (Comparator)
    persons.sortWith(CompareNames())
    display("List after sorting by last and first name", persons)
    // sort by decreasing age, with an anonymous object
    persons.sortWith(object : Comparator<Person> {
        override fun compare(p1: Person, p2: Person) = p2.age.compareTo(p1.age)
    })
    display("List after sorting by decreasing age", persons)
    // the > operator uses the compareTo method of Comparable
    println("${persons[0]} > ${persons[1]} : ${persons[0] > persons[1]}")
    // comparators built by compareBy and thenBy; sortedWith returns a new list
    val collator = Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRENCH)
    val byNames = compareBy<Person, String>(collator) { it.lastName }.thenBy(collator) { it.firstName }
    display("New list sorted by last and first name", persons.sortedWith(byNames))
    // a sort on a single property
    display("New list sorted by first name", persons.sortedBy { it.firstName })
    // the original list has not changed
    display("Original list", persons)
}

// display of a list of persons
fun display(text: String, persons: List<Person>) {
    println(text + "-".repeat(50 - text.length))
    for (p in persons) {
        println(p)
    }
}

// a person, comparable to another person
class Person(val firstName: String, val lastName: String, val age: Int) : Comparable<Person> {
    // the natural order of persons: the order of ages
    override fun compareTo(other: Person) = age.compareTo(other.age)

    override fun toString() = "[$firstName, $lastName, $age]"
}

// comparison of the last and first names of two persons
class CompareNames : Comparator<Person> {
    // string comparison according to the rules of the French language
    private val collator = Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRENCH)

    override fun compare(p1: Person, p2: Person): Int {
        // we compare the last names
        val i = collator.compare(p1.lastName, p2.lastName)
        if (i != 0) {
            return i
        }
        // equal last names: we compare the first names
        return collator.compare(p1.firstName, p2.firstName)
    }
}
  • lines 8–11: the editable list of people. The Java version sorted an array; the same functions [sort] and [sortWith] exist for Kotlin arrays;
  • Lines 47–51: The class [Person] implements the generic interface [Comparable<Person>]: its objects are comparable to other people. Its method [compareTo] (line 49) defines the natural order of people, in this case, the order of ages. The [a.compareTo(b)] method for integers returns a negative, zero, or positive number depending on whether [a] is less than, equal to, or greater than [b]: this is exactly what the [compareTo] method expects (Java writes [Integer.compare(a, b)]). The parameter is called [other] in the interface; we keep this name when redefining it, otherwise the compiler—which allows named arguments—would issue a warning;
  • line 16: sorting in natural order;
  • line 19: sorting the list of people by last name and first name. The parameter of the function [sortWith] is an instance of the class [CompareNames], which implements the generic interface [Comparator<Person>];
  • lines 55–66: the class [CompareNames]. Its method [compare] implements the method [compare(a: T, b: T)] of the interface [Comparator<T>], where [T] = [Person]. Strings are not compared using the [compareTo] method, which follows the order of character codes (uppercase letters before lowercase, accented letters after "z"), but rather by a [java.text.Collator] object (line 57) that applies the sorting rules for the French language. Kotlin directly uses a class from JDK here;
  • lines 22–24: sorting by descending age. This time, the comparator is an anonymous object: the expression [object : Comparator<Person> { ... }] declares an unnamed class that implements the [Comparator<Person>] interface and immediately creates an instance of that class. This is equivalent to Java’s anonymous class ([new Comparator<Person>() { ... }]). The body of the object provides the method [compare]. An anonymous object avoids having to declare a class that is used only once;
  • Line 27: The method [compareTo] of the interface [Comparable] is declared as [operator]: the operators [<], [>], [<=], and [>=] can therefore be applied to people ([p1 > p2] is translated to [p1.compareTo(p2) > 0]), as we saw earlier with operator overloading;
  • Lines 29–30: The Kotlin library creates comparators: [compareBy(comparator) { it.lastName }] returns a comparator for people that compares their names (the value calculated by the lambda) using the specified comparator, in this case [Collator]; [thenBy(comparator) { it.firstName }] adds a second criterion, used in case of a tie on the first criterion. Both types of [compareBy] (the element and the key) are specified between angle brackets, as the compiler cannot infer them from the lambda alone. Without a specific comparator, we simply write [compareBy<Person> { it.lastName }.thenBy { it.firstName }]: the keys are then compared in their natural order. The comparator [byNames] is a better replacement for the class [CompareNames];
  • line 31: the function [sortedWith] returns a new list sorted by the comparator; the list [persons] remains unchanged;
  • line 33: The function [sortedBy] sorts according to the key calculated by the lambda expression—in this case, the first name—in its natural order ([sortedByDescending] would sort in descending order);
  • line 35: the original list has not been modified by the functions [sortedWith] and [sortedBy];
  • line 40: the function [repeat] repeats a string: the title line is padded with dashes up to 50 characters.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes20.Classes20Kt
List to sort--------------------------------------
[claude, pollon, 25]
[valentine, germain, 35]
[paul, germain, 32]
List after sorting by age-------------------------
[claude, pollon, 25]
[paul, germain, 32]
[valentine, germain, 35]
List after sorting by last and first name---------
[paul, germain, 32]
[valentine, germain, 35]
[claude, pollon, 25]
List after sorting by decreasing age--------------
[valentine, germain, 35]
[paul, germain, 32]
[claude, pollon, 25]
[valentine, germain, 35] > [paul, germain, 32] : true
New list sorted by last and first name------------
[paul, germain, 32]
[valentine, germain, 35]
[claude, pollon, 25]
New list sorted by first name---------------------
[claude, pollon, 25]
[paul, germain, 32]
[valentine, germain, 35]
Original list-------------------------------------
[valentine, germain, 35]
[paul, germain, 32]
[claude, pollon, 25]

In this case, the Java version featured three types of classes declared inside another class. Kotlin has the same types, but with different names: a class declared inside another class is nested by default (the equivalent of the Java class [static class]: it is not bound to any object of the enclosing class); an inner class, associated with an object of the enclosing class, is declared using the keyword [inner] ([inner class]); finally, the expression [object : ...] creates an anonymous object. We’ll see in Chapter 7 that we can make it even shorter than an anonymous object for an interface that has only one abstract method, such as [Comparator]: a lambda, [persons.sortWith { p1, p2 -> p2.age.compareTo(p1.age) }], or, as we just did, a comparator built from a lambda: [persons.sortWith(compareByDescending { it.age })].

docs.title: 4.8.4. Variance, projections, and type erasure
docs.text:
A [MutableList<Int>] is not a [MutableList<Number>], even though [Int] derives from [Number]: if it were, one could add a [Double] to a list of integers via a variable of type [MutableList<Number>]. The type [MutableList<T>] is said to be invariant: a function that accepts a [MutableList<Number>] rejects a [MutableList<Int>]. In contrast, a read-only list of type [List<Int>] is a [List<Number>]: since nothing can be added to it, the previous risk does not exist, and every integer read from the list is indeed a number. The type [List<T>] is said to be covariant.

This is a significant difference from Java. In Java, all generic interfaces are invariant, and you have to write wildcards for each use: [List<? extends Number>] for a list you’re reading from, [List<? super Integer>] for a list you’re populating. Kotlin allows you to specify the variance once and for all, at the declaration of the class or interface: this is declaration variance. The interface [List] is declared as [interface List<out E>]: the keyword [out] means that the type [E] appears only as an “output” (the result of methods and properties of type [val]), which makes the type covariant. Similarly, the interface [Comparable] is declared as [interface Comparable<in T>]: the type [T] appears there only as an “input” (parameter of [compareTo]), which makes the type contravariant: a [Comparable<Number>] is a [Comparable<Int>] (anyone who can compare any number can compare an integer). The compiler verifies that the class adheres to its declaration.

For invariant types like [MutableList], Kotlin also offers type projections, which are equivalent to Java’s wildcards:

KotlinJavaMeaning[MutableList<out Number>][List<? extends Number>]A list of elements of an unknown type derived from [Number]: you can read [Number] from it, but you cannot add elements to it[MutableList<in Int>][List<? super Integer>]a list of elements of an unknown type from which [Int] is derived ([Int], [Number], [Any]): [Int] can be added to this list[MutableList<*>][List<?>]a list of elements of an unknown type (star projection): you can read [Any?]

The program [Classes21.kt] illustrates variance, projections, and a specific feature of the generics in JVM—type erasure—as well as Kotlin’s partial solution to this issue: reified type parameters:

package classes21

// variance (out, in), projections, star projection, type erasure and reified types
fun main() {
    val integers: List<Int> = listOf(1, 2, 3)
    val reals: List<Double> = listOf(1.5, 2.25)
    // List<out E> is covariant: a List<Int> is a List<Number>
    println("Sum of integers: ${sum(integers)}")
    println("Sum of reals: ${sum(reals)}")
    // MutableList<in Int>: a mutable list that can receive Ints
    val numbers = mutableListOf<Number>()
    addIntegers(numbers, 3)
    numbers.add(2.5)
    println("numbers=$numbers, sum=${sum(numbers)}")
    // MutableList<out Number>: a mutable list whose elements are only read
    val mutableIntegers = mutableListOf(10, 20)
    println("Sum of a mutable list: ${mutableSum(mutableIntegers)}")
    // a recursive bound: T must be comparable to itself
    println("max : ${max(listOf("paul", "jean", "valentine"))}, ${max(integers)}")
    // declaration-site variance in our own classes
    val box: Box<Number> = Box(5)
    println("box : ${box.content}")
    // the star projection: a list of elements of an unknown type
    displaySize(listOf("a", "b"))
    displaySize(mutableIntegers)
    // type erasure: at runtime, a list is a list
    val l1 = ArrayList<String>()
    val l2 = ArrayList<Int>()
    println("same class: ${l1.javaClass == l2.javaClass} (${l1.javaClass.name})")
    // the reified type parameters of inline functions
    val mixed = listOf(1, "two", 3.0, "four", 5)
    println("strings : ${countOf<String>(mixed)}, integers : ${countOf<Int>(mixed)}")
    println("the strings : ${mixed.filterIsInstance<String>()}")
    println("type name : ${typeName<Double>()}")
}

// sum of the elements of a list of numbers (List is covariant)
fun sum(values: List<Number>): Double {
    var sum = 0.0
    for (value in values) {
        sum += value.toDouble()
    }
    return sum
}

// sum of the elements of a mutable list of numbers (MutableList is invariant)
fun mutableSum(values: MutableList<out Number>): Double {
    // values.add(1)   // rejected: the exact type of the elements is unknown
    return values.sumOf { it.toDouble() }
}

// adding the integers 1, 2, ..., n to a list able to receive Ints
fun addIntegers(list: MutableList<in Int>, n: Int) {
    for (i in 1..n) {
        list.add(i)
    }
}

// the largest element of a non-empty list
fun <T : Comparable<T>> max(elements: List<T>): T {
    var max = elements.first()
    for (element in elements) {
        if (element > max) {
            max = element
        }
    }
    return max
}

// a covariant class: T only appears in output (method result, val property)
class Box<out T>(val content: T)

// a list whose element type is unknown
fun displaySize(list: List<*>) {
    println("list of ${list.size} elements, first element: ${list.firstOrNull()}")
}

// the type T is known at runtime thanks to reified (inline function)
inline fun <reified T> countOf(elements: List<Any>) = elements.count { it is T }

inline fun <reified T : Any> typeName() = T::class.simpleName
  • lines 38–43: The function [sum] accepts a [List<Number>]; therefore, because [List] is covariant, it accepts a list of elements of any type derived from [Number]: [Int], [Double], [BigDecimal]… It reads the elements as [Number] and uses their [toDouble] method. Kotlin, like Java, does not support generic arithmetic: you cannot write [a + b] for two objects of type [T] or [Number], hence the use of [Double]. Where Java would have to write ***[List<? extends Number>], the simple type ***[List<Number>] is sufficient;
  • lines 8–9: the same function adds a list of [Int] to a list of [Double]. [listOf(...)] creates a read-only list;
  • Lines 47–49: An editable list, on the other hand, is invariant. To accept a [MutableList<Int>] (line 17), the function declares a projection [MutableList<out Number>]. It can read elements such as [Number], but adding an element (line 48) is rejected: the compiler does not know whether it is a list of [Int] or [Double] ([receiver type 'MutableList<out Number>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean']);
  • lines 53–55: the function [addIntegers] accepts any mutable list capable of holding [Int], in this case a [MutableList<Number>] (line 11). We follow the rule “producer: [out], consumer: [in]”: a list whose elements are read is written as [out], and a list that is filled is written as [in]. Kotlin’s keywords directly express what Java conveys using [extends] and [super];
  • lines 60–67: The generic function [max] returns the largest element in a list. The bound [T : Comparable<T>] requires that the elements be comparable to one another; it applies to strings as well as integers (line 19). In Java, you must write [T extends Comparable<? super T>] to also accept a type whose parent class is comparable; in Kotlin, since the [Comparable] interface is contravariant ([in T]), [T : Comparable<T>] is sufficient. The function [first] returns the first element of the list, and the operator [>] calls [compareTo]. (The Kotlin library already provides the function [maxOf] and, for collections, [max()].);
  • Line 71: our own covariant class. The type *[T] appears there only as an output, as the type of a property *[val]*. Line 21: A ***[Box<Int>] is therefore accepted where a ***[Box<Number>] is expected. If we add a method [fun replace(newValue: T)] to the class, where [T] appears as an input, the compiler rejects the class: [type parameter 'T' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position in type 'T (of class Box<out T>)']*;
  • Lines 74–75: The function [displaySize] accepts a list of elements of any type: [List<*>]. It cannot make any assumptions about its elements, which it reads as [Any?]. The function [firstOrNull] returns the first element, or [null] if the list is empty;
  • lines 27–29: at runtime, a ***[ArrayList<String>] and a ***[ArrayList<Int>] are two objects of the same class *[java.util.ArrayList] (*[javaClass] returns the Java class of an object). The compiler checks the generic types and then erases them: the compiled code only recognizes [ArrayList] and [Object], and conversions are inserted where necessary. This “type erasure,” adopted by Java in 2004 to ensure that generic code remains compatible with existing code, also applies to Kotlin, which generates code for the same JVM. This explains several limitations: you cannot write [T()] or test [o is List<String>] ([cannot check for instance of erased type 'List<String>']); however, you can test [o is List<*>];
  • Lines 79–81: Kotlin partially bypasses type erasure for the [inline] functions. The code for a [inline] function is copied by the compiler at every point where it is called (we’ll return to this in Chapter 7): at that point, the type [T] is known. If the type parameter is declared as [reified] (“reified”), the function can then use it as a true type: to test [it is T] (line 79), or to obtain its class [T::class] (line 81). Without [reified], the test [it is T] is rejected: [cannot check for instance of erased type 'T (of fun <T> countOf)'];
  • lines 31–34: use of reified functions. The type is specified between angle brackets: [countOf<String>(mixed)] counts the strings in the list. The Kotlin library makes extensive use of this mechanism, for example in the function [filterIsInstance<String>()], which returns the elements of a collection that are strings as type [List<String>].

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes21.Classes21Kt
Sum of integers: 6.0
Sum of reals: 3.75
numbers=[1, 2, 3, 2.5], sum=8.5
Sum of a mutable list: 30.0
max : valentine, 3
box : 5
list of 2 elements, first element: a
list of 2 elements, first element: 10
same class: true (java.util.ArrayList)
strings : 2, integers : 2
the strings : [two, four]
type name : Double

Unlike other languages such as C#, where interfaces can declare abstract static members to implement generic computations, Kotlin does not allow a type [T] to be required to have a “class” method: the members of an interface’s companion object are called using the interface’s name and are not inherited by the classes that implement it.

docs.title: 4.9. Packages
docs.text:
To print a line to the screen, we use the function [println(...)]. If we look at its definition in the Kotlin library documentation (kotlinlang.org/api), we find that it is part of the [kotlin.io] package. This means that its full name is [kotlin.io.println] and that we could write [kotlin.io.println(...)]. A Kotlin package contains classes, as well as functions, properties, and top-level objects. Several packages are automatically imported into every Kotlin file: [kotlin.*] ([Any], [String], [Int]…), [kotlin.io.*] ([println], [readln]), [kotlin.collections.*] ([List], [listOf]…), [kotlin.text.*] ([StringBuilder], [Regex]…), [kotlin.ranges.*], [kotlin.sequences.*], [kotlin.comparisons.*] ([compareBy]…), [kotlin.annotation.*], and, on JVM, [java.lang.*], and [kotlin.jvm.*]. For the others, a [import] clause is used, placed at the beginning of the file, after the package declaration:

  • [import java.text.Collator] imports the class [Collator] from the package [java.text] (without a trailing semicolon, as with all Kotlin statements);
  • [import java.util.*] imports all public declarations from the [java.util] package on demand;
  • [import kotlin.math.sqrt] imports a top-level function, which can then be used without its package: [sqrt(2.0)]. Kotlin does not require Java’s [import static] clause: classes, functions, properties, and even static members of a Java class ([import java.lang.Math.PI]) are imported in the same way;
  • [import namespaces.e2.Person as PersonE2] imports a declaration under a different name—an alias—that is valid only within that file.

When the compiler encounters a simple name, it looks for it in the current package and among the imported declarations. A [import] clause adds nothing to the program: it simply avoids having to write out the full names.

When you create a class, you place it in a package. The purpose of packages is to prevent name conflicts between classes, for example, when they are distributed. Consider two companies, E1 and E2, distributing classes packaged in the archives [e1.jar] and [e2.jar], respectively. Suppose a customer C purchases these two sets of classes, in which both companies have defined a class named [Person]. If company E1 creates its classes in a package named [e1] and company E2 creates its classes in a package named [e2], the two classes [Person] will then be named [e1.Person] and [e2.Person]. The client can import one of them and refer to the other by its full name, or give it an alias. The package resolves the ambiguity. By convention, package names are in lowercase and begin with the reverse domain name of the organization that publishes them ([com.mysql.cj.jdbc], [org.hibernate], [kotlinx.coroutines]…); for our examples, we will use short names.

To place a file’s declarations in a package, you write the declaration [package name] at the top of the file. This is what we’ve been doing since the beginning of this course: each program is in a package with its own name. Unlike Java, Kotlin does not require a one-to-one correspondence between packages and folders, but it does recommend it, and IntelliJ IDEA indicates a file that is not properly organized: The source files for the [namespaces.e1] package are located in a folder named [namespaces/e1], starting from the source root ([src/main/kotlin]). The [namespaces] package and its two subpackages illustrate these concepts:

src/main/kotlin/namespaces/
  Main.kt               the main program (namespaces package)
  e1/
    Person.kt           the namespaces.e1.Person class
  e2/
    Person.kt           the namespaces.e2.Person class

The first class [Person] [e1/Person.kt]:

// the declarations of this file belong to the namespaces.e1 package
package namespaces.e1

class Person(private val firstName: String, private val lastName: String) {
    override fun toString() = "e1.Person[$firstName, $lastName]"
}

// a top-level function also belongs to a package
fun greet(person: Person) = "Hello $person"
  • Line 2: the package declaration. All declarations in the file belong to this package: the class [Person] and the top-level function [greet] (line 9), whose full name is [namespaces.e1.greet]. In JVM, this function is placed in a class named [namespaces.e1.PersonKt], which is named after the file.

The second one, [e2/Person.kt]:

// the declarations of this file belong to the namespaces.e2 package
package namespaces.e2

class Person(val name: String) {
    override fun toString() = "e2.Person[$name]"
}

// a constant visible in the whole module, and only in the module
internal const val VERSION = "e2-1.0"

// a function visible in this file only
private fun tool() = "private tool"
  • line 4: a class named [Person], which shares the same name as the previous one but is in a different package;
  • line 9: a visibility constant [internal]: it is accessible only to declarations within the same module. In Kotlin, a module is a set of files compiled together: a Gradle project (or subproject), a module IntelliJ, IDEA… Here, it is the project [04-classes];
  • Line 12: a private top-level function: it is accessible only to declarations within its own file. An attempt to import it from [Main.kt] is rejected: [cannot access 'fun tool(): String': it is private in file].

Both classes are public, which is Kotlin’s default visibility (a Java class without the [public] keyword is accessible only to classes in its own package). Let’s summarize the four visibility levels of a top-level declaration:

VisibilityAccessible from[public] (default)everywhere[internal]the same module[private]the same file[protected](only applies to members of a class: the class and its derived classes)

Kotlin does not have an equivalent to Java’s “package” visibility—the default visibility of Java declarations without a modifier: in Kotlin, a package is merely a namespace, and it is the module that defines what a library exposes to its users. The main program [Main.kt] is as follows:

package namespaces

// importing a class from a package
import namespaces.e1.Person
// importing a top-level function
import namespaces.e1.greet
// importing a class under another name
import namespaces.e2.Person as PersonE2
// importing a constant internal to the module
import namespaces.e2.VERSION
// importing a function of the Kotlin library
import kotlin.math.sqrt

fun main() {
    // Person designates namespaces.e1.Person, which has been imported
    val p1 = Person("Jean", "Dupont")
    // the full name of a class removes any ambiguity
    val p2 = namespaces.e2.Person("Durand")
    // the alias PersonE2 designates the class namespaces.e2.Person
    val p3 = PersonE2("Martin")
    println("$p1 $p2 $p3")
    // a top-level function of the namespaces.e1 package
    println(greet(p1))
    // full name and package of a class
    println("${Person::class.qualifiedName}, ${PersonE2::class.qualifiedName}")
    println("package of the Person class: ${Person::class.java.packageName}")
    // the JPMS module that contains a class
    println("e1.Person is in a named module: ${Person::class.java.module.isNamed}")
    println("${String::class.java.name} is in the module ${String::class.java.module.name}")
    // StringBuilder is known without an import
    val sb = StringBuilder("abc")
    println(sb.append("def"))
    // sqrt is known thanks to the import
    println("sqrt(2)=${sqrt(2.0)}")
    // an internal declaration is accessible in the whole module
    println("version=$VERSION")
}
  • line 4: import of the [namespaces.e1.Person] class;
  • line 6: import of the top-level function [greet], just as one imports a class;
  • Line 8: Importing the class [namespaces.e2.Person] under the name [PersonE2]. In this file, the name [PersonE2] refers to this class. Java does not support aliases: you cannot give a class a different name in Java. (Kotlin also allows you to declare a type alias for the entire package, such as [typealias PersonE2 = namespaces.e2.Person]: we’ve seen examples of this, where [Comparator] and [Exception] are aliases for Java types);
  • line 10: import of the constant [internal], which is allowed since [Main.kt] is in the same module;
  • line 12: import of the function [sqrt] from the package [kotlin.math];
  • line 16: [Person] refers to the class [namespaces.e1.Person], which was imported;
  • line 18: the full name of the class [namespaces.e2.Person] removes any ambiguity;
  • line 20: the alias yields the same result, but is more readable;
  • line 23: call to the imported function;
  • lines 25–26: the property [qualifiedName] of the Kotlin description of a class ([Person::class]) returns its full name, prefixed with its package. The property [java] returns the Java description of the class ([java.lang.Class]), whose method [getPackageName]—viewed in Kotlin as a property [packageName]—returns the package name;
  • lines 28–29: the [getModule] method of the Java class returns the JPMS module that contains the class (see below);
  • lines 31–32: the class [StringBuilder] is recognized without an import (it is an alias, defined in the package [kotlin.text], for the class [java.lang.StringBuilder]);
  • line 34: use of the imported function;
  • line 36: use of the constant [internal].

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=namespaces.MainKt
e1.Person[Jean, Dupont] e2.Person[Durand] e2.Person[Martin]
Hello e1.Person[Jean, Dupont]
namespaces.e1.Person, namespaces.e2.Person
package of the Person class: namespaces.e1
e1.Person is in a named module: false
java.lang.String is in the module java.base
abcdef
sqrt(2)=1.4142135623730951
version=e2-1.0

If we replace the imports of [Person] with the two on-demand imports [import namespaces.e1.*] and [import namespaces.e2.*], without the alias, the name [Person] becomes ambiguous. The two imports cancel each other out, and the compiler can no longer find the class:

Main.kt:7:14: error: unresolved reference 'Person'.

Note that an import with an alias masks the original name in the file: With the clause [import namespaces.e2.Person as PersonE2], the name [Person] can now only refer to the class in the package [e1], even if both packages are imported on demand.

docs.title: 4.9.1. Modules
docs.text: The term module has two meanings for a Kotlin developer. We’ve just seen the first: the Kotlin module, a set of files compiled together, which defines the scope [internal]. The second meaning is from Java: since Java 9, packages have been grouped into modules (the “Java Platform Module System,” JPMS). JDK is divided into modules: [java.base] contains the core packages ([java.lang], [java.util], [java.math], [java.io]…), [java.sql] provides database access, [java.net.http] is the client, HTTP, and so on. A module named JPMS declares, in a file named [module-info.java], its name, the modules it depends on ([requires java.sql;]), and the packages it makes available to other modules ([exports tax.business;]). A Kotlin project can declare one (the file [module-info.java], written in Java, is placed alongside the Kotlin source files and must then depend on the module [kotlin.stdlib]). Classes in an application that does not declare a JPMS module—such as ours—belong to the unnamed module (line 5 of the output), which has access to all modules. This is the case for most applications, and for all those in this course: the JPMS modules are primarily of interest to library authors, and the JDK module itself.

docs.title: 4.10. Data Classes
docs.text:
Many classes are used solely to carry data: a person, a grade, a tax bracket… For these, we always write the same code: read-only properties, a [toString] method that displays them, and the [equals] and [hashCode] methods. Kotlin’s primary constructor already saves you from having to write the fields, the constructor, and the accessors; the keyword [data], placed before [class], also instructs the compiler to generate the rest. Data classes have existed since the first version of Kotlin (2016); Java caught up with them, with its records, in 2021. We encountered them earlier (in the “Immutable Objects” section) and several times since then; the program [Classes22.kt] presents them more fully:

package classes22

// data classes (data class)
fun main() {
    val r1 = Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)
    val r2 = Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)
    // toString generated by the compiler
    println(r1)
    // the properties are those declared by the primary constructor
    println("firstName=${r1.firstName}, identity=${r1.identity()}")
    // equality by value: r1 and r2 are two different but equal objects
    println("r1 == r2 : ${r1 == r2}, r1 === r2 : ${r1 === r2}, equal hashCodes : ${r1.hashCode() == r2.hashCode()}")
    // val properties are read-only
    // r1.age = 31   // rejected: age is a val property
    // a modified copy, with the copy method and a named argument
    val r3 = r1.copy(age = 31)
    println(r3)
    println("r1 == r3 : ${r1 == r3}")
    // destructuring into variables, thanks to the functions component1(), component2()...
    val (firstName, lastName, age) = r1
    println("firstName=$firstName, lastName=$lastName, age=$age")
    println("component2()=${r1.component2()}")

    // the same thing with an ordinary class
    val c1 = PersonC("Jean", "Dupont", 30)
    val c2 = PersonC("Jean", "Dupont", 30)
    println(c1)
    println("c1 == c2 : ${c1 == c2}")

    // two data classes that implement the same interface
    val e = Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61)
    println(e)
    println(e.identity())
    // equality takes the type into account: a Person is not equal to a Teacher
    val pe = Person("Lucile", "Dumas", 56)
    println("pe == e : ${pe == e}")
    // the common type: the HasIdentity interface
    val identities = listOf(pe, e)
    for (i in identities) {
        println(i.identity())
    }
}

// an interface implemented by the data classes
interface HasIdentity {
    fun identity(): String
}

// a data class: firstName, lastName, age are its properties
data class Person(val firstName: String, val lastName: String, val age: Int) : HasIdentity {
    // methods can be added
    override fun identity() = "[$firstName, $lastName, $age]"
}

// a data class cannot be derived from (it is final)
data class Teacher(val firstName: String, val lastName: String, val age: Int, val section: Int) : HasIdentity {
    override fun identity() = "Teacher[[$firstName, $lastName, $age],$section]"
}

// an equivalent ordinary class... or almost
class PersonC(val firstName: String, val lastName: String, val age: Int)
  • lines 50–52: the data class [Person]. The declaration [data class Person(val firstName: String, val lastName: String, val age: Int)] generates, from the properties declared in the primary constructor:
    • three read-only properties [firstName], [lastName], [age] (which a regular class also does), accessed by their names: [r1.firstName] (line 10);
    • a method [toString] that displays the class name and its properties (line 1 of the results);
    • the methods [equals] and [hashCode], which compare property values rather than references;
    • a method [copy], which creates a copy of the object whose properties can be modified;
    • the methods [component1], [component2], and [component3], which return the properties in the order in which they were declared and allow for destructuring;
  • the primary constructor of a data class must have at least one parameter, and all of its parameters must be properties ([val] or [var]). Properties of type [var] can be declared: the data class is then mutable. This is allowed but not recommended, because an object whose [hashCode] changes is lost in a set or dictionary that contains it; data classes are reserved for immutable data;
  • line 52: A data class, like a class, can have additional methods and implement interfaces (line 50);
  • Line 12: [r1] and [r2] are two distinct objects ([===], where the references are equal, results in [false]) but they are equal in the sense of [==], which calls [equals], because their properties have the same values. Their hash codes are therefore equal. For an ordinary class, [equals] compares the references (line 28);
  • line 14: when uncommented, this line is rejected: ['val' cannot be reassigned];
  • line 16: an immutable data class cannot be modified; a modified copy is created. The generated method [copy] has one parameter per property, whose default value is the property’s value in the copied object; with a named argument, only the properties that change are specified. This is the [with] expression that was missing in Java, where you have to manually write “wither” methods ([withAge(31)]);
  • Line 20: destructuring: the properties of *[r1] are extracted into the variables *[firstName]*, *[lastName], and *[age]. The compiler translates this declaration into [val firstName = r1.component1()], [val lastName = r1.component2()], etc.: the mapping is based on position and not on the name (line 22, the [component2] method is called directly). A property can be skipped using the character [_]: [val (firstName, _, age) = r1]. This is equivalent to the Java 21 record pattern ([r1 instanceof Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age)]*); we’ll revisit destructuring with pattern filtering;
  • lines 56–57: A data class is final; it cannot be subclassed (the keyword [open] is prohibited here). Unlike a Java record, however, it can itself be derived from an open, abstract, or sealed class. To give the classes [Person] and [Teacher] a common type, we have them implement the same interface, in this case [HasIdentity] (lines 45–46). The class [Teacher] therefore inherits the properties of the person;
  • line 36: the equality of data classes takes into account the actual type of the objects: a [Person] is never equal to a [Teacher], even if their shared properties are equal;
  • lines 38–40: The common interface allows both classes to be handled polymorphically. The type of the list, [List<HasIdentity>], is inferred by the compiler: it is the most specific common type of the two elements;
  • line 61: an ordinary class that resembles the class [Person]. Thanks to the primary constructor, it also fits on a single line… but equality by value, [toString], [copy], and destructuring are not provided. In Java, you also had to write the fields, the constructor, and the getters and setters.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes22.Classes22Kt
Person(firstName=Jean, lastName=Dupont, age=30)
firstName=Jean, identity=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
r1 == r2 : true, r1 === r2 : false, equal hashCodes : true
Person(firstName=Jean, lastName=Dupont, age=31)
r1 == r3 : false
firstName=Jean, lastName=Dupont, age=30
component2()=Dupont
classes22.PersonC@4554617c
c1 == c2 : false
Teacher(firstName=Lucile, lastName=Dumas, age=56, section=61)
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
pe == e : false
[Lucile, Dumas, 56]
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]

Note that the method [toString] of the class [PersonC] is the same as that of the class [Any]: the full class name followed by a hash code, which changes from one execution to the next (line 8 of the results), and that the equality of the two [PersonC] objects is false (line 9). The format of the [toString] for a data class, [Person(firstName=Jean, lastName=Dupont, age=30)], differs slightly from that of a Java record, [Person[firstName=Jean, lastName=Dupont, age=30]].

Let’s summarize the differences between a regular class and a data class:

ClassData ClassEquality: [==] ([equals])same object (unless overridden)same values for the primary constructor’s properties, same type[toString]class name and hash codeclass name and propertiesProperties, constructordeclared by the primary constructordeclared by the primary constructor (at least one property, only properties)stateeditable or notimmutable with [val] (recommended); other properties may be declared in the bodymodified copyto be written[copy(prop = value)] generateddestructuringto be written ([operator fun componentN])generatedinheritanceof a class, of multiple interfaces; open with [open]of a class, of multiple interfaces; always final

A data class is used for data defined by its value (a person retrieved from a database, a message exchanged over the network, a tax bracket), while an ordinary class is used for an object with an identity and behavior (a calculation service, a connection, a mutable list). We will see in Chapter 11 that Hibernate entities, which have an identity, are not data classes. Note: A data class with properties of type [val] is “superficially” immutable: if a property references a mutable object—a [MutableList], for example—the contents of that list remain mutable. In this case, we use read-only properties of type [List], initialized with a copy ([list.toList()]). For readers coming from Java: a data class is compiled into a regular, final Java class (not a record); the [@JvmRecord] annotation allows it to be compiled into a true Java record if necessary.

docs.title: 4.11. Data Class Constructors
docs.text:
The primary constructor of a data class simply copies its parameters into the properties. However, you may want to validate or normalize these parameters. Java provides the compact constructor for records for this purpose, which can modify the parameters before storing them. Kotlin does not have an exact equivalent: the parameters of a data class are its properties, stored as-is. On the other hand, we have the tools available to any class: the [init] block for validation, secondary constructors, and the companion object’s factories for normalization. The program [Classes23.kt] illustrates these:

package classes23

import kotlin.math.sqrt

// constructors of data classes: validation, secondary constructor, factory
fun main() {
    val p = Person.create("  Jean ", "Dupont", 30)
    println(p.identity())
    // a data class is immutable: growOlder returns a new person
    val p2 = p.growOlder()
    println("${p.identity()} -> ${p2.identity()}")
    // a secondary constructor
    val unknown = Person("Martin")
    println(unknown.identity())
    // the checks of the factory and of the init block
    try {
        Person.create("Paul", " ", 20)
    } catch (ex: IllegalArgumentException) {
        println(ex.message)
    }
    try {
        Person.create("Paul", "Martin", -4)
    } catch (ex: IllegalArgumentException) {
        println(ex.message)
    }
    // a data class with a computed property and a companion object
    val pt = Point(3.0, 4.0)
    println("pt=$pt, distance to the origin: ${pt.distance}, origin=${Point.ORIGIN}")
}

// the primary constructor is private: a person is created with the create factory
// or with the secondary constructor; copy is private like it (@ConsistentCopyVisibility)
@ConsistentCopyVisibility
data class Person private constructor(val firstName: String, val lastName: String, val age: Int) {
    // the init block checks the object, whatever the way it is constructed
    init {
        require(age >= 0) { "invalid age ($age)" }
    }

    // a secondary constructor must call the primary constructor
    constructor(lastName: String) : this("?", validate(lastName, "last name"), 0)

    // a method that returns a new person
    fun growOlder() = copy(age = age + 1)

    fun identity() = "[$firstName, $lastName, $age]"

    companion object {
        // the factory: it checks and normalizes the parameters before construction
        fun create(firstName: String, lastName: String, age: Int) =
            Person(validate(firstName, "first name"), validate(lastName, "last name"), age)

        // a private validation function
        private fun validate(value: String, label: String): String {
            require(value.isNotBlank()) { "invalid $label ($value)" }
            return value.trim()
        }
    }
}

data class Point(val x: Double, val y: Double) {
    // a property declared in the body of the class: it is not part
    // of the properties used by toString, equals, hashCode, copy
    val distance: Double
        get() = sqrt(x * x + y * y)

    companion object {
        val ORIGIN = Point(0.0, 0.0)
    }
}
  • lines 36–37: The block [init] executes on every construction, after the primary constructor’s properties have been initialized. It validates the object: a negative age is rejected. The function [require(condition) { message }] throws a [IllegalArgumentException] exception with the message calculated by the lambda if the condition is false: this is the exception intended for an invalid parameter. All constructors of a class go through the primary constructor, and therefore through the [init] block: there is no way to create a [Person] with a negative age, not even with [copy], which also calls the primary constructor;
  • Line 34: The block [init] cannot modify the [val] properties of the primary constructor, which are already initialized. To normalize the parameters (in this case, removing the spaces around the first and last names), we make the primary constructor private ([private constructor]) and provide a factory method instead: the [create] function of the companion object (lines 50–51). It validates and normalizes the parameters before calling the primary constructor, which it is authorized to call since it is part of the class. It is called using the class name: [Person.create(" Jean ", "Dupont", 30)] (line 7);
  • line 33: the generated method [copy] calls the primary constructor; if it were public, it would allow the factory method ([p.copy(firstName = " x ")]) to be bypassed. The annotation [@ConsistentCopyVisibility] instructs the compiler to give it the visibility of the primary constructor, which is private here. Without it, Kotlin 2.4 issues the warning [non-public primary constructor is exposed via the generated 'copy()' method of the 'data' class], specifying that the visibility of the generated method [copy] will change in a future version (it will then have the same visibility as the constructor);
  • line 41: a secondary constructor, which takes only the name. Like any secondary constructor of a class with a primary constructor, it must call the primary constructor with [: this(...)]; to calculate the parameters, it may call functions of the companion object, even private ones ([validate]). A secondary constructor can be public when the primary constructor is private;
  • line 44: a data class is immutable: aging means creating a new instance, which is done by the method [copy] (private, but usable within the class);
  • lines 54–56: a private validation function in the companion object. [isNotBlank()] returns true if the string contains anything other than spaces; [trim()] removes leading and trailing spaces from the string. The error message is constructed using a string template within the lambda passed to [require]: it is calculated only if an error occurs;
  • Lines 61–68: A data class may have, in addition to the properties of its primary constructor, properties declared within its body—in this case, the computed property [distance]. These do not contribute to [toString], [equals], [hashCode], or [copy]. It may also have a companion object, in this case with the property [ORIGIN], which is equivalent to the static field in the Java version. (Unlike a record, a data class can even have properties stored within its body, but this is of little use for immutable data.)

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes23.Classes23Kt
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Jean, Dupont, 30] -> [Jean, Dupont, 31]
[?, Martin, 0]
invalid last name ( )
invalid age (-4)
pt=Point(x=3.0, y=4.0), distance to the origin: 5.0, origin=Point(x=0.0, y=0.0)

The first name, provided with spaces on either side (line 7), was stored without them (lines 1 and 2 of the results). The [init] block is the idiomatic way to ensure that an object is always valid; a factory, with a private constructor, also allows the data to be normalized.

docs.title: 4.12. Extension Functions
docs.text:
How do you add a method to a class that cannot be modified, such as the [String] class? Java doesn’t provide a built-in solution: you write static methods, grouped into a utility class ([Arrays], [Collections], [Objects], [Math]…), and we call them using their class name, passing the object as a parameter: [Tools.initials(p)]. Kotlin, like C# with its extension methods, offers extension functions: functions declared outside the class that are used as methods of the extended class: [p.initials()]. We’ve been using them since the beginning of this course: [toInt], [sumOf], [contentToString], [toMutableList], [repeat], [also]… are extension functions from the Kotlin library, which enhance the classes in JDK ([String], arrays, collections) without modifying them. The program [Classes24.kt] shows how to write your own:

package classes24

import java.time.DayOfWeek
import java.time.LocalDate

// extension functions and properties
fun main() {
    val p = Person("jean", "dupont", 30)
    // extension functions are called like methods of the object
    println(p.initials())
    println("jean".firstUpper())
    println("${p.fullName} is an adult: ${p.isAdult}")
    println("\"the weather is fine\" has ${"the weather is fine".nbWords()} words")
    // a function of the companion object of the class itself
    val unknown = Person.unknown()
    println("${unknown.fullName} is an adult: ${unknown.isAdult}")
    // an extension of a Java class
    val date = LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 4)
    println("$date is a weekend day: ${date.isWeekend}")
    // an extension of a nullable type: callable on null
    val absent: Person? = null
    println("${p.description()} / ${absent.description()}")
    // the resolution of extensions is static: the declared type is what counts
    val shape: Shape = Square()
    println("shape.name()=${shape.name()}, Square().name()=${Square().name()}")
    // ...whereas the call of an overridden method is polymorphic
    println("shape.category()=${shape.category()}")
}

// a person
data class Person(val firstName: String, val lastName: String, val age: Int) {
    companion object {
        // factory: an unknown person
        fun unknown() = Person("?", "?", 0)
    }
}

// extension functions of the Person class
fun Person.initials() = "${firstName[0].uppercaseChar()}.${lastName[0].uppercaseChar()}."

// extension properties (computed: an extension cannot store a value)
val Person.isAdult: Boolean
    get() = age >= 18

val Person.fullName: String
    get() = "${firstName.firstUpper()} ${lastName.uppercase()}"

// extension functions of the String class
fun String.firstUpper() = if (isEmpty()) this else this[0].uppercaseChar() + substring(1)

fun String.nbWords() = if (isBlank()) 0 else trim().split(Regex("\\s+")).size

// an extension property of a JDK class
val LocalDate.isWeekend: Boolean
    get() = dayOfWeek == DayOfWeek.SATURDAY || dayOfWeek == DayOfWeek.SUNDAY

// an extension function of a nullable type
fun Person?.description() = if (this == null) "absent person" else "person $firstName"

// static resolution of extensions
open class Shape {
    open fun category() = "shape"
}

class Square : Shape() {
    override fun category() = "square"
}

fun Shape.name() = "a shape"

fun Square.name() = "a square"
  • line 39: an extension function for the [Person] class. The function name is prefixed by the extended type, known as the receiver type ([Person.]). In the body of the function, [this] refers to the object on which the function is called—the receiver—and its members are accessible without a prefix, just as in a method: [firstName], [lastName]. [firstName[0]] returns the first character of the string, and [uppercaseChar()] capitalizes it;
  • lines 42–46: two extension properties. They are declared like functions, with a receiver type, and must have an accessor [get]: an extension does not add anything to the object, so it cannot store a value (an extension property has no field and cannot have an initializer). They are read like properties: [p.isAdult], [p.fullName] (line 12);
  • lines 49–51: two extensions of the [String] class, used as methods of any string: ["jean".firstUpper()]. In [firstUpper], [this] is the string itself. The function [nbWords] splits the string using the function [split], to which a regular expression ([Regex]) is passed: ["\\s+"] refers to a sequence of one or more space characters (regular expressions are covered in Chapter 5);
  • lines 54–55: an extension property of a Java class, JDK, [java.time.LocalDate]. An extension applies to any type, including a Java class or a final class. Note that the [getDayOfWeek] method of the Java class is treated by Kotlin as a [dayOfWeek] property;
  • Line 58: a nullable type extension, [Person?]. It can be called on a reference to [null] without the [?.] operator (line 22): this is what checks whether [this] is equal to [null]. After the check, the compiler knows that [this] is not [null] in the [else] branch and allows access to [firstName] (this is smart type casting, which the following paragraph explains in more detail). The function [toString()] from the Kotlin library, which can be called on a null reference, is declared as follows: [fun Any?.toString(): String];
  • lines 8–13: extension functions and properties are called as members: [p.initials()], not [Tools.initials(p)];
  • lines 32–34: when the type can be modified, its methods are naturally placed there: the factory [unknown] is a function of the companion object of the [Person] class (line 15);
  • lines 61–71: a class [Shape] and its derived class [Square], each equipped with a redefined method [category] and an extension function [name]. On line 25, the variable [shape], declared as type [Shape], references a [Square]: however, the call to [shape.name()] actually executes the extension of [Shape]. Extension resolution is static: the compiler selects the function based on the variable’s declared type rather than on the actual type of the object at runtime. On line 27, the method [category] is polymorphic: the method of the class [Square] is the one that is executed.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes24.Classes24Kt
J.D.
Jean
Jean DUPONT is an adult: true
"the weather is fine" has 4 words
? ? is an adult: false
2026-10-04 is a weekend day: true
person jean / absent person
shape.name()=a shape, Square().name()=a square
shape.category()=square

This behavior is explained by the way the compiler translates an extension function: into a static method, whose first parameter is the receiver. The function [fun Person.initials()] in the file [Classes24.kt] becomes the Java method [public static final String initials(Person $this$initials)] of the class [classes24.Classes24Kt] (the extension property *[isAdult] likewise becomes a static method ***[isAdult(Person)]), and the call ***[p.initials()] becomes ***[Classes24Kt.initials(p)]**. In other words, Kotlin writes the Java utility class for us and makes its usage more readable. A Java program that uses a Kotlin library calls its extensions in this way. This leads to several rules:

  • an extension has access only to the receiver’s public members: it cannot see its private or protected members;
  • an extension cannot be overridden in a derived class: it is not polymorphic;
  • if the class has a member with the same signature, that member is always called, and the compiler warns that the extension is unnecessary ([this extension is shadowed by a member: 'fun g(): Int' defined in 'C']);
  • To be used in another package, an extension must be imported, just like a top-level function ([import tools.initials]).

Extension functions are one of Kotlin’s most distinctive features. They are used to enrich types over which we have no control, but also to separate, within our own classes, the core of the class (its members) from utility functions that only access it from the outside. In Chapter 7, we’ll look at lambdas with receivers, which are based on the same principle ([buildString { append(...) }]).

docs.title: 4.13. Pattern matching on objects
docs.text:
The expression [when] is not limited to simple values (numbers, strings, enumerations): it also applies to objects. You can check an object’s type, add a condition, and use the object in the correct type without explicit conversion—all in a single expression. Kotlin does not, strictly speaking, have “patterns” like Java 21: it achieves essentially the same result using the [is] operator, smart casting, and destructuring. The program [Classes25.kt] uses a sealed interface and three data classes that implement it:

package classes25

// pattern matching on objects: is, smart cast, when, destructuring
fun main() {
    val objects: List<Any?> = listOf(
        Individual("Jean", "Dupont", 30),
        Individual("Lise", "Morel", 12),
        Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61),
        Teacher("Marc", "Petit", 44, 27),
        Student("Paul", "Martin", 19, "computer science"),
        "a string",
        42,
        null,
    )

    // 1 - the is type test and the smart cast
    for (o in objects) {
        if (o is Person) {
            // here o is a Person
            println("${o.firstName} is of type ${o::class.simpleName}")
        }
    }

    // 2 - the type test followed by a condition
    for (o in objects) {
        if (o is Person && o.age >= 18) {
            println("${o.firstName} is an adult")
        }
    }

    // 3 - when on the type of the object, with guards and destructuring
    for (o in objects) {
        println(describe(o))
    }

    // 4 - an exhaustive when on a sealed interface
    for (o in objects) {
        if (o is Person) {
            println("${o.firstName} : ${category(o)}")
        }
    }

    // 5 - the explicit casts as and as?
    val first = objects[0] as Person
    val string = objects[0] as? String
    println("first=${first.firstName}, string=$string")
    try {
        val s = objects[0] as String
        println(s)
    } catch (ex: ClassCastException) {
        println("ClassCastException : ${ex.message}")
    }
}

fun describe(o: Any?): String = when (o) {
    is Teacher if o.section == 27 -> "${o.firstName} teaches computer science"
    is Teacher -> "${o.firstName} teaches in section ${o.section}"
    is Student -> {
        val (firstName, _, _, major) = o
        "$firstName studies $major"
    }
    is Person if o.age < 18 -> "${o.firstName} is a minor"
    is Person -> "${o.firstName} is ${o.age} years old"
    is String -> "a string of ${o.length} characters"
    is Int if o > 0 -> "the positive integer $o"
    null -> "the null reference"
    else -> "an unknown object"
}

// no else: the compiler knows that the three cases cover all persons
fun category(p: Person) = when (p) {
    is Individual -> "individual"
    is Teacher -> "teacher"
    is Student -> "student"
}

// a sealed interface and the three data classes that implement it
sealed interface Person {
    val firstName: String
    val lastName: String
    val age: Int
}

data class Individual(override val firstName: String, override val lastName: String, override val age: Int) : Person

data class Teacher(
    override val firstName: String,
    override val lastName: String,
    override val age: Int,
    val section: Int,
) : Person

data class Student(
    override val firstName: String,
    override val lastName: String,
    override val age: Int,
    val major: String,
) : Person
  • Lines 78–97: A sealed interface [Person] ([sealed interface]), implemented by three data classes: [Individual], [Teacher], and [Student]. Like a sealed class (see the section “Final, Open, and Sealed Classes”), a sealed interface can only be implemented by classes in the same package and the same module: the compiler therefore knows all of its implementations without needing to list them explicitly, as is required by the Java clause [permits]. The interface declares the abstract properties [firstName], [lastName], and [age]; the data classes implement them using properties of their primary constructor, prefixed with [override];
  • lines 5–13: a list of objects of various types, including an integer and the reference [null]. Its type is [List<Any?>]: [Any?] is Kotlin’s most general type, which accepts any object and the value [null];
  • line 18: the expression [o is Person] is true if [o] refers to an object of type [Person] (it is false if [o] is equal to [null]). In the following block, the compiler knows that [o] is a [Person]: it allows [o.firstName] without conversion. This is smart type casting: the type of a variable is tested, and the variable itself changes type where the test is guaranteed to be true. Java 16 achieves the same result by declaring a new variable ([o instanceof Person p]); Kotlin doesn’t need to do this. Smart type conversion applies to local variables [val], to variables [var] that haven’t changed between the test and the use, and to properties [val] in the same module without custom accessors: the compiler must be certain that the value could not have changed between the test and the use;
  • line 26: smart type conversion also applies in the remainder of the condition, after [&&];
  • lines 55–67: the expression [when] with a subject evaluates the branches in order and returns the value associated with the first one that matches:
    • line 56: a teacher from section 27. In a branch [is Type], the subject [o] is intelligently type-cast; the clause [if] adds a condition, called a guard (Kotlin 2.2), which is the equivalent of [when] in Java patterns;
    • line 57: any other teacher. The order is important: if placed before the previous one, this case would have made it inaccessible. The Kotlin compiler does not flag this (Java would reject it): the branch would simply never be chosen;
    • lines 58–60: a student, whose properties are extracted via destructuring: [val (firstName, _, _, major) = o] calls [component1()] and [component4()] from the data class ([_] ignores a property). This is equivalent to Java’s record pattern ([case Student(var firstName, _, _, var major)]), in two steps: the type check, followed by destructuring. A branch may contain a block; its value is that of the last expression in the block;
    • lines 62–63: a minor, then any other person;
    • line 64: a string, whose property [length] can be used;
    • line 65: a positive integer. The type [Int] is checked, not [Integer] as in Java;
    • line 66: the case [null], a simple value, compared to the subject by [==]. Without this case, the null reference would fall into the [else] branch: a [when] on a null reference never throws an exception;
    • line 67: the branch [else] covers everything else. Without it, the compiler would report that the expression [when] does not handle all cases: an expression [when], which returns a value, must be exhaustive;
  • Lines 71–74: a [when] on a [Person], without a [else]. However, it is exhaustive: since the interface is sealed, the compiler knows that a person is a [Individual], a [Teacher], or a [Student];
  • lines 44–51: explicit type conversions. [o as Person] converts [o] to [Person] and throws a [ClassCastException] exception if the object is not a person (line 48); this is the equivalent of [(Person) o] in Java. [o as? String] is the “safe” type conversion: it returns [null] instead of throwing an exception, which works well with the Elvis operator ([o as? String ?: "default"]). With smart type conversion, this is rarely needed.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes25.Classes25Kt
Jean is of type Individual
Lise is of type Individual
Lucile is of type Teacher
Marc is of type Teacher
Paul is of type Student
Jean is an adult
Lucile is an adult
Marc is an adult
Paul is an adult
Jean is 30 years old
Lise is a minor
Lucile teaches in section 61
Marc teaches computer science
Paul studies computer science
a string of 8 characters
the positive integer 42
the null reference
Jean : individual
Lise : individual
Lucile : teacher
Marc : teacher
Paul : student
first=Jean, string=null
ClassCastException : class classes25.Individual cannot be cast to class java.lang.String (classes25.Individual is in unnamed module of loader 'app'; java.lang.String is in module java.base of loader 'bootstrap')

If you remove the case [Student] from the function [category], the compiler flags it:

Classes25.kt:71:27: error: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Student' branch or an 'else' branch.

This is the great benefit of combining sealed types with the expression [when]: if a fourth class is added to the hierarchy, the compiler flags all instances of [when] as needing to be completed. Note also that the [is] test corresponds to the types that implement the interface: the type-checking loop (lines 16–20) has identified the three types of people. The [when] test on types is a useful replacement for cascading [if (o is ...)] tests; however, it should not replace polymorphism: when behavior depends on the object’s type and you have control over the class hierarchy, a method redefined in each class is often the object-oriented solution. Filtering using [when] is well-suited for data hierarchies (sealed data classes) on which you want to write processing logic external to that data.

docs.title: 4.14. Handling the null value
docs.text:
In Java, any reference-type variable can be null, and using a null reference causes the NullPointerException, the most common runtime error. We saw in Chapter 3 how Kotlin handles this: the compiler distinguishes between types that can be [null] ([String?]) and those that cannot ([String]), and only allows access to the members of a nullable reference after a check, or through the operators [?.], [?:], and [!!]. Where Java uses the [Optional<T>] class, the [Objects.requireNonNull] and [Objects.requireNonNullElse] methods, or annotations such as those in the JSpecify library ([@Nullable], [@NullMarked]), Kotlin relies on the type system itself. Here, we explore these concepts in more detail in the context of classes: nullable properties, late-initialized properties, and the boundary with Java code. The program [Classes26.kt] uses the example from the Java version:

package classes26

// handling the null value in classes: nullable types, ?., ?:, ?.let, requireNotNull, !!,
// lateinit, platform types
fun main() {
    val jean = Person("Jean", "Dupont")
    jean.middleName = "Marie"
    val persons = listOf(jean, Person("Paul", "Martin"))
    for (p in persons) {
        // a default value when the reference is null: the Elvis operator
        val middle = p.middleName ?: "(none)"
        // the safe call ?.: null if the reference is null
        val length = p.middleName?.length
        println("${p.firstName} : middle name=$middle, length=$length")
    }

    // a function that may find nothing: it returns a Person?
    var found = find(persons, "Durand")
    println("Durand found: ${found != null}")
    println(found?.firstName ?: "Durand: person not found")
    // the reference is tested before being used: smart cast
    found = find(persons, "Martin")
    if (found != null) {
        println("Martin : ${found.firstName}")
    }
    // ?.let: the block is executed only if the reference is not null
    find(persons, "Dupont")?.let { it.middleName = "Louise" }
    find(persons, "Durand")?.let { it.middleName = "Louise" }
    println(jean.middleName)
    // requireNotNull: we assert that the reference is not null, otherwise an exception is thrown
    val martin = requireNotNull(find(persons, "Martin")) { "Martin cannot be found" }
    println(martin.firstName)
    try {
        requireNotNull(find(persons, "Durand")) { "Durand cannot be found" }
    } catch (ex: IllegalArgumentException) {
        println("Error: ${ex.message}")
    }
    // the !! operator: a NullPointerException if the reference is null
    try {
        val lise = Person("Lise", "Morel")
        println(lise.middleName!!.length)
    } catch (ex: NullPointerException) {
        println("Error: $ex")
    }

    // a lateinit property: initialized after construction
    val paul = persons[1]
    println("Paul's email initialized: ${paul.hasEmail}")
    try {
        println(paul.email)
    } catch (ex: UninitializedPropertyAccessException) {
        println("Error: ${ex.message}")
    }
    paul.email = "paul.martin@example.com"
    println("Paul's email: ${paul.email}, initialized: ${paul.hasEmail}")

    // platform types: a Java method can return null
    val variable = System.getenv("NONEXISTENT_VARIABLE")
    println("variable=$variable, length=${variable?.length}")
    try {
        val value: String = System.getenv("NONEXISTENT_VARIABLE")
        println(value.length)
    } catch (ex: NullPointerException) {
        println("Error: ${ex.message}")
    }
}

// search for a person by last name: null if not found
fun find(persons: List<Person>, lastName: String): Person? = persons.firstOrNull { it.lastName == lastName }

class Person(val firstName: String, val lastName: String) {
    // optional property: null means "no middle name"
    var middleName: String? = null

    // mandatory property, but initialized after construction
    lateinit var email: String

    // has the lateinit property been initialized?
    val hasEmail: Boolean
        get() = this::email.isInitialized
}
  • Lines 71–80: The class [Person] has two required properties, of type [String], initialized by the primary constructor, and one optional property, [middleName], of type [String?]: [null] means “no middle name.” The constructor does not need to validate its parameters as the Java version did with [Objects.requireNonNull]: the compiler rejects a call to [Person(null, "Morel")] ([null cannot be a value of a non-null type 'String']). The error is detected even before execution;
  • line 11: the Elvis operator [?:] returns the left-hand value if it is not equal to [null], and the right-hand value otherwise. This is equivalent to [Objects.requireNonNullElse(value, defaultValue)];
  • line 13: the safe call [?.] returns [null] if the reference is [null], and otherwise the length of the string: [length] is of type [Int?]. Direct access to [p.middleName.length] is rejected by the compiler: [only safe (?.) or non-null asserted (!!.) calls are allowed on a nullable receiver of type 'String?'];
  • line 69: the function [find] returns the person being searched for, or [null] if it cannot find them: its return type, [Person?], warns the caller that the result may be missing, and the compiler requires the caller to handle this case in order to use the person. This is the role played by [Optional<Person>] in Java, without any additional objects. The extension function [firstOrNull] returns the first element in the list that satisfies the condition, or [null];
  • line 19: the presence of a value is tested by comparing it to [null] (the equivalent of [isPresent()]);
  • line 20: the combination [?.] followed by [?:] converts any person present into their first name and provides a default value. This is equivalent to [found.map(Person::getFirstName).orElse(...)];
  • Lines 23–24: After the [found != null] test, intelligent type conversion changes [found] to [Person] within the block: [found.firstName] is accessed directly. Smart type conversion works here even though [found] is a variable of type [var], because it is not modified between the test and its use;
  • Lines 27–28: [x?.let { ... }] executes the block only if [x] is not equal to [null]; within the block, [it] refers to the value, which is of a non-nullable type. This is equivalent to [ifPresent]. Dupont exists and is assigned a new middle name; Durand does not exist, and the statement does nothing;
  • Line 31: [requireNotNull(value) { message }] returns the value if it is not [null], as a non-nullable type, and otherwise throws a [IllegalArgumentException] exception with the specified message (lines 34–36). It is used when the absence of a value constitutes an error: it is the equivalent of [orElseThrow]. Its counterpart, [checkNotNull], throws a [IllegalStateException] exception;
  • Lines 40–41: The operator [!!] checks whether the reference is equal to [null] and throws the exception [NullPointerException] if it is. Here, the exception has no message: we prefer [requireNotNull] or [checkNotNull], which do provide one. The operator [!!] should be reserved for cases where you are certain… and where the compiler cannot know this;
  • Line 76: a [lateinit] property (“initialized late”). A non-nullable property must normally be initialized at construction. But some values are only known afterward: a dependency injected by Spring (Chapter 6), an object prepared by a test initialization method, etc. Rather than declaring the property as nullable—and having to write [?.] or [!!] each time it is used—we declare it as [lateinit var]: it is of type [String] and is used as such. A property named [lateinit] must be a [var] of a non-nullable, non-primitive type ([lateinit var n: Int] is prohibited);
  • lines 50–51: Reading a [lateinit] property before it is initialized throws the [UninitializedPropertyAccessException] exception, whose message names the property; this is clearer than a [NullPointerException] exception occurring later;
  • lines 79–80: The expression [this::email.isInitialized] indicates whether the property has been initialized. [this::email] is a property reference (Chapter 7); this test is permitted only within the class that declares the property;
  • lines 58–62: the boundary with Java. The Java method [System.getenv(name)] returns the value of an environment variable, or [null] if it does not exist; however, nothing in its Java signature indicates this to the Kotlin compiler. Its return value has a platform type, denoted as [String!] in compiler messages and in IntelliJ IDEA: a type for which Kotlin does not know whether it is nullable, and which it allows the developer to use as a *[String] or as a *[String?], at their own risk. On line 58, the variable [variable] is of the platform type, and we treat it cautiously as [?.]. On line 61, we assert that it is not null by declaring it as [String]: the compiler then inserts a check, and the [NullPointerException] exception is thrown immediately upon assignment, with a message that identifies the offending method ([getenv(...) must not be null]), rather than later, during use. When the Java code is annotated ([@Nullable], [@NonNull] from JSpecify, or from JetBrains), Kotlin takes this into account, and the type is no longer a platform type: this is the case for much of Spring Framework 7, which we will be using.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=classes26.Classes26Kt
Jean : middle name=Marie, length=5
Paul : middle name=(none), length=null
Durand found: false
Durand: person not found
Martin : Paul
Louise
Paul
Error: Durand cannot be found
Error: java.lang.NullPointerException
Paul's email initialized: false
Error: lateinit property email has not been initialized
Paul's email: paul.martin@example.com, initialized: true
variable=null, length=null
Error: getenv(...) must not be null

The Java class *[Optional]* remains usable in Kotlin when a Java library provides one (the extension function ***[getOrNull()] from the package *[kotlin.jvm.optionals] then converts it to a nullable type), but we do not use it in the Kotlin code: a nullable type does the same thing—verified by the compiler—without creating an object. In this course, we declare only optional values as nullable; we prefer objects that are always complete (constructed with all their required values) to objects that are populated incrementally; we reserve [lateinit] for properties initialized by a grid, and we handle values coming from Java with caution.

docs.title: 4.15. Example Application - V2
docs.text:
We revisit the tax calculation already covered in the previous chapter (version 1) and now implement it using classes and interfaces. Let’s review the problem. We aim to write a program to calculate a taxpayer’s tax. We’ll consider the simplified case of a taxpayer who has only their salary to report (the 2004 tax schedule for 2003 income, used as-is: this is an exercise):

  • we calculate the employee’s number of shares: shares = nbChildren / 2 + 1 if they are unmarried, nbChildren / 2 + 2 if he is married, where nbChildren is the number of his children;
  • if he has at least three children, he receives an additional half-share;
  • his taxable income R is calculated as R = 0.72 × S, where S is his annual salary;
  • his family quotient is calculated as QF = R / shares;
  • his tax I is calculated using the following table:
thresholdcoeffRcoeffN49620083820.068291.0914,7530.1911,322.9223,8880.2832,668.3938,8680.3744,846.9847,9320.4266,883.6600.4819,505.54

Each row has three fields. To calculate tax I, find the first row where QF ≤ the limit. For example, if QF = 5,000, the row (8,382; 0.068; 291.09) will be found. Tax I is then equal to 0.068 × R - 291.09 × shares. If QF is such that the condition QF ≤ limit is never satisfied, then the coefficients of the last row are used, resulting in tax I = 0.481 × R - 9,505.54 × shares.
