    // the Regex object wraps a java.util.regex.Pattern object
    val pattern: java.util.regex.Pattern = date.toPattern()
    println("date.toPattern().matcher(\"18/05/97\").matches() : ${pattern.matcher("18/05/97").matches()}")
}

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=regex01.Regex01Kt
[  123  ] matches the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$]
[  123a  ] does not match the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$]
[4567] matches the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$]
containsMatchIn("abc 123") : true, matches("abc 123") : false
"18/05/97" matches date : true
"5/1/01".matches(date) : false
date.toPattern().matcher("18/05/97").matches() : true

Comments:

  • Line 6: The pattern is an unsigned integer, possibly surrounded by spaces, that occupies the entire string (anchors [^] and [$]). Thanks to the raw string, the [\] entries are not duplicated: the template is written exactly as it appears in the results;
  • line 7: the template is compiled by the [Regex] class constructor;
  • line 10: [containsMatchIn] searches for the pattern in the string. The string “123a,” surrounded by spaces, does not match the pattern: the character “a” cannot be a digit or a space. Without the anchors [^] and [$], the string would match, since it contains a number. This is the equivalent of [regex1.matcher(sample).find()] in Java;
  • line 17: the extension function [toRegex] of [String] is another way to compile a pattern;
  • lines 18–19: the difference between [containsMatchIn], which searches for the pattern in the string, and [matches], which requires that the entire string match the pattern, as if it were bounded by [^] and [$];
  • Lines 21–23: The extension function [matches] of [String] takes a [Regex] object; it is declared as [infix] and can be written without a dot or parentheses (line 22). Unlike Java, Kotlin does not provide a function [matches(String)] that would take the template as a string and compile it on each call: the call ["5/1/01".matches("\\d{2}")] is rejected by the compiler ([argument type mismatch: actual type is 'String', but 'Regex' was expected]). The model must be compiled explicitly, which encourages doing so only once;
  • Lines 25–26: The object [Regex] wraps an object [java.util.regex.Pattern]*, which is returned by the function *[toPattern]. All of the Java code in API thus remains accessible; Conversely, the extension function [toRegex] of [Pattern] transforms a [Pattern] into a [Regex]. We will use this in the program [Regex06.kt].

docs.title: 5.8.2. Find all occurrences of a pattern in a string
docs.text:
The function [find] returns the first occurrence of the pattern in a string, or [null] if there are none. The function [findAll] returns all occurrences as a sequence ([Sequence], evaluated lazily: each occurrence is looked up only when requested). An occurrence is a [MatchResult] object, which provides information about the found element:

  • [value]: the text of the occurrence, i.e., an element matching the pattern;
  • [range]: the range [IntRange] of the element’s positions in the searched string; [range.first] is the position where the element was found, and [range.last] is the position of its last character;
  • [next()]: the next occurrence, or [null] if there are no more.

The program [Regex02.kt] is as follows:

package regex02

// finding all the occurrences of a pattern in a string
fun main() {
    val pattern2 = """\d+"""
    val regex2 = Regex(pattern2)
    val sample3 = "  123  456  789 "
    println("Pattern=[$pattern2], sample=[$sample3]")
    // findAll returns the sequence of occurrences
    var nbOccurrences = 0
    for (occurrence in regex2.findAll(sample3)) {
        nbOccurrences++
        println("[${occurrence.value}] found at position ${occurrence.range.first}")
    }
    println("There are $nbOccurrences occurrences of the pattern in the sample")
    // find returns the first occurrence (or null); next returns the next occurrence (or null)
    var result = regex2.find(sample3)
    while (result != null) {
        print("${result.value} : ${result.range}  ")
        result = result.next()
    }
    println()
    // operations on sequences apply to the occurrences
    val sum = regex2.findAll(sample3).sumOf { it.value.toInt() }
    println("sum of the numbers found: $sum")
    val vowels = Regex("[aeiouy]").findAll("antidisestablishmentarianism").count()
    println("number of vowels of \"antidisestablishmentarianism\": $vowels")
}

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=regex02.Regex02Kt
Pattern=[\d+], sample=[  123  456  789 ]
[123] found at position 2
[456] found at position 7
[789] found at position 12
There are 3 occurrences of the pattern in the sample
123 : 2..4  456 : 7..9  789 : 12..14
sum of the numbers found: 1368
number of vowels of "antidisestablishmentarianism": 11

Comments:

  • Line 5: The pattern being searched for is a sequence of digits;
  • line 7: the string in which this pattern is searched for;
  • Lines 10–15: The loop [for] iterates through the sequence of occurrences returned by [findAll]. Each occurrence and its position are displayed. There is neither a [Matcher] object nor repeated calls to [find], as in Java;
  • lines 17–20: the same step-by-step traversal: [find] returns the first occurrence, of type [MatchResult?], and [next] returns the next one, until [null] is reached. Within the loop, the compiler knows that [result] is not [null] (intelligent type conversion, Chapter 4). The display of [range] shows the position ranges: 2..4 for 123;
  • line 24: the sequence of occurrences lends itself to all sequence operations; here, we sum the numbers found using [sumOf]. In Java, you must use the [results] method of [Matcher], which returns a stream of the API Stream;
  • Line 26: The number of occurrences of the pattern [[aeiouy]], which denotes a vowel, is the number of elements in the sequence, returned by [count].

docs.title: 5.8.3. Retrieving Parts of a Pattern
docs.text:
As mentioned, the parts of a pattern enclosed in parentheses are stored: these are the groups. A [MatchResult] object provides them in several ways:

  • [groups]: the collection of groups, of type [MatchGroupCollection]. Its element #0 is the entire occurrence; the following elements are groups #1, #2, … Each group is a [MatchGroup] object, which has the properties [value] (the captured text) and [range] (its positions); it is of type [MatchGroup?], since an optional group, such as [(\.\d+)?], may capture nothing;
  • [groupValues]: the list of captured texts, of type [List<String>]; a group that has not captured anything is represented there by an empty string;
  • [destructured]: groups No. 1 and subsequent, ready to be parsed: [val (h, m, s) = result.destructured].

The program [Regex03.kt] uses them:

package regex03

import java.time.LocalDate
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter

// retrieving parts of a pattern: the groups
fun main() {
    val pattern3 = """(\d\d):(\d\d):(\d\d)"""
    val regex3 = Regex(pattern3)
    val sample4 = "It is 18:05:49"
    // find searches for the first occurrence of the pattern; null if there is none
    val result = regex3.find(sample4)
    if (result != null) {
        println("The sample [$sample4] matches the pattern [$pattern3]")
        // we display the parenthesized groups; group 0 is the whole occurrence
        result.groups.forEachIndexed { i, group ->
            println("groups[$i]=[${group?.value}] found at position ${group?.range?.first}")
        }
        // the values of groups 1, 2, 3 by destructuring
        val (hours, minutes, seconds) = result.destructured
        println("hours=$hours, minutes=$minutes, seconds=$seconds")
    } else {
        println("The sample [$sample4] does not match the pattern [$pattern3]")
    }

    // named groups: (?<name>...)
    val regexDate = Regex("""(?<day>\d{1,2})/(?<month>\d{1,2})/(?<year>\d{4})""")
    val text = "Appointment on 3/10/2026, then on 15/11/2026."
    val format = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("EEEE d MMMM yyyy")
    for (m in regexDate.findAll(text)) {
        // a group is designated by its name rather than by its number
        val day = m.groups["day"]!!.value.toInt()
        val month = m.groups["month"]!!.value.toInt()
        val year = m.groups["year"]!!.value.toInt()
        val date = LocalDate.of(year, month, day)
        println("[${m.value}] : day=$day, month=$month, year=$year -> ${date.format(format)}")
    }

    // replace: the groups can be reused in the replacement string
    // $$"...": only $$ introduces a template, $ is an ordinary character
    val reversed = regexDate.replace(text, $$"${year}-${month}-${day}")
    println("replace(string) : $reversed")
    // replace with a lambda: the replacement is computed for each occurrence
    val iso = regexDate.replace(text) { r ->
        val (day, month, year) = r.destructured
        LocalDate.of(year.toInt(), month.toInt(), day.toInt()).toString()
    }
    println("replace(lambda) : $iso")
    // matchEntire: the whole string must match the pattern; groupValues: the values of the groups
    println("matchEntire(\"25/12/2026\") : ${regexDate.matchEntire("25/12/2026")?.groupValues}")
    println("matchEntire(\"on 25/12/2026\") : ${regexDate.matchEntire("on 25/12/2026")?.groupValues}")
}

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=regex03.Regex03Kt
The sample [It is 18:05:49] matches the pattern [(\d\d):(\d\d):(\d\d)]
groups[0]=[18:05:49] found at position 6
groups[1]=[18] found at position 6
groups[2]=[05] found at position 9
groups[3]=[49] found at position 12
hours=18, minutes=05, seconds=49
[3/10/2026] : day=3, month=10, year=2026 -> Saturday 3 October 2026
[15/11/2026] : day=15, month=11, year=2026 -> Sunday 15 November 2026
replace(string) : Appointment on 2026-10-3, then on 2026-11-15.
replace(lambda) : Appointment on 2026-10-03, then on 2026-11-15.
matchEntire("25/12/2026") : [25/12/2026, 25, 12, 2026]
matchEntire("on 25/12/2026") : null

Comments:

  • Line 12: The string [sample4] is compared to the pattern [regex3]; [find] searches for the first occurrence of the pattern and returns [null] if none is found. The test in line 13 then determines that [result] can be used without caution;
  • lines 16–17: the collection [groups] is traversed using its index: element #0 is the entire occurrence, and elements #1 through #3 are the parentheses groups. Since the elements are of type [MatchGroup?], they are accessed using the operator [?.]; here, all groups have captured some text. [range.first] is the position of this text within the explored string;
  • Line 20: The [destructured] property allows you to retrieve groups #1, #2, and #3 into three variables in a single statement, using destructuring (Chapter 3). This is the most concise way to process a template when you know its groups;
  • line 27: A group can be named using the syntax [(?<name>...)]. Here, the template recognizes a date in the d/m/yyyy format, with a one- or two-digit day and month;
  • lines 32–34: a named group is referred to by its name rather than its number, using the indexing operator [groups]: the code is more readable and does not depend on the order of the parentheses. The result is of the type [MatchGroup?] (an unknown name causes a [IllegalArgumentException] exception; a group that has not captured anything yields [null]); here, the three groups always capture text when the template is found, and the operator [!!] expresses this certainty;
  • lines 35–36: The class [java.time.LocalDate] represents a date without a time. It is displayed using the template [EEEE d MMMM yyyy]: the day of the week appears in English. Kotlin uses the classes [java.time] and JDK directly;
  • line 41: the function [replace] replaces each occurrence of the template with a string in which [${name}] (or [$1], [$2]… for numbered groups) denotes the value of a group. Dates are thus reformatted to the year-month-day format. But in Kotlin, [${year}] in a string is a template, which would insert the value of a variable [year]! We could write ["\${year}-\${month}-\${day}"]. The string is written here using Kotlin 2.2’s multi-dollar sign interpolation: in a string preceded by [$$], a template is written as [$${...}], and the isolated character [$] is a regular character. With ***[$$$]***, three would be needed, and so on;
  • lines 44–46: a variant of *[replace] takes a lambda (Chapter 7) that calculates the replacement text from each occurrence, of the form *[MatchResult]. Written after the parentheses, in accordance with Kotlin convention for the last parameter of a function, the lambda retrieves the groups via destructuring, constructs the date, and returns its normalized form ISO 8601, which is produced by the function [toString] from [LocalDate]: Days and months are always two digits long. This is equivalent to the method *[replaceAll] from *[Matcher], which takes a function (Java 9);
  • Lines 50–51: The [matchEntire] function, like [matches], requires that the entire string match the pattern, but returns the result of the comparison ([MatchResult]), or [null] if the comparison fails: This is the function to use to check a string and extract parts of it. Here, the [groupValues] property of the result is displayed: the entire occurrence, followed by the value of each group.

docs.title: 5.8.4. A Learning Program
docs.text:
Finding the regular expression that verifies whether a string matches a certain pattern can sometimes be a real challenge. The program [Regex04.kt] lets you practice. It takes a pattern and a string as input and indicates whether or not the string matches the pattern.

package regex04

import java.util.regex.PatternSyntaxException
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds
import kotlin.time.TimeSource

// a program for learning regular expressions
fun main() {
    while (true) {
        // we ask for the pattern
        val pattern = read("Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: ")
        // finished?
        if (pattern.isBlank()) break
        // we compile the regular expression; an incorrect pattern causes an exception
        val regex = try {
            Regex(pattern)
        } catch (e: PatternSyntaxException) {
            println("Error: ${e.description} (position ${e.index})")
            continue
        }
        // we ask for the samples to compare with the pattern
        while (true) {
            val string = read("Type the string to compare with the pattern [$pattern] or nothing to stop: ")
            // finished?
            if (string.isBlank()) break
            try {
                // we do the comparison, with a limit of one second
                val deadline = TimeSource.Monotonic.markNow() + 1.seconds
                var found = false
                for (m in regex.findAll(TimeLimitedString(string, deadline))) {
                    found = true
                    // we display the element matching the pattern
                    println("I found the match [${m.value}] at position [${m.range.first}]")
                    // and its sub-elements (groups 1, 2, ...)
                    for (group in m.groups.drop(1)) {
                        println("    sub-element [${group?.value}] at position [${group?.range?.first}]")
                    }
                }
                if (!found) println("I did not find any matches")
            } catch (_: TimeoutExceededException) {
                println("The search was abandoned: it lasted more than one second")
            }
        }
    }
}

// reading a line on the keyboard; "" at end of stream
fun read(prompt: String): String {
    print(prompt)
    return readlnOrNull() ?: ""
}

// a string that refuses to be read beyond a deadline
// the members of CharSequence that are not overridden (length) are delegated to the [text] object
class TimeLimitedString(
    private val text: CharSequence,
    private val deadline: TimeSource.Monotonic.ValueTimeMark
) : CharSequence by text {

    // the regular expression engine reads the string character by character
    override fun get(index: Int): Char {
        if (deadline.hasPassedNow()) throw TimeoutExceededException()
        return text[index]
    }

    override fun subSequence(startIndex: Int, endIndex: Int): CharSequence =
        TimeLimitedString(text.subSequence(startIndex, endIndex), deadline)

    override fun toString() = text.toString()
}

// the exception thrown when the deadline is exceeded
class TimeoutExceededException : RuntimeException()

Comments:

  • Lines 15–19: Compilation of the template entered via the keyboard. An incorrect template causes a [java.util.regex.PatternSyntaxException] exception: the [Regex] class passes through the exception from the [Pattern] class that it wraps. Its properties [description] and [index] (the Java methods [getDescription] and [getIndex], treated as properties by Kotlin) provide the error description and its position in the template. Its full message, the property [message], spans multiple lines and displays the model with a marker below the error. Note that [try] is an expression (Chapter 3): its value is that of the block [try], the object [Regex], or that of the block [catch]. This block ends with [continue], an expression of type [Nothing] that never returns a value: the compiler infers that [regex] is of type [Regex];
  • lines 28–30: the search is not performed directly on the typed string, but on a [TimeLimitedString] object (lines 55–69), which limits the search duration to one second: if the search takes longer, a [TimeoutExceededException] exception is thrown and then caught on line 40. We’ll see later why this is useful and how it works. The time limit is calculated using the [kotlin.time] classes from the standard library: [TimeSource.Monotonic.markNow()] is the current time, measured by a monotonic clock (insensitive to changes in the system time), and [1.seconds] is a duration [Duration], written using an extension property of [Int];
  • lines 35–36: for each match, groups #1 and subsequent groups are displayed, if any: [drop(1)] excludes element #0 from the collection [groups], the entire occurrence;
  • line 40: the name [_] indicates that the intercepted exception is not used;
  • lines 48–50: Unlike previous programs, the entered line is not stripped of its spaces; they may be part of the template or the string to be tested. At the end of the input stream, [readlnOrNull] returns [null], replaced by an empty string, which terminates the program.

Here is an example of the program in action (the input, redirected from a file, has been reinserted after the prompts):

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=regex04.Regex04Kt
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: \d+
Type the string to compare with the pattern [\d+] or nothing to stop: 123 456 789
I found the match [123] at position [0]
I found the match [456] at position [4]
I found the match [789] at position [8]
Type the string to compare with the pattern [\d+] or nothing to stop:
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: (\d{2}):(\d\d)
Type the string to compare with the pattern [(\d{2}):(\d\d)] or nothing to stop: 14:15 abcd 17:18 xyzt
I found the match [14:15] at position [0]
    sub-element [14] at position [0]
    sub-element [15] at position [3]
I found the match [17:18] at position [11]
    sub-element [17] at position [11]
    sub-element [18] at position [14]
Type the string to compare with the pattern [(\d{2}):(\d\d)] or nothing to stop:
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: ^\s*\d+\s*$
Type the string to compare with the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$] or nothing to stop:    1456
I found the match [   1456] at position [0]
Type the string to compare with the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$] or nothing to stop:
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: ^\s*(\d+)\s*$
Type the string to compare with the pattern [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] or nothing to stop: 1456
I found the match [1456] at position [0]
    sub-element [1456] at position [0]
Type the string to compare with the pattern [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] or nothing to stop: abcd 1456
I did not find any matches
Type the string to compare with the pattern [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] or nothing to stop:
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: ^(a+)+$
Type the string to compare with the pattern [^(a+)+$] or nothing to stop: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!
I did not find any matches
Type the string to compare with the pattern [^(a+)+$] or nothing to stop:
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: ^(a+)+\1$
Type the string to compare with the pattern [^(a+)+\1$] or nothing to stop: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!
The search was abandoned: it lasted more than one second
Type the string to compare with the pattern [^(a+)+\1$] or nothing to stop:
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: (\d+
Error: Unclosed group (position 4)
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop:

The templates [^\s*\d+\s*$] and [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] demonstrate the value of groups: the first recognizes the string “1456” preceded by three spaces, including the spaces; the second additionally allows the number to be extracted without the spaces. The patterns [^(a+)+$] and [^(a+)+\1$] are examined below. The last pattern, which is incorrect, is rejected: it is missing a closing parenthesis (“Unclosed group”), which the engine detects at position 4, at the end of the pattern. The exception message, generated by JDK, is in English.

docs.title: 5.8.5. The split function
docs.text:
We have already encountered the [split] function from the [String] class. The [Regex] class has the same function, which uses the already-compiled template:

functionrole[split(input, limit = 0)]The string [input] is split into fields, with each field separated by a delimiter corresponding to the template; returns a list [List<String>]. If [limit] is positive, it sets the maximum number of fields[splitToSequence(input)]Same as above, but the fields are returned as a sequence, evaluated lazily[CharSequence.split(regex)]extension function of [String]: [line.split(separator)] is equivalent to [separator.split(line)]

Suppose, for example, that a text file contains lines of the form field1, field2, ..., fieldn. The fields are separated by a comma, but the comma may be preceded or followed by spaces. The [\s*,\s*] template describes this separator exactly, as shown by the [Regex05.kt] program:

package regex05

// split: the separator is defined by a pattern
fun main() {
    val line = "abc  , def  ,ghi ,   jkl"
    // a comma preceded and followed by any number of spaces
    val separator = Regex("""\s*,\s*""")
    val fields = separator.split(line)
    fields.forEachIndexed { i, field -> println("fields[$i]=[$field]") }
    // several possible separators: ; or | or a sequence of spaces
    val words = "one;two|three   four".split(Regex("""[;|]|\s+"""))
    println("words=$words")
    // caution: with a String parameter, split splits on a text, not on a pattern
    println("\"1.5.2\".split(\".\") : ${"1.5.2".split(".")}")
    // the trailing empty fields are kept; limit sets the maximum number of fields
    println("\"a,b,,\".split(\",\") : ${"a,b,,".split(",")}")
    println("separator.split(line, 2) : ${separator.split(line, 2)}")
    // splitToSequence: the fields in the form of a sequence
    println("splitToSequence : ${separator.splitToSequence(line).map { it.uppercase() }.toList()}")
}

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=regex05.Regex05Kt
fields[0]=[abc]
fields[1]=[def]
fields[2]=[ghi]
fields[3]=[jkl]
words=[one, two, three, four]
"1.5.2".split(".") : [1, 5, 2]
"a,b,,".split(",") : [a, b, , ]
separator.split(line, 2) : [abc, def  ,ghi ,   jkl]
splitToSequence : [ABC, DEF, GHI, JKL]

Comments:

  • line 7: the separator: a comma preceded and followed by any number of spaces. The spaces are removed along with the separator. Once compiled, the template can split as many lines as desired without being recompiled: this is the method for splitting all the lines in a file;
  • line 9: the result of [split] is a list, iterated over using its indices by [forEachIndexed];
  • line 11: a separator that can take several forms: a semicolon or a vertical bar ([[;|]]), or ([|]) a sequence of spaces ([\s+]). The model is passed to the [split] function from [String] in the form of a [Regex] object;
  • Line 14: Note that this is an important difference from Java. When the Kotlin function [split] receives a string ([String]), it is treated as a literal separator, not a template: ["1.5.2".split(".")] splits the string based on the period character and returns [[1, 5, 2]]. In Java, the [split] method of [String] always interprets its parameter as a regular expression, in which the period matches any character: ["1.5.2".split(".")] returns an empty array—a classic pitfall. In Kotlin, there’s no room for error: a template is passed as a [Regex] object, and a string is always taken literally;
  • Line 16: Another difference from Java: empty fields at the end of the string are preserved. The string “a,b,,” yields four fields, the last two of which are empty, whereas Java’s [split] method returns only two. The number of fields in a malformed line is thus never distorted: a line ending with an extra separator has one too many fields;
  • line 17: the [limit] parameter limits the number of fields; the last field then contains the remainder of the string;
  • line 18: [splitToSequence] returns the fields as a sequence, to which the [map] operation is applied here, before converting it into a list. The fields are split only as needed, which is useful for a very long string where only the first few fields are used. This is equivalent to the [splitAsStream] method of [Pattern].

docs.title: 5.8.6. Precompiled templates, options, and searches that take too long
docs.text:
Unlike other platforms, neither Java nor Kotlin has a mechanism that generates the code for a regular expression search at program compilation time: a pattern is always parsed at runtime by the [Regex] constructor. This compilation comes at a cost; therefore, best practice is to compile each known pattern once and for all in advance and store the [Regex] object in a read-only property ([val]), either at the top level or within a *[companion object], as the program *[Regex06.kt] does. In particular, avoid writing ["""\\d+""".toRegex()] inside a loop: the template would be recompiled on every iteration. A [Regex] object is immutable and can be used simultaneously by multiple threads: unlike Java’s [Matcher] object, it does not store the state of a search, as each search produces its own results.

package regex06

import java.util.regex.Pattern
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds
import kotlin.time.TimeSource
import kotlin.time.measureTimedValue

// patterns compiled once and for all, options, protection against searches that take too long

// a time hh:mm:ss with named groups
val TIME = Regex("""(?<h>\d\d):(?<m>\d\d):(?<s>\d\d)""")
// yes, whatever the case
val YES = Regex("""^\s*yes\s*$""", RegexOption.IGNORE_CASE)
// a pathological pattern: a repeated group followed by a backreference to this group
val CATASTROPHIC = Regex("""^(a+)+\1$""")

fun main() {
    // 1 - patterns compiled only once, stored in top-level properties
    println("TIME.containsMatchIn(\"It is 18:05:49\") : ${TIME.containsMatchIn("It is 18:05:49")}")
    TIME.find("departure at 07:45:00")?.let { m ->
        val (h, mn, s) = listOf("h", "m", "s").map { name -> m.groups[name]?.value }
        println("hours=$h, minutes=$mn, seconds=$s")
    }

    // 2 - the options: here IGNORE_CASE, set when the pattern is compiled
    for (answer in listOf("yes", "YES", "Yes", "no", "yesss")) {
        print("$answer=${YES.matches(answer)} ")
    }
    println()
    // IGNORE_CASE also ignores the case of accented letters
    println("Regex(\"éclair\", IGNORE_CASE) on \"ÉCLAIR\" : "
            + Regex("éclair", RegexOption.IGNORE_CASE).matches("ÉCLAIR"))
    // MULTILINE: ^ and $ match each start and end of line; \w only recognizes [a-zA-Z0-9_]
    val text = "price: 10\ncafé: 3\ntotal: 30"
    display(Regex("""^(\w+): (\d+)$""", RegexOption.MULTILINE), text)
    // (?U) at the start of the pattern: \w also recognizes accented letters
    display(Regex("""(?U)^(\w+): (\d+)$""", RegexOption.MULTILINE), text)
    // an option of java.util.regex missing from RegexOption: we compile a Pattern and convert it
    val unicode = Pattern.compile("""^(\w+): (\d+)$""", Pattern.MULTILINE or Pattern.UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS)
    display(unicode.toRegex(), text)
    // the options can also be written in the pattern: (?i) for IGNORE_CASE, (?m) for MULTILINE
    println("(?i)yes on \"YES\" : ${"YES".matches(Regex("(?i)yes"))}")

    // 3 - a pattern with catastrophic backtracking, without then with a time limit
    for (n in listOf(10, 15, 20)) {
        val string = "a".repeat(n) + "!"
        val (found, duration) = measureTimedValue { CATASTROPHIC.containsMatchIn(string) }
        println("$n a : $found in ${duration.inWholeMilliseconds} ms")
    }
    val string = "a".repeat(30) + "!"
    try {
        val deadline = TimeSource.Monotonic.markNow() + 100.milliseconds
        println(CATASTROPHIC.containsMatchIn(TimeLimitedString(string, deadline)))
    } catch (e: TimeoutExceededException) {
        println("30 a : ${e.javaClass.simpleName} : search abandoned after 100 ms")
    }
    // the Java engine recognizes the pattern (a+)+ without a backreference and answers immediately
    val (found, duration) = measureTimedValue { Regex("""^(a+)+$""").containsMatchIn(string) }
    println("^(a+)+$ on 30 a : $found, answer in less than one second : ${duration < 1.seconds}")
}

// display of the name=value pairs found in a text
fun display(pattern: Regex, text: String) {
    for ((name, value) in pattern.findAll(text).map { it.destructured }) {
        print("[$name=$value] ")
    }
    println()
}

// a string that refuses to be read beyond a deadline
class TimeLimitedString(
    private val text: CharSequence,
    private val deadline: TimeSource.Monotonic.ValueTimeMark
) : CharSequence by text {

    override fun get(index: Int): Char {
        if (deadline.hasPassedNow()) throw TimeoutExceededException()
        return text[index]
    }

    override fun subSequence(startIndex: Int, endIndex: Int): CharSequence =
        TimeLimitedString(text.subSequence(startIndex, endIndex), deadline)

    override fun toString() = text.toString()
}

// the exception thrown when the deadline is exceeded
class TimeoutExceededException : RuntimeException()

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=regex06.Regex06Kt
TIME.containsMatchIn("It is 18:05:49") : true
hours=07, minutes=45, seconds=00
yes=true YES=true Yes=true no=false yesss=false
Regex("éclair", IGNORE_CASE) on "ÉCLAIR" : true
[price=10] [total=30]
[price=10] [café=3] [total=30]
[price=10] [café=3] [total=30]
(?i)yes on "YES" : true
10 a : false in 1 ms
15 a : false in 6 ms
20 a : false in 238 ms
30 a : TimeoutExceededException : search abandoned after 100 ms
^(a+)+$ on 30 a : false, answer in less than one second : true

Comments:

  • Lines 12–16: The program’s templates are compiled once and stored in top-level properties, written in uppercase as is customary for constants. They cannot be declared [const]: only values of basic types and strings, known at compile time, can be declared; an object [Regex] is created at runtime, the first time the file is used;
  • Lines 20–23: The properties are used in the same way as the [Regex] objects in the previous programs. The function [let], called by the operator [?.], executes its block only if [find] has found a match; line 22 retrieves the three named groups in a single statement, using a [map] projection followed by a destructuring;
  • Line 14: The second parameter of the [Regex] constructor is an option from the [RegexOption] enumeration. [IGNORE_CASE] is case-insensitive: “YES” and “Yes” match the pattern (line 3 of the results). Several options are specified as a set: [Regex(pattern, setOf(RegexOption.MULTILINE, RegexOption.IGNORE_CASE))], where Java combines integers using the [|] operator;
  • lines 31–33: for JVM, Kotlin always adds Java’s [UNICODE_CASE] option to the [IGNORE_CASE] option; the case of accented letters is also ignored, “ÉCLAIR” corresponds to “éclair” (line 4 of the results). In Java, [CASE_INSENSITIVE] alone would not do so;
  • lines 35–36: [MULTILINE] matches [^] and [$] at the beginning and end of each line in the string, rather than just at the beginning and end of the string itself. However, with the default options, [\w] recognizes only unaccented letters: the line “café: 3” is not recognized (line 5 of the results);
  • line 38: the [RegexOption] enumeration does not include the Java option [UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS], which provides [\w], [\d], [\s], and [\b] their Unicode meanings. This is achieved by writing [(?U)] at the beginning of the template: accented letters are then treated as word characters (line 6 of the results). This should be used for all French text;
  • lines 40–41: Another solution is to compile the template with the Java class [Pattern], which provides all available options (combined here with the operator [or], Kotlin’s bitwise “or” operator), and then convert the [Pattern] object to [Regex] using the extension function [toRegex] (line 7 of the results). The other options for [RegexOption] are [DOT_MATCHES_ALL] ([.] also corresponds to a line break), [COMMENTS] (spaces in the template are ignored, allowing it to be written across multiple lines, with comments, in a raw string), [LITERAL] (the template is plain text; see also [Regex.escape] and [Regex.fromLiteral]), [UNIX_LINES], and [CANON_EQ];
  • line 43: options can also be written at the beginning of the template: [(?i)] for [IGNORE_CASE], [(?m)] for [MULTILINE], [(?s)] for [DOT_MATCHES_ALL], [(?U)]…;
  • Lines 64–66: The function [display] iterates through the sequence of [destructured] values for the occurrences and parses each one directly within the [for] loop: [(name, value)] are groups 1 and 2.

The rest of the program addresses a security issue. Some patterns are pathological: when applied to certain strings, they force the regular expression engine to try an enormous number of ways to match the string to the pattern before reaching a conclusion. The Java engine—the one Kotlin uses on the JVM—uses a process called “backtracking”: when an attempt fails, it returns to the last choice made and tries another one. The [^(a+)+\1$] pattern on line 16 is an example of this: When applied to a sequence of “a”s ending with a different character, it tries every possible way to distribute the “a”s among the repetitions of the group and its backward reference [\1] before concluding that it has failed, and the number of attempts multiplies with each additional “a.” This is known as a catastrophic backtrack. When applied to user-entered strings, such a pattern constitutes a security vulnerability (known as ReDoS, “regular expression denial of service”): just a few requests are enough to bring a server to a standstill.

  • Lines 46–49: The search duration is measured for 10, 15, and 20 a. The function *[measureTimedValue] of *[kotlin.time] executes the block it receives and returns both its value and its duration, a [Duration] object, in the form of a [TimedValue] object that is unpacked. The duration increases very rapidly (lines 9–11 of the results; durations vary from one execution and one machine to another). Since the execution time roughly doubles with each additional a, the search would take several minutes with 30 a;
  • lines 51–56: Neither the [Regex] class nor the [Pattern] class has a timeout option. A standard technique is used: the search is performed in a [TimeLimitedString] object (lines 72–85), which implements the [CharSequence] interface accepted by the functions of [Regex]. The regular expression engine reads the string character by character using the [charAt] method of the Java interface [CharSequence], which corresponds to the [get] operator in Kotlin: this is what checks the time and throws a [TimeoutExceededException] exception (line 89) if the deadline—stored when the object was created—has passed. The search is abandoned after 100 ms;
  • lines 72–75: the class *[TimeLimitedString] has two properties, the text and the deadline, a time stamp from the monotonic clock of *[kotlin.time] ([ValueTimeMark]), whose function [hasPassedNow] indicates whether it has been exceeded. The clause [CharSequence by text] is a delegation: the class implements the [CharSequence] interface by delegating all members it does not override—in this case, the [length] property—to the [text] object. The compiler generates the functions that forward the calls; in Java, these must be written by hand. The only members that are redefined are the [get] operator, which monitors the time, and the [subSequence] function, which returns a [TimeLimitedString] subject to the same deadline. The function [toString], which is a member of [Any] but not of the interface, is not delegated: it is also overridden;
  • line 89: the [TimeoutExceededException] exception is derived from [RuntimeException]. Since Kotlin does not have checked exceptions, any exception could be thrown by [get]; Deriving from [RuntimeException] remains the standard practice, and Java code that calls the class would treat it as an unchecked exception. The [serialVersionUID] field found in Java exceptions is unnecessary here: the Kotlin compiler does not flag its absence;
  • Lines 59–60: The Java runtime can recognize and efficiently handle simple cases of nested repetitions: the [^(a+)+$] pattern, which is problematic with other runtimes, resolves immediately here. It is the backward reference [\1] that prevents this optimization in the pattern on line 16. Durations of the type [Duration] are compared using the operator [<].

It is important to note that one must be wary of patterns containing nested repetitions ([(a+)+], [(\w+\s?)*]…) and limit the duration of searches as soon as the pattern or the string being searched comes from outside the program. The Java engine’s possessive quantifiers ([a++], [a*+]), which prevent backtracking within the element they repeat, also allow you to write safe patterns, provided you fully understand their meaning.

docs.title: 5.9. Example Application - V3
docs.text: We’ll revisit the application discussed in Chapter 3 (Version 1) and Chapter 4 (Version 2). Remember that this is an exercise: the tax schedule used is the 2004 schedule (based on 2003 income), which has remained unchanged since the original course.

docs.title: 5.9.1. Data in a File
docs.text:
In Version 2, the tax calculation was performed in the abstract class [AbstractTax], which we are reusing here in the project’s package [taxv3]: as in Java, Version 3 is self-contained and does not depend on the classes from Chapter 4. The tax brackets are provided by an abstract property—a read-only list—and the division is performed with 16 significant digits, which is more than sufficient:

package taxv3

import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.math.MathContext

abstract class AbstractTax : ITax {

    // the tax brackets needed for the calculation come from an external source
    // that only the derived classes know
    protected abstract val taxBrackets: List<TaxBracket>

    // tax calculation
    override fun calculate(married: Boolean, nbChildren: Int, salary: Int): Int {
        // calculation of the number of shares
        var shares = nbChildren.toBigDecimal().divide(BigDecimal.TWO)
        shares += if (married) BigDecimal.TWO else BigDecimal.ONE
        if (nbChildren >= 3) {
            shares += "0.5".toBigDecimal()
        }
        // calculation of the taxable income and of the family quotient
        val income = "0.72".toBigDecimal() * salary.toBigDecimal()
        val quotient = income.divide(shares, MathContext.DECIMAL64)
        // search for the tax bracket: the last one is used if no limit fits
        val bracket = taxBrackets.dropLast(1).firstOrNull { quotient <= it.limit } ?: taxBrackets.last()
        // tax calculation
        return (income * bracket.coeffR - shares * bracket.coeffN).toInt()
    }
}

The function [calculate] uses the tax brackets returned by the abstract property [taxBrackets] (line 10). The class [AbstractTax] does not know where these brackets come from: it is up to the derived classes to provide them by redefining the property. In version 2, the derived class [HardwiredTax] hard-coded them directly into its code. The calculations are performed using exact decimal numbers [java.math.BigDecimal] (Chapter 3), which the Kotlin standard library makes easy to work with:

  • the extension functions [toBigDecimal] of [Int] and [String] replace [BigDecimal.valueOf(...)] and [new BigDecimal(...)] (["0.72".toBigDecimal()], line 21);
  • the operators [+], [-], [*], and [+=] are defined for [BigDecimal] (these are extension functions of [plus], [minus], [times], declared in [operator], Chapter 4): line 26 reads as the formula it calculates;
  • [BigDecimal] implements [Comparable<BigDecimal>]: the comparison operators are applied ([quotient <= it.limit], line 24) and call [compareTo];
  • Be careful, however, with the operator [/]: it calls [divide(other, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)], which preserves the number of decimal places in the dividend. For two integers, the result is rounded to the nearest integer: [3.toBigDecimal() / 2.toBigDecimal()] equals 2, and [1.toBigDecimal() / 2.toBigDecimal()] equals 0. The function’s two division operations are therefore implemented using the [divide] method: exact division by 2 (line 15), which would throw an exception if the result were not a finite decimal, and division with 16 significant digits ([MathContext.DECIMAL64], line 22);
  • line 24: the search for the bracket is written using collection operations: [dropLast(1)] excludes the last bracket, [firstOrNull] returns the first bracket whose limit is not exceeded by the family quotient, or [null] if there is none, and the operator [?:] then selects the last bracket, [last()];
  • [toInt] returns the integer part of the result (method [intValue] of [BigDecimal]).

A bracket is represented by the data class [TaxBracket]:

package taxv3

import java.math.BigDecimal

// a bracket of the tax scale
data class TaxBracket(val limit: BigDecimal, val coeffR: BigDecimal, val coeffN: BigDecimal)

and the calculation is described by the [ITax] interface, documented here by a KDoc comment—the Kotlin equivalent of Javadoc (same tags as [@param] and [@return]):

package taxv3

/**
 * The tax calculation.
 */
interface ITax {

    /**
     * Calculates the tax of a taxpayer.
     *
     * @param married true if the taxpayer is married
     * @param nbChildren number of children
     * @param salary annual salary in euros
     * @return the amount of the tax, in euros
     */
    fun calculate(married: Boolean, nbChildren: Int, salary: Int): Int
}

The new version stores the data in a file, which allows you to change the scale without recompiling the program. We write two new classes derived from [AbstractTax]:

  • [FileTax] reads the brackets from a text file [TaxData.txt];
  • [JsonTax] reads them from a JSON file [TaxData.json].

The text file [TaxData.txt] contains one bracket per line, in the format limit:coeffR:coeffN :

4962:0:0
8382:0.068:291.09
14753:0.191:1322.92
23888:0.283:2668.39
38868:0.374:4846.98
47932:0.426:6883.66
0:0.481:9505.54

The numbers in the file are written with a decimal point. A data file must not depend on the language of the machine reading it: a file written with decimal commas and interpreted according to French rules ([NumberFormat.getInstance(Locale.FRANCE)]) would be rejected or, worse, misinterpreted on an English-language machine. The function [toBigDecimal] of [String], like [toDouble], always expects a decimal point, regardless of the machine’s language. This is also the convention for JSON and most data formats.

The file [TaxData.json] contains the same data, in the form of a JSON array of objects:

[
  { "limit": 4962, "coeffR": 0, "coeffN": 0 },
  { "limit": 8382, "coeffR": 0.068, "coeffN": 291.09 },
  { "limit": 14753, "coeffR": 0.191, "coeffN": 1322.92 },
  { "limit": 23888, "coeffR": 0.283, "coeffN": 2668.39 },
  { "limit": 38868, "coeffR": 0.374, "coeffN": 4846.98 },
  { "limit": 47932, "coeffR": 0.426, "coeffN": 6883.66 },
  { "limit": 0, "coeffR": 0.481, "coeffN": 9505.54 }
]

docs.title: 5.9.2. Errors
docs.text:
Processing these files may fail due to a missing file, a malformed line, an incorrect number, etc. We create a special exception class to report these errors, [TaxException]. It will also be used for other data sources (the JSON file here, and databases later). It carries an error code:

package taxv3

// the exception thrown by the classes that read the tax brackets
// code: the code of the error (a combination of ErrorCode values)
// cause: the exception at the origin of the error, if there is one
class TaxException(message: String, val code: Int, cause: Throwable? = null) :
    RuntimeException(message, cause)

Comments:

  • Line 6: The entire class fits within its header. The primary constructor receives the message, the code, and the cause of the error; the code becomes a read-only property ([val]), while the message and cause, which are simple parameters, are passed to the constructor of the parent class *[RuntimeException]*, which makes them available via the properties *[message]* and *[cause]*;
  • the parameter [cause], the exception that caused the error, has a default value, [null]: a single constructor replaces the two constructors in the Java version; [TaxException(message, code)] and [TaxException(message, code, e)] are defined using the same constructor. Subsequent versions of the application will adopt this exception, which carries an integer code, with a slightly different constructor (Chapter 6);
  • Line 7: The class extends [RuntimeException]. Since Kotlin does not have checked exceptions (Chapter 3), the choice of parent class does not impose any restrictions here; however, for Java code that uses the class, [TaxException] will be an unchecked exception, which is the intended behavior, as we will see. The [serialVersionUID] field in the Java version is unnecessary: the Kotlin compiler does not issue a warning about it.

Possible error codes are defined by an enumeration:

package taxv3

import java.util.EnumSet

// the error codes: powers of 2, which can be combined
enum class ErrorCode(val value: Int) {
    ACCESS(1),      // the file cannot be read
    LINE(2),        // a line does not have three fields
    FIELD1(4),      // field 1 (limit) is incorrect
    FIELD2(8),      // field 2 (coeffR) is incorrect
    FIELD3(16),     // field 3 (coeffN) is incorrect
    JSON(32);       // the JSON document is incorrect

    companion object {
        // the codes present in a combination of codes
        fun decode(code: Int): EnumSet<ErrorCode> =
            entries.filterTo(EnumSet.noneOf(ErrorCode::class.java)) { code and it.value != 0 }
    }
}

Comments:

  • lines 7–12: possible error codes:
    • [ACCESS]: error accessing the data file;
    • [LINE]: row missing the three expected fields, or file containing no brackets;
    • [FIELD1], [FIELD2], [FIELD3]: Field 1, 2, or 3 in a row is incorrect;
    • [JSON]: The JSON document is incorrect;
  • line 6: A Kotlin enum ([enum class], Chapter 3) can have properties, declared in its primary constructor, and functions. Each constant is constructed with its integer value, enclosed in parentheses; the list of constants ends with a semicolon when followed by other members;
  • Lines 14–17: Some errors can occur simultaneously; all three fields in a line may be incorrect. Therefore, the code values are powers of 2: each corresponds to a bit of the integer. An error in fields 2 and 3 will result in the code [8 or 16] = 24 ([or] is the bitwise “OR” operator in Kotlin). The function [decode], placed within [companion object] in the enumeration to be called by [ErrorCode.decode(code)], performs the inverse operation: it converts the set of codes present into an integer by testing each bit with the [and] operator. The property [entries] (Kotlin 1.9) is the list of constants in the enum, and [filterTo] places those that satisfy the condition into the collection passed to it, in this case an empty [java.util.EnumSet]. This collection, specialized for the constants of an enum, stores them internally as the bits of an integer; its method [toString] displays a combination in the form “[FIELD2, FIELD3].” We could just as easily return a Kotlin [Set<ErrorCode>] ([entries.filter { ... }.toSet()]), which would be displayed the same way.

docs.title: 5.9.3. The FileTax class
docs.text:
The [FileTax] class provides the brackets read from a text file:

package taxv3

import java.io.IOException
import kotlin.io.path.Path
import kotlin.io.path.useLines

// the tax brackets read from a text file of limit:coeffR:coeffN lines
class FileTax(fileName: String) : AbstractTax() {

    companion object {
        // the field separator: the : character surrounded by optional spaces
        private val SEPARATOR = Regex("""\s*:\s*""")
        // a positive or zero number: digits, optionally followed by a dot and digits
        private val NUMBER = Regex("""\d+(\.\d+)?""")
        // the error codes of the three fields of a line
        private val FIELD_CODES = listOf(ErrorCode.FIELD1, ErrorCode.FIELD2, ErrorCode.FIELD3)
    }

    // the tax brackets read from the file (implementation of the abstract property of the parent)
    override val taxBrackets: List<TaxBracket>

    init {
        // the file name, without its path, for the error messages
        val path = Path(fileName)
        val name = path.fileName.toString()
        val brackets = try {
            // reading the file line by line; useLines closes it in all cases
            path.useLines { lines ->
                lines.mapIndexed { index, line -> index + 1 to line.trim() }
                    // empty lines are ignored
                    .filter { (_, line) -> line.isNotEmpty() }
                    .map { (lineNumber, line) -> bracket(lineNumber, line) }
                    .toList()
            }
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            // file access error: it is wrapped in a TaxException
            throw TaxException("Error while reading the file $name", ErrorCode.ACCESS.value, e)
        }
        // at least one bracket is needed
        if (brackets.isEmpty()) {
            throw TaxException("The file $name does not contain any bracket", ErrorCode.LINE.value)
        }
        taxBrackets = brackets
    }

    // the tax bracket described by a line of the file
    private fun bracket(lineNumber: Int, line: String): TaxBracket {
        // the line must have three fields
        val fields = line.split(SEPARATOR)
        if (fields.size != 3) {
            throw TaxException("Line no. $lineNumber is incorrect ($line)", ErrorCode.LINE.value)
        }
        // three positive or zero decimal numbers, written with a decimal point
        val code = FIELD_CODES.zip(fields)
            .filter { (_, field) -> !NUMBER.matches(field) }
            .fold(0) { code, (errorCode, _) -> code or errorCode.value }
        if (code != 0) {
            throw TaxException("Line no. $lineNumber is incorrect ($line)", code)
        }
        // the new tax bracket
        val (limit, coeffR, coeffN) = fields.map { it.toBigDecimal() }
        return TaxBracket(limit, coeffR, coeffN)
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 8: The [FileTax] class derives from the [AbstractTax] class, just as the [HardwiredTax] class did in version 2. Its primary constructor takes the name of the text file containing the data. The parameter [fileName], declared without [val], is not a property: it is used only during object construction;
  • lines 10–16: two regular expressions, compiled once and for all and stored in the class’s [companion object], the Kotlin equivalent of Java’s [private static final] constants: the field separator for a limit:coeffR:coeffN line (the character [:], preceded and followed by any number of spaces), and a positive or zero number, consisting of digits possibly followed by a period and more digits. Raw strings prevent duplication of [\]. The list [FIELD_CODES] associates an error code with each field;
  • line 20: the property that redefines the abstract property of [AbstractTax]. It is declared without an initial value: it will be initialized in the block [init], where the compiler requires that it be assigned a value—and only one;
  • lines 22–43: The block [init] executes when the object is constructed, similar to the body of a Java constructor. Its role is to populate the list [taxBrackets];
  • line 25: the filename without its path, used in error messages. The constructor can indeed receive a full path, which does not need to be displayed to the user. The function [Path] of [kotlin.io.path] creates the object [java.nio.file.Path]; [fileName] is the Java method [getFileName] treated as a property;
  • Lines 26–33: Reading the file. The extension function [useLines] of [Path] opens the file (in UTF-8), passes the sequence of its lines to the lambda, and then closes the file regardless of how the lambda is exited—whether normally or via an exception: This is the equivalent of [try] using Java resources. Since reading a text file is a sequential process, the number of lines is not known until the end; the sequence lends itself to string processing:
    • [mapIndexed] associates each line—with spaces removed by [trim]—with its number (the index starts at 0, line numbering at 1), in the form of a pair [number to line];
    • [filter] removes empty lines; the pair is unpacked into the lambda’s parameters, [(_, line)], with the unnecessary number replaced by [_];
    • [map] converts each line into a bracket using the function [bracket];
    • [toList] iterates over the sequence and stores the brackets in a list. This call must be made within the lambda: a sequence is evaluated lazily, and a sequence returned as-is by [useLines] would be iterated over after the file is closed;
  • the block [try] is an expression: its value is the list of brackets, stored in the variable [brackets];
  • lines 35–37: file access errors ([IOException] and its variants, such as [NoSuchFileException] for a missing file, [AccessDeniedException] for insufficient permissions, or [MalformedInputException] for a file that is not in UTF-8) are wrapped in a [TaxException] with code [ACCESS], with the original exception becoming its cause. The [TaxException] exceptions thrown by the [bracket] function are not [IOException] exceptions: they are not intercepted by this [catch] clause and exit the constructor as-is, though the file is still closed by [useLines];
  • lines 40–43: an empty file is rejected; otherwise, the list becomes the value of the [taxBrackets] property, which was the purpose of the [init] block;
  • lines 49–51: The function [bracket] parses a line. The line is split into fields using a regular expression; if there are not three fields, a [TaxException] exception with code [LINE] is thrown. Note that [split] retains empty fields at the end in Kotlin: a line ending with an extra separator, “4962:0:0: ”, has four fields and is rejected, whereas the Java method [split], which removes empty fields at the end, would accept it;
  • Lines 54–58: validation of the three fields. The function [zip] associates each error code with the corresponding field, in the form of pairs; [filter] retains the fields that do not match the [NUMBER] template, and [fold] accumulates their codes using the [or] operator, starting from 0. Errors are thus reported collectively. The [matches] function requires that the entire field match the [NUMBER] template: no signs, spaces, or commas. Negative numbers are thus rejected, which validates the data at the same time it is being checked;
  • lines 61–62: the fields, now validated, are converted to [BigDecimal] by [toBigDecimal], using a decimal point regardless of the machine’s language; the list of three numbers is unpacked to construct the bracket.

Encapsulating low-level exceptions ([IOException]) within an application-specific exception ([TaxException]) allows the calling code to handle only a single type of exception, regardless of the data source: a text file, a JSON file, and, later in the course, a database. In Java, this is also why [TaxException] is an unchecked exception: a checked exception would need to be declared by every method it passes through, which would tie the calling code to the details of the data source. Kotlin, which does not have checked exceptions, does not enforce this choice, but encapsulation remains just as important: the calling code does not need to know about file-related exceptions in API.

docs.title: 5.9.4. The JsonTax class
docs.text:
The [JsonTax] class returns the brackets read from a JSON file. It uses the Jackson 3 library, which has already been declared in the project’s [build.gradle.kts] file:

package taxv3

import java.io.IOException
import java.math.BigDecimal
import kotlin.io.path.Path
import kotlin.io.path.readText
import tools.jackson.core.JacksonException
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper

// the tax brackets read from a JSON file
class JsonTax(fileName: String) : AbstractTax() {

    companion object {
        // the JsonMapper is reusable and usable by several threads: only one is created
        private val MAPPER = JsonMapper.builder().build()

        // a negative value is incorrect
        private fun negative(value: BigDecimal) = value.signum() < 0
    }

    // the tax brackets read from the file
    override val taxBrackets: List<TaxBracket>

    init {
        // the file name, without its path, for the error messages
        val path = Path(fileName)
        val name = path.fileName.toString()
        // reading the file
        val json = try {
            path.readText()
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            throw TaxException("Error while reading the file $name", ErrorCode.ACCESS.value, e)
        }
        // deserialization of the array of brackets; the null JSON document gives the null value
        val brackets: Array<TaxBracket>? = try {
            MAPPER.readValue(json, Array<TaxBracket>::class.java)
        } catch (e: JacksonException) {
            val position = "line ${e.location?.lineNr}, column ${e.location?.columnNr}"
            throw TaxException("The file $name is incorrect: ${e.originalMessage} ($position)",
                ErrorCode.JSON.value, e)
        }
        // at least one bracket is needed, without a negative value
        if (brackets.isNullOrEmpty()) {
            throw TaxException("The file $name does not contain any bracket", ErrorCode.JSON.value)
        }
        if (brackets.any { negative(it.limit) || negative(it.coeffR) || negative(it.coeffN) }) {
            throw TaxException("The file $name contains a negative value", ErrorCode.JSON.value)
        }
        taxBrackets = brackets.toList()
    }
}

Comments:

  • Line 15: A single [JsonMapper], stored within the [companion object], is used for all [JsonTax] objects. The properties JSON, [limit], [coeffR], and [coeffN] are named after the parameters of the constructor for the data class [TaxBracket]: No annotations are necessary, because the compiler preserves these names in the compiled code (option [javaParameters = true] in the file [build.gradle.kts]), and Jackson 3 can read them;
  • Lines 29–32: Reading the file using the [readText] extension function from [Path]; an access error is handled as in [FileTax];
  • line 36: a single instruction converts the JSON text into an array of brackets; [Array<TaxBracket>::class.java] is the Java class for the array, equivalent to [TaxBracket[].class]. Jackson constructs each bracket by calling the data class’s constructor and converts the numbers JSON to [BigDecimal] without any loss of precision. Since the Java method [readValue] can return [null] (for the JSON document [null]), the result is stored in a variable of type [Array<TaxBracket>?]: without this declaration, Kotlin would assign it a “platform” type, and it does not know whether that type accepts [null];
  • lines 37–40: an invalid document causes a [JacksonException], encapsulated in a [TaxException] with code [JSON]. The message indicates the location of the error, specified by the [location] property ([getLocation] method); the [?.] operator protects against an unknown position;
  • lines 43–49: deserialization checks the document format, not the validity of the data: it remains to be verified that there is at least one bracket (the document [null] or [[]] is a valid JSON), which [isNullOrEmpty] does in a single test, and that no values are negative, which is done by the operation [any], applied directly to the array. After the first test, the compiler knows that [brackets] is not [null]. The array is finally converted to a list by [toList];
  • line 18: the function that tests a value, written as an expression.

The Java version also checked that no values were missing: a missing property of an object JSON assigns the value [null] to the corresponding component of a record. In Kotlin, this check is unnecessary: the properties of [TaxBracket] are of type *[BigDecimal]*, not ***[BigDecimal?]. The Kotlin compiler adds a check for each non-nullable parameter at the beginning of the class’s constructor: if Jackson passes it [null], the constructor throws an exception, which Jackson propagates as a [JacksonException]. Safety with respect to *[null] thus extends to objects created by a Java library: an incomplete bracket cannot exist. We’ll verify this later.

Comparing the two classes is instructive: with a structured data format and a library that understands it, parsing the file requires almost no code. Note that there is a Kotlin-specific Jackson module, [jackson-module-kotlin], which takes into account parameter defaults and nullable types, and offers functions such as [mapper.readValue<Array<TaxBracket>>(json)], where the type is specified by a generic parameter ([reified], Chapter 4). JetBrains also offers its own serialization library, [kotlinx.serialization], which generates serialization code at compile time using a compiler plugin. For a data class as simple as [TaxBracket], Jackson alone is sufficient.

docs.title: 5.9.5. The Main Program
docs.text:
Unlike the Java version, which was part of a separate Maven project, Version 3 is a multi-file program within the chapter’s Gradle project, organized into its own package, [taxv3]. The relevant part of the project has the following directory structure:

05-classes-kotlin/
  build.gradle.kts
  TaxData.json
  TaxData.txt
  TaxDataIncomplete.json
  TaxDataInvalid.json
  TaxDataInvalid.txt
  src/main/kotlin/taxv3/
    AbstractTax.kt
    ErrorCode.kt
    FileTax.kt
    ITax.kt
    JsonTax.kt
    Main.kt
    TaxBracket.kt
    TaxException.kt

The data files are placed in the project root directory, next to the [build.gradle.kts] file: This is the current directory of the program when it is run using the [gradlew run] command, or by clicking the green triangle in IntelliJ or IDEA. The Jackson library is declared in the project’s [build.gradle.kts] file, which is used by all the programs in this chapter:

dependencies {
    // the libraries used by the programs of the project
    // JSON: Jackson 3
    implementation("tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind:3.1.5")
}

The main program is the file [Main.kt]; its class JVM is [taxv3.MainKt]:

package taxv3

import kotlin.system.exitProcess

// tax calculation, version 3: the tax brackets are read from a file
// syntax: gradlew -q run -Pmain=taxv3.MainKt [--args="file"]
// file: TaxData.txt by default, or a .json file

private val SYNTAX = """
    syntax: Married NbChildren Salary
    Married: y for married, n for not married
    NbChildren: number of children
    Salary: annual salary in euros""".trimIndent()

// the prompt of the input loop
private const val PROMPT =
    "Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: "

// the separator of the typed parameters: a sequence of spaces
private val SPACES = Regex("""\s+""")

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    // the data file is looked for in the current folder
    val fileName = args.firstOrNull() ?: "TaxData.txt"
    println("Tax brackets read from [$fileName]")

    // creation of an ITax object; the class depends on the file extension
    val tax: ITax = try {
        when (fileName.substringAfterLast('.').lowercase()) {
            "json" -> JsonTax(fileName)
            else -> FileTax(fileName)
        }
    } catch (e: TaxException) {
        // display of the error; the code is displayed as a set of ErrorCode
        val origin = e.cause?.let { ", original exception: ${it.javaClass.simpleName}" } ?: ""
        println("The following error occurred: [Code=${ErrorCode.decode(e.code)}, "
                + "Message=${e.message}$origin]")
        // stopping the program
        exitProcess(1)
    }

    // input loop
    while (true) {
        // we ask for the tax calculation parameters
        print(PROMPT)
        val parameters = readlnOrNull()?.trim() ?: ""
        // anything to do?
        if (parameters.isEmpty()) break
        // checking the number of fields of the typed line
        val fields = parameters.split(SPACES)
        if (fields.size != 3) {
            println(SYNTAX)
            continue
        }
        // checking the validity of the parameters
        // married
        val married = fields[0].lowercase()
        if (married != "y" && married != "n") {
            println("$SYNTAX\nIncorrect married argument: type y or n")
            continue
        }
        // nbChildren: a positive or zero integer
        val nbChildren = fields[1].toIntOrNull()?.takeIf { it >= 0 }
        if (nbChildren == null) {
            println("$SYNTAX\nIncorrect NbChildren argument: type a positive or zero integer")
            continue
        }
        // salary: a positive or zero integer
        val salary = fields[2].toIntOrNull()?.takeIf { it >= 0 }
        if (salary == null) {
            println("$SYNTAX\nIncorrect salary argument: type a positive or zero integer")
            continue
        }
        // the parameters are correct: we calculate the tax
        println("Tax=${tax.calculate(married == "y", nbChildren, salary)} euros")
    }
}

Comments:

  • Lines 9–13: the help text, in a raw string from which [trimIndent] removes the common indentation and the first, empty line. Since the result of a function call is not a compile-time constant, the property cannot be declared as [const]: [const val SYNTAX = """...""".trimIndent()] is rejected by the compiler ([const 'val' initializer must be a constant value]). The prompt for the input loop, a string literal, is, however, a constant [const val] (line 16);
  • line 20: the separator for the entered parameters, compiled once and for all;
  • line 24: the name of the data file is passed as an argument; by default, it is [TaxData.txt]. [firstOrNull] returns the first argument, or [null] if there is none, in which case it is replaced by the default value using the operator [?:]. With Gradle, the program’s arguments are passed via the [--args] option: [gradlew -q run -Pmain=taxv3.MainKt --args="TaxData.json"];
  • lines 28–31: a [when] expression (Chapter 3) selects the class to instantiate based on the file extension, extracted from the filename using [substringAfterLast]. The two branches return objects of different types, [JsonTax] and [FileTax], both of type [ITax], which is the declared type of the variable [tax]. The rest of the program only recognizes the [ITax] interface and is unaware of where the data comes from;
  • lines 33–39: creating the object may throw a [TaxException], which is displayed before the program terminates. The code is decoded into a set of [ErrorCode] to be displayed in plain text; the original exception, if any, is indicated by its type: [e.cause?.let { ... } ?: ""] constructs the text if the cause exists and returns an empty string otherwise. The [exitProcess] function from the standard library terminates the program; it is of type [Nothing]: the compiler knows that it never returns control, and therefore that the variable [tax] is initialized after the block [try]. The unnecessary instruction [return], which followed [System.exit] in the Java version and was required by the Java compiler, is removed;
  • lines 43–75: The dialog loop is the same as in version 2. The line read by [readlnOrNull] is [null] at the end of the stream, which is then replaced by an empty string (line 46). The number of children and the salary are converted by [toIntOrNull], which returns [null] if the string is not an integer, and [takeIf { it >= 0 }] also returns [null] for a negative integer (lines 63, 69): A single test on [null] detects both errors. The expression is written directly, without the [positiveInteger] function from version 2 (or the [integer] function from the Java version, which returned -1 in case of an error). After this test, the compiler knows that [nbChildren] and [salary] are of type [Int].

With the file [TaxData.json]:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=taxv3.MainKt --args="TaxData.json"
Tax brackets read from [TaxData.json]
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2 60000
Tax=4282 euros
