import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException
import java.util.concurrent.Executors
import java.util.concurrent.Future

fun main() {
    println("Main thread: ${Thread.currentThread()}")

    // 1 - a pool of 2 threads, closed automatically at the end of the use block
    Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2).use { pool ->
        // three tasks that each return a result of type Int
        val futures: List<Future<Int>> = List(3) { number ->
            pool.submit<Int> {
                val name = Thread.currentThread().name
                println("${time()} : task $number runs in thread $name")
                // work
                Thread.sleep(500L * (number + 1))
                // the result of the task
                number * 10
            }
        }
        // the results: get() waits for the end of the task
        futures.forEachIndexed { i, future ->
            try {
                println("task $i: result ${future.get()}, state ${future.state()}")
            } catch (e: ExecutionException) {
                println("task $i in error: ${e.cause}")
            }
        }

        // a task that throws an exception
        val failed = pool.submit<Int> { fail() }
        try {
            failed.get()
        } catch (e: ExecutionException) {
            // the exception of the task is wrapped in an ExecutionException
            val cause = e.cause!!
            println("${e::class.simpleName} containing ${cause::class.simpleName} : ${cause.message}")
        }
        println("task in error: state ${failed.state()}")
    }

    // 2 - one virtual thread per task; invokeAll submits a collection of tasks and waits for their end
    Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { executor ->
        val jobs = List(3) { number ->
            Callable {
                Thread.sleep(300)
                "job $number executed by ${Thread.currentThread()}"
            }
        }
        for (future in executor.invokeAll(jobs)) {
            // the task is finished: resultNow() returns its result without waiting
            println(future.resultNow())
        }
    }
}

// the work of the failing task
fun fail(): Int = throw IllegalStateException("test....")

// the current time, to the millisecond
fun time(): String = LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"))

Comments:

  • line 15: a pool of 2 threads, created by [Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)] and closed at the end of the [use] block;
  • lines 17–24: Each task is a lambda that displays the thread executing it, sleeps for 0.5, 1, or 1.5 seconds, and then returns an integer result—the value of its last expression. The function [List] constructs the list of the three [Future<Int>] objects returned by [submit];
  • Line 18: Be careful with the submit overload. The *[submit] method exists in several versions, including ***[submit(Runnable)] and ***[submit(Callable<T>)]***. With a lambda, Java chooses the [Callable] version if the lambda returns a value. Kotlin, on the other hand, treats any lambda as convertible to [Runnable]* (in which case its value is ignored) and chooses [submit(Runnable)]! If you write ***[val f = pool.submit { 10 }], the compiler simply issues a warning:
warning: expression is unused.

and [f.get()] produces [null], the "result" of a [Runnable]. We impose the [Callable] version by specifying the type argument, [submit<Int> { … }], as shown here, or by explicitly creating a [Callable]: [pool.submit(Callable { … })]. The [Thread.sleep] on line 22 does not need to be surrounded by a [try]: Kotlin does not have controlled exceptions, and any potential [InterruptedException] would be logged in the [Future];

  • Line 28: The function [forEachIndexed] iterates through the list, returning the index and the element;
  • line 30: [future.get()] waits for the task to finish and returns its result; [future.state()] returns its status. Since [state] is not an accessor for [getXxx], Kotlin treats it as a method, not a property;
  • line 37: a task that executes the function [fail] (line 64), which throws an exception. The return type of [fail] is [Int]: the expression [throw …] is of type [Nothing], which is compatible with all types;
  • lines 39–43: the exception thrown in the task is not lost; it is stored in the object [Future], then rethrown in the thread requesting the result, wrapped in a *[ExecutionException] whose property [cause]* (the Java method *[getCause]*) contains the original exception. This property is of type [Throwable?]; the operator [!!] asserts that it is not [null], which is guaranteed here. The expression [e::class.simpleName] provides the short name of the exception’s class;
  • lines 49–58: an executor that creates one virtual thread per task. Tasks are explicitly created as [Callable], using the SAM constructor [Callable { … }] (line 51): the list [jobs] is therefore of type [List<Callable<String>>]. The method [invokeAll] (line 56) assigns the three jobs to the executor and waits for them to finish. Once the tasks are complete, [resultNow] returns their results immediately.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=threads26.Threads26Kt
Main thread: Thread[#3,main,5,main]
13:01:08.772 : task 0 runs in thread pool-1-thread-1
13:01:08.769 : task 1 runs in thread pool-1-thread-2
13:01:09.291 : task 2 runs in thread pool-1-thread-1
task 0: result 0, state SUCCESS
task 1: result 10, state SUCCESS
task 2: result 20, state SUCCESS
ExecutionException containing IllegalStateException : test....
task in error: state FAILED
job 0 executed by VirtualThread[#24]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1
job 1 executed by VirtualThread[#27]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2
job 2 executed by VirtualThread[#29]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2
  • the tasks run in the pool’s threads ([pool-1-thread-1] and [pool-1-thread-2]);
  • Task 2 did not start until Task 0 had finished, in the thread that Task 0 had freed up: the pool has only 2 threads, and Task 2 waited in the queue. This behavior is reproducible;
  • The results are retrieved after the tasks have finished, and their status is [SUCCESS];
  • the exception from the task that failed was caught by the main thread, and the task’s status is [FAILED];
  • the three jobs in the second part were executed by three different virtual threads, mounted on the carrier threads [ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1] and [ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2] (the distribution among carriers varies from one execution to another).

Blocking a thread in [get] to wait for a result is simple, but you cannot chain processing operations to the completion of a task without waiting. The following chapter introduces the [CompletableFuture] class from JDK, which allows this, and, most importantly, Kotlin’s solution: coroutines, with [async] and [Deferred] (the equivalent of a [Future] whose result is awaited by [await] without blocking a thread). Finally, note that Java 25 offers, as a preview, structured concurrency ([StructuredTaskScope]), which treats a group of subtasks as a single unit of work (if one fails, the others are canceled). It is not used in this course: Kotlin coroutines are based on this same principle, which has long been a standard feature in Kotlin, and Chapter 9 focuses extensively on it.

docs.title: 8.11.1. Parallel streams
docs.text:
Let’s return to the primary use of threads: utilizing all processors for a time-consuming computation. The Kotlin standard library does not provide parallel operations on collections: its functions ([filter], [map], [count]…) and its sequences are sequential. However, a Kotlin program has access to Java’s API Stream (Chapter 5), whose streams can be executed in parallel: simply call [parallel()] on a stream, or [parallelStream()] instead of [stream()] on a collection (a Kotlin list is a [java.util.List]: it has these methods). The stream then splits the data into chunks, has the chunks processed by multiple threads, and then combines the partial results. The threads used are those from the shared pool ([ForkJoinPool.commonPool()]), joined by the thread executing the stream. By default, the shared pool has as many threads as there are processors, minus one: the calling thread performs the count.

These flows are only suitable if the processing of each element is independent of the others: the processing order is undefined, and if the processing updates shared data, it must be protected. The program [Threads27.kt] is as follows:

// parallel streams: IntStream.parallel and parallelStream
package threads27

import java.time.LocalTime
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap
import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool
import java.util.stream.IntStream
import kotlin.time.measureTimedValue

fun main() {
    // 1 - counting the prime numbers less than N
    val N = 5_000_000
    // sequential version: a for loop
    val (nbLoop, durationLoop) = measureTimedValue {
        var nb = 0
        for (i in 2..<N) {
            if (isPrime(i)) nb++
        }
        nb
    }
    display("sequential for", nbLoop.toLong(), durationLoop.inWholeMilliseconds)

    // sequential version: Kotlin's count function on a range
    val (nbKotlin, durationKotlin) = measureTimedValue { (2..<N).count { isPrime(it) } }
    display("sequential count", nbKotlin.toLong(), durationKotlin.inWholeMilliseconds)

    // sequential version: a Java stream
    val (nbStream, durationStream) = measureTimedValue { IntStream.range(2, N).filter { isPrime(it) }.count() }
    display("sequential stream", nbStream, durationStream.inWholeMilliseconds)

    // parallel version: the same stream, made parallel
    val (nbParallel, durationParallel) = measureTimedValue {
        IntStream.range(2, N).parallel().filter { isPrime(it) }.count()
    }
    display("parallel stream", nbParallel, durationParallel.inWholeMilliseconds)

    // the threads that worked and the number of prime numbers found by each one
    val threads = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Int>()
    IntStream.range(2, N).parallel()
        .filter { isPrime(it) }
        .forEach { threads.merge(Thread.currentThread().name, 1, Int::plus) }
    for ((name, nb) in threads.toSortedMap()) {
        println("  thread %-30s : %,d prime numbers found".format(name, nb))
    }

    // 2 - processing a collection in parallel
    val files = listOf("a.txt", "b.txt", "c.txt", "d.txt", "e.txt")
    files.parallelStream().forEach { file ->
        println("${time()} : processing of $file in thread ${Thread.currentThread().name}")
        // simulated processing
        sleep(500)
    }
    println("parallel forEach finished")
    println("Parallelism of the common pool: ${ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism()}")
}

// display of a result and of its duration
fun display(method: String, nb: Long, ms: Long) {
    println("%-20s : %,d prime numbers in %d ms".format(method, nb, ms))
}

// primality test (deliberately simple)
fun isPrime(n: Int): Boolean {
    if (n < 2) return false
    var d = 2
    while (d * d <= n) {
        if (n % d == 0) return false
        d++
    }
    return true
}

// sleep for [ms] milliseconds
fun sleep(ms: Long) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms)
    } catch (_: InterruptedException) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt()
    }
}

// the current time, to the millisecond
fun time(): String = LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"))

Comments:

  • Lines 15–22: Prime numbers less than 5,000,000 are counted using a standard [for] loop. The function [isPrime] (lines 64–71) tests divisors up to the square root of the number: this is a time-consuming process, and the iterations are independent. The duration is measured by the [measureTimedValue] function from the standard library ([kotlin.time]): it executes its lambda and returns a [TimedValue] object that contains the value returned by the lambda and the duration of its execution (a *[Duration]*); this is unpacked into two variables. The *[inWholeMilliseconds] property gives the duration in milliseconds. Java measured durations using ***[System.nanoTime()]**;
  • line 25: the same calculation, written in the Kotlin style: the function [count] from the interval [2..<N] counts the elements that satisfy the predicate. This is sequential;
  • line 29: the same calculation using a sequential Java stream: [IntStream.range(2, N)] generates the integers from 2 to N - 1, [filter] keeps only the prime numbers, and [count] counts them (the result is a [Long]). The lambda [{ isPrime(it) }] is converted to [IntPredicate], the functional interface expected by [filter];
  • lines 33–34: the same flow, made parallel by [parallel()]. Nothing else needs to be changed: each thread counts the prime numbers in its segments, and the flow adds up the partial counts. No data is shared between threads;
  • lines 39–44: To determine which threads have completed their work, the parallel stream counts, for each thread, the prime numbers it has found and stores them in a shared [ConcurrentHashMap]. This is shared data, updated by an atomic operation ([merge]);
  • lines 48–52: The [parallelStream()] method of a Kotlin list of filenames returns a parallel stream; [forEach] processes each file (the processing is simulated by a half-second pause). With a parallel stream, [forEach] does not preserve the order of the list; [forEachOrdered] would preserve it, at the cost of some parallelism;
  • Line 55: the number of threads in the shared pool;
  • Lines 59–60: Displaying a result: [%-20s] left-aligns the method name to 20 characters.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=threads27.Threads27Kt
sequential for       : 348,513 prime numbers in 2523 ms
sequential count     : 348,513 prime numbers in 1891 ms
sequential stream    : 348,513 prime numbers in 3697 ms
parallel stream      : 348,513 prime numbers in 4583 ms
  thread ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 : 224,082 prime numbers found
  thread main                           : 124,431 prime numbers found
12:56:50.425 : processing of b.txt in thread ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1
12:56:50.440 : processing of c.txt in thread main
12:56:50.943 : processing of e.txt in thread main
12:56:50.955 : processing of a.txt in thread ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1
12:56:51.451 : processing of d.txt in thread main
parallel forEach finished
Parallelism of the common pool: 1
  • All four versions find the same number of prime numbers;
  • Two threads participated in the parallel processing: the thread [main] and the single thread from the shared pool ([ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1]): on this dual-processor machine, the shared pool has only one thread (last line);
  • files are processed in pairs, half a second apart, and in an order that does not match the list;
  • here, the parallel flow was no faster than the sequential versions, and was in fact the slowest. This is not a flaw in parallel processing: at the time of the test, the machine (2 processors) was running many other very active programs (an average load of about ten threads ready to run for 2 processors), so the second processor, on which the parallel process relied, was not available. The measured execution times also varied significantly from one run to the next for all versions. On a lightly loaded machine with n processors, a parallel thread like this one can be nearly n times faster than the sequential thread. It is always necessary to measure performance under real-world conditions before drawing conclusions: parallelization comes at a cost (work partitioning, synchronization, result merging) that is only worthwhile if processing each element requires enough computation, and if processors are available to execute it.

In the next chapter, we will also parallelize calculations using coroutines, launching them on the [Dispatchers.Default] dispatcher, whose threads are also as numerous as the processors.

docs.title: 8.11.2. Divide and Conquer: ForkJoinPool and RecursiveTask
docs.text:
Parallel streams are based on the Fork/Join framework (Java 7), which can also be used directly. It is well-suited for “divide and conquer” algorithms: a task that is too large is broken down into subtasks, which are in turn broken down, until the pieces are small enough to be processed directly; the results of the subtasks are then combined. A task is a class derived from [RecursiveTask<V>] (a task that returns a result of type V) or from [RecursiveAction] (no result), for which the [compute] method is overridden. In [compute], a subtask’s [fork()] method immediately submits it to the pool, and its [join()] method waits for its result.

The tasks are executed by a [ForkJoinPool], in which each thread has its own task queue. A thread that has nothing left to do “steals” tasks from another thread’s queue (“work stealing”): the load is thus distributed automatically. The threads carrying the virtual threads also form a [ForkJoinPool]: this is the one we saw in the textual representation of the virtual threads ([ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1]). The program [Threads28.kt] counts prime numbers using a recursive task:

// divide and conquer: ForkJoinPool and RecursiveTask
package threads28

import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap
import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool
import java.util.concurrent.RecursiveTask
import kotlin.time.measureTimedValue

fun main() {
    val N = 5_000_000
    // the common pool, used by default by parallel streams
    val (nb, duration) = measureTimedValue { ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(CountPrimes(2, N)) }
    println("common pool       : %,d prime numbers in %d ms".format(nb, duration.inWholeMilliseconds))

    // a pool of 4 threads, closed at the end of the use block
    ForkJoinPool(4).use { pool ->
        CountPrimes.chunks.clear()
        val (nb4, duration4) = measureTimedValue { pool.invoke(CountPrimes(2, N)) }
        println("pool of 4 threads : %,d prime numbers in %d ms".format(nb4, duration4.inWholeMilliseconds))
        println("tasks stolen by one thread from another: ${pool.stealCount}")
    }
    // the distribution of the chunks among the threads of the last pool
    for ((name, nbChunks) in CountPrimes.chunks.toSortedMap()) {
        println("  %-25s : %d chunks processed".format(name, nbChunks))
    }
}

// a task that counts the prime numbers of the interval [start, end[
class CountPrimes(private val start: Int, private val end: Int) : RecursiveTask<Int>() {
    companion object {
        // below this threshold, the chunk is processed directly
        const val THRESHOLD = 100_000
        // the number of chunks processed by each thread
        val chunks = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Int>()
    }

    override fun compute(): Int {
        // chunk small enough: it is processed sequentially
        if (end - start <= THRESHOLD) {
            chunks.merge(Thread.currentThread().name, 1, Int::plus)
            return (start..<end).count { isPrime(it) }
        }
        // otherwise, it is cut in two
        val middle = (start + end) ushr 1
        val left = CountPrimes(start, middle)
        val right = CountPrimes(middle, end)
        // the left half is handed to the pool (another thread may "steal" it)
        left.fork()
        // the right half is processed by the current thread
        val nbRight = right.compute()
        // we wait for the result of the left half and combine the two results
        return left.join() + nbRight
    }
}

// primality test (deliberately simple)
fun isPrime(n: Int): Boolean {
    if (n < 2) return false
    var d = 2
    while (d * d <= n) {
        if (n % d == 0) return false
        d++
    }
    return true
}

Comments:

  • lines 29–52: The task [CountPrimes] counts prime numbers in the interval [start, end[. It is derived from [RecursiveTask<Int>]: The Java class is abstract; its parameterless constructor ([RecursiveTask<Int>()]) is called in the class header. The bounds [start] and [end] are private properties declared in the primary constructor;
  • lines 30–34: The class members are grouped in the companion object: the threshold [THRESHOLD] (below 100,000 numbers, an interval is processed directly) and, for each thread, the number of chunks it has processed ([chunks]). Fork/Join tasks are serializable; Java declared a serialization version number ([serialVersionUID]), which was required by its compilation option [-Xlint:all]. The Kotlin compiler does not require it, and we will never serialize these tasks: we omit it;
  • line 37: the redefinition of the method [compute], declared as [protected] in Java: the redefinition remains [protected] without us having to specify it;
  • lines 39–41: a relatively small chunk is processed sequentially by the function [count] within the interval;
  • lines 44–46: a chunk that is too large is split into two subtasks. The expression [(start + end) ushr 1] calculates the middle using an unsigned right shift (the infix function [ushr], which corresponds to the Java operator [>>>]), which prevents an overflow if the sum exceeds the capacity of a [Int];
  • line 48: the left half is placed in the pool: another thread may take it;
  • line 50: the right half is processed by the current thread via a direct call to [compute]. There is no need to assign both halves to the pool: the current thread would have nothing left to do but wait;
  • line 52: the thread waits for the result of the left half (which it will process itself if no one has “stolen” it) and combines the two results;
  • Line 12: The task is first executed by the shared pool. The [invoke(task)] method submits the task and waits for its result;
  • Lines 16–20: Then by a pool of 4 threads, used in a [use] block ([ForkJoinPool] is a [ExecutorService]). The [stealCount] property (Java method [getStealCount]) returns the number of tasks stolen by one thread from another;
  • lines 23–24: the distribution of chunks among the threads in this pool.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=threads28.Threads28Kt
common pool       : 348,513 prime numbers in 3638 ms
pool of 4 threads : 348,513 prime numbers in 2568 ms
tasks stolen by one thread from another: 6
  ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1   : 13 chunks processed
  ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2   : 16 chunks processed
  ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3   : 14 chunks processed
  ForkJoinPool-1-worker-4   : 21 chunks processed
  • the shared pool was no faster than a sequential loop (compare with the previous program): on this machine, it has only one thread, and the main thread—which waits for the result in [invoke]—does not participate in the computation as it does in a parallel flow;
  • the 4-thread pool was faster because it was able to use both processors, but not twice as fast, since the machine was still heavily loaded by other programs. Having more threads than processors offers no benefit for a pure computation, but doesn’t cost much here;
  • the 64 chunks (5,000,000 / 100,000, rounded up to the next power of 2 due to halving) were distributed among the 4 threads via task stealing. This distribution, like the execution times, varies from one run to the next; the number of chunks and the result of the calculation are reproducible.

Parallel streams are sufficient in most cases; a Fork/Join task is written only for a recursive algorithm that cannot be easily expressed as a stream (sorting, tree traversal, etc.).

docs.title: 8.12.1. The Principle
docs.text:
Consider a three-tier application:

Suppose the application is multi-user, such as a web application. Each user request is handled by a thread. The thread’s lifecycle is as follows:

  • the thread is created (virtual thread) or requested from a thread pool to fulfill a user’s request;
  • if this request requires data, the thread executes a function in the [ui] layer, which calls a function in the [business] layer, which in turn calls a function in the [dao] layer;
  • the thread returns the response to the user. It then either terminates or is returned to the thread pool.

During the second step, it may be useful for the thread to have its own data—that is, data not shared with other threads. This data could, for example, belong to the specific user that the thread is serving and be used across the various [ui, business, dao] layers without being passed as a parameter to each function.

JDK provides two tools for this purpose, which Kotlin uses as-is:

  • the [ThreadLocal<T>] class (Java 1.2): an object whose value—read by [get()] and written by [set(value)]—is different for each thread. The constructor [ThreadLocal.withInitial(factory)] provides the initial value for each thread; the method [remove()] clears the value of the current thread. The derived class [InheritableThreadLocal<T>] passes the value of the creating thread to the newly created thread;
  • the [ScopedValue<T>] class (final in Java 25): a value bound to a thread for a limited scope of the code, which cannot be modified within that scope.

docs.title: 8.12.2. The ThreadLocal class
docs.text:
The program [Threads29.kt] compares a regular property, a [ThreadLocal], and a [InheritableThreadLocal]:

// thread-local data: ThreadLocal and InheritableThreadLocal
package threads29

import kotlin.concurrent.thread

// the program's data
object Context {
    // an ordinary (volatile) property: a single copy, shared by all the threads
    @Volatile
    var shared = 0
    // one copy per thread; initial value null
    val perThread = ThreadLocal<Int?>()
    // one copy per thread, initialized for each thread by the supplied factory
    val user: ThreadLocal<String> =
        ThreadLocal.withInitial { "anonymous (thread ${Thread.currentThread().name})" }
    // one copy per thread, whose initial value is inherited from the creating thread
    val language = InheritableThreadLocal<String?>()
}

fun main() {
    Thread.currentThread().name = "Main"
    // the main thread writes its own values
    Context.shared = 100
    Context.perThread.set(100)
    Context.user.set("admin")
    Context.language.set("fr")

    // three threads write then read the data again
    val threads = List(3) { number ->
        thread(name = "T$number") {
            // writing
            Context.shared = number
            Context.perThread.set(number)
            // thread T2 does not set a user: it will have the initial value
            if (number != 2) {
                Context.user.set("user$number")
            }
            // thread T1 changes the language inherited from the main thread
            if (number == 1) {
                Context.language.set("en")
            }
            // the other threads are allowed to write in their turn
            sleep(200)
            // reading again
            display()
        }
    }
    threads.forEach { it.join() }
    // reading again by the main thread
    display()
}

// displays the data seen by the current thread
fun display() {
    println("%-4s : shared=%-3d perThread=%-3d user=%-20s language=%s".format(
        Thread.currentThread().name, Context.shared, Context.perThread.get(),
        Context.user.get(), Context.language.get()))
}

// sleep for [ms] milliseconds
fun sleep(ms: Long) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms)
    } catch (_: InterruptedException) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt()
    }
}

Comments:

  • lines 9–10: a regular property of the [Context] object. There is only one instance of it, shared by all threads. It is [@Volatile], so that each thread sees the latest value written by the others;
  • line 12: a [ThreadLocal<Int?>] object. Each thread has its own value; as long as a thread has not written to it, [get] returns [null]. We declare the type of the [Int?] values so that the compiler knows that [get] can yield [null]: with [ThreadLocal<Int>], Kotlin would treat the result of *[get]* as a platform type (***[Int!]***), on which it performs no checks;
  • Lines 14–15: A [ThreadLocal<String>] object created by [ThreadLocal.withInitial { … }]. The lambda passed to this method (converted to [Supplier]) is executed the first time a thread reads the value without having written it; it provides the initial value for that thread. Here, [get] never returns [null]: the type [String] is justified. Kotlin also provides an extension function, [getOrSet { … }] (package [kotlin.concurrent]), which returns the value of the current thread after initializing it with the lambda if it is [null];
  • line 17: a [InheritableThreadLocal<String?>] object: when a thread is created, its initial value is a copy of the value that the creating thread had at that time;
  • lines 23–26: the main thread writes its own values;
  • lines 32–40: each thread writes its own values, except for the thread T2, which does not set a user, and the thread T1, which is the only one to change the language;
  • line 43: each thread waits for the others to write before reading the values again;
  • lines 54–57: the data displayed as seen by the current thread. The format [%-3d] accepts a value of [null], which it displays as [null].

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=threads29.Threads29Kt
T0   : shared=1   perThread=0   user=user0                language=fr
T2   : shared=1   perThread=2   user=anonymous (thread T2) language=fr
T1   : shared=1   perThread=1   user=user1                language=en
Main : shared=1   perThread=100 user=admin                language=fr
  • the ordinary property [shared] has the same value for all threads: the last value written (in this execution, that of thread T1; another execution may yield a different value);
  • [perThread] retained, in each thread, the value that thread had written to it;
  • [user] has the value written by each thread; the thread T2, which had not written to it, obtained the initial value provided by the lambda of [withInitial];
  • [language] is equal to [fr] for the threads T0 and T2, which inherited it from the main thread without ever writing to it. The thread T1 changed it to [en] only for itself: the main thread and the other threads do not see this change;
  • except for the value of [shared] and the order of the first three lines, these results are reproducible.

A [ThreadLocal] requires some precautions. A thread’s value exists only as long as the thread itself: with a thread pool, the thread that serves one request will then serve other requests, and you must call [remove] at the end of each request; otherwise, the next request would find the data from the previous one (and the memory would never be freed). With virtual threads, you can create millions of threads, each with its own copy of the data: [InheritableThreadLocal] then copies its values into each of them. Finally, a value that can be modified by any function within the thread makes the code difficult to follow. The [ScopedValue] class avoids these issues.

The coroutines in Chapter 9 pose a particular problem: a coroutine can begin execution in one thread and continue in another, and a *[ThreadLocal] would not track it. To address this, the coroutine library provides the extension function [asContextElement(value)] of [ThreadLocal], which sets the value of [ThreadLocal] in every thread where the coroutine executes; coroutines also have their own context data mechanism, the coroutine context*. We’ll cover this in the next chapter.

docs.title: 8.12.3. The ScopedValue class
docs.text:
A [ScopedValue<T>] value is bound to a value for the execution of a piece of code, called its scope:

  • [ScopedValue.newInstance()] creates a bound value, typically stored in a top-level property or an object’s property, which is read-only ([val]);
  • [ScopedValue.where(sv, value).run(action)] executes the action (a [Runnable]) by binding [sv] to [value]. While the action—and all the functions it calls—is executing in the current thread, [sv.get()] returns [value]. When the action finishes, the binding disappears: there is nothing to clean up;
  • [ScopedValue.where(sv, value).call(op)] does the same with an operation that returns a result;
  • within the scope, the value cannot be modified; it can only be bound to another value for a nested scope;
  • [isBound()] indicates whether the value is bound in the current thread (Kotlin treats this as a property [isBound]); [orElse(other)] binds the value, or, if that fails, [other]. Outside any scope, [get()] throws the [NoSuchElementException] exception.

The [ScopedValue] class has been final since Java 25: a Kotlin program compiled for Java 25 uses it without any special options or warnings. The program is as follows:

// values bound to a scope: ScopedValue (Java 25)
package threads30

// the user on whose behalf the code runs
val USER: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance()

fun main() {
    println("Outside any scope, is USER bound? ${USER.isBound}")
    try {
        USER.get()
    } catch (e: NoSuchElementException) {
        println("get() out of scope: ${e::class.simpleName}")
    }

    // 1 - two simultaneous processings, each for its own user
    val t1 = Thread.ofVirtual().start { ScopedValue.where(USER, "alice").run(::process) }
    val t2 = Thread.ofVirtual().start { ScopedValue.where(USER, "bob").run(::process) }
    t1.join()
    t2.join()

    // 2 - a scope can contain another one, which temporarily binds another value
    ScopedValue.where(USER, "admin").run {
        display("outer scope")
        ScopedValue.where(USER, "guest").run { display("inner scope") }
        display("back in the outer scope")
        // a thread created in the scope does not inherit the binding
        val child = Thread.ofVirtual().start { println("child thread: bound? ${USER.isBound}") }
        child.join()
    }

    // 3 - call: a bound processing that returns a result
    val message = ScopedValue.where(USER, "carole")
        .call<String, RuntimeException> { "hello ${USER.get()}" }
    println(message)
    // after the scope, the binding has disappeared
    println("After the scopes: bound? ${USER.isBound}, orElse: ${USER.orElse("nobody")}")
}

// the [business] layer calls the [dao] layer without passing it the user
fun process() {
    display("[business] layer")
    dao()
}

// the [dao] layer finds the user in the current scope
fun dao() {
    display("[dao] layer")
}

// displays the user bound in the current scope
fun display(place: String) {
    println("$place : USER = ${USER.get()}")
}

Comments:

  • line 5: the bound value [USER], a read-only top-level property. Its type, [ScopedValue<String>], is declared: the generic method [newInstance] cannot infer it;
  • Lines 8–12: Outside of any scope, the value is unbound, and [get] throws an exception. The class [NoSuchElementException] does not need to be imported: Kotlin treats it as a type alias for the standard library ([kotlin.NoSuchElementException]);
  • Lines 16–17: Two virtual threads execute the function [process], each in a scope where [USER] is bound to a different user. The function reference [::process] is converted to [Runnable];
  • lines 40–47: the function [process] (the [business] layer) calls the function [dao] (the [dao] layer) without passing the user to it: each retrieves it via [USER.get()] (line 52);
  • lines 22–28: a scope where [USER] equals [admin] contains a nested scope (line 24) where it equals [guest]. Upon exiting the nested scope, we find [admin]. A note on the notation [where(…).run { … }]: the Kotlin standard library also has a function [run], applicable to any object ([obj.run { … }]). Here, it is indeed the method [run] of the class [ScopedValue.Carrier] that is called, because in Kotlin a member method always takes precedence over an extension function with the same name. The results confirm this: if the Kotlin function [run] had been called, no value would have been bound, and [get] would have thrown an exception;
  • Lines 27–28: A thread created within the scope does not see the binding: unlike a *[InheritableThreadLocal]*, a [ScopedValue] is not passed to threads created by *[Thread]. It is, however, passed to the sub-tasks of structured concurrency ([StructuredTaskScope]*, previewed in Java 25), which ensures that these sub-tasks complete before the scope ends;
  • lines 32–33: [call] performs an operation within a scope and returns its result. Its parameter is of type [ScopedValue.CallableOp<T, X>], where [X] is the type of exceptions (controlled, in Java) that the operation can throw. Kotlin cannot infer [X] from the lambda (it does not declare any exceptions); without the type arguments, the compiler reports:
error: cannot infer type for type parameter 'X'. Specify it explicitly.

We therefore specify [call<String, RuntimeException>]: the result is a [String], and the operation does not throw a checked exception;

  • line 36: after the scopes, the value is no longer bound.

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=threads30.Threads30Kt
Outside any scope, is USER bound? false
get() out of scope: NoSuchElementException
[business] layer : USER = bob
[dao] layer : USER = bob
[business] layer : USER = alice
[dao] layer : USER = alice
outer scope : USER = admin
inner scope : USER = guest
back in the outer scope : USER = admin
child thread: bound? false
hello carole
After the scopes: bound? false, orElse: nobody

The messages from the virtual threads in lines 3–6 may appear in a different order (bob before alice); the rest is reproducible. A [ScopedValue] is suitable for context data passed “downward,” from the caller to the called functions: authenticated user, transaction, regional settings, etc. When a called function needs to modify the data for subsequent processing, a [ThreadLocal] is required.

docs.title: 8.12.4. Application: a transaction shared across layers
docs.text:
Consider the following three-layer application, in which the [dao] layer manages a table of items:

Suppose that the interface of layer [dao] is initially as follows:

interface IDao {
    fun insertArticle(article: Article): Int
    fun getAllArticles(): List<Article>
    fun deleteAllArticles()
}

Later, the need arises to insert a list of items within a transaction, because the requirement is all-or-nothing: either all items are inserted, or none are. A function [insertArticles(articles: List<Article>)] can be added to the interface. Then, for another application, the need arises to delete a list of items, again within a transaction… To meet different business requirements, the [dao] layer will grow. We can take a different approach:

  • include only the basic operations (insert, update, delete, read an item) in the [dao] layer;
  • move operations that simultaneously update multiple items to the [business] layer. These operations use the basic operations from the [dao] layer.

The advantage of this solution is that the same [dao] layer can be used without modification with different [business] layers. It introduces a challenge in managing the transaction that groups the updates to be performed atomically:

  • the transaction must be initiated by the [business] layer before it calls the functions of the [dao] layer;
  • the functions in the [dao] layer must be aware of the transaction’s existence in order to participate in it;
  • the transaction must be completed (committed or rolled back) by the [business] layer.

To ensure that the functions in the [dao] layer are aware of any ongoing transaction, the transaction could be added as a parameter to each function in the [dao] layer. This parameter would then appear in the signature of the interface functions, thereby binding the interface to a specific data source. Thread-local data provides a more elegant solution: the [business] layer places the transaction in the thread-local data, and that is where the [dao] layer retrieves it. The function signatures of the [dao] layer do not need to be changed. Multiple threads (multiple users) can work simultaneously: each has its own transaction.

Databases will be covered in Chapters 10 and 11. To keep the focus on threads, we are using an in-memory table and a simulated transaction here. The program [Threads31.kt] combines all the layers into a single source file. The entities are as follows:

// an article
data class Article(
    val id: Int, val name: String, val price: Double, val currentStock: Int, val minimumStock: Int
)

// a simulated transaction: it notes how to undo each update
class Transaction {
    companion object {
        private val counter = AtomicInteger()
    }

    private val undos = ArrayDeque<() -> Unit>()
    val number = counter.incrementAndGet()

    // records the operation that undoes an update
    fun log(undo: () -> Unit) {
        undos.addFirst(undo)
    }

    // commits the transaction: the updates are kept
    fun commit() {
        undos.clear()
    }

    // rolls back the transaction: the updates are undone, from the last to the first
    fun rollback() {
        while (true) {
            val undo = undos.removeFirstOrNull() ?: break
            undo()
        }
    }
}

// the thread-local data shared by the layers
object ThreadContext {
    // the current transaction of the thread (null if there is none)
    val transaction = ThreadLocal<Transaction?>()
}
  • lines 2–3: an article is a data class whose identifier [id] is set by the [dao] layer;
  • lines 7–29: a simulated transaction. Each update made within the transaction records the operation needed to undo it (function [log]); [commit] commits the transaction while ignoring these operations; [rollback] rolls it back by executing the rollback operations, from the last to the first. A rollback operation is a function of type [() -> Unit]: in Kotlin, a functional type replaces the Java interface [Runnable]. The operations are stored in a stack, in this case a *[ArrayDeque] from the Kotlin standard library (*[kotlin.collections.ArrayDeque], imported automatically): the [addFirst] function pushes to the top, the [removeFirstOrNull] function pops from the top, and returns [null] if the stack is empty. In the [rollback] loop, the Elvis operator [?: break] exits the loop when the stack is empty; otherwise, the popped operation is executed by [undo()]. A real database operates in a similar way, using a transaction log;
  • lines 8–13: Each transaction is assigned a unique number, the read-only property [number], calculated when the object is created. Since transactions can be created by multiple threads simultaneously, the counter—stored in the companion object—is a [AtomicInteger], which is incremented atomically;
  • lines 35–37: the thread-local data shared across layers: the thread’s current transaction, or [null] if there is none, hence the type [ThreadLocal<Transaction?>].

The [dao] layer is as follows:

// the [dao] layer: an in-memory table of articles with a uniqueness constraint on the name
interface IDao {
    fun insertArticle(article: Article): Int
    fun getAllArticles(): List<Article>
    fun deleteAllArticles()
}

class Dao : IDao {
    // the table, shared by all the threads, and its lock
    private val table = mutableListOf<Article>()
    private val lock = Any()
    private var nextId = 1

    override fun insertArticle(article: Article): Int {
        // is there a transaction in progress in the current thread?
        val transaction = ThreadContext.transaction.get()
        synchronized(lock) {
            check(table.none { it.name == article.name }) { "an article named [${article.name}] already exists" }
            val inserted = article.copy(id = nextId++)
            table += inserted
            // in a transaction, we note how to undo the insertion
            transaction?.log {
                synchronized(lock) { table -= inserted }
            }
            val mode = if (transaction == null) "outside a transaction"
                       else "in transaction ${transaction.number}"
            val name = Thread.currentThread().name
            println("[$name] [dao] insertion of ${inserted.name} (id ${inserted.id}) $mode")
            return 1
        }
    }

    override fun getAllArticles(): List<Article> = synchronized(lock) { table.toList() }

    override fun deleteAllArticles() {
        synchronized(lock) { table.clear() }
    }
}
  • Lines 10–11: the item table, shared by all threads. Access to it is protected by the lock on line 11;
  • line 16: the function [insertArticle] retrieves any transaction that the [business] layer has placed in the current thread’s local data. Its variable [transaction] is of type [Transaction?];
  • line 18: The table has a uniqueness constraint on item names: inserting an item with a name that already exists throws an exception. The Kotlin function [check] (Chapter 3) throws a [IllegalStateException], with the message calculated by the lambda, if the condition is false; the function [none] verifies that no element in the table satisfies the predicate;
  • lines 19–20: The inserted record is a copy of the received record, with an identifier assigned by the [dao] layer. Since a read-only data class cannot be modified, a new object is created using the [copy] function, which changes only the named property;
  • lines 22–23: If there is a transaction, the [dao] layer participates by recording how to undo the insertion. The safe call to [?.] calls [log] only if [transaction] is not equal to [null]. The rollback lambda, passed as the final lambda, captures the variable [inserted];
  • lines 25–28: a trace output shows the thread, the inserted record, and any transaction. In the branch [else], the compiler knows that [transaction] is not [null] (smart type conversion);
  • line 33: The returned list of items is a copy of the table ([table.toList()]), so that the caller does not iterate through it while another thread is modifying it. The function [synchronized] returns the value of its block.

The [business] layer is as follows:

// the [business] layer
interface IBusiness {
    fun insertArticlesInTransaction(articles: List<Article>)
    fun insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(articles: List<Article>)
    fun getAllArticles(): List<Article>
    fun deleteAllArticles()
}

class Business(private val dao: IDao) : IBusiness {
    // insertion of a list of articles: all or nothing
    override fun insertArticlesInTransaction(articles: List<Article>) {
        val name = Thread.currentThread().name
        // start of the transaction, stored in the thread-local data
        val transaction = Transaction()
        ThreadContext.transaction.set(transaction)
        try {
            for (article in articles) {
                // the [dao] layer will find the transaction in the thread
                dao.insertArticle(article)
                // simulated processing, which gives other threads time to intervene
                sleep(200)
            }
            transaction.commit()
            println("[$name] [business] transaction ${transaction.number} committed")
        } catch (e: RuntimeException) {
            transaction.rollback()
            println("[$name] [business] transaction ${transaction.number} rolled back")
            // the exception is rethrown to the caller
            throw e
        } finally {
            // the thread no longer has a transaction in progress
            ThreadContext.transaction.remove()
        }
    }

    // insertion of a list of articles without a transaction
    override fun insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(articles: List<Article>) {
        articles.forEach(dao::insertArticle)
    }

    override fun getAllArticles(): List<Article> = dao.getAllArticles()

    override fun deleteAllArticles() = dao.deleteAllArticles()
}
  • line 9: the [dao] layer is injected by the primary constructor, which makes it a private property;
  • lines 14–15: the function [insertArticlesInTransaction] starts a transaction and saves it in the thread’s local data;
  • line 19: the insertion function of the [dao] layer is called for each item, without passing the transaction to it;
  • line 21: a pause simulates processing, in order to give another thread time to intervene during the transaction (third part of the test program);
  • line 23: if the program reaches this point, no exception has occurred: the transaction is committed;
  • lines 25–29: if an exception occurs, the transaction is rolled back and the exception is rethrown to the caller;
  • line 32: In all cases, the thread no longer has an active transaction: [remove()] clears the thread’s value. This is essential if the thread is reused (a pooled thread);
  • lines 37–38: the same insertion, without a transaction. The linked reference [dao::insertArticle] points to the function [insertArticle] of the object [dao];
  • The last two functions delegate their work to the [dao] layer, with a body reduced to a single expression.

The test program is as follows:

fun main() {
    // the layers of the application
    val dao: IDao = Dao()
    val business: IBusiness = Business(dao)
    Thread.currentThread().name = "Main"

    // two articles with the same name: the second violates the uniqueness constraint on the name
    val articles = listOf(Article(0, "article", 100.0, 10, 1), Article(0, "article", 100.0, 10, 1))

    // 1 - insertion outside a transaction
    println("Inserting the articles outside a transaction...")
    execute { business.insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(articles) }
    displayArticles(business)

    // 2 - insertion in a transaction
    business.deleteAllArticles()
    println("Inserting the articles in a transaction...")
    execute { business.insertArticlesInTransaction(articles) }
    displayArticles(business)

    // 3 - two simultaneous threads: the transaction of thread A is not seen by thread B
    business.deleteAllArticles()
    println("Two simultaneous threads...")
    val articlesA = listOf(Article(0, "keyboard", 20.0, 5, 1), Article(0, "mouse", 10.0, 5, 1),
        Article(0, "keyboard", 20.0, 5, 1))
    val articlesB = listOf(Article(0, "screen", 150.0, 2, 1))
    val threadA = thread(name = "A") { execute { business.insertArticlesInTransaction(articlesA) } }
    Thread.sleep(100)
    val threadB = thread(name = "B") { execute { business.insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(articlesB) } }
    threadA.join()
    threadB.join()
    displayArticles(business)
}

// executes an action, displaying the exception if any
fun execute(action: () -> Unit) {
    try {
        action()
    } catch (e: RuntimeException) {
        println("[${Thread.currentThread().name}] ${e::class.simpleName} : ${e.message}")
    }
}

// sleep for [ms] milliseconds
fun sleep(ms: Long) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms)
    } catch (_: InterruptedException) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt()
    }
}

// displays the list of articles
fun displayArticles(business: IBusiness) {
    println("List of articles:")
    for (article in business.getAllArticles()) {
        println("  $article")
    }
}
  • Line 8: A list of two items with the same name is created. The insertion of the second item will be rejected. If the insertion is performed outside a transaction, the first item is inserted and remains in the list. If it is performed within a transaction, the first item is inserted and then removed when the transaction is rolled back;
  • Lines 11–13: Insert the list outside a transaction, then display the table;
  • lines 16–19: same as above, but within a transaction;
  • lines 22–31: Two threads are running simultaneously. Thread A inserts three items within a transaction (the third violates the uniqueness constraint); meanwhile, Thread B, launched one-tenth of a second later, inserts an item outside a transaction;
  • lines 36–40: the function [execute] performs an action of type [() -> Unit] and displays any exception, preceded by the thread name. It is called with a trailing lambda: [executer { … }].

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=threads31.Threads31Kt
Inserting the articles outside a transaction...
[Main] [dao] insertion of article (id 1) outside a transaction
[Main] IllegalStateException : an article named [article] already exists
List of articles:
  Article(id=1, name=article, price=100.0, currentStock=10, minimumStock=1)
Inserting the articles in a transaction...
[Main] [dao] insertion of article (id 2) in transaction 1
[Main] [business] transaction 1 rolled back
[Main] IllegalStateException : an article named [article] already exists
List of articles:
Two simultaneous threads...
[A] [dao] insertion of keyboard (id 3) in transaction 2
[B] [dao] insertion of screen (id 4) outside a transaction
[A] [dao] insertion of mouse (id 5) in transaction 2
[A] [business] transaction 2 rolled back
[A] IllegalStateException : an article named [keyboard] already exists
List of articles:
  Article(id=4, name=screen, price=150.0, currentStock=2, minimumStock=1)
  • The insert outside a transaction left the first record in the table (row 5). The function [toString] generated for a data class displays the name and value of each of its properties;
  • The insertion performed within a transaction left no items in the table: the item with ID 2 was removed by the rollback;
  • In the third part, thread B inserted the screen while thread A’s transaction 2 was in progress: it did so outside a transaction, since the transaction is a local variable of thread A. The rollback of transaction 2 removed the keyboard and mouse inserted by A, but not the screen inserted by B. This result is reproducible.

docs.title: 8.12.5. Conclusion
docs.text: The previous example demonstrated the value of thread-local data for transaction management. It should not be replicated exactly as shown, but it accurately describes how frameworks work: Spring’s transaction management ([@Transactional] annotation) places the transaction and the database connection into [ThreadLocal], which the data access layers consult without their code having to manipulate the transaction; Hibernate can similarly associate the working session with the current thread. We’ll revisit these tools in Chapter 11. In new code, particularly with virtual threads, a *[ScopedValue]* is the recommended way to pass this type of context information; with coroutines, this role falls to the coroutine context (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 8.13. Further Reading
docs.text:
Thread synchronization is a challenging field. This chapter has introduced the main tools; to learn more:

  • the book by Brian Goetz et al., [Java Concurrency in Practice] (Addison-Wesley), which remains the definitive reference on the subject, even though it predates virtual threads. Its examples are in Java, but everything it says applies to Kotlin on the JVM;
  • the “Concurrency” section of Oracle’s Java tutorial: Lesson: Concurrency—it’s old but still accurate for the basics;
  • the documentation for the [java.util.concurrent] package: Package java.util.concurrent, whose “Memory Consistency Properties” section summarizes the “earlier-than” relationships;
  • the documentation for the [kotlin.concurrent] package in the Kotlin standard library ([thread], [withLock], [read], [write], [getOrSet]…): kotlin.concurrent;
  • the Java improvement proposals (JEP) that introduced virtual threads and scoped values: JEP 444: Virtual Threads and JEP 506: Scoped Values.

In modern code, objects ([Thread]) are rarely manipulated directly. In Java, we prefer to use executors ([ExecutorService]), parallel streams for computations, and virtual threads for tasks that involve waiting. Kotlin has all these tools, but it offers its own solution, which is presented in the next chapter: coroutines. A coroutine is a task that can suspend itself (during network access, database access, or file access) without blocking the thread executing it, and then resume, possibly in a different thread; structured concurrency ensures that no coroutine is forgotten and that errors and cancellations propagate correctly. The concepts in this chapter are nonetheless essential: coroutines run in threads, and the data they share must be protected using the same tools (locks, atomic classes, concurrent collections), or their equivalents for coroutines ([Mutex], [Channel]…).

docs.title: 7. Functional Types, Lambdas, and Events
docs.text:
In many programs, we need to pass not data but behavior to a function: the sorting criterion, the filtering condition, or the action to be performed when something happens. Kotlin addresses this need by treating functions as values just like any other: a function has a type—the functional type, denoted, for example, as [(Int, Int) -> Int]; it can be stored in a variable, passed as a parameter, returned as the result of another function, and executed whenever desired. A function that takes or returns a function is called a higher-order function.

Java, as a reminder, does not have functional types: it relies on functional interfaces—interfaces with a single abstract method ([Runnable], [Comparator], [Function<T, R>]…), and it wasn’t until Java 8 (2014) that it allowed them to be implemented using lambda expressions and method references. Kotlin has supported lambdas since its very first version, and it can also work with Java’s functional interfaces, since it directly uses Java libraries. We’ve already used lambdas extensively without going into detail, in the collection operations covered in Chapter 5: in [persons.filter { it.age >= 18 }], we pass a lambda to the function [filter]. This chapter explains what lies behind this syntax. It concludes with events, which Kotlin—like Java—handles using “listeners”: functions, most often lambdas, that register with an emitter to be notified of what is happening there. Graphical user interfaces (Swing, JavaFX, Compose) and web frameworks alike rely on this mechanism: a button click or the arrival of a HTTP request is signaled to registered listeners. This course does not cover graphical user interfaces; all examples are console programs.

The programs in this chapter are organized in the Gradle project [07-lambdas], with one package per program: [src/main/kotlin/lambdas01/Lambdas01.kt], [src/main/kotlin/lambdas02/Lambdas02.kt]… They are run using [gradlew -q run -Pmain=lambdas01.Lambdas01Kt] or by clicking the green triangle in IntelliJ or IDEA. The project requires no libraries other than the standard Kotlin library: functional types, lambdas, and scope functions are included, and the interfaces in the [java.util.function] package are the same as those in JDK.

docs.title: 7.1. Functional types and predefined functional interfaces
7.1.1. The Concept of a Functional Type
docs.text:
A functional type describes a model (also called a signature or a form) of a function: the types of its parameters, enclosed in parentheses, followed by an arrow, and then the type of its return value. A variable of a functional type can refer to any function of this form and execute it. Here are a few examples:

  • [() -> Unit]: a function with no parameters that returns no useful result ([Unit] plays the role of Java’s [void]);
  • [() -> String]: a function with no parameters that returns a string;
  • [(Int) -> Boolean]: a function that takes an integer and returns a boolean, in other words, a predicate;
  • [(Int, Int) -> Int]: a function that takes two integers and returns an integer;
  • [(String) -> (Int) -> Int]: a function that takes a string and returns… a function of type [(Int) -> Int] (the arrow is read from right to left);
  • [(() -> Unit)?]: a function that may be absent; the parentheses are necessary because [() -> Unit?] would otherwise denote a function returning a [Unit?]. Here we see the safety property with respect to [null] from Chapter 3: such a function is denoted by [f?.invoke()];
  • [String.(Int) -> String]: a function with a receiver; it is applied to a string—which its code denotes as [this]—as an extension function (Chapter 4). It can be called as an extension (["ab".f(3)]) or as an ordinary function whose receiver is the first parameter ([f("ab", 3)]).

Parameters can be named to document the type: [(n1: Int, n2: Int) -> Int] is the same type as [(Int, Int) -> Int].

There are three ways to obtain a value of a function type:

  • write a reference to an existing function that has the correct form: [val task: () -> Unit = ::display];
  • Write a lambda expression: [val task: () -> Unit = { println("task") }];
  • write an anonymous function: [val task = fun() { println("task") }], or an object of a class that implements the functional type (a functional type is an interface, as we’ll see). These two notations are less common.

The function is then executed like an ordinary function: [task()]. This is a shorthand notation for calling the method [invoke] of the function object: [task.invoke()]. This is the first noticeable difference from Java, where you must call the interface’s method by name ([run], [apply], [test]…); Kotlin behaves here like C#, where a delegate is called like a method.

docs.title: 7.1.2. Kotlin Functional Types and java.util.function Interfaces
docs.text:
Before Java 8, each Java library defined its own single-method interfaces ([Runnable], [Comparator], [ActionListener]…). Java 8 introduced the [java.util.function] package, which provides 43 generic functional interfaces. Kotlin does not need them: a functional type is written directly. However, these interfaces can still be used from Kotlin, and you’ll encounter them whenever you call a Java library. The following table maps the main Java interfaces to Kotlin’s functional types:

Java InterfaceKotlin TypeFunctions Represented[Runnable]: [void run()][() -> Unit]No parameters, no results[Supplier<T>] : [T get()][() -> T]No parameters, one result: one “supplier”[Consumer<T>]: [void accept(T t)][(T) -> Unit]one parameter, no result: a “consumer”[BiConsumer<T, U>][(T, U) -> Unit]two parameters, no results[Function<T, R>]: [R apply(T t)][(T) -> R]one parameter, one result[BiFunction<T, U, R>][(T, U) -> R]two parameters, one result[UnaryOperator<T>][(T) -> T]Parameter and result of the same type[BinaryOperator<T>][(T, T) -> T]Two parameters and one result of the same type[Predicate<T>]: [boolean test(T t)][(T) -> Boolean]one parameter, a Boolean result: a “predicate”[BiPredicate<T, U>][(T, U) -> Boolean]two parameters, a Boolean result[Comparator<T>]: [int compare(T o1, T o2)][(T, T) -> Int]two parameters of the same type, an integer result[Callable<V>] : [V call()][() -> V]such as [Supplier<V>]; in Kotlin, no checked exception needs to be declared[IntBinaryOperator], [IntPredicate]…[(Int, Int) -> Int], [(Int) -> Boolean]…The Java versions for primitive types

In Kotlin, there is no practical limit to the number of parameters a function type can have: [(Int, Int, Int) -> Int] is written just as simply as the others, whereas in Java, since there is no predefined interface with three parameters, you have to define your own.

How does the Java Virtual Machine, which only recognizes classes and interfaces, represent a functional type? Through generic interfaces from the Kotlin library: [kotlin.jvm.functions.Function0<R>], [Function1<P1, R>], [Function2<P1, P2, R>]… all the way up to [Function22], followed by an interface [FunctionN] beyond that. Each has a single method, [invoke]: [(Int, Int) -> Int] is compiled into [Function2<Integer, Integer, Integer>], whose method is [operator fun invoke(p1: Int, p2: Int): Int]. It is the modifier [operator] of [invoke] (see operator overloading in Chapter 4) that allows the notation [f(2, 3)]. A functional type is therefore, for JVM, a functional interface like those in Java. Since Java generics apply only to object types, [Int] values passed to a [(Int, Int) -> Int] are converted to [Integer] and vice versa (boxing and unboxing). Java avoids these conversions with its specialized interfaces ([IntBinaryOperator]…); Kotlin avoids them in a different way, using the [inline] functions, which we’ll discuss later.

The program [Lambdas01.kt] uses these types with function references:

package lambdas01

import java.util.function.IntBinaryOperator
import java.util.function.Predicate
import java.util.function.Supplier

// Kotlin function types and Java functional interfaces

fun main() {
    // 1 - () -> Unit: no parameter, no result
    val task: () -> Unit = ::display
    // execution: the function is called like an ordinary function
    task()
    // which is shorthand for calling its invoke method
    task.invoke()

    // 2 - (Int, Int) -> Int: two parameters, one result
    val operation: (Int, Int) -> Int = ::add
    println("operation(2, 3)=${operation(2, 3)}")
    // () -> String: no parameter, one result
    val greet: () -> String = ::greet
    println("greet()=${greet()}")

    // 3 - (String) -> Unit: one parameter, no result
    val write: (String) -> Unit = ::println
    write("(String) -> Unit executed println")

    // 4 - (Int) -> Boolean: a predicate
    val isEven: (Int) -> Boolean = ::isEven
    println("isEven(8)=${isEven(8)}")
    val numbers = mutableListOf(3, 8, 1, 6, 5, 4)
    // removeAll from the Kotlin library expects an (Int) -> Boolean
    val modified = numbers.removeAll(isEven)
    println("even numbers removed: $modified, remaining: $numbers")

    // 5 - a Comparator<T> (Java interface) built from a function (SAM conversion)
    val names = mutableListOf("Paul", "Mélanie", "Jo", "Sébastien")
    names.sortWith(Comparator(::compareLengths))
    println("sorted by length: $names")

    // 6 - the java.util.function interfaces remain usable
    val supplier: Supplier<String> = Supplier(::greet)
    val multiply = IntBinaryOperator(::multiply)
    val predicate = Predicate<Int> { it > 4 }
    println("supplier.get()=${supplier.get()}")
    println("multiply.applyAsInt(2, 3)=${multiply.applyAsInt(2, 3)}")
    // removeIf is a Java method (Collection): it expects a Predicate
    val values = mutableListOf(10, 3, 8, 7, 2, 1)
    values.removeIf(predicate)
    // a Kotlin function is automatically converted to a Predicate (SAM conversion)
    values.removeIf(isEven)
    values.removeIf { it == 1 }
    println("after removeIf: $values")

    // 7 - a nullable function type: the function may be absent
    execute(null)
    execute(task)

    // 8 - a function type with receiver: String.(Int) -> String
    val times: String.(Int) -> String = String::repeat
    println("\"ab\".times(3)=${"ab".times(3)}, times(\"cd\", 2)=${times("cd", 2)}")

    // 9 - a function is an object, an instance of a class that implements an interface
    println("class: ${operation::class.java.name}")
    println("interfaces: ${operation::class.java.interfaces.contentToString()}")
    val sum: (Int, Int) -> Int = { n1, n2 -> n1 + n2 }
    println("class of the lambda: ${sum::class.java.name}")
    println("interfaces: ${sum::class.java.interfaces.contentToString()}")
}

// a function that receives a possibly absent function
fun execute(callback: (() -> Unit)?) {
    // safe call: nothing is executed if callback is null
    callback?.invoke()
    println("callback ${if (callback == null) "absent" else "present"}")
}

// the referenced functions: top-level functions of the file
fun display() {
    println("display() executed by task()")
}

fun add(n1: Int, n2: Int): Int = n1 + n2

fun multiply(n1: Int, n2: Int): Int = n1 * n2

fun greet(): String = "Hello"

fun isEven(n: Int): Boolean = n % 2 == 0

fun compareLengths(s1: String, s2: String): Int = s1.length.compareTo(s2.length)

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=lambdas01.Lambdas01Kt
display() executed by task()
display() executed by task()
operation(2, 3)=5
greet()=Hello
(String) -> Unit executed println
isEven(8)=true
even numbers removed: true, remaining: [3, 1, 5]
sorted by length: [Jo, Paul, Mélanie, Sébastien]
supplier.get()=Hello
multiply.applyAsInt(2, 3)=6
after removeIf: [3]
callback absent
display() executed by task()
callback present
"ab".times(3)=ababab, times("cd", 2)=cdcd
class: lambdas01.Lambdas01Kt$main$operation$1
interfaces: [interface kotlin.jvm.functions.Function2]
class of the lambda: lambdas01.Lambdas01Kt$$Lambda/0x000000001f04a7f0
interfaces: [interface kotlin.jvm.functions.Function2]

Comments:

  • line 11: the variable [task] is of type [() -> Unit]. It is assigned a function reference: [::display] refers to the top-level function [display] declared later in the file (line 79). The compiler verifies that it has the required form (no parameters, no return value) and creates the function object that calls it. In Java, an auxiliary class would have been needed to contain these methods, since the implicit class of a compact source file cannot be named; in Kotlin, top-level functions are referenced directly;
  • line 13: the function is executed by calling it as an ordinary function. The function [display] is executed (line 1 of the results). Line 15: the same result is obtained by explicitly calling the method [invoke] (line 2 of the results);
  • Line 18: [(Int, Int) -> Int] refers to a function with two parameters, [Int], and returning an [Int]. The function [add] (line 83) is appropriate. The function is called via [operation(2, 3)] (line 19);
  • line 21: a parameterless function returning a string, the equivalent of Java’s [Supplier<String>]. Note that the local variable [greet] has the same name as the function [greet]: in [::greet], this refers to the function, and in [greet()], it refers to the local variable, which masks the function;
  • Line 25: a function with one parameter, [String], that returns nothing—the equivalent of Java’s [Consumer<String>]. The standard library function [println] is overloaded ([println(Int)], [println(Any?)]…): it is the expected type, [(String) -> Unit], that allows the compiler to choose the correct overload;
  • Line 29: a predicate, equivalent to [Predicate<Integer>]. Line 33: the Kotlin library’s extension function [removeAll] specifically expects a parameter of type [(T) -> Boolean]: it removes from the mutable list all elements for which the predicate evaluates to [true], and returns [true] if it has removed at least one element (line 7 of the results);
  • Line 38: The function [sortWith] expects a [Comparator<T>]. In Kotlin, [Comparator] is an alias for the Java interface [java.util.Comparator]. [Comparator(::compareLengths)] creates a [Comparator<String>] from the function [compareLengths]: this is a SAM conversion (“Single Abstract Method”), which creates the object implementing the Java interface from a Kotlin function of the same form. The function [compareLengths] (line 91) uses [compareTo], which compares two [Int] objects without the risk of capacity overflow (which a simple subtraction does not guarantee);
  • lines 42–44: the interfaces of *[java.util.function] can be used as-is. They are constructed in the same way, via an explicit SAM conversion: the interface name followed by a function reference or a lambda. They are then executed via their Java method ([get], [applyAsInt]*, [test]…), just as in Java;
  • lines 49–52: [removeIf] is a Java method of the [Collection] interface; it expects a [Predicate]. You can pass it a *[Predicate] (line 49), but also directly a value of type *[(Int) -> Boolean] (line 51) or a lambda (line 52): When calling a Java method that expects a functional interface, Kotlin automatically performs the SAM conversion. This is what makes Java libraries just as pleasant to use from Kotlin as they are from Java. The initial list (10, 3, 8, 7, 2, 1) successively removes elements greater than 4, even elements, and then the element 1 (line 11 of the results);
  • lines 56–57 and 72–75: the function *[execute] is passed a function that may be absent, of type *[(() -> Unit)?]. The safe call [callback?.invoke()] does nothing if [callback] is equal to [null]. You cannot write [callback?()]: the safe call to a nullable function goes through [invoke]. This will be the standard notation for optional listeners;
  • Line 60: a functional type with a receiver. The reference [String::repeat] refers to the method [repeat] of the class [String], which applies to a string and takes an integer. Line 61 is referred to in two ways: as an extension, ["ab".times(3)], or as a function with two parameters, [times("cd", 2)]. We’ll see functions with receivers again in the scope functions [apply] and [with];
  • lines 64–68: a function is an object. The class of the function reference [operation] (line 16 of the output) is a class generated by the Kotlin compiler, named after the location where the reference appears; the class of the lambda [sum] (line 18 of the results) is generated at runtime by the virtual machine, just like Java lambdas: its name contains [$$Lambda] followed by an address that changes from one execution to the next. In both cases, the class implements the [kotlin.jvm.functions.Function2] interface (lines 17 and 19 of the results). A Kotlin function is therefore not a new type of object: it is an instance of an ordinary class that implements a functional interface.

docs.title: 7.2. Defining Your Own Functional Types
docs.text:
Functional types are often sufficient, but you may want to give a name to a function model. Kotlin offers two tools for this purpose, which are very different in nature.

The first is a type alias, declared using the keyword [typealias]:

  • [typealias BinaryOperation = (n1: Int, n2: Int) -> Int]

An alias does not create a new type: [BinaryOperation] is another name for [(Int, Int) -> Int], and the two notations are interchangeable. The alias makes the code more readable when the functional type is long or appears frequently.

The second is the functional interface, declared by [fun interface]:

  • [fun interface Operation { fun calculate(n1: Int, n2: Int): Int }]

This is the exact equivalent of a functional Java interface: an interface with only one abstract method (also known as a SAM, or “Single Abstract Method” interface). It may also have methods with bodies and non-abstract properties; these do not count. The keyword [fun] preceding [interface] serves the same purpose as the Java annotation [@FunctionalInterface], with one important difference: it is not optional. It is this keyword that enables the SAM conversion—that is, the creation of an [Operation] object from a lambda or a function reference: [Operation { n1, n2 -> n1 + n2 }]. Without the keyword [fun], a Kotlin interface—even one reduced to a single method—can only be implemented by a class or an anonymous object ([object : Operation { … }]).

Compared to the type [(Int, Int) -> Int], the type [Operation] is a truly new type, distinct from all others: it has a name that describes its purpose, its method has a descriptive name ([calculate] rather than [invoke]), it can have additional methods, and it can be implemented by a named class. Conversely, it is executed by its method name ([op.calculate(2, 3)]), not by [op(2, 3)].

A variable named [op] of type [Operation], like a variable of type [(Int, Int) -> Int], references only one function at a time. Unlike C#, which offers “multicast delegates,” neither Java nor Kotlin provides a way to store multiple functions in a single variable and execute them all with a single call: when needed, we store the functions in a list and execute them one by one. This is exactly what we’ll do with event listeners.

Consider the example [Lambdas02.kt]:

package lambdas02

import java.util.function.IntBinaryOperator

// defining your own function types: fun interface and typealias

fun main() {
    // a variable of type Operation receives the increase function of the companion object
    var op = Operation(Calculations::increase)
    // the operation is executed
    var n = op.calculate(4, 7)
    println("n=$n")

    // creation of an object c1 of type Calculations
    val c1 = Calculations()
    // op is given the add method of the object c1
    op = Operation(c1::add)
    n = op.calculate(2, 3)
    println("n=$n")
    // then the subtract method of c1
    op = Operation(c1::subtract)
    n = op.calculate(2, 3)
    println("n=$n")

    // a variable references only one function: to execute several, a list is used
    val operations = listOf(
        Operation(c1::add),
        Operation(c1::subtract),
        Operation { n1, n2 -> n1 * n2 },
    )
    for (operation in operations) {
        println("-> ${operation.calculate(10, 4)}")
    }

    // a method of the interface builds a new operation
    val squaredSum = Operation(c1::add).then { x -> x * x }
    println("squaredSum.calculate(1, 2)=${squaredSum.calculate(1, 2)}")

    // Operation and IntBinaryOperator have the same shape but are two different types
    val other = IntBinaryOperator(op::calculate)
    println("other.applyAsInt(5, 1)=${other.applyAsInt(5, 1)}")

    // a generic functional interface
    val length = Transformation(String::length)
    val stars = Transformation("*"::repeat)
    println("length(\"Hello\")=${length.transform("Hello")}")
    println("stars(5)=${stars.transform(5)}")

    // a type alias: simply another name for (Int, Int) -> Int
    val f: BinaryOperation = { n1, n2 -> n1 - n2 }
    // BinaryOperation and (Int, Int) -> Int are the same type
    val g: (Int, Int) -> Int = f
    // but Operation is a different type: a conversion is needed
    val op2 = Operation(g)
    println("f(5, 1)=${f(5, 1)}, g(5, 1)=${g(5, 1)}, op2.calculate(5, 1)=${op2.calculate(5, 1)}")
}

// definition of a functional interface: a single abstract method
// taking two integers as parameters and returning an integer
fun interface Operation {
    fun calculate(n1: Int, n2: Int): Int

    // a method with a body does not count: the interface remains functional
    fun then(next: (Int) -> Int): Operation = Operation { n1, n2 -> next(calculate(n1, n2)) }
}

// a generic functional interface: T -> R
fun interface Transformation<T, R> {
    fun transform(value: T): R
}

// a type alias: no new type is created
typealias BinaryOperation = (n1: Int, n2: Int) -> Int

// a class whose methods have the shape of the Operation interface
class Calculations {
    // two instance methods
    fun add(n1: Int, n2: Int): Int {
        println("add($n1,$n2)")
        return n1 + n2
    }

    fun subtract(n1: Int, n2: Int): Int {
        println("subtract($n1,$n2)")
        return n1 - n2
    }

    // a method of the companion object: the equivalent of a static method
    companion object {
        fun increase(n1: Int, n2: Int): Int {
            println("increase($n1,$n2)")
            return n1 + 2 * n2
        }
    }
}

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=lambdas02.Lambdas02Kt
increase(4,7)
n=18
add(2,3)
n=5
subtract(2,3)
n=-1
add(10,4)
-> 14
subtract(10,4)
-> 6
-> 40
add(1,2)
squaredSum.calculate(1, 2)=9
subtract(5,1)
other.applyAsInt(5, 1)=4
length("Hello")=5
stars(5)=*****
f(5, 1)=4, g(5, 1)=4, op2.calculate(5, 1)=4

Comments:

  • lines 60–64: definition of the functional interface [Operation]. In Kotlin, type declarations can be placed anywhere in the file, before or after the function [main]; we place them after it;
  • Line 64: A functional interface can have methods with a body (the equivalent of Java’s [default] methods). The method [then] constructs a new [Operation]: this object performs the current operation, then applies the function [next] to its result. It returns a lambda converted to [Operation], which we will examine in the next section. Note that the [next] parameter does not require an interface like the [IntUnaryOperator] in the Java version: the functional type [(Int) -> Int] is sufficient, and it is executed via [next(…)];
  • lines 76–89: the class [Calculations] has two instance methods, [add] and [subtract], and a method of its companion object, [increase] (the equivalent of a static method, see Chapter 4), all three of which have the same form as the method [calculate];
  • line 9: the variable [op] is of type [Operation]. It is assigned the object obtained by converting the reference [Calculations::increase] to SAM, which refers to the method [increase] of the companion object of the class [Calculations].
