  • the Java class [java.beans.PropertyChangeSupport], which manages the list of listeners for us. The listeners implement the functional interface [PropertyChangeListener], whose method [void propertyChange(PropertyChangeEvent evt)] receives an event containing the source, the property name, and its old and new values.

The delegate [observable] knows when a property changes, and [PropertyChangeSupport] knows who to notify: the program [Lambdas12.kt] links them together:

package lambdas12

import java.beans.PropertyChangeListener
import java.beans.PropertyChangeSupport
import kotlin.properties.Delegates
import kotlin.properties.ReadWriteProperty

// property change events: Delegates.observable, vetoable and PropertyChangeSupport

fun main() {
    val thermometer = Thermometer("living room")
    // a listener of all the properties
    val log = PropertyChangeListener { e ->
        val source = e.source as Thermometer
        println("Log: ${source.name}.${e.propertyName} : ${e.oldValue} -> ${e.newValue}")
    }
    thermometer.addPropertyChangeListener(log)
    // a listener of the temperature property only
    thermometer.addPropertyChangeListener("temperature") { e ->
        if (e.newValue as Double > 19) {
            println("Alert: temperature too high")
        }
    }

    thermometer.temperature = 18.0
    thermometer.temperature = 21.5
    // same value: no event
    thermometer.temperature = 21.5
    thermometer.name = "lounge"
    // unregistration of the log
    thermometer.removePropertyChangeListener(log)
    thermometer.temperature = 22.0
    println("remaining listeners: ${thermometer.nbListeners}")

    // a property that can refuse a new value
    for (value in listOf(21.0, 45.0)) {
        thermometer.setpoint = value
        println("requested setpoint: $value, retained setpoint: ${thermometer.setpoint}")
    }
}

// a class whose properties signal their changes
class Thermometer(name: String) {
    // listener management is delegated to a PropertyChangeSupport object
    private val changes = PropertyChangeSupport(this)

    // an observable property: after each write, the change is signaled
    private fun <T> observable(initialValue: T): ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> =
        Delegates.observable(initialValue) { property, old, new ->
            changes.firePropertyChange(property.name, old, new)
        }

    var name: String by observable(name)
    var temperature: Double by observable(0.0)

    // a property that refuses values outside the interval [5, 30]
    var setpoint: Double by Delegates.vetoable(20.0) { _, _, new -> new in 5.0..30.0 }

    // registration and unregistration of the listeners
    fun addPropertyChangeListener(listener: PropertyChangeListener) {
        changes.addPropertyChangeListener(listener)
    }

    fun addPropertyChangeListener(property: String, listener: PropertyChangeListener) {
        changes.addPropertyChangeListener(property, listener)
    }

    fun removePropertyChangeListener(listener: PropertyChangeListener) {
        changes.removePropertyChangeListener(listener)
    }

    val nbListeners: Int
        get() = changes.propertyChangeListeners.size
}

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=lambdas12.Lambdas12Kt
Log: living room.temperature : 0.0 -> 18.0
Log: living room.temperature : 18.0 -> 21.5
Alert: temperature too high
Log: lounge.name : living room -> lounge
Alert: temperature too high
remaining listeners: 1
requested setpoint: 21.0, retained setpoint: 21.0
requested setpoint: 45.0, retained setpoint: 21.0

Comments:

  • Lines 3–4: The [java.beans] package belongs to the [java.desktop] module of JDK, not to the [java.base] module. Since our program is not a Java module, all classes in JDK are accessible to it: we simply need to import them;
  • Line 45: The [Thermometer] class delegates the management of its listeners to a [PropertyChangeSupport] object, constructed using the event source ([this]). The methods on lines 60–69 simply pass subscription and unsubscription events to it, and the [nbListeners] property (lines 72–73) returns the number of registered listeners;
  • lines 48–50: a small generic function that creates a [Delegates.observable] delegate whose lambda passes each change to [firePropertyChange], along with the property name ([property.name]), the old value, and the new value. It returns a *[ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T>]*, the interface for delegates of mutable properties. Like a method, a lambda written within a class can access the object’s private properties, in this case [changes];
  • lines 53–54: the class’s two observable properties. The keyword [by] delegates their management to a delegate created by our function [observable]. Compared to the Java version, where each setter must store the old value, save the new one, and call *[firePropertyChange] with the property name written as a string, the Kotlin version fits into a single line per property, and the property name cannot be misspelled. The delegate executes the lambda on every write, even if the value doesn’t change; however, [firePropertyChange]* only notifies the listeners if the two values are different: the write on line 28, which doesn’t change the value, therefore produces no output;
  • lines 13–17: a first observer, a lambda converted to [PropertyChangeListener] and stored in a variable so it can be unsubscribed (line 31). It is subscribed to all of the object’s properties. [e.source] (i.e., [e.getSource()], viewed from Kotlin as a property) is of type [Any], which must be cast to [as]. The values are objects: [Double] objects are displayed using their [toString] method, which uses the decimal point;
  • Lines 19–21: A second listener, registered solely for the property [temperature]. The lambda is moved out of the parentheses and converted to [PropertyChangeListener] (conversion SAM). It triggers an alert when the temperature exceeds 19 °C. [e.newValue as Double] converts the new value to the type [Any?];
  • Lines 25–33: property changes are made via simple assignments. The name change (line 29) is reported only to the log. On line 4 of the results, the log displays the new source name, [lounge]: the event is reported after the change. After unsubscribing from the log, only the alert is displayed, and only one listener remains;
  • line 57: the property [setpoint] uses the delegate [vetoable]. Its lambda, called before each write operation, accepts the new value only if it is between 5 and 30 °C ([new in 5.0..30.0]); its first two parameters, which are unnecessary here, are denoted as [_]. Lines 36–38: the value 21 is accepted, while the value 45 is rejected; the property retains its previous value (lines 7–8 of the results). The JavaBeans instances have an equivalent mechanism, with [VetoableChangeSupport] and listeners that throw a [PropertyVetoException].

Without writing an event class or a listener type, we thus obtain a complete mechanism. [PropertyChangeSupport] is the one used by Swing GUI components and JavaBeans; JavaFX has its own, very similar mechanism for observable properties. The delegates [observable] and [vetoable], on the other hand, are sufficient on their own when there is only one observer, known at the time the class is written. Finally, note that for asynchronous event streams, Kotlin provides the [Flow] from the kotlinx.coroutines library, which we’ll cover in Chapter 9 ([StateFlow], in particular, acts as an observable property).

docs.title: 7.7. Lambdas, Collections, and Sequences
docs.text:
In Chapter 5, we used the functional operations of collections ([filter], [map], [sortedBy]…) and sequences by passing lambdas to them. We now know what these parameters are: the function [filter] is declared as follows in the standard library: [inline fun <T> Iterable<T>.filter(predicate: (T) -> Boolean): List<T>].

It is an extension function, [inline], whose parameter is a functional type: any function or lambda that takes an element and returns a Boolean is suitable. Similarly, [map] expects a [(T) -> R], [sortedBy] expects a [(T) -> R?], and [R] is comparable, [forEach] corresponds to a [(T) -> Unit], [reduce] to a [(S, T) -> S]… To fully understand how they work, let’s write our own filtering and transformation operations. Here is the program [Lambdas13.kt]:

package lambdas13

// lambdas, collections and sequences

fun main() {
    val numbers = listOf(3, 8, 1, 6, 5, 4, 9, 2)

    // 1 - filter and map expect functions (T) -> Boolean and (T) -> R
    val isEven: (Int) -> Boolean = { it % 2 == 0 }
    val square: (Int) -> Int = { it * it }
    println("collections: ${numbers.filter(isEven).map(square)}")
    // the Java Stream API remains usable: the lambdas are converted to Predicate and Function
    println("Stream: ${numbers.stream().filter { it % 2 == 0 }.map { it * it }.toList()}")

    // 2 - our own filtering function, called with a lambda then a reference
    println("filterBy(n > 4): ${numbers.filterBy { it > 4 }}")
    println("filterBy(isOdd): ${numbers.filterBy(::isOdd)}")

    // 3 - a collection is evaluated immediately: each step produces a complete list
    val largeList = numbers.filter {
        print("[test $it] ")
        it > 7
    }
    println()
    println("the list is already computed: $largeList")

    // 4 - a sequence is evaluated on demand:
    //     the predicate is only called by the terminal operation
    val large = numbers.asSequence().filter {
        print("[test $it] ")
        it > 7
    }
    println("the sequence is defined, nothing has been executed yet")
    large.forEach { print("-> $it ") }
    println()

    // 5 - our own intermediate operations on sequences, lazy as well
    val cities = listOf("Angers", "Paris", "Lyon", "Nantes", "Aix")
    val result = cities.asSequence()
        .keep { it.length <= 5 }
        .transform(String::uppercase)
        .toList()
    println("our operations: $result")
    // an infinite sequence: only the requested elements are computed
    val powersOfTwo = generateSequence(1) { it * 2 }
    val firstOnes = powersOfTwo.transform { "2^${it.countTrailingZeroBits()}=$it" }.take(5)
    println("powers of 2: ${firstOnes.toList()}")
}

// filters a list with a predicate: the work that filter does
inline fun <T> List<T>.filterBy(predicate: (T) -> Boolean): List<T> {
    val result = mutableListOf<T>()
    for (element in this) {
        if (predicate(element)) {
            result.add(element)
        }
    }
    return result
}

fun isOdd(n: Int) = n % 2 != 0

// an intermediate sequence operation that lets through only the elements satisfying the predicate
fun <T> Sequence<T>.keep(predicate: (T) -> Boolean): Sequence<T> = sequence {
    for (element in this@keep) {
        if (predicate(element)) yield(element)
    }
}

// an intermediate operation that transforms each element: the equivalent of map
fun <T, R> Sequence<T>.transform(transformation: (T) -> R): Sequence<R> = sequence {
    for (element in this@transform) {
        yield(transformation(element))
    }
}

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=lambdas13.Lambdas13Kt
collections: [64, 36, 16, 4]
Stream: [64, 36, 16, 4]
filterBy(n > 4): [8, 6, 5, 9]
filterBy(isOdd): [3, 1, 5, 9]
[test 3] [test 8] [test 1] [test 6] [test 5] [test 4] [test 9] [test 2]
the list is already computed: [8, 9]
the sequence is defined, nothing has been executed yet
[test 3] [test 8] -> 8 [test 1] [test 6] [test 5] [test 4] [test 9] -> 9 [test 2]
our operations: [PARIS, LYON, AIX]
powers of 2: [2^0=1, 2^1=2, 2^2=4, 2^3=8, 2^4=16]

Comments:

  • Lines 9–11: The lambdas from [filter] and [map] are first assigned to variables to reveal their types. [map] transforms each element: this yields the squares of even numbers;
  • line 13: the same calculation using the Java API stream, which can be used as-is from Kotlin: the Java method [filter] expects a [Predicate], [map] expects a [Function], and Kotlin lambdas are automatically converted (SAM conversion). It is rarely used in Kotlin for sequential computations, since collection and sequence functions are simpler; it remains useful for the parallel streams in Chapter 8, or when a Java library returns a [Stream];
  • Lines 51–58: Our function [filterBy], written as an extension function of [List<T>] and declared as [inline], just like [filter]. It is generic: it filters a list of elements of any type [T]. It iterates over the list ([this]), calls the predicate on each element (line 54), and returns the list of selected elements;
  • Line 16: call to [filterBy] with a lambda, outside the parentheses. The type [T] is inferred from the list: [Int]. On line 17, a function reference is passed to it: [isOdd] (line 61) has the form [(Int) -> Boolean];
  • Lines 20–25: a verbose predicate, which displays each element it tests, applied to a list. Collection operations are immediate: [filter] tests all elements and constructs the complete result list before returning it (lines 5–6 of the results). In a chain [list.filter { … }.map { … }], each step thus creates an intermediate list;
  • lines 29–34: the same predicate applied to a sequence ([asSequence()]). The result (lines 7–8) shows that the sequence definition does not execute anything: the message on line 33 is displayed before the first test. It is only when the terminal operation [forEach] requests the elements that the predicate executes, and the tests alternate with the displays from [forEach]: each element passes through the entire chain before the next one enters it. This is the deferred (or lazy) execution of sequences, the same as that of Java streams. The intermediate operations of the sequences are not [inline]: they must retain the lambdas in order to execute them later;
  • lines 64–73: To write our own intermediate operations—which are lazy, like those in the library—we use the sequence constructor [sequence]. It takes a lambda in which the function [yield] produces an element of the sequence: for each element requested by the downstream, the lambda resumes execution where it left off, until the next [yield] (this is a coroutine, a concept we will study in Chapter 9). The label of [this@keep] designates the receiver of the extension function [keep], that is, the original sequence: without a label, [this] would denote the receiver of the lambda in [sequence], since that lambda is a lambda with a receiver. The function [keep] passes only those elements that satisfy the predicate; the function [transform], which is doubly generic ([T] is the type of the received elements, [R] is the type of the produced elements), returns the result of the function applied to each element. Java 24 introduced intermediate collectors ([Gatherer]) for the same purpose, which have a significantly more complex syntax;
  • lines 39–42: Our extension functions are inserted into the string just like library operations: we keep cities with at most 5 letters, then convert them to uppercase. The terminal operation [toList] triggers the calculation;
  • lines 45–47: [generateSequence(1) { it * 2 }] defines an infinite sequence: 1, followed by each element obtained by doubling the previous one. It is usable only thanks to lazy evaluation: [take(5)] requests only the first five elements, and only those are computed. The lambda passed to [transform] displays each power in the form [2^n=value] ([countTrailingZeroBits] counts the rightmost zeros in the binary representation, i.e., the exponent).

All operations on collections and sequences are built on this model: higher-order functions that take functional types. For collections, these functions are [inline] and immediate; for sequences, they preserve the lambdas and compute the elements only when requested by the terminal operation.

docs.title: 7.8. Expression Trees
docs.text:
Some languages, such as C#, allow a lambda to be converted not into executable code, but into a data structure that describes it (an “expression tree”): a program can then parse the lambda [t => t.Limit > 20000] and translate it, for example, into a clause SQL [WHERE limits > 20000] executed by the database server.

Kotlin, like Java, has no equivalent: a Kotlin lambda is always compiled into executable code; it can be called, but its internal workings cannot be examined. Several tools come close, however:

  • Property references: [Person::age] is an object ([KProperty1<Person, Int>]) that knows the property name ([Person::age.name]) and its type. A library can use this to construct a query without writing a string: this is what Spring Data MongoDB does, for example, with its Kotlin extensions, which allow you to write a criterion such as [Person::age gt 18];
  • Internal DSL (“Domain-Specific Languages”): thanks to lambdas with receivers, [infix] functions, and operator overloading, a Kotlin library can offer a syntax similar to SQL, which the program executes to construct a data structure describing the query. This is the principle behind the Exposed library, from JetBrains: [Brackets.selectAll().where { Brackets.limit greater 20000 }];
  • compiler plugins: the Kotlin compiler can be extended with plugins that transform the code. This is how kotlinx.serialization works, the [all-open] and [no-arg] plugins used with Spring and Hibernate, or the [power-assert] plugin, which analyzes an assertion’s expression to display its details in case of failure. However, these are development tools, not built-in features of the program.

Hibernate, which we will cover in Chapter 11, offers the same solutions as in Java: a query language similar to SQL but expressed in terms of classes and properties, HQL (["from Bracket t where t.limit > 20000"]), and Jakarta Persistence’ API Criteria, which constructs the query through method calls ([cb.gt(t.get("limit"), 20000)]). In both cases, the query is data (a string or an object tree) that Hibernate translates into SQL, whereas a lambda passed to [filter] is executed within the Kotlin program.

docs.title: 7.9. Conclusion
docs.text:
Key takeaways from this chapter:

  • In Kotlin, functions are values: they have a functional type ([(Int, Int) -> Int], [() -> Unit], [(T) -> Boolean], [(() -> Unit)?], [T.() -> R]…), can be stored in variables, passed as parameters, returned as results, and called like ordinary functions. To the virtual machine, they are objects that implement the interfaces [Function0], [Function1]…;
  • the interfaces of [java.util.function] ([Function], [Supplier], [Consumer], [Predicate]…), along with [Runnable], [Callable], and [Comparator], remain usable: when a Java method expects a functional interface, Kotlin automatically converts a lambda or a reference to it (conversion SAM); elsewhere, the conversion is written explicitly: [Comparator { … }];
  • to name a function type, we have the alias [typealias] (simply an alias) and [fun interface] (a true new type, implementable via a lambda);
  • A function can be obtained via a lambda expression ([{ a, b -> a + b }], [{ it * it }]—written outside parentheses when it is the last parameter, and closed with [return@label]), via an anonymous function, via an anonymous object, or via a reference ([::function], [object::method], [Class::method], [::Class]). Two references to the same function of the same object are equal; two lambdas are never equal;
  • lambdas capture the variables surrounding them, including the [var], which they can modify (the compiler stores them in [Ref] objects); they then see the value of the variable at the time of their execution, which requires caution in loops and between threads;
  • Functions that return functions and extensions on functional types ([then], [and], [or]…) compose new functions; [compareBy], [thenBy], and [reversed] construct comparators;
  • the functions [inline] copy their code and that of the lambdas to the call site, without an object or conversion, and allow non-local returns; [noinline] and [crossinline] handle special cases. The scope functions [let], [run], [with], [apply], and [also] are the most common applications of this;
  • a functional type is chosen for short-term, one-off behavior; a [fun interface] for a distinct type; or a API that can be used from Java; a multi-member interface (or a “business” interface) for an application role;
  • an event is set up using the listener pattern: an [XxxEvent] class, a listener type (often a functional-type [typealias]), [addXxxListener] / [removeXxxListener], and a list of functions ([CopyOnWriteArrayList]) iterated over by a [fireXxx] method. The delegated properties [Delegates.observable] and [Delegates.vetoable] signal or filter changes to a property, and [PropertyChangeSupport] manages the list of listeners for them;
  • collection operations (immediate, [inline]) and sequence operations (lazy) are higher-order functions; Kotlin does not have expression trees, and Hibernate expresses its queries using HQL or the Criteria API.

Lambdas will reappear in all subsequent chapters: a thread executes a lambda ([thread { … }]), and an [ExecutorService] executes a [Callable] (Chapter 8); a coroutine is launched by [launch { … }] or [async { … }] (Chapter 9), extension functions of [ResultSet] will receive, in the form of a lambda, the transformation of a line from the result into an object (Chapter 10), and Spring Boot web services process HTTP requests in methods that the framework calls as listeners (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 14. Further Reading
docs.text: This document introduced the Kotlin language and the most commonly used libraries for writing layered applications, network clients and servers, and web services on the Java Virtual Machine. Here are the main topics that build on this.

docs.title: 14.1. Processing XML documents
docs.text:
JSON has largely replaced XML for data exchange, but XML is still in use (configuration files, document formats, existing SOAP services). Kotlin directly uses the XML API of the JDK, within the [javax.xml] package:

  • DOM ([DocumentBuilder], [Document], [Element]): the document is loaded into memory as a tree, which is then traversed and modified;
  • StAX ([XMLStreamReader], [XMLStreamWriter]): the document is read or written on the fly, without being loaded entirely into memory;
  • XPath ([javax.xml.xpath]) to query a document, and XSLT ([javax.xml.transform]) to transform it.

Aside from JDK, Jackson can read and write XML using its [jackson-dataformat-xml] module, just as it does for JSON (Chapter 5), and the kotlinx.serialization library for JetBrains, which generates serialization code at compile time, also supports XML formats developed by the community.

docs.title: 14.2. Web Applications
docs.text:
Chapter 13 covers only web services (applications that produce data). For web applications that generate HTML pages, or for other ways to write web services in Kotlin, the following are available:

  • Spring MVC with a template engine like Thymeleaf: server-side generated pages. Spring supports Kotlin just as it does Java (data classes, coroutines in controllers, Kotlin for route configuration); the author wrote the course “Step-by-Step Introduction to the Spring Web Framework” (September 2026);
  • Ktor, the JetBrains web framework, written in and for Kotlin: HTTP servers and clients built on the coroutines from Chapter 9, configured using Kotlin code rather than annotations;
  • other JVM frameworks that support Kotlin: Quarkus, Micronaut, Javalin, and the Jakarta application servers EE;
  • interfaces written in JavaScript (Vue.js, Angular, React) that consume Kotlin web services; the author wrote the course “Step-by-Step Introduction to the Vue.js Framework” (September 2026). Kotlin itself can be compiled to JavaScript (Kotlin/JS) or to WebAssembly (Kotlin/Wasm), which also allows the client-side to be written in Kotlin.

docs.title: 14.3. Mobile and Desktop Applications
docs.text:
This document does not cover graphical user interfaces: today, management applications are most often built with web interfaces. However, this is an area where Kotlin is widely used:

  • on Android, Kotlin is the language recommended by Google, and the UI is built using Jetpack Compose, a declarative library written entirely in Kotlin; coroutines (Chapter 9) are used to keep the UI responsive during network or database access;
  • Compose Multiplatform, by JetBrains, extends Compose to write desktop (Windows, Linux, macOS), iOS, and web interfaces using the same code;
  • More generally, Kotlin Multiplatform allows business logic code (the [business] and [dao] layers in Chapter 6, for example) to be shared between JVM, Android, iOS (via Kotlin/Native, which generates machine code without a virtual machine), and the web;
  • on JVM, the Java Swing and JavaFX libraries remain usable from Kotlin. The concepts covered in Chapters 7 (event listeners) and 9 (returning to the GUI thread with [Dispatchers.Main]) apply directly here.

docs.title: 14.4. Tests
docs.text:
Chapter 6 introduces JUnit and [kotlin.test]. These are often supplemented by:

  • Kotest, a testing framework written for Kotlin, offering multiple test-writing styles and a rich library of assertions ([list shouldHaveSize 7]);
  • MockK, the library of “mocks” (simulated objects) for the layers on which the layer under test depends, designed for Kotlin (final classes, objects, suspension functions); Mockito remains usable;
  • kotlinx-coroutines-test, which runs tests on coroutine-based code using a virtual clock: a [delay(10_000)] runs instantly;
  • Testcontainers, which launches a real database (MySQL, PostgreSQL…) in a Docker container for the duration of integration tests;
  • Spring Boot testing tools ([@SpringBootTest], [MockMvc]) for testing a web service without deploying it.

docs.title: 14.5. Performance
docs.text:
A Kotlin program is executed by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM): it benefits from just-in-time compilation and runtime optimizations, with performance equivalent to that of a Java program. Among the tools that go a step further:

  • the JMH tool (“Java Microbenchmark Harness”), which can be used directly in Kotlin or via the kotlinx-benchmark Gradle plugin, to precisely measure code performance while accounting for virtual machine warm-up;
  • JDK Flight Recorder and JDK Mission Control, which record and analyze a program’s behavior in production; IntelliJ IDEA includes a profiler and a coroutine debugger;
  • ahead-of-time compilation to native code with GraalVM Native Image: a standalone executable that launches in a few milliseconds, at the cost of restrictions on reflection; Spring Boot and Quarkus can generate such executables from Kotlin code;
  • the choice of garbage collector (G1 by default, ZGC for very short pauses on large memory heaps).

docs.title: 14.6. Deployment
docs.text: A Kotlin program is deployed just like a Java program: as a [.jar] archive executed by a JDK installed on the machine ([java -jar application.jar]), provided that the standard Kotlin library is included (this is what the scripts generated by [gradlew installDist] do, Chapter 2; Spring Boot generates a standalone [.jar] that contains all its libraries), as a standalone application that embeds a virtual machine reduced to only what it needs (tools [jlink] and [jpackage] from JDK), or in a Docker container (Spring Boot directly generates a container image via [gradlew bootBuildImage]).

docs.title: 14.7. Resources
docs.text:
• the official Kotlin website, with its documentation, tutorials, and “What’s New” pages for each release: https://kotlinlang.org;
  • the Kotlin Playground online sandbox, for trying out Kotlin code in a browser;
  • the Kotlin Koans exercises, available on the Kotlin website and in IntelliJ IDEA;
  • language evolution proposals (KEEP), to stay up to date on what’s new in upcoming versions: https://github.com/Kotlin/KEEP;
  • the source code for the compiler and the standard library, available at GitHub: https://github.com/JetBrains/kotlin, and the source code for coroutines: https://github.com/Kotlin/kotlinx.coroutines;
  • the documentation for Java API SE 25, for the JDK classes used from Kotlin: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/;
  • the books *Kotlin in Action* (Manning) and *Effective Kotlin* by Marcin Moskała, and, for concurrency in JVM, *Java Concurrency in Practice* by Brian Goetz et al. (Addison-Wesley).

docs.title: 11. Hibernate
docs.text:
The previous chapter demonstrated how a Kotlin application interacts with a database through a JDBC driver: a connection is opened, SQL commands are executed, the result rows are read column by column, and they are copied into objects. This process of copying—from rows to objects and from objects to the [INSERT], [UPDATE], and [DELETE] commands—is repetitive. It can be automated using a tool: an “Object-Relational Mapper” (ORM). This chapter introduces the most widely used ORM in the Java world, Hibernate, and the standard it implements, Jakarta Persistence. Kotlin does not have its own ORM of the same caliber: it directly uses those from the Java platform—Hibernate foremost among them—just as it uses ORMs. You only need to know a few rules to write Kotlin entities that work with Hibernate: this chapter introduces them as we go along.

The chapter revisits the sample code from the articles in Chapter 10 and concludes with version 7 of the tax calculation application, whose [dao] layer uses Hibernate.

docs.title: 11.1.1. Objects and Tables
docs.text:
A Kotlin application works with objects: an item has a name, a price, and a stock level; an order has a customer and a list of line items, each of which refers to an item. A relational database stores this same information in tables: one row in the [articles] table per item, one row in the [orders] table per order, with the relationships between rows expressed by foreign keys. The two worlds do not quite align:

  • an object directly references other objects ([order.client]); a row contains the primary key value of another row ([client_id]);
  • an object can contain a collection ([order.lines]); a table contains only single values; the collection is represented by the rows of another table that point to the order;
  • the Kotlin types ([String], [BigDecimal], [LocalDate], [Boolean]) and the SQL types ([varchar(30)], [decimal(10,2)], [date], [bit]) are not the same;
  • objects are queried using Kotlin (the [filter], [map]... operations on collections) and tables are queried using SQL.

A ORM bridges the two worlds. We define the correspondence between classes and tables (the model, or “mapping”) once and for all; it then takes care of:

  • translating queries written in an object-oriented language (HQL) or constructed using code (API Criteria) into SQL and [SELECT] commands ;
  • create objects from the read lines (this is called materialization);
  • to store the read objects and detect those that have been modified, added, or deleted;
  • to generate the [INSERT], [UPDATE], and [DELETE] commands that reflect these changes in the database;
  • and, if necessary, to create and update the database schema (tables, columns, indexes) based on the classes.

The architecture of an application that uses Hibernate with MySQL is as follows:

  • [1]: the application. Its [dao] layer no longer communicates directly with the JDBC driver but with Hibernate, through a [Session] object and HQL queries;
  • [2]: Hibernate, independent of the DBMS: model, query translation, change tracking, schema generation;
  • [3]: the dialect specific to the DBMS (here, [MySQLDialect]): it knows the SQL syntax of the DBMS, its column types, and its functions. The dialects of the main DBMSs are part of Hibernate itself: nothing needs to be added to the project;
  • [4]: the JDBC driver for the DBMS, the one discussed in Chapter 10 (MySQL Connector/J): Hibernate does not replace JDBC; it uses it;
  • [5]: the DBMS.

Whether the application is written in Java or Kotlin does not change this pattern: Hibernate is a Java library that Kotlin code calls just like any other Java library (Chapter 5), and the compiled Kotlin classes are, to Hibernate, Java classes just like any others.

docs.title: 11.1.2. Jakarta Persistence and Hibernate
docs.text:
Hibernate was created in 2001 by Gavin King in response to the cumbersomeness of the “entity beans” in the Java platform EE of that time. Its success was such that its ideas were incorporated into a standard, JPA (Java Persistence API), released in 2006 with Java EE 5. When Java EE was transferred to the Eclipse Foundation and renamed Jakarta EE, JPA became Jakarta Persistence, and its packages changed from [javax.persistence] to [jakarta.persistence] (version 3.0, 2020). The current version is Jakarta Persistence 3.2 (2024).

Jakarta Persistence is a specification: a set of interfaces ([EntityManagerFactory], [EntityManager]...), annotations ([@Entity], [@Id], [@Column]...), and a query language, JPQL. It is implemented by several products: Hibernate ORM (the most widely used, used in Spring Boot and Quarkus), EclipseLink (the reference implementation)... This course uses Hibernate ORM 7.4.5, which implements Jakarta Persistence 3.2.

Hibernate offers two ways to use it:

  • exclusively through the standard interfaces: in this case, the code depends only on [jakarta.persistence], and it would, in principle, be possible to switch implementations;
  • through its own (“native”) API, which is more feature-rich and whose interfaces extend those of the standard: a [SessionFactory] is a [EntityManagerFactory], and a [Session] is a [EntityManager].

We use Hibernate’s own API, as recommended in its documentation: It provides all the standard methods ([persist], [find], [merge], [remove]...) as well as Hibernate’s extensions. The annotations, however, are always those defined by the standard. The following table shows the correspondences:

Jakarta PersistenceHibernateRole[EntityManagerFactory][SessionFactory]Hibernate configuration for a database: a heavy object, created once, shared by the entire application[EntityManager][Session]A database session: a lightweight, short-lived object[EntityTransaction][Transaction]a transactionJPQLHQLthe query language; HQL is a superset of JPQL[CriteriaBuilder][HibernateCriteriaBuilder]query construction via code

In the Kotlin ecosystem, you’ll also encounter data access libraries of a different nature, such as Exposed (from JetBrains), which allows you to write SQL queries using a dedicated Kotlin language. These are lighter than a full ORM; Hibernate remains the standard for Spring applications, in both Java and Kotlin, and that is what we are studying.

docs.title: 11.1.3. Libraries
docs.text:
The libraries used in this chapter are as follows (they are summarized in the appendix on dependencies):

Gradle DependencyRole[org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-core] 7.4.5.FinalHibernate itself; it includes the API from Jakarta Persistence 3.2 ([jakarta.persistence-api]) and its own dependencies (Byte Buddy for class generation, ANTLR for query analysis, JBoss Logging for logging, etc.)[com.mysql:mysql-connector-j] 9.7.0the JDBC driver for MySQL, the one from Chapter 10[ch.qos.logback:logback-classic] 1.5.38Logback, which will receive the Hibernate log

Hibernate writes its log (executed SQL commands, warnings, etc.) through JBoss Logging, a small library that simply forwards messages to the logging system it finds in the classpath: Log4j 2, or Logback (via SLF4J), or, failing that, the one from JDK or [java.util.logging]. Without configuration, the latter displays each message on two lines, in red in most consoles, which makes the program output difficult to read. We therefore add Logback to our projects and configure it using a [logback.xml] file.

In addition to these libraries, there are two Kotlin compiler plugins that adapt Kotlin classes to Hibernate’s requirements: [kotlin("plugin.jpa")] and [kotlin("plugin.allopen")]. We’ll see why they’re necessary when we look at the first entity.

docs.title: 11.1.4. Code-First or Database-First
docs.text:
The model (the mapping between classes and tables) can be built in two ways:

  • code-first: you write the Kotlin classes, and Hibernate infers the database schema from them, which it can then create on its own. This is the approach taken in this chapter;
  • database-first: the database already exists, and the classes are generated from its schema using Hibernate’s reverse-engineering tools (Hibernate Tools) or those provided by development environments (IntelliJ IDEA can generate entities from database tables in both Java and Kotlin). This is the approach used for applications that need to work with an existing database. The generated code is similar to what we would write by hand.

docs.title: 11.2.1. The project
docs.text:
The examples in this chapter are subprojects of a multi-project Gradle build (see Chapter 6), located in the [11-hibernate] folder:

11-hibernate/
  settings.gradle.kts     the list of the subprojects
  build.gradle.kts        the root project: the plugins and their versions
  gradlew, gradlew.bat    the Gradle wrapper
  tools/                  library: the compact SQL log
  articles/               library: the Article entity and the [hbarticles] database
  first/                  a first example
  model/                  the model: annotations, XML file, creation script
  crud/                   persist, find, merge, remove
  hql/                    HQL queries
  criteria/               Criteria API queries
  relations/              relationships between entities
  clients/                the evolution of the database schema
  async/                  Hibernate, virtual threads and coroutines
  transactions/           transactions
  concurrency/            optimistic concurrency
  rawsql/                 native SQL
  bulkupdate/             bulk updates
  injection/              Hibernate and Spring
  TaxV7/                  the tax calculation application, version 7

The file [settings.gradle.kts] declares the subprojects:

// chapter 11: Hibernate

// Gradle downloads the JDK requested by jvmToolchain(25) itself if it does not find it on the machine
plugins {
    id("org.gradle.toolchains.foojay-resolver-convention") version "1.0.0"
}

rootProject.name = "hibernate"

// two libraries common to the examples of the chapter
include("tools", "articles")
// the examples
include("first", "model", "crud", "hql", "criteria", "relations", "clients",
    "async", "transactions", "concurrency", "rawsql", "bulkupdate", "injection")
// version 7 of the [Tax] application: a [dao] layer written with Hibernate
include("TaxV7:tax-dao-hibernate", "TaxV7:tax-ui-hibernate")

// the [business] and [ui] layers of version 5 (chapter 6) are reused: composite build
includeBuild("../06-architectures")
  • lines 3–6: the plugin that allows Gradle to download JDK 25 itself if it cannot find it on the machine (Chapter 2);
  • line 8: the name of the root project;
  • line 11: the two libraries common to the examples;
  • lines 13–14: a subproject, for example. Gradle does not require them to be listed in the order of their dependencies; it deduces this itself from the dependencies declared between subprojects;
  • Line 16: The two subprojects for version 7 of the tax calculation application. The name [TaxV7:tax-dao-hibernate] refers to the folder [TaxV7/tax-dao-hibernate];
  • Line 19: the composite structure of Chapter 6, whose application TaxV7 will reuse the layers [business] and [ui].

The root project declares, along with their versions, the plugins used by the subprojects:

// chapter 11: root project. The plugins are declared here (with their version) and applied by the subprojects
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.20" apply false
    kotlin("plugin.jpa") version "2.4.20" apply false
    kotlin("plugin.allopen") version "2.4.20" apply false
    kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.4.20" apply false
}
  • line 3: the Kotlin plugin for JVM;
  • lines 4–5: the two Kotlin compiler plugins required by the entities (described later);
  • line 6: the “all-open” plugin configured for Spring (Chapter 6), used by the [injection] example;
  • [apply false]: The plugins are only declared here, along with their versions; each subproject applies the ones it needs, without repeating the version.

The first example is the subproject [first]. It is independent of the others:

// a first example: an entity, a database, a few SQL statements generated by Hibernate
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    // the parameterless constructor of the entities ("no-arg" plugin configured for JPA)
    kotlin("plugin.jpa")
    // entities and properties made open (non-final): Hibernate can derive proxies from them
    kotlin("plugin.allopen")
    application
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // Hibernate and the MySQL JDBC driver
    implementation("org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-core:7.4.5.Final")
    runtimeOnly("com.mysql:mysql-connector-j:9.7.0")
    // Logback: it receives the Hibernate log (only at runtime)
    runtimeOnly("ch.qos.logback:logback-classic:1.5.38")
}

// the classes annotated this way are opened by the [allopen] plugin
allOpen {
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.Entity")
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.MappedSuperclass")
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.Embeddable")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
    // the program run by [gradlew -q :first:run], launched in the 11-hibernate folder
    mainClass = "first.MainKt"
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}
  • lines 3–8: the applied plugins: Kotlin, the two entity plugins, and [application] to run the program;
  • lines 17–20: Hibernate, the JDBC driver for MySQL, and Logback. The driver and Logback are used only at runtime ([runtimeOnly]): the program code does not reference any of their classes;
  • lines 24–27: the configuration of the [allopen] plugin (described below);
  • lines 31–34: the standard compilation options for the course (JDK 25, warnings treated as errors);
  • line 40: the main class of the subproject. A [Main.kt] file from the [first] package is compiled into a [first.MainKt] class (Chapter 3);
  • lines 43–46: The programs launched by Gradle write their output to UTF-8 so that accented characters display correctly on Windows (Chapter 2).

To run an example, navigate to the [11-hibernate] folder and specify the subproject’s task [run] by its path ([:first:run]); Gradle first builds the subprojects it depends on (on Linux and macOS, type [./gradlew]):

> cd 11-hibernate
> gradlew -q :first:run

The program is executed in the subproject folder ([11-hibernate/first]). The database used is the [hbfirst] database on the local MySQL server, which is the Laragon server (see appendices). It does not need to exist: MySQL will create it.

docs.title: 11.2.2. The entity [Article]
docs.text:
A class whose objects are stored in a table is called an entity. Our first entity is a store item, as in the table [articles] from Chapter 10:

package first

import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import java.math.BigDecimal

// an article of the shop: an ordinary Kotlin class, plus a few annotations
@Entity
class Article(
    // the columns of the table, declared as properties of the primary constructor
    var name: String,
    var price: BigDecimal,
    var currentStock: Int,
    var minimumStock: Int,
) {
    // the primary key, generated by the DBMS: null as long as the article is not saved
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null

    // display
    override fun toString() = "[%d, %s, %.2f, %d, %d]".format(id, name, price, currentStock, minimumStock)
}
  • Line 10: The annotation [@Entity] (package [jakarta.persistence]) makes the class an entity. This is a regular Kotlin class that does not extend any Hibernate class; it is referred to as a POJO (“Plain Old Java Object”);
  • lines 13–16: the properties declared in the primary constructor (Chapter 4). These are [var]: Hibernate must be able to modify their values, and so must the application (to change a price or inventory level). Each property becomes a column with the same name;
  • lines 19–21: the primary key is designated by the [@Id] annotation. There is no naming convention: the annotation is required. [@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)] indicates that its values will be generated by the DBMS (the [AUTO_INCREMENT] column of MySQL). The identifier is not a constructor parameter: it will be provided by the DBMS. Its type is [Int?], and its initial value is [null], which means “not yet recorded in the database.” The type [Int?] is compiled into [java.lang.Integer], and the type [Int] into [int] (Chapter 3);
  • line 24: a convenient display of the item. The format [%.2f] displays the price with two decimal places, in accordance with common cultural conventions (a comma in France, a point in the English locale used for the results).

Where do annotations go? In bytecode, a Kotlin property corresponds to several Java elements: a private field, an accessor ([getX]), a modifier ([setX]), and, in this case, a constructor parameter. An annotation placed before a property, without further specification, is positioned by Kotlin 2.4 based on the targets it accepts: on the constructor parameter if it is a constructor property and if the annotation allows it, and additionally on the Kotlin property itself if the annotation allows it; otherwise, on the field. Jakarta Persistence annotations ([@Id], [@Column]...) do not apply to Kotlin parameters or properties, but only to Java fields and methods: they are therefore placed on the field. This is exactly what we want: since the [@Id] annotation is on a field, Hibernate accesses the fields directly (it reads and writes them via reflection, even if they are private). You can verify this using the [javap] tool from JDK, which displays the contents of a [.class] file. You can also specify the target of an annotation using a prefix: [@field:Column(length = 30)] places it on the field, [@get:Transient] on the accessor.

Jakarta Persistence requires two things that Kotlin classes do not provide out of the box:

  • a parameterless constructor, which Hibernate uses to create objects read from the database (it then populates their fields). Our class has only one constructor, with four parameters. In Java, you manually add a protected parameterless constructor. In Kotlin, it is the compiler plugin [no-arg], configured for JPA ([kotlin("plugin.jpa")]), that adds it to any class annotated with [@Entity], [@Embeddable], or [@MappedSuperclass]. This constructor exists in the bytecode, where Hibernate finds it through reflection, but it is not visible from the Kotlin code: [Article()] remains a compilation error (“[no value passed for parameter 'name'.]”). Note that it does not execute property initializations: a property declared as [var x = "a"] is set to [null] in an object created by Hibernate, as long as Hibernate has not assigned a value to it (the [noArg { invokeInitializers = true }] option in the build file changes this behavior). This is not a problem for properties stored in the database, since Hibernate assigns them the value that was read;
  • non-final classes and methods. To implement lazy loading (which we’ll cover when discussing relationships), Hibernate creates proxies at runtime: classes derived from the entities, whose methods load the object from the database on the first call. For this to work, the class and its methods must be overridable. In Java, this is the default behavior; in Kotlin, classes and their members are final by default (Chapter 4). The [all-open] ([kotlin("plugin.allopen")]) plugin, configured by the [allOpen] block in the build file, makes classes bearing one of the listed annotations—as well as their properties and methods—non-final ([open]). The [plugin.spring] plugin from Chapter 6 is the same plugin, configured for Spring annotations.

With these two plugins, the entity is written as a regular Kotlin class. Without them, you would have to write [open class Article(...)], declare [open] for each property, and add a secondary constructor with no parameters: we’ll do this for a class without annotations in the following example.

Why not use a data class ([data class], Chapter 4)? It would seem ideal for representing a table row. However, this is a bad idea for an entity, for several reasons:

  • The generated methods [equals] and [hashCode] compare all properties of the primary constructor, which are modifiable. The hash code of an entity therefore changes as soon as its price is modified: an item stored in a [HashSet] or serving as the key of a [HashMap] becomes untraceable. Hibernate itself stores the elements of relationship collections ([Set]) using these methods;
  • two objects representing two different rows (with two different identifiers) but with the same values would be considered equal, whereas an item read from the database and then modified would no longer be equal to itself when read again;
  • the generated [toString] method displays all properties: with relationships, it iterates through the linked objects, which can cause them to be loaded from the database (unexpected SQL queries), an exception if the session is closed, or even an infinite recursion between two entities that reference each other;
  • The method [copy] creates a new object with the same identifier, which is unknown to the session: this results in two objects for the same row, which can lead to confusion;
  • A data class cannot be declared as open ([open]) by the programmer. The [all-open] plugin opens it anyway, which allows proxies to be created (we verified this using the [javap] tool), but it does not correct any of the previous issues.

An entity is therefore an ordinary class: its identity is that of the table row, not the value of its properties. As in Java, it retains the [equals]/[hashCode] inherited from [Any] (object identity), which is fine as long as you do not mix objects from different sessions. Data classes remain very useful with Hibernate for query results that are not entities (projections), as we will see. This is the same rule as in Java, where an entity cannot be a record.

One final note: Hibernate does not recognize Kotlin’s nullable types. The fact that the property [name] is of type [String] (non-nullable) does not tell Hibernate that the column is required; only the annotation [@Column(nullable = false)] tells it that, as we’ll see in the results.

docs.title: 11.2.3. [SessionFactory] and [Session]
docs.text:
The program uses three Hibernate objects:

  • the [SessionFactory] represents Hibernate configured for a database: the list of entities, the database, and the options. Its creation is resource-intensive (Hibernate analyzes the entities, connects to the server to determine its version, and prepares the SQL for common operations): only one is created per database and per application, at startup. It is thread-safe: all application threads can use it;
  • the [Session] represents a working session with the database. It obtains a connection when needed, stores the entities it has read or saved, and knows how to commit their changes to the database. It is a lightweight, short-lived object that is not thread-safe: one is opened for each unit of work and then closed;
  • [Transaction]: With Hibernate, all writes to the database occur within an explicit transaction, opened by [session.beginTransaction()] and closed by [commit] (commit) or [rollback] (rollback).

[SessionFactory] and [Session] implement the [AutoCloseable] interface: they are used with the Kotlin function [use] (Chapter 3), which closes them at the end of the block, whether it terminates normally or with an exception (the equivalent of the [try] statement with Java resources).

docs.title: 11.2.4. The program
docs.text:
package first

import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import java.math.BigDecimal

fun main() {
    // the SessionFactory: Hibernate configured for the [hbfirst] database
    HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("first")
        // the entities
        .managedClass(Article::class.java)
        // the database; MySQL creates it if it does not exist
        .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbfirst?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
        .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
        // display of the SQL statements, formatted, without colors
        .showSql(true, true, false)
        .createEntityManagerFactory().use { sessionFactory ->

            // the tables are dropped then recreated from the entities
            sessionFactory.schemaManager.drop(false)
            sessionFactory.schemaManager.create(false)

            // adding three articles, in a transaction
            sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
                val transaction = session.beginTransaction()
                println("--- persist")
                session.persist(Article("bike", BigDecimal(500), 10, 5))
                session.persist(Article("pump", BigDecimal(10), 10, 2))
                session.persist(Article("bow", BigDecimal(600), 4, 1))
                println("--- commit")
                transaction.commit()
            }

            // reading the table, with a new session
            println("--- reading the articles")
            sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
                val articles: List<Article> = session
                    .createSelectionQuery("from Article order by name", Article::class.java)
                    .resultList
                articles.forEach { println(it) }
            }
        }
}
  • lines 8–16: creation of the [SessionFactory]. There are several ways to configure Hibernate (we’ll discuss them later); we’re using the [HibernatePersistenceConfiguration] class from Hibernate 7, an enhanced version of the [PersistenceConfiguration] class introduced with Jakarta Persistence 3.2, which allows you to configure everything via code. Its parameter is the name of the persistence unit—a freely chosen name that appears in Hibernate messages. Each method returns the configuration itself, allowing calls to be chained together;
  • line 10: the list of entities. [Article::class.java] is the Java object [Class] (the Kotlin class [KClass] is not suitable: Hibernate is a Java library);
  • Lines 12–13: the URL JDBC from the [hbfirst] database, in the same format as in Chapter 10, and the user ([root], with no password in Laragon). The parameter [createDatabaseIfNotExist=true] of URL is an option of the driver MySQL: it creates the database if it does not exist;
  • Line 15: [showSql(true, true, false)] instructs Hibernate to print each SQL command it executes to the console, formatted across multiple lines (second parameter), without colors (third parameter). Looking at the SQL sent to the server is the best way to understand what Hibernate does: we’ll do this in all the examples;
  • Line 16: [createEntityManagerFactory] constructs [SessionFactory] (the method name follows the standard; the returned type is Hibernate’s). The function [use] will close it at the end of the program; within the block, it is called [sessionFactory];
  • Lines 19–20: The [SchemaManager] object of [SessionFactory] (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) manages the entity tables: [drop(false)] deletes them if they exist, while [create(false)] creates them (the parameter [false] specifies that the database itself should not be deleted or created). This is convenient for examples and tests; a real-world application manages its database differently, as we will see. Kotlin presents the Java method [getSchemaManager()] as a property, [schemaManager] (Chapter 4);
  • line 23: [openSession()] opens a session, which is closed at the end of the [use] block;
  • line 24: the start of a transaction;
  • lines 26–28: [persist] adds three new items to the session: they will be stored in the database. No value is specified for the identifier; it will be generated by the DBMS;
  • line 30: [commit] commits the transaction. Prior to this, the session sends the SQL commands to the server, which are still necessary to save the changes it has stored: this is referred to as “flushing” the session to the database;
  • lines 36–38: a query written in HQL, Hibernate’s query language: the articles in alphabetical order by name. It refers to the entity [Article] and its property [name], not to the table. The second parameter of [createSelectionQuery] is the result type: the property [resultList] (the Java method [getResultList]) returns a [List<Article>];
  • Line 39: Displaying the items.

If an exception were to occur between [beginTransaction] and [commit], the transaction would neither be committed nor explicitly rolled back by our code: we’ll see later a safer way to write a transaction using a higher-order function.

The [src/main/resources/logback.xml] file in the subproject configures Logback. It displays Hibernate messages of level [INFO] or higher, one per line (level, log name, message):

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- Logback configuration: Hibernate information messages, one line each -->
<configuration>
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%-5level %logger - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>
    <root level="INFO">
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>

--- persist
