Comments:

  • Lines 2–17: Hibernate informational messages: the name of the persistence unit, the Hibernate version, and database characteristics (URL, driver, selected dialect, server version, transaction isolation level, connection pool size). Hibernate queried the server to select the [MySQLDialect] dialect appropriate for its version;
  • line 4: a warning. Hibernate manages its own small connection pool, which is not intended for a production application. We’ll see, with Spring, how to provide it with the HikariCP pool from Chapter 10; for our examples, the built-in pool is sufficient;
  • Lines 18–28: Deleting and then creating the table [Article] based on the entity: the table name is the same as the entity’s name, the columns are named after the properties, and the column [id] is the primary key, with a generated value ([auto_increment]). The columns for properties of type [Int] are [not null]: compiled into [int]; a [Int] cannot equal [null]. Properties of type [String] and [BigDecimal] accept the value [NULL], even though these types are non-nullable in Kotlin: for Hibernate, these are Java references ([java.lang.String], [java.math.BigDecimal]), which can be set to [null];
  • note the default types: [varchar(255)] for a string, and [decimal(38,2)] for a [BigDecimal] (38 digits, including 2 decimal places). These are rarely the ones you want: the following paragraph shows how to specify them;
  • Lines 29–51: The three configured [INSERT] commands were executed as soon as [persist] was called, before [commit]. This is a consequence of the key being generated by the DBMS ([IDENTITY]): the session must know an entity’s identifier as soon as it takes over that entity, and to obtain it, it must execute the insertion (the JDBC driver returns the generated key; see Chapter 10). With other generation methods, insertions are deferred until the session is synchronized. The parameter values ([?]) are not displayed: we will see how to make them appear;
  • lines 53–63: the query HQL [from Article order by name] was translated into a statement [SELECT ... ORDER BY]. Hibernate assigned the alias [a1_0] to the table and created a [Article] object for each row read (lines 64–66), using the parameterless constructor added by the [no-arg] plugin.

We did not write any SQL statements or any column-reading code: that is the whole point of a ORM. We can also see that this does not eliminate the need to understand SQL: to determine whether the generated SQL is correct and effective, you need to know how to read it.

docs.title: 11.3. The Model
docs.text:
Hibernate builds its model from entities in three steps:

  • First, it applies its default rules: anything that isn’t specified is assigned a reasonable value (this is known as “configuration by exception”);
  • it then supplements or corrects these values using the annotations placed on the entities;
  • finally, it applies the mapping files XML ([orm.xml]), which can fully describe a class without annotations or modify what its annotations specify.

docs.title: 11.3.1. Default Rules
docs.text:
We saw the essentials of this in the first example:

  • an entity carries the annotation [@Entity] and has an identifier designated by [@Id]; both of these annotations are required;
  • the placement of the [@Id] annotation determines the access mode: when placed on a field, Hibernate reads and writes the fields directly; When placed on a getter or setter ([getId]), access goes through the getters and setters ([getX]/[setX]). Access via fields is the most common: it allows the class to have whatever methods it wants. In Kotlin, an annotation placed before a property is applied to the field (as we’ve seen): this provides access via fields without any explicit specification. For access via getters and setters, you would need to write [@get:Id];
  • any property that has a backing field is stored in a column, unless it bears the Jakarta Persistence annotation [@Transient] or the annotation [@kotlin.jvm.Transient] (which adds the Java modifier [transient] to the field); a calculated property, whose custom accessor does not use [field] (Chapter 4), has no field: it is never stored;
  • the table name is the entity name (the simple class name), and the column name is the property name. These names then go through a naming strategy: Hibernate’s strategy keeps the names as-is, while another strategy—which we’ll try below—converts them to “snake case” ([currentStock] becomes [current_stock]). Spring Boot uses the latter by default;
  • a column of a type compiled to a primitive type (non-nullable [Int], [Double], [Boolean]) becomes [NOT NULL]; a column of a type compiled to a reference ([Int?], [String], [BigDecimal], [LocalDate], whether nullable or not for Kotlin) accepts the value [NULL]. To make a column of a property of type [String] mandatory, you must therefore use the annotation [@Column(nullable = false)], even though the Kotlin type already prohibits the value [null];
  • The SQL types are selected based on the dialect. With MySQL: [integer] for [Int], [bigint] for [Long], [bit] for [Boolean], [varchar(255)] for [String], [decimal(38,2)] for [BigDecimal], [date] for [LocalDate], [datetime(6)] (to the microsecond) for [LocalDateTime]. An enumeration ([enum class]) is registered by default by its sequence number (see Chapter 3); the annotation [@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)] registers it by its name, which is more reliable;
  • a property that refers to another entity, or to a collection of entities, defines a relationship (we will discuss this later).

docs.title: 11.3.2. The annotations and the mapping file XML
docs.text:
The subproject [model] defines two entities configured in two different ways. Its build file is that of [first], with the Logback dependency replaced by a dependency on the [tools] library described below (which provides Logback and its configuration). The first entity is configured using annotations:

package model

import jakarta.persistence.Column
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.Table
import jakarta.persistence.Transient
import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.time.LocalDate

// an entity configured by annotations
@Entity
@Table(name = "products")
class Product(
    // required string of 50 characters at most
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 50)
    var name: String,

    // name and SQL type of the column imposed
    @Column(name = "price_excl_tax", nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    var priceExclTax: BigDecimal,

    // optional string (NULL column) of 200 characters at most
    @Column(length = 200)
    var description: String? = null,

    // an optional date: a nullable type
    var withdrawalDate: LocalDate? = null,
) {
    // the primary key: @Id, whatever its name
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var code: Int? = null

    // a property without a column
    @Transient
    var selected = false

    // a computed property has no field: it is never saved
    val priceInclTax: BigDecimal
        get() = priceExclTax * BigDecimal("1.2")
}
  • lines 3–9: the Jakarta Persistence annotations. The explicit import of [jakarta.persistence.Transient] takes precedence over the annotation [kotlin.jvm.Transient]—which has the same name—that Kotlin imports by default;
  • line 15: [@Table] specifies the table name;
  • lines 18–19: [@Column] specifies the column; [nullable = false] makes it required ([NOT NULL]); [length = 50] sets its length ([varchar(50)]);
  • lines 22–23: [@Column] also specifies the column name ([price_excl_tax]) and, for a decimal number, its precision (the total number of digits) and its scale (the number of digits after the decimal point): [decimal(10,2)];
  • lines 26–27: an optional description of up to 200 characters: the column will accept the value [NULL]. The property is of type [String?], with the default value [null]: the Kotlin type matches the column. It is good practice to match the property’s nullable or non-nullable type with the column’s optional or required nature, even though Hibernate only reads the annotation;
  • line 30: an optional date. The type [LocalDate] (Chapter 5) represents a date without a time: it is associated with the types SQL and [date];
  • lines 32–35: the primary key, designated by [@Id] regardless of its name;
  • lines 38–39: [@Transient] excludes a property from the model: in this case, information useful to the user interface that does not belong in the database;
  • lines 42–43: a computed property. Its accessor does not use a field: there is nothing to save, and Hibernate, which accesses the fields, ignores it. The operator [*] between two [BigDecimal] is the function [times] that the Kotlin standard library adds to [BigDecimal] (Chapter 4, Operator Overloading): we write [priceExclTax * BigDecimal("1.2")] instead of Java’s [priceExclTax.multiply(new BigDecimal("1.2"))].

The second entity has no annotations:

package model

import java.time.LocalDateTime

// a class without any annotation: its mapping is described by the [supplier.orm.xml] file
// the [jpa] and [allopen] plugins do not see it: it is declared [open]
// and has its own parameterless constructor
open class Supplier(
    private var companyName: String,
    private var phone: String?,
) {
    private var number: Int? = null
    private var creationDate: LocalDateTime? = null

    // the parameterless constructor required by Hibernate
    protected constructor() : this("", null)
}
  • Line 8: Since the class is not annotated with [@Entity], the [no-arg] and [all-open] plugins do not recognize it. So we declare it ourselves as [open], so that Hibernate can derive proxies from it;
  • lines 9–13: private properties: Kotlin generates neither accessors nor mutators for them, only a private field, which Hibernate will read from and write to. This is the exact equivalent of private fields in a Java class;
  • Line 16: The parameterless constructor required by Hibernate, written by hand: a secondary constructor that calls the primary constructor (Chapter 4) with arbitrary values, which Hibernate will replace with those read from the database. It is protected: the application code will not use it.

Its mapping to the table is described by a file named XML, located in the [src/main/resources/META-INF] folder of the subproject (this is the same file as in Java):

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- the mapping of the [Supplier] class to its table, described in XML (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) -->
<entity-mappings xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm"
                 xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
                 xsi:schemaLocation="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm
                                     https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm/orm_3_2.xsd"
                 version="3.2">
    <entity class="model.Supplier" access="FIELD">
        <table name="suppliers">
            <!-- a unique index: two suppliers cannot have the same company name -->
            <index name="ix_suppliers_company_name" column-list="companyName" unique="true"/>
        </table>
        <attributes>
            <id name="number">
                <generated-value strategy="IDENTITY"/>
            </id>
            <basic name="companyName">
                <column nullable="false" length="60"/>
            </basic>
            <basic name="phone">
                <column name="tel" length="20"/>
            </basic>
            <!-- a default value computed by the DBMS: Hibernate never writes this column -->
            <basic name="creationDate">
                <column nullable="false" insertable="false" updatable="false"
                        column-definition="datetime(6) default current_timestamp(6)"/>
            </basic>
        </attributes>
    </entity>
</entity-mappings>
  • lines 3–7: the XML schema for Jakarta Persistence 3.2 mapping files;
  • line 8: the described class, with access via fields;
  • lines 9–12: the table, and a unique index on the company name: no two suppliers can have the same one. The equivalent annotation is [@Table(name = "suppliers", indexes = [Index(...)])] (in Kotlin, an array passed as an annotation argument is written in square brackets);
  • lines 14–16: the identifier, generated by the DBMS;
  • lines 17–18: a required column with a maximum of 60 characters;
  • lines 20–21: the property [phone] is stored in the column [tel];
  • lines 24–26: the creation date has a default value, calculated by the DBMS. The [column-definition] attribute provides the text SQL from the column definition, copied verbatim in the order [CREATE TABLE]; [insertable="false"] and [updatable="false"] indicate that Hibernate must never write to this column, which allows the DBMS to use [current_timestamp(6)].

Everything that annotations do can be done in XML. Annotations have the advantage of placing the configuration next to the property, and this is the most common approach; the XML file, on the other hand, keeps the classes independent of Jakarta Persistence and centralizes the configuration in a single location. The two approaches can be combined: the XML file takes precedence in case of a conflict. Jakarta Persistence does not support configuring the model via code, as other frameworks such as ORM (for example, Entity Framework in C# or Exposed in Kotlin) do.

The program displays the model built by Hibernate, followed by the SQL script that would create the tables:

package model

import jakarta.persistence.metamodel.SingularAttribute
import org.hibernate.boot.model.naming.PhysicalNamingStrategySnakeCaseImpl
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import java.io.StringWriter

fun main() {
    // the table creation script will be written into this object
    val script = StringWriter()
    // a SessionFactory that never connects to the server
    HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("model")
        // an annotated entity and a mapping described in XML
        .managedClass(Product::class.java)
        .mappingFile("META-INF/supplier.orm.xml")
        // no database: the DBMS and its version are given, for the SQL dialect
        .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_DB_NAME, "MySQL")
        .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_DB_MAJOR_VERSION, "8")
        .property(AvailableSettings.ALLOW_METADATA_ON_BOOT, false)
        // the column names in "snake case": companyName -> company_name
        .property(AvailableSettings.PHYSICAL_NAMING_STRATEGY,
            PhysicalNamingStrategySnakeCaseImpl::class.java.name)
        // the table creation script, without executing it
        .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_ACTION, "create")
        .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_CREATE_TARGET, script)
        .property(AvailableSettings.HBM2DDL_DELIMITER, ";")
        .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
        .createEntityManagerFactory().use { sessionFactory ->

            // the model built by Hibernate: entities and attributes (Jakarta Persistence API)
            for (entity in sessionFactory.metamodel.entities) {
                println("entity ${entity.name} (${entity.javaType.name})")
                for (attribute in entity.attributes) {
                    val id = attribute is SingularAttribute<*, *> && attribute.isId
                    println("  %-14s %s%s".format(attribute.name, attribute.javaType.simpleName,
                        if (id) " (identifier)" else ""))
                }
            }
        }
    // the table creation script, without the 4-space indentation of its lines
    println("--- creation script")
    script.toString().trim().lines()
        .map { it.removePrefix("    ") }
        .forEach { println(it.trimEnd()) }
}
  • line 11: a [StringWriter] (package [java.io]), a write stream to a string in memory, will receive the script SQL;
  • lines 15–16: the annotated entity is declared by [managedClass], and the file XML by [mappingFile];
  • lines 18–20: The database will never exist: this [SessionFactory] is used solely to examine the model. Therefore, there is no URL or JDBC. To select the SQL dialect without querying the server, Hibernate needs the name of the DBMS and its version; the [ALLOW_METADATA_ON_BOOT] property ([hibernate.boot.allow_jdbc_metadata_access]) prevents it from connecting at startup. The names of the configuration properties are constants in the [AvailableSettings] interface;
  • line 22: the “snake case” naming convention, denoted by the name of its class ([::class.java.name]);
  • lines 25–28: Hibernate will write the table creation script (["create"]) to the [script] object without executing it; the commands are terminated by a semicolon and formatted across multiple lines;
  • line 32: the property [metamodel] (the [getMetamodel] method from Jakarta Persistence) provides access to the model: its entities ([EntityType]) and, for each one, its attributes ([Attribute]);
  • Lines 33–37: For each entity, its name and class; for each attribute, its name, Java type, and whether it is the identifier. On line 35, the [attribute is SingularAttribute<*, *>] test is followed by a smart type conversion (Chapter 4): in the continuation of the expression [&&], [attribute] is a [SingularAttribute], from which the property [isId] can be read. The [<*, *>] projection replaces Java’s [<?, ?>];
  • Lines 42–45: The script as displayed, without the four spaces that Hibernate adds to its lines ([removePrefix] removes the prefix only if it is present).

Results:

> gradlew -q :model:run
WARN  connection - HHH102003: No appropriate connection provider encountered; client must supply connections
entity Product (model.Product)
  code           Integer (identifier)
  description    String
  name           String
  priceExclTax   BigDecimal
  withdrawalDate LocalDate
entity Supplier (model.Supplier)
  number         Integer (identifier)
  companyName    String
  creationDate   LocalDateTime
  phone          String
--- creation script
create table products (
    code integer not null auto_increment,
    price_excl_tax decimal(10,2) not null,
    withdrawal_date date,
    name varchar(50) not null,
    description varchar(200),
    primary key (code)
) engine=InnoDB;

create table suppliers (
    number integer not null auto_increment,
    creation_date datetime(6) default current_timestamp(6) not null,
    tel varchar(20),
    company_name varchar(60) not null,
    primary key (number)
) engine=InnoDB;

alter table suppliers
   add constraint ix_suppliers_company_name unique (company_name);
  • Line 2: The Hibernate warning confirms that it has no way to establish a connection;
  • lines 3–13: the two entities and their attributes (the identifier first, then the others in alphabetical order; the order of the entities is not significant). The property [selected] and the calculated property [priceInclTax] do not appear in the model. The types are the Java types: [Integer] for [Int?];
  • lines 15–21: the table [suppliers], described by the file XML. The naming strategy has changed [companyName] and [creationDate] to [company_name] and [creation_date]; the column [tel], whose name is fixed, remains unchanged. The definition of the column [creation_date] is that of the file XML, supplemented by [not null];
  • Lines 23–30: the table [products]. The types SQL come from annotations ([varchar(50)], [decimal(10,2)]) or from dialect-specific choices for a type ([integer], [date]);
  • lines 32–33: the unique index, created under MySQL by a uniqueness constraint ([unique]).

docs.title: 11.3.3. Generated identifiers
docs.text:
The annotation [@GeneratedValue] indicates that the identifier value is generated. Its parameter [strategy] specifies how:

StrategyIdentifier Generation[IDENTITY]by the DBMS, when inserting the row (column [AUTO_INCREMENT] of MySQL, [IDENTITY] of SQL Server, and PostgreSQL)[SEQUENCE]by a sequence from the DBMS (PostgreSQL, Oracle), which Hibernate queries before insertion[TABLE]by a counter table managed by Hibernate[UUID]by Hibernate: a random universal identifier, such as [java.util.UUID][AUTO] (by default)Hibernate chooses; with MySQL, which has no sequences, it simulates them using a table named [<table>_SEQ]

With MySQL, we always use [IDENTITY], which corresponds to the natural behavior of the [AUTO_INCREMENT] column. We’ve seen the result of this: the [INSERT] command is executed as soon as [persist] is called, and Hibernate cannot group multiple inserts into a batch (we’ll discuss batches later). The [SEQUENCE] strategy, which allows you to know the ID before the insertion, is preferred for the DBMS methods that use sequences.

In Kotlin, the generated identifier should preferably be declared as [var id: Int? = null]: the value [null] clearly indicates “not yet registered.” We also encounter [var id: Int = 0], where the value 0 serves this purpose; Hibernate accepts it (for an identifier of a primitive type, it treats 0 as the “not yet registered” value), but this convention is less readable.

docs.title: 11.3.4. Optional Values and Columns [NULL]
docs.text:
Whether a column is optional is therefore determined by the property’s type (compiled as a primitive type or a reference) and by the [nullable] attribute of [@Column]; in Kotlin, the property type also specifies whether the value may be missing ([String?]) or not ([String]). You must choose carefully and ensure that the two match: the rule expresses both a code constraint (“this value may be missing”) and a database constraint. A few notes:

  • [@Column(nullable = false)] represents the constraint [NOT NULL] from the schema created by Hibernate, and Hibernate also uses it before sending a command [INSERT] or [UPDATE]: if the field is [null], it does not send the command and throws a [PropertyValueException] error (“not-null property references a null or transient value”). This Hibernate check is disabled by default when Jakarta Validation (below) is present: validation then falls back to its annotations, or, failing that, to the DBMS, which rejects the command. In Kotlin, this scenario is less common than in Java: the compiler prohibits assigning [null] to a property of type [String];
  • for a more comprehensive validation performed before any database access, we use Jakarta Validation ([hibernate-validator] library) and its annotations [@NotNull], [@Size(max = 30)], [@Positive]... When present in the classpath, Hibernate validates entities before saving them and uses these annotations to create the columns. In Kotlin, these annotations also accept parameters as targets: when applied to a constructor property, Kotlin 2.4 applies them to both the parameter and the field, which the validator reads. Earlier versions placed them only on the parameter: you had to specify the field target, [@field:Size(max = 30)], a form that is still encountered in many examples;
  • there is no need to use [Optional] (Chapter 4): Kotlin’s nullable type ([var description: String? = null]) directly indicates that a value is optional, and it is read using the operators [?.] and [?:] (Chapter 3): [product.description ?: "(no description)"].

docs.title: 11.4. The following examples: two common libraries
docs.text: The examples in the following paragraphs almost all use the [hbarticles] database and its [articles] table, populated with the six entries from Chapter 10. Rather than repeating the Hibernate entity and configuration in each subproject, we place them in a library—the [articles] subproject—on which the other subprojects depend. We also replace the SQL log from [showSql]—which is too verbose for our examples—with a more compact log, placed in a second library, the [tools] subproject.

docs.title: 11.4.1. The compact SQL log
docs.text:
Rather than writing directly to the console ([showSql]), Hibernate can forward its activity to the logging system (in this case, Logback), with each message category written to a different logger:

LogLevelMessages[org.hibernate.SQL][DEBUG]SQL orders executed[org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind][TRACE]the value of each parameter in an order SQL[org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc][TRACE]including, among other things, the initiation, confirmation, and cancellation of transactions[org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.batch][TRACE]execution of order batches SQL[org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error][WARN]Errors reported by the DBMS

A log only records messages of a level equal to or higher than its own. Therefore, you simply need to set the desired level for these logs in the [logback.xml] file to capture these messages. We process them through a layout class that makes them more compact:

package tools

import ch.qos.logback.classic.Level
import ch.qos.logback.classic.Logger
import ch.qos.logback.classic.spi.ILoggingEvent
import ch.qos.logback.core.LayoutBase
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory

// a compact log of the SQL statements executed by Hibernate: a Logback layout
class SqlLog : LayoutBase<ILoggingEvent>() {

    // layout of a message: the text to write is returned ("": nothing is written)
    override fun doLayout(event: ILoggingEvent): String {
        val message = event.formattedMessage
        return when (event.loggerName) {
            SQL -> sqlStatement(message)
            PARAMETERS -> parameter(message)
            TRANSACTIONS -> transaction(message)
            ERRORS -> dbError(message)
            BATCHES -> batch(message)
            else -> ""
        }
    }

    companion object {
        // the Hibernate loggers used
        const val SQL = "org.hibernate.SQL"
        const val PARAMETERS = "org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind"
        const val TRANSACTIONS = "org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc"
        const val ERRORS = "org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error"
        const val BATCHES = "org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.batch"

        // the maximum length of a clause written on a single line
        private const val WIDTH = 100

        // the execution of a batch of SQL statements: "Executing JDBC batch (3 / 3) - [...]"
        private val BATCH = Regex("""Executing JDBC batch \((\d+) / \d+\).*""")

        // a parameter bound to an SQL statement: "binding parameter (1:VARCHAR) <- [bike]"
        private val PARAMETER = Regex("""binding parameter \((\d+):\w+\) <- \[(.*)]""")

        // the SQL statement formatted by Hibernate, made more compact: one line per clause (select, from...)
        private fun sqlStatement(sql: String): String {
            // the non-empty lines, without the trailing spaces
            val lines = sql.lines().map { it.trimEnd() }.filter { it.isNotBlank() }
            // the clauses: a top-level line (the least indented) and the lines that follow it
            val indentation = lines.minOfOrNull { indentation(it) } ?: 0
            val clauses = mutableListOf<MutableList<String>>()
            for (line in lines) {
                if (clauses.isEmpty() || indentation(line) == indentation) clauses.add(mutableListOf())
                clauses.last().add(line.substring(indentation))
            }
            // each clause is written on one line, if it is not too long
            var start = ""
            return buildString {
                for (clause in clauses) {
                    val line = start + clause.joinToString(" ") { it.trim() }
                    if (line == "insert" || line == "delete") {
                        // [insert into ...], [delete from ...]: a single line
                        start = "$line "
                        continue
                    }
                    if (line.length <= WIDTH) {
                        append("    SQL> ").append(line).append('\n')
                    } else {
                        // clause too long: the Hibernate lines are kept
                        clause.forEachIndexed { i, l ->
                            append("    SQL> ").append(if (i == 0) start else "").append(l).append('\n')
                        }
                    }
                    start = ""
                }
            }
        }

        // the number of spaces at the start of the line
        private fun indentation(line: String) = line.length - line.trimStart().length

        // the value of a parameter of the SQL statement
        private fun parameter(message: String): String =
            PARAMETER.matchEntire(message)
                ?.let { "    SQL> -- parameter ${it.groupValues[1]} = ${it.groupValues[2]}\n" } ?: ""

        // start, commit and rollback of the transactions (the other messages are ignored)
        private fun transaction(message: String): String = when {
            message.startsWith("HHH10003002") -> "    SQL> -- start of transaction\n"
            message.startsWith("HHH10003004") -> "    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)\n"
            message.startsWith("HHH10003006") -> "    SQL> -- transaction rolled back (ROLLBACK)\n"
            else -> ""
        }

        // the error reported by the DBMS (the line that gives its error codes is ignored)
        private fun dbError(message: String): String =
            if (message.startsWith("HHH000247")) "" else "    SQL> -- failure: $message\n"

        // the execution of a batch of SQL statements (the other messages are ignored)
        private fun batch(message: String): String =
            BATCH.matchEntire(message)
                ?.let { "    SQL> -- execution of a batch of ${it.groupValues[1]} statement(s)\n" } ?: ""

        // executes an action without an SQL log and returns its result
        fun <T> withoutLog(action: () -> T): T {
            val loggers = listOf(SQL, PARAMETERS, TRANSACTIONS, ERRORS, BATCHES)
                .map { LoggerFactory.getLogger(it) as Logger }
            // the current levels, restored at the end
            val levels: List<Level?> = loggers.map { it.level }
            loggers.forEach { it.level = Level.OFF }
            try {
                return action()
            } finally {
                loggers.zip(levels).forEach { (logger, level) -> logger.level = level }
            }
        }
    }
}
  • line 10: a Logback layout derives from the Java class [LayoutBase<ILoggingEvent>] (note the parentheses: the call to the parent class’s constructor, Chapter 4); its method [doLayout] (lines 13–21) receives each message (a [ILoggingEvent]) and returns the text to be written. Logback creates the object itself, via reflection, based on the class name: it requires a parameterless constructor, which is the class’s implicit primary constructor;
  • lines 15–21: the processing depends on the log that sent the message (a ***[when] on a channel, Chapter 3). The branches use the constants from ***[companion object];
  • line 25: the class’s “static” members are stored in its companion object (Chapter 4);
  • lines 27–31: the names of the Hibernate logs used and the public compilation constants ([const val]); other subprojects refer to them as [SqlLog.SQL]...;
  • lines 37–40: two regular expressions (Chapter 5), written as raw strings (["""..."""]), which avoids having to double the backslashes, as Java does (["\\((\\d+)..."]);
  • lines 43–71: the order SQL, as formatted by Hibernate ([format_sql]), spread across many lines, with one column per line. We make it more compact. Non-empty lines are grouped into clauses (lines 47–51): a clause begins with a top-level line ([select], [from], [where]...) and includes the indented lines that follow it. [minOfOrNull] specifies the smallest indentation, or [null] if there is no line, in which case it is replaced by 0 using the operator [?:]. Each clause is then written on a single line, preceded by [SQL>], if it does not exceed 100 characters (lines 63–64); otherwise, its lines are retained (lines 67–68). The clauses [insert] and [delete] are combined with the following one (lines 58–61). The text is constructed by [buildString] (Chapter 5), whose block has a [StringBuilder] as its receiver: [append] is called there without a prefix;
  • lines 80–82: the Hibernate message that returns the value of a parameter resembles [binding parameter (1:VARCHAR) <- [bike]]. [matchEntire] returns a [MatchResult] if the entire message matches the regular expression, and [null] otherwise; [?.let] constructs the text from the captured groups (the parameter number and its value), and [?: ""] returns an empty string when there is no match;
  • Lines 85–89: Among the many messages in the [org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc] log, only those indicating the start, commit, and rollback of a transaction are retained. Each Hibernate message begins with a code ([HHH10003002]...) that uniquely identifies it. A [when] without arguments (Chapter 3) replaces Java’s [if] sequence;
  • lines 93–94: an error in the DBMS. Hibernate writes this as two messages: one providing the error codes (which we ignore) and the other providing the error text;
  • lines 97–99: execution of a batch of SQL commands, which we will encounter at the end of the chapter;
  • lines 102–111: the function [withoutLog] executes a logless action SQL. This is a higher-order function (Chapter 7): its parameter is a function [() -> T], and it returns the result of the action (Java, which uses a [Runnable], does not allow this quite so easily). It uses Logback’s API: each log ([Logger]) has a level, which can be modified at runtime (the [level] property, which corresponds to the Java methods [getLevel]/[setLevel]). We set the five logs to level [OFF], execute the action, and then restore the original levels in a [finally] clause, so that they remain at those levels even if the action throws an exception. The original level may be [null] (a log that inherits its level from its parent), hence the type [List<Level?>]; [zip] associates each log with its original level, and the [(logger, level)] decomposition (Chapter 3) names the two elements of each pair;
  • line 104: [LoggerFactory] is the class of SLF4J that returns a log; Since Logback is the current implementation of SLF4J, the rendered object is a [ch.qos.logback.classic.Logger], as indicated by the type conversion [as Logger].

The [tools] subproject also contains the [logback.xml] file used by the examples (it is the same file as in Java). Placed at the root of the classpath ([src/main/resources]), it is found by Logback when the program starts:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- Logback configuration for the examples of the chapter -->
<configuration>

    <!-- the compact SQL log: layout by the [tools.SqlLog] class -->
    <appender name="SQL" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder class="ch.qos.logback.core.encoder.LayoutWrappingEncoder">
            <layout class="tools.SqlLog"/>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <!-- the other messages: level, short name of the logger, text -->
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%-5level %logger{0} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <!-- the SQL statements (DEBUG), their parameters, the transactions, the batches (TRACE) and the errors -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.SQL" level="DEBUG" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind" level="TRACE" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc" level="TRACE" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.batch" level="TRACE" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error" level="WARN" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>

    <!-- Hibernate's built-in connection pool is enough for our examples: its warning is silenced -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.connections.pooling" level="ERROR"/>

    <!-- dropping the tables of an empty database causes harmless errors: they are silenced -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.tool.schema" level="OFF"/>

    <!-- all the other loggers: warnings and errors only -->
    <root level="WARN">
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>
  • lines 6–10: An “appender” writes the messages, in this case to the console. It uses our layout, identified by its class name ([tools.SqlLog]);
  • lines 13–17: a second “appender” for the other messages: level, short log name, text;
  • Lines 20–34: The Hibernate logs from the previous table, along with their levels. Their messages are sent to the “appender” [SQL] and only to it ([additivity="false"]: they are not additionally forwarded to the root log);
  • line 37: the warning regarding Hibernate’s built-in connection pool is suppressed;
  • line 40: Hibernate deletes tables starting with their foreign keys; on an empty database, these deletions fail without consequence, but Hibernate logs this at length. These messages are suppressed;
  • lines 43–45: the other logs record only warnings and errors.

The build file for the [tools] subproject is that of a library (Chapter 6):

// library: the compact log of the SQL statements executed by Hibernate
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    // the library plugin: it adds the [api] configuration
    `java-library`
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // Logback, which will receive the Hibernate log (JBoss Logging detects it);
    // [api]: the SqlLog class derives from a Logback class, its users must see it
    api("ch.qos.logback:logback-classic:1.5.38")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}
  • line 5: the library plugin, which adds the [api] configuration;
  • line 15: the only dependency, Logback. It is declared by [api] and not by [implementation]: the class [SqlLog] derives from a Logback class, and the subprojects that use it must be able to see this parent class at compile time. A dependency on [api] is provided to users of the library, for both compilation and runtime.

A library does not typically impose its logging configuration on the applications that use it; we are doing so here to avoid repeating this file in every example.

docs.title: 11.4.2. The Entity and the Article Database
docs.text:
The [Article] entity in the [articles] subproject uses the annotations from the previous paragraph:

package articles

import jakarta.persistence.Column
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.Table
import jakarta.persistence.UniqueConstraint
import java.math.BigDecimal

// an article of the shop, with the annotations that specify its table
// an ordinary class (not a data class); the [jpa] plugin adds a parameterless constructor to it,
// the [allopen] plugin makes it open (non-final), as well as its properties
@Entity
@Table(
    name = "articles",
    uniqueConstraints = [UniqueConstraint(name = "uk_articles_name", columnNames = ["name"])]
)
class Article(
    // name of the article: mandatory, at most 30 characters, unique (see @Table)
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    var name: String,
    // price: 10 digits of which 2 after the decimal point
    @Column(nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    var price: BigDecimal,
    // current stock and minimum stock below which restocking is needed
    var currentStock: Int,
    var minimumStock: Int,
) {
    // primary key, generated by the DBMS (AUTO_INCREMENT): null as long as the article is not saved
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
        // no modification by the application: the identifier is managed by Hibernate
        protected set

    // display
    override fun toString() = "[%d, %s, %.2f, %d, %d]".format(id, name, price, currentStock, minimumStock)
}
  • lines 13–14: a reminder of what the [jpa] and [allopen] plugins do for this class;
  • lines 16–18: the table is named [articles], as in Chapter 10. The parameter [uniqueConstraints] declares a uniqueness constraint, named [uk_articles_name], on the column [name]: two items cannot have the same name. Without an explicit name, Hibernate would generate an unreadable one ([UK3f8k...]), which would appear in error messages. Array-type annotation parameters are written in Kotlin within square brackets ([[UniqueConstraint(...)]], [["name"]]); an annotation used as an argument for another annotation is written without [@];
  • lines 22–23: a required name of no more than 30 characters;
  • lines 25–26: a price in the format [decimal(10,2)];
  • lines 28–29: the two stock levels, of type [Int]: columns [NOT NULL];
  • lines 32–36: the identifier. The property modifier is declared as [protected]: the application can read the identifier but cannot change it, since it is managed by Hibernate (the Java class does not have a [setId] method, for the same reason). It could not be [private]: the property is public ([all-open]), and Kotlin prohibits a private modifier on a public property, which a derived class could redefine (“[private setters for open properties are prohibited.]”);
  • line 39: the same method [toString] as in the first example.

The Java version of this class has nearly ninety lines, including the two constructors and about ten accessors ([getX]/[setX]); in Kotlin, the properties of the primary constructor and the two plugins serve this purpose.

The [BaseArticles] object contains the Hibernate configuration for the [hbarticles] database:

package articles

import org.hibernate.SessionFactory
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import tools.SqlLog
import java.math.BigDecimal

// the [hbarticles] database: Hibernate configuration and database initialization
// an [object]: a single instance, without a constructor (Java's utility class)
object BaseArticles {

    // the database; MySQL creates it if it does not exist (createDatabaseIfNotExist)
    const val URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbarticles?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true"
    const val USER = "root"
    const val PASSWORD = ""

    // the Hibernate configuration: entities, database, formatting of the logged SQL
    fun configuration(): HibernatePersistenceConfiguration =
        HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("articles")
            .managedClass(Article::class.java)
            .jdbcUrl(URL)
            .jdbcCredentials(USER, PASSWORD)
            .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)

    // a SessionFactory for the [hbarticles] database, with the previous configuration
    fun createSessionFactory(): SessionFactory = configuration().createEntityManagerFactory()

    // (re)creation of the [articles] table with its six articles, without an SQL log
    fun initialize(sessionFactory: SessionFactory) = SqlLog.withoutLog {
        // dropping then creating the tables of the entities
        sessionFactory.schemaManager.drop(false)
        sessionFactory.schemaManager.create(false)
        // the six articles, added in a transaction
        sessionFactory.inTransaction { session ->
            session.persist(Article("bike", BigDecimal(500), 10, 5))
            session.persist(Article("pump", BigDecimal(10), 10, 2))
            session.persist(Article("bow", BigDecimal(600), 4, 1))
            session.persist(Article("arrows - set of 6", BigDecimal(100), 12, 20))
            session.persist(Article("diving suit", BigDecimal(300), 8, 2))
            session.persist(Article("diver's oxygen tanks", BigDecimal(120), 10, 5))
        }
    }
}
  • line 11: a [object] (Chapter 4): a singleton, created on first use. This is equivalent to a Java utility class (a [final] class with static members and a private constructor);
  • lines 14–16: the base URL and the user URL, which are public so that other subprojects can use them;
  • Lines 19–24: The Hibernate configuration. It is returned by a public function, which will allow an example to complete it before creating the [SessionFactory]. The [FORMAT_SQL] ([hibernate.format_sql]) property instructs Hibernate to format the SQL, which it then passes to the [org.hibernate.SQL] log: it is this formatted output that the [SqlLog] class then condenses;
  • line 27: the [SessionFactory] from the [hbarticles] base, a function whose body is an expression;
  • lines 30–41: a function that recreates the table [articles] with its six entries, without the log SQL: we do not want to see the SQL from this initialization in the example results. The block passed to [withoutLog] is a lambda written after the parentheses, which are omitted here (Chapter 7);
  • line 35: [sessionFactory.inTransaction { session -> ... }] opens a session, starts a transaction, executes the lambda by passing it the session, commits the transaction (or rolls it back if the lambda throws an exception), and closes the session. This is the shortest way to write a unit of work; we’ll use it often, along with its variants [inSession] (a session without a transaction), [fromTransaction], and [fromSession] (which return the result of the lambda). The parameter for these Java methods is a functional interface ([Consumer<Session>], [Function<Session, R>]): Kotlin directly accepts a lambda there (conversion SAM, Chapter 7);
  • lines 36–41: [BigDecimal(500)] calls the constructor of [BigDecimal], which takes an integer; it returns the same value as the Java method [BigDecimal.valueOf(500)].

The [articles] subproject depends on the [tools] subproject, Hibernate, and the JDBC driver:

// library: the [Article] entity and the factory of the SessionFactory of the [hbarticles] database
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    // the parameterless constructor of the entities ("no-arg" plugin configured for JPA)
    kotlin("plugin.jpa")
    // entities and properties made open (non-final): Hibernate can derive proxies from them
    kotlin("plugin.allopen")
    // the library plugin: it adds the [api] configuration
    `java-library`
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // the compact SQL log (and Logback)
    api(project(":tools"))
    // Hibernate: [api], because the users of the library handle SessionFactory, Session...
    api("org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-core:7.4.5.Final")
    // the MySQL JDBC driver: only useful at runtime
    runtimeOnly("com.mysql:mysql-connector-j:9.7.0")
}

// the classes annotated this way are opened by the [allopen] plugin
allOpen {
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.Entity")
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.MappedSuperclass")
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.Embeddable")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}
  • lines 5–9: the library defines an entity; it applies both entity plugins and the library plugin;
  • line 18: the dependency on another subproject in the build, identified by its path ([":tools"]);
  • line 20: Hibernate, declared by [api]: subprojects that use the library directly manipulate its types ([SessionFactory], [Session]...);
  • line 22: the driver JDBC, required only at runtime;
  • lines 26–29: the configuration for the [all-open] plugin.

The example subprojects then require only one dependency: the [articles] subproject. Gradle adds its dependencies (known as transitive dependencies): the [api] dependencies for compilation and execution, and the [runtimeOnly] dependency for execution. Here is the build file for the [crud] subproject:

// the basic operations: persist, find, merge, remove; the states of an entity
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    // no [jpa] or [allopen] plugin: the subproject does not define any entity
    // (the Article class is compiled in the [articles] subproject)
    application
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // the [Article] entity and the [hbarticles] database (Hibernate, MySQL and the SQL log included)
    implementation(project(":articles"))
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
    // the program run by [gradlew -q :crud:run], launched in the 11-hibernate folder
    mainClass = "crud.MainKt"
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}
  • line 4: the subproject does not define any entities: it does not need the plugins [jpa] and [allopen], which are used when compiling annotated classes, in this case those from the [articles] subproject;
  • line 15: the only dependency;
  • Lines 31–34: The programs launched by Gradle write their output to UTF-8 so that accented characters display correctly on Windows (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 11.4.3. Other Ways to Configure Hibernate
docs.text:
We configure Hibernate programmatically using [HibernatePersistenceConfiguration]. There are other ways to do this, which can be found in applications and documentation:

  • a [META-INF/persistence.xml] file, the traditional approach used by Jakarta Persistence: it describes one or more persistence units (entity classes, connection properties, options), and the factory is created using [Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("articles")];
  • a [hibernate.properties] (or [hibernate.cfg.xml]) file, specific to Hibernate, read by the [org.hibernate.cfg.Configuration] class: [Configuration().addAnnotatedClass(Article::class.java).buildSessionFactory()]. This is the approach used in older versions of Hibernate;
  • In a Spring Boot application, the properties [spring.datasource.*] and [spring.jpa.*] in the file [application.properties]: Spring Boot creates the factory itself.

The properties are the same everywhere ([hibernate.format_sql], [jakarta.persistence.jdbc.url]...): only the way they are specified changes.

docs.title: 11.5. Basic operations: add, read, update, delete
11.5.1. The [crud] program
docs.text:
The [crud] subproject demonstrates the four basic operations (CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete), as well as entity tracking via the session. To make this tracking visible, it uses a few internal Hibernate methods (its “SPI,” Service Provider Interface), intended for Hibernate extensions rather than applications: they are grouped in the utility functions at the end of the file, written as extension functions of [Session] (Chapter 4). Transactions are written using the session’s [inTransaction] method, a higher-order function: [session.inTransaction { ... }] starts a transaction, executes the block, and then commits the transaction or rolls it back if the block throws an exception. The code can no longer omit [commit] or [rollback] in the event of an error.

package crud

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import org.hibernate.Session
import org.hibernate.engine.spi.PersistenceContext
import org.hibernate.engine.spi.SessionImplementor
import java.math.BigDecimal

fun main() {
    BaseArticles.createSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
        // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
        BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory)
        sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
            // 1 - search by the primary key
            println("--- find(1)")
            val bike = session.find(Article::class.java, 1) ?: error("no article no. 1")
            println(bike)
            println("--- find(1) a second time")
            val bike2 = session.find(Article::class.java, 1)
            println("same object: ${bike === bike2}")

            // 2 - adding an article, in a transaction
            println("--- persist")
            val x = Article("x", BigDecimal(100), 10, 1)
            session.inTransaction {
                println("before persist: state=${session.state(x)}, id=${x.id}")
                session.persist(x)
                println("after persist: state=${session.state(x)}, id=${x.id}")
            }

            // 3 - modification: it is enough to modify the object
            println("--- modification of the price")
            session.inTransaction {
                x.price *= BigDecimal("1.1")
                println("session modified: ${session.isDirty}, " +
                    "original price=${session.originalValue(x, "price")}, current price=${x.price}")
                println("--- commit")
            }
            println("after commit: session modified: ${session.isDirty}")

            // 4 - deletion
            println("--- remove")
            session.inTransaction {
                session.remove(x)
                println("before commit: state=${session.state(x)}")
            }
            println("after commit: state=${session.state(x)}")

            // 5 - a detached object, modified then merged with the session
            println("--- detach and merge")
            val bow = session.find(Article::class.java, 3) ?: error("no article no. 3")
            session.detach(bow)
            println("after detach: state=${session.state(bow)}")
            bow.price = BigDecimal(550)
            session.inTransaction {
                val managedBow = session.merge(bow)
                println("merge: same object=${bow === managedBow}, " +
                    "state of the returned object=${session.state(managedBow)}")
            }

            // 6 - the entities tracked by the session
            println("--- the tracked entities")
            bike.currentStock--
            session.displayTrackedEntities()
        }
    }
}

// the persistence context of the session (Hibernate internal API): an extension property
private val Session.trackingContext: PersistenceContext
    get() = unwrap(SessionImplementor::class.java).persistenceContext

// the state of an article with respect to the session (Hibernate internal API)
private fun Session.state(article: Article): String = when {
    // an object tracked by the session: MANAGED, DELETED...
    trackingContext.isEntryFor(article) -> trackingContext.getEntry(article).status.name
    // an object unknown to the session: never saved (without an identifier) or detached
    article.id == null -> "TRANSIENT"
    else -> "DETACHED"
}

// the value of a property as it was read from the database (Hibernate internal API)
private fun Session.originalValue(entity: Any, property: String): Any? =
    trackingContext.getEntry(entity).getLoadedValue(property)

// the entities of the persistence context of the session (Hibernate internal API)
private fun Session.displayTrackedEntities() {
    for ((entity, entry) in trackingContext.reentrantSafeEntityEntries()) {
        val persister = entry.persister
        println("${persister.entityName} #${entry.id} ${entry.status}")
        // current values of the properties, compared with the values read from the database
        val current = persister.getValues(entity)
        val originals = entry.loadedState
        persister.propertyNames.forEachIndexed { i, name ->
            val modification = if (current[i] == originals[i]) ""
                else " (modified, original value: ${originals[i]})"
            println("    $name : ${current[i]}$modification")
        }
    }
    println("session modified: $isDirty")
}

Comments:

  • Line 17: [session.find(Article::class.java, 1)] searches for the primary key record 1. It returns [null] if the key does not exist; the operator [?:] then throws an exception ([error], Chapter 3), and [bike] is of type [Article], which is non-nullable. The generated SQL (lines 3–6 of the results) is a parameterized [SELECT], whose parameter is set to 1: the compact log now displays the parameter values;
  • line 20: the second call to [find(Article::class.java, 1)] does not send any SQL commands and returns the same object (line 9). The [===] operator compares references (the Java [] operator), whereas [] would call [equals] (Chapter 3). The session stores the entities it has read or saved in its persistence context—also known as the first-level cache: before querying the database, [find] checks to see if the requested entity is already there. A session never contains two objects for the same row in the database;
  • Lines 25–29: adding an item. Before [persist], the object is [TRANSIENT] (“transient”): the session does not recognize it, and its identifier is [null] (line 12). [persist] brings it into the session, which immediately executes the command [INSERT] (lines 13–18) to obtain the generated key, and places it in the field [id] (Hibernate writes to the field directly: the property’s protected modifier does not prevent this). The item is then [MANAGED] (“managed” or “persistent”), and its identifier is 7 (line 19). The transaction is opened at the beginning of the block [inTransaction] and committed at its end (lines 11 and 20 of the results). The block parameter ([Transaction]) is not used: it is not named;
  • line 35: to modify a row in the database, simply modify the object. No [update] method is required: the session has retained a copy of the read or saved values (the original state) and compares the current values to those. This is known as “dirty checking.” The [*=] operator is translated here by Kotlin into [x.price = x.price * BigDecimal("1.1")]: a new [BigDecimal] object (which is immutable) is assigned to the property;
  • Lines 36–37: The property [isDirty] (the Java method [isDirty()]) indicates whether the session contains changes that have not yet been committed to the database: this is the case (line 23). The function [originalValue] (lines 84–85) reads the original price value, 100, from the persistence context, whereas the current value is 110.0;
  • line 38: the end of the block. The subsequent [commit] synchronizes the session with the database (“flush”): the [UPDATE] command is executed (lines 25–32), and then the transaction is committed. After that, the session has no pending changes (line 34);
  • Note that the [UPDATE] command writes all columns in the table, not just the one that has changed. This is Hibernate’s default behavior: a single SQL command, prepared once and for all, is used for all article modifications. In contrast, the [@DynamicUpdate] annotation placed on the entity instructs it to generate a query limited to the modified columns each time;
  • Lines 45–48: deletion. [remove] changes the article’s status to [DELETED] (line 37); [commit] sends the command [DELETE] (lines 38–40). The object is then no longer recognized by the session: it becomes [DETACHED] (“detached,” line 42);
  • lines 52–55: the bow is read (lines 44–47), then detached from the session by [detach]: the session forgets it (line 48). Any change to its price is then ignored. A detached object is a common occurrence in an application: it is an object read by a session that is now closed—for example, during a previous HTTP query—and subsequently modified by the user;
  • line 57: [session.merge(bow)] merges the detached object with the session. The session reads the item from the database (lines 50–53), copies the state of the detached object into the entity it manages, and returns the latter: this is not the same object (line 54). The object passed to [merge] remains detached; the returned object is the one that must be used next. [commit] records the new price (lines 55–62);
  • line 64: the bike’s inventory is updated, without a transaction;
  • lines 71–72: the session’s persistence context, obtained via an extension property: in the following functions, [trackingContext] is treated as a session property. [unwrap] provides access to the session’s internal interface [SessionImplementor];
  • lines 75–80: the status of an item, calculated by a [when] without arguments. First, [isEntryFor] is used to check whether the session is associated with the item: the [getEntry] method, which returns [null] for an unknown object (which is what the Java code tests for), is nevertheless annotated as [@NonNull] in Hibernate. Kotlin takes these nullability annotations from the Java libraries into account: it considers that [getEntry] returns a non-nullable [EntityEntry] and flags a check for [?.] on its result (“[unnecessary safe call on a non-null receiver of type 'EntityEntry'.]”) as unnecessary ( a warning, and thus an error with our compilation options). This is a rare but instructive case: the types in a Java library are always exactly what their annotations specify;
  • Lines 88–101: display of the persistence context. For each tracked entity ([EntityEntry]), its name, identifier, and state are displayed, followed by the current value of each property and its original value if it differs. The [EntityPersister] object is the one in Hibernate that knows the mapping between an entity and its table: it provides the names of the properties and their values. The [for ((entity, entry) in ...)] loop unpacks each element of the array, a [Map.Entry] (Chapter 5); [forEachIndexed] iterates over the property names along with their indices. The [==] operator between two values—which can be [null]—replaces Java’s [Objects.equals]. In an extension function, [isDirty] refers to the receiver’s property, the session;
  • Lines 65–75 of the results: The session tracks the bike, whose stock has changed from 10 to 9, and the bow. The change to the bike is not saved: the session is closed without synchronization. There is no [commit], and a session does not synchronize automatically upon closure.

docs.title: 11.5.2. The States of an Entity
docs.text:
An entity is, with respect to a session, in one of the following states (Jakarta Persistence refers to them as “new,” “managed,” “detached,” and “removed”):

StateMeaningtransient ([TRANSIENT])The object was created by a constructor call and has never been registered: it has no identifier, and no session is aware of itManaged ([MANAGED])The object has been read or saved by the session, which is tracking it: changes to it will be reflected in the database during the next synchronizationDeleted ([DELETED])The object has been marked for deletion ([remove]): the next synchronization will send the command [DELETE]detached ([DETACHED])The object corresponds to a row in the database, but the session that read it is closed or has forgotten it ([detach], [clear]): its changes are ignored unless it is merged with a session ([merge])

Synchronizing (“flushing”) the session sends the SQL commands to the DBMS, which propagate the changes to the managed entities. This occurs:

  • during the [commit] phase of the transaction;
  • before executing a query whose result might depend on changes that have not yet been committed ([FlushMode.AUTO] mode, the default mode): the query thus sees the session data;
  • during an explicit call to [session.flush()]. The commands are then executed, but they will not be permanently saved until the transaction’s [commit].

Here’s an overview of the workflow with Hibernate: we open a session and a transaction, read entities, modify them as ordinary objects, add them ([persist]), and delete them ([remove]), then commit the transaction, which sends all necessary commands to the database in a single batch. The session acts as a “unit of work.” It is a lightweight object designed for a short lifespan: a unit of work, such as a HTTP request in a web application. You do not use the same session throughout the entire lifetime of an application—it would accumulate the tracked entities in its persistence context.

In Kotlin, this cycle is naturally implemented using Hibernate’s higher-order functions: [sessionFactory.inTransaction { session -> ... }] for a complete unit of work (session and transaction), [sessionFactory.fromTransaction { session -> ... }] when it returns a result, and [session.inTransaction { ... }] for a transaction within an already open session. In short, these are the equivalents of the [use] function for transactions.

docs.title: 11.6.1. HQL and JPQL
docs.text:
To retrieve entities other than by their primary key, queries are written in a language similar to SQL, but one that refers to entities and attributes rather than tables and columns: HQL (Hibernate Query Language). Jakarta Persistence defines a similar language, JPQL (Jakarta Persistence Query Language), of which HQL is a superset: a JPQL query is a valid HQL query. Hibernate translates the query into SQL, in the DBMS dialect, and it is the DBMS that executes it.

Some differences from SQL:

  • We use the entity name ([Article]), not the table name ([articles]), and the attribute names ([currentStock]), not the column names. Entity and attribute names are case-sensitive, just like in Kotlin. With our Kotlin entities, an attribute’s name is the same as the property’s name (Hibernate accesses the field that stores it, and that field is named after the property);
  • the clause [select] is optional in HQL: [from Article] returns entities [Article]. JPQL requires writing [select a from Article a];
  • relationships between entities are traversed using a dot ([p.category.name]), with Hibernate writing the joins itself, as we will see.

A query is created by the session's [createSelectionQuery] method, which receives the text HQL and the result type ([Article::class.java], the Java class of the entity), and returns a [SelectionQuery<T>] object. You can then assign values to its parameters and execute it with [getResultList] (a list), [getSingleResult] (a single result; an exception if there are zero or more), [getSingleResultOrNull] ([null] if there are none), or [getResultStream] (a stream). As is always the case with Java classes, Kotlin allows you to write these parameterless [getXxx] methods as properties: [query.resultList], [query.singleResult], [query.singleResultOrNull]. The [createQuery] method from Jakarta Persistence also exists; it is used for both read queries and updates.

docs.title: 11.6.2. The program [hql]
docs.text:
The [hql] subproject provides several examples of queries. It has only one dependency: the [articles] library (which provides Hibernate, the MySQL driver, and the compact SQL log); it does not define any entities, and therefore does not require either the [jpa] plugin or the [allopen] plugin:

// HQL / JPQL queries
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    // no [jpa] or [allopen] plugin: no entity here (Article is compiled in [articles])
    application
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // the [Article] entity and the [hbarticles] database (Hibernate, MySQL and the SQL log included)
    implementation(project(":articles"))
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
    // the program run by [gradlew -q :hql:run]
    mainClass = "hql.MainKt"
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}

The program:

package hql

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import org.hibernate.query.SemanticException
import java.math.BigDecimal

// HQL / JPQL queries on the [articles] table

// a projection: the name of an article and the value of its stock (a data class, not an entity)
data class StockValue(val name: String, val value: BigDecimal)

// a business rule written in Kotlin (an extension function):
// an article is out of stock if its stock is below the minimum stock
fun Article.isOutOfStock() = currentStock < minimumStock

fun main() {
    BaseArticles.createSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
        // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
        BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory)
        sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
            // 1 - filtering and sorting
            println("--- the articles to restock, in alphabetical order")
            val hql = "from Article where currentStock < minimumStock order by name"
            val toOrder = session.createSelectionQuery(hql, Article::class.java).resultList
            toOrder.forEach(::println)

            // 2 - projection: only the useful columns are requested
            println("--- value of the stock of each article")
            val values = session
                .createSelectionQuery(
                    """
                    select name, price * currentStock from Article
                    order by price * currentStock desc""", StockValue::class.java
                )
                .resultList
            for ((name, value) in values) {
                println("%s : %.2f euros".format(name, value))
            }

            // 3 - a single result; the value [minPrice] is passed by a named parameter
            println("--- the first article over 200 euros")
            val minPrice = BigDecimal(200)
            val article: Article? = session
                .createSelectionQuery(
                    """
                    select a from Article a
                    where a.price > :minPrice order by a.price""", Article::class.java
                )
                .setParameter("minPrice", minPrice)
                .setMaxResults(1)
                .singleResultOrNull
            println(article ?: "none")

            // 4 - aggregates: the computation is done by the DBMS
            println("--- aggregates")
            val nbArticles = session
                .createSelectionQuery("select count(*) from Article", Long::class.java)
                .singleResult
            val stockValue = session
                .createSelectionQuery("select sum(price * currentStock) from Article", BigDecimal::class.java)
                .singleResult
            println("%d articles, value of the stock: %.2f euros".format(nbArticles, stockValue))

            // 5 - like and in; a Kotlin list as the value of a parameter
            println("--- like and in")
            val names = listOf("bow", "pump", "racket")
            val results = session
                .createSelectionQuery(
                    """
                    select name from Article
                    where name like 'b%' or name in :names""", String::class.java
                )
                .setParameter("names", names)
                .resultList
            println(results.joinToString(", "))

            // 6 - pagination: the third page of two articles, by ascending price
            println("--- pagination")
            val pageSize = 2
            val pageNumber = 3
            val page = session.createSelectionQuery("from Article order by price", Article::class.java)
                .setFirstResult((pageNumber - 1) * pageSize)
                .setMaxResults(pageSize)
                .resultList
            val text = page.joinToString(", ") { "%s (%.2f euros)".format(it.name, it.price) }
            println("page $pageNumber : $text")

            // 7 - an incorrect query is rejected as soon as it is created, before any execution
            println("--- incorrect query")
            try {
                session.createSelectionQuery("from Article where stock < minimumStock", Article::class.java)
            } catch (e: SemanticException) {
                println("${e.javaClass.simpleName} : ${e.message}")
            }

            // 8 - a rule written in Kotlin cannot be translated into SQL: in-memory filtering
            println("--- in-memory filtering")
            session.createSelectionQuery("from Article", Article::class.java).resultStream.use { stream ->
                stream.filter { it.isOutOfStock() }.forEach(::println)
            }
        }
    }
}
