Comments:

  • Lines 24–26: The clause [where] compares two attributes of the entity; the clause [order by] sorts by name: they become the clauses [WHERE] and [ORDER BY] in the order SQL. The query is executed by [resultList] (the [getResultList] method), which returns a [List<Article>]; [forEach(::println)] displays each item using its method [toString];
  • Lines 30–38: a projection. The query does not return entities, but rather two values per item: the name and the stock value. The generated SQL retrieves only the necessary columns and performs the calculation itself. The result type is the [StockValue] data class from line 11: Hibernate creates one object per row, passing the values from the [select] clause to its constructor in order (the Java course used a record). These objects are not entities: the session does not track them. A data class is perfectly suited for this role, and we take advantage of its destructuring: [for ((name, value) in values)] (line 37);
  • lines 32–34: the query is written in a raw string (["""..."""], Chapter 5), which is more readable than a long string on a single line. Unlike Java text blocks, a raw string preserves its line indentation and the initial line break; this is irrelevant here, since spaces and line breaks do not matter in HQL: there is no need to call [trimIndent];
  • lines 44–53: a query written as in JPQL, with an alias ([a]). [:minPrice] is a named parameter, whose value is given by [setParameter]. It becomes a parameter of the order SQL (the [?] from the clause [WHERE], whose value is displayed by the log): so there is no need to worry about SQL injections, since the value is passed separately from the order text. This is the rule that Chapter 10 applied to prepared statements. [setMaxResults(1)] limits the result to a single row: the [LIMIT] clause of MySQL. [singleResultOrNull] returns a [Article?]: the nullable type clearly states that there may be no result, and the Elvis operator [?:] displays [none] in this case;
  • It’s important to highlight a pitfall specific to Kotlin. Its string templates make it very tempting to write ["... where a.price > $minPrice"]. The program would work, but the value would then be copied into the query text: it is precisely this concatenation that opens the door to injections (Chapter 10), and Hibernate would have to parse a new query for each value. We never use the character [$] to set a value in a query HQL: values are passed via named parameters. A literal value written in the query text (such as ['b%'] on line 72) is also copied into the text of the SQL command, as shown in the log: this is acceptable for a program constant, but never for a value coming from an external source;
  • Lines 57–63: The aggregates [count] and [sum] are calculated by the DBMS: only the result is transferred, not the rows. [Long::class.java] refers to the class of the primitive type [long] in Java (the Kotlin type [Long] is compiled to [long]), whereas the Java course used [Long.class], the wrapper class [java.lang.Long]; Hibernate accepts both (the wrapper class would be written as [Long::class.javaObjectType]). HQL also recognizes [avg], [min], [max], the clauses [group by] and [having];
  • lines 67–76: the [like] operator of SQL, and the [in] operator, whose operand is a parameter that accepts a Kotlin list (a Kotlin [List] is a Hibernate [java.util.List]): Hibernate expands it into as many SQL parameters as there are elements in the list. HQL supports numerous functions on strings ([upper], [length], [substring]...), dates, and numbers, which it translates into the DBMS dialect;
  • lines 82–85: pagination, to display a long list page by page. [setFirstResult] skips the entries from the previous pages, while [setMaxResults] keeps those from the requested page: the [LIMIT ?, ?] clause of MySQL, whose two parameters are 4 and 2. Pagination only makes sense on a sorted list ([order by]). Lines 86–87 construct the page display using [joinToString] and its transformation function (Chapter 5);
  • lines 91–94: a query that uses a [stock] attribute that does not exist. The error is detected as soon as the query is created, before any execution, because Hibernate parses the text HQL and compares it to the model: it throws a [SemanticException] (Hibernate messages are in English). A syntax error would result in a [SyntaxException]. Note that the value returned by [createSelectionQuery] is ignored: in Kotlin, there is no requirement to use the result of a function;
  • lines 15 and 99–100: a query cannot use a Kotlin function, such as the extension function [isOutOfStock]: Hibernate does not know its code, and even if it did, it would not necessarily know how to write it as SQL. You can read all entities and filter them in memory: [resultStream] (the [getResultStream] method) returns a Java [Stream<Article>], which holds a JDBC resource open and must be closed after use: the [use] function handles this, since a [Stream] is a [AutoCloseable]. The result is correct, but the entire table was transferred (the last SQL order has no [WHERE] clause): with a large table, this should be avoided. It’s better to write the condition in the query, as shown on line 24. The extension function also demonstrates a very “Kotlin”-like way of writing a business rule on an entity without modifying its class (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 11.6.3. Named Queries and Compile-Time Validation
docs.text:
A query written in a string is only parsed at runtime. There are two ways to detect errors earlier:

  • Named queries: The [@NamedQuery(name = "Article.outOfStock", query = "from Article where currentStock < minimumStock")] annotation, applied to the entity, declares a query that Hibernate parses at startup, when creating the [SessionFactory]. It is then executed by its name: [session.createNamedSelectionQuery("Article.outOfStock", Article::class.java)]. It is written in Kotlin exactly the same way as in Java; the annotation is repeatable: it is applied as many times as there are queries to declare;
  • the Hibernate annotation processor (“Hibernate Processor,” library [org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-processor]). In Java, it is executed by [javac] during compilation: it checks the queries in the annotations and generates, for each entity, a “metamodel” class ([Article_] for [Article]), which we’ll see again with the API Criteria. This mechanism does not apply solely to Kotlin: we’ll return to this below when discussing the static metamodel.

docs.title: 11.7.1. Queries Built with Code
docs.text:
A HQL query is a string that can be constructed through concatenation (or, in Kotlin, using templates): this approach is unreliable and hard to read as soon as the query depends on many optional criteria (a search form, for example). Jakarta Persistence offers another way to write queries: API Criteria, where the query is a tree of objects built through method calls. Hibernate translates this tree into SQL, just like a HQL query (it also translates HQL into such a tree). The subproject [criteria] (its [build.gradle.kts] is that of the subproject [hql], except for the program name) includes several queries from the previous program:

package criteria

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import jakarta.persistence.criteria.Path
import jakarta.persistence.criteria.Predicate
import org.hibernate.Session
import java.math.BigDecimal
import kotlin.reflect.KProperty1

// queries built with the Criteria API

// a projection: the name of an article and the value of its stock
data class StockValue(val name: String, val value: BigDecimal)

// an attribute designated by a property reference (Article::price), and not by a string ("price"):
// the name is checked by the compiler, and the type of the returned path is that of the property
fun <X, T> Path<X>.get(property: KProperty1<X, T>): Path<T> = get(property.name)

fun main() {
    BaseArticles.createSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
        // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
        BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory)
        sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
            // the factory of the query elements
            val cb = session.criteriaBuilder

            // 1 - filtering and sorting; the attributes are designated by strings
            println("--- the articles to restock, in alphabetical order")
            val query = cb.createQuery(Article::class.java)
            val a = query.from(Article::class.java)
            query.select(a)
                .where(cb.lt(a.get<Int>("currentStock"), a.get<Int>("minimumStock")))
                .orderBy(cb.asc(a.get<String>("name")))
            session.createSelectionQuery(query).resultList.forEach(::println)

            // 2 - projection to a data class; the attributes are designated by references
            println("--- value of the stock of each article")
            val projection = cb.createQuery(StockValue::class.java)
            val p = projection.from(Article::class.java)
            val value = cb.prod(p.get(Article::price), p.get(Article::currentStock))
                .`as`(BigDecimal::class.java)
            projection.select(cb.construct(StockValue::class.java, p.get(Article::name), value))
                .orderBy(cb.desc(value))
            for ((name, v) in session.createSelectionQuery(projection).resultList) {
                println("%s : %.2f euros".format(name, v))
            }

            // 3 - a query built according to the criteria supplied
            println("--- search: maximum price 150 euros")
            search(session, maxPrice = BigDecimal(150)).forEach(::println)
            println("--- search: maximum price 150 euros and name starting with [d]")
            search(session, maxPrice = BigDecimal(150), nameStart = "d").forEach(::println)

            // 4 - aggregates
            println("--- aggregates")
            val count = cb.createQuery(Long::class.java)
            count.select(cb.count(count.from(Article::class.java)))
            val nbArticles = session.createSelectionQuery(count).singleResult
            val sum = cb.createQuery(BigDecimal::class.java)
            val s = sum.from(Article::class.java)
            val articleValue = cb.prod(s.get(Article::price), s.get(Article::currentStock))
                .`as`(BigDecimal::class.java)
            sum.select(cb.sum(articleValue))
            val stockValue = session.createSelectionQuery(sum).singleResult
            println("%d articles, value of the stock: %.2f euros".format(nbArticles, stockValue))
        }
    }
}

// the articles whose price does not exceed [maxPrice] and whose name starts with [nameStart],
// each criterion being used only if it is not null
fun search(session: Session, maxPrice: BigDecimal? = null, nameStart: String? = null): List<Article> {
    val cb = session.criteriaBuilder
    val query = cb.createQuery(Article::class.java)
    val a = query.from(Article::class.java)
    // the conditions, added one by one
    val conditions = buildList<Predicate> {
        maxPrice?.let { add(cb.le(a.get(Article::price), it)) }
        nameStart?.let { add(cb.like(a.get(Article::name), "$it%")) }
    }
    query.select(a).where(conditions).orderBy(cb.asc(a.get(Article::price)))
    return session.createSelectionQuery(query).resultList
}

Results:

> gradlew -q :criteria:run
--- the articles to restock, in alphabetical order
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.currentStock<a1_0.minimumStock
    SQL> order by a1_0.name
[4, arrows - set of 6, 100.00, 12, 20]
--- value of the stock of each article
    SQL> select a1_0.name, (a1_0.price*a1_0.currentStock)
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> order by (a1_0.price*a1_0.currentStock) desc
bike : 5000.00 euros
bow : 2400.00 euros
diving suit : 2400.00 euros
arrows - set of 6 : 1200.00 euros
diver's oxygen tanks : 1200.00 euros
pump : 100.00 euros
--- search: maximum price 150 euros
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.price<=?
    SQL> order by a1_0.price
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 150
[2, pump, 10.00, 10, 2]
[4, arrows - set of 6, 100.00, 12, 20]
[6, diver's oxygen tanks, 120.00, 10, 5]
--- search: maximum price 150 euros and name starting with [d]
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.price<=? and a1_0.name like ? escape ''
    SQL> order by a1_0.price
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 150
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = d%
[6, diver's oxygen tanks, 120.00, 10, 5]
--- aggregates
    SQL> select count(a1_0.id)
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> select sum((a1_0.price*a1_0.currentStock))
    SQL> from articles a1_0
6 articles, value of the stock: 12300.00 euros

Comments:

  • line 26: the session returns a [HibernateCriteriaBuilder] ([criteriaBuilder], the [getCriteriaBuilder] method), the Hibernate-enhanced version of Jakarta Persistence’s [CriteriaBuilder]: This is the factory for all elements of a query (conditions, expressions, sorts);
  • lines 30–34: the query from the first example, HQL. [createQuery(Article::class.java)] creates a query that returns articles; [from(Article::class.java)] declares the queried entity and returns its root ([Root<Article>]), which is the equivalent of the alias [a] for [from Article a]; [a.get<Int>("currentStock")] designates an attribute. The condition is constructed by [cb.lt(x, y)] (“less than,” [x < y]), and the sort by [cb.asc(...)]. The explicit type argument [<Int>] (in Java: [a.<Integer>get(...)]) specifies the attribute’s type, which cannot be determined from the string ["currentStock"]. The compiler cannot verify that it is correct: it takes our word for it;
  • line 35: the query is executed by the session, as a HQL query. The generated SQL is the same as that of the HQL query;
  • line 18: an extension function of the Jakarta Persistence interface [Path], which refers to an attribute using a property reference ([Article::price], of type [KProperty1<Article, BigDecimal>], Chapter 7) rather than a string. It simply passes the property name ([property.name], here ["price"]) to the original [get] method, but it provides two guarantees: the compiler verifies that the property exists, and the type of the rendered path ([Path<BigDecimal>]) is inferred from that of the property, without an explicit type argument. This relies on the fact that the attribute name JPA is the same as the Kotlin property name, which is the case for our entities;
  • Lines 39–46: a projection to the data class [StockValue], using the extension function: [p.get(Article::price)]. [cb.prod(x, y)] is the product of two expressions; [as(BigDecimal::class.java)] specifies the result type ([as] is a Kotlin keyword: to call the Java method with this name, it is enclosed in grave accents); [cb.construct(StockValue::class.java, ...)] indicates that each line of the result must be passed to the data class’s constructor;
  • Lines 73–83: This is where the API Criteria function is most useful. The [search] function constructs a query based on the criteria provided. Its criteria are nullable parameters with a default value ([maxPrice: BigDecimal? = null]), which allows for the named-argument calls in lines 51 and 53 (in Java, [null] had to be passed explicitly). The list of conditions is constructed by [buildList]: each condition is added to it only if the corresponding criterion is not [null] ([maxPrice?.let { ... \}]), and the clause [where] receives the entire list ([where(conditions)], an overhead introduced with Jakarta Persistence 3.2), with the conditions combined by [and]. The first call produces a query with one condition; the second produces a query with two conditions. Note that with the API Criteria, Hibernate passes the values ([150], [d%]) as parameters in the order SQL: the template ["$it%"] on line 80 constructs the value for the parameter (the pattern for [like]), not the query text;
  • Lines 57–64: the aggregates [count] and [sum].

docs.title: 11.7.2. The Static Metamodel
docs.text:
The weakness of the queries in the first example is that attributes are designated by strings ([a.get<Int>("currentStock")]): a typo will not be detected until runtime, and the compiler ignores the attribute’s type. To address this, Jakarta Persistence provides a static metamodel: for each entity [Article], there is a class [Article_] that contains one field per attribute, describing its name and type. In Java, you then write ***[cb.lt(a.get(Article\_.currentStock), a.get(Article\_.minimumStock))]***, which the compiler fully validates. These classes are not written by hand: they are generated during compilation by Hibernate’s annotation processor. This is the recommended approach in a Java project that uses the API Criteria.

In Kotlin, it’s not quite that simple. The Hibernate annotation processor is a Java annotation processor: it is executed by [javac] on Java source code, but our entities are compiled by the Kotlin compiler. The Kotlin tool for this type of code generation is KSP (Kotlin Symbol Processing), but Hibernate does not provide a KSP processor. That leaves kapt (“Kotlin annotation processing tool”), which runs Java processors on “stubs ” generated from Kotlin code; however, kapt is in maintenance mode at JetBrains (which recommends KSP), it slows down compilation, and the kapt + Hibernate Processor combination is not a configuration documented by Hibernate. Therefore, we do not use it. Kotlin’s property references provide much of the benefit without any tools: with the program’s extension function, a typo is detected at compile time. Here’s what the compiler says for [a.get(Article::stock)], compiled into a test file:

Typo.kt:9:50: error: unresolved reference 'stock'.
fun condition(a: Path<Article>) = a.get(Article::stock)
                                                 ^^^^^

(The compiler also displays, beforehand, the list of candidate [get] methods, none of which are suitable.) However, the check is not comprehensive: a Kotlin property that is not a persistent attribute (a computed property, for example) would be accepted by the compiler but rejected by Hibernate at runtime.

For a fixed query, HQL is more readable than the API Criteria; for a query that is constructed based on the circumstances, the API Criteria is safer. The two can be combined: Hibernate allows you to create a Criteria query from a HQL ([cb.createQuery(hql, Article::class.java)]) string and then supplement it with code.

docs.title: 11.8.1. The Store Model
docs.text:
The tables in a database are linked to one another. Hibernate represents these links as associations: properties that reference another entity or a collection of entities. The [relations] subproject uses a [hbshop] database that describes a small store with six entities. Since it defines entities, its [build.gradle.kts] applies the [jpa] and [allopen] plugins, just like the one in the [articles] library; it depends directly on the [tools] library (the SQL log), Hibernate, and the MySQL driver:

// relationships between entities: the [hbshop] database
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    // the parameterless constructor of the entities ("no-arg" plugin configured for JPA)
    kotlin("plugin.jpa")
    // entities and properties made open (non-final): Hibernate can derive proxies from them
    kotlin("plugin.allopen")
    application
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // the compact SQL log (and Logback)
    implementation(project(":tools"))
    // Hibernate and the MySQL JDBC driver
    implementation("org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-core:7.4.5.Final")
    runtimeOnly("com.mysql:mysql-connector-j:9.7.0")
}

// the classes annotated this way are opened by the [allopen] plugin
allOpen {
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.Entity")
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.MappedSuperclass")
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.Embeddable")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
    // the program run by [gradlew -q :relations:run]
    mainClass = "relations.MainKt"
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}

A category groups products together:

package relations

import jakarta.persistence.CascadeType
import jakarta.persistence.Column
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.OneToMany
import jakarta.persistence.Table

// a category groups several products (one-to-many relationship)
@Entity
@Table(name = "categories")
class Category(
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    var name: String,
) {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
        protected set

    // the products of the category: the inverse side of the relationship, described by Product.category
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "category", cascade = [CascadeType.PERSIST])
    val products: MutableList<Product> = mutableListOf()

    // adding a product: the two sides of the relationship are updated
    fun add(product: Product) {
        products += product
        product.category = this
    }
}

A product belongs to a category and has tags:

package relations

import jakarta.persistence.CascadeType
import jakarta.persistence.Column
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.FetchType
import jakarta.persistence.ForeignKey
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.JoinColumn
import jakarta.persistence.JoinTable
import jakarta.persistence.ManyToMany
import jakarta.persistence.ManyToOne
import jakarta.persistence.Table
import java.math.BigDecimal

// a product belongs to a category and carries several tags
@Entity
@Table(name = "products")
class Product(
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    var name: String,
    @Column(nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    var price: BigDecimal,
    vararg tags: Tag,
) {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
        protected set

    // many-to-one relationship: the foreign key [category_id] of the [products] table
    // [lateinit]: the category is filled in after construction, by Category.add
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "category_id", foreignKey = ForeignKey(name = "fk_products_category"))
    lateinit var category: Category
        internal set

    // many-to-many relationship, stored in an association table
    @ManyToMany(cascade = [CascadeType.PERSIST])
    @JoinTable(
        name = "products_tags",
        joinColumns = [JoinColumn(name = "product_id")],
        inverseJoinColumns = [JoinColumn(name = "tag_id")],
        foreignKey = ForeignKey(name = "fk_products_tags_product"),
        inverseForeignKey = ForeignKey(name = "fk_products_tags_tag"),
    )
    val tags: MutableSet<Tag> = mutableSetOf()

    init {
        // only the owning side of the relationship is filled in: it is the one Hibernate saves
        this.tags += tags
    }
}

A tag is assigned to multiple products:

package relations

import jakarta.persistence.Column
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.ManyToMany
import jakarta.persistence.Table

// a tag (promo, new...) is carried by several products
@Entity
@Table(name = "tags")
class Tag(
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 20)
    var label: String,
) {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
        protected set

    // the inverse side of the relationship described by Product.tags
    @ManyToMany(mappedBy = "tags")
    val products: MutableSet<Product> = mutableSetOf()
}

A customer places orders:

package relations

import jakarta.persistence.CascadeType
import jakarta.persistence.Column
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.OneToMany
import jakarta.persistence.Table

// a client places orders
@Entity
@Table(name = "clients")
class Client(
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    var name: String,
) {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
        protected set

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "client", cascade = [CascadeType.PERSIST])
    val orders: MutableList<CustomerOrder> = mutableListOf()

    // adding an order: the two sides of the relationship are updated
    fun add(order: CustomerOrder) {
        orders += order
        order.client = this
    }
}

An order belongs to a customer and contains line items:

package relations

import jakarta.persistence.CascadeType
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.FetchType
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.JoinColumn
import jakarta.persistence.ManyToOne
import jakarta.persistence.OneToMany
import jakarta.persistence.Table
import java.time.LocalDate

// an order of a client, made of lines
@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
class CustomerOrder(
    var date: LocalDate,
) {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
        protected set

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "client_id")
    lateinit var client: Client
        internal set

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = [CascadeType.PERSIST])
    val lines: MutableList<OrderLine> = mutableListOf()

    // adding a line: the two sides of the relationship are updated
    fun add(line: OrderLine) {
        lines += line
        line.order = this
    }
}

An order line has an ID, a quantity, and two many-to-one associations—one to its order and one to its product:

package relations

import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.FetchType
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.JoinColumn
import jakarta.persistence.ManyToOne
import jakarta.persistence.Table

// an order line: a quantity of a product
@Entity
@Table(name = "order_lines")
class OrderLine(
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "product_id")
    var product: Product,
    var quantity: Int,
) {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
        protected set

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "order_id")
    lateinit var order: CustomerOrder
        internal set
}

It contains three types of associations:

  • a many-to-one relationship ([@ManyToOne]): a product belongs to a category (the property [category] of [Product]). In the database, this is represented by a foreign key, the column [category_id] in the table [products], where [@JoinColumn] specifies the name and the constraint name ([fk_products_category]). [optional = false] makes the relationship mandatory: the column will be [NOT NULL]. Note the syntax for nested annotations in Kotlin: an annotation passed as an argument to another is written without [@] ([foreignKey = ForeignKey(name = ...)]), and an array of annotations is written in square brackets ([joinColumns = [JoinColumn(name = "product_id")]]), such as the array [cascade = [CascadeType.PERSIST]];
  • the inverse, one-to-many relationship ([@OneToMany]): a category contains multiple products (the property [products] of [Category]). It does not create anything in the database: [mappedBy = "category"] indicates that it is described by the property [category] of the entity [Product]. [Product.category] is said to be the owner side of the relationship, and [Category.products] its inverse side: Hibernate stores the value of the owner side. However, both sides must be kept consistent in memory: this is the role of the function [add] of [Category], which adds the product to the list ([products += product], the [+=] operator for a mutable collection, Chapter 5) and sets its category;
  • a many-to-many relationship ([@ManyToMany]): a product has multiple tags, and a tag is associated with multiple products. It is stored in an association table, [products_tags], for which [@JoinTable] specifies the name, the names of the two columns, and the names of the two foreign keys (the property [tags] of [Product]). The reverse side is [Tag.products] ([mappedBy = "tags"]). For a many-to-many relationship, a set ([MutableSet]) is preferred over a list ([MutableList]): with a list, Hibernate deletes and re-inserts all rows in the association table every time the collection is modified;
  • [fetch = FetchType.LAZY] requests lazy loading of a product’s category: it will only be read when it is used. This is the default behavior for collections ([@OneToMany], [@ManyToMany]), but not for relationships to a single entity ([@ManyToOne]), which the standard loads immediately by default ([EAGER]): [fetch = FetchType.LAZY] is systematically added to them, as recommended by the Hibernate documentation;
  • [cascade = [CascadeType.PERSIST]] propagates the operation [persist]: persisting a category persists its products, and persisting a product persists its tags. The other values ([MERGE], [REMOVE], [ALL]...) propagate the other operations.

The transition to Kotlin warrants several comments:

  • Collections are declared using Kotlin's mutable interfaces, [MutableList] and [MutableSet], which are initialized by [mutableListOf()] and [mutableSetOf()]. This choice is mandatory: Hibernate replaces the collection of an entity it reads with its own collection (a [PersistentBag] or a [PersistentSet]), which is a mutable [java.util.List] or [java.util.Set], and which can be loaded on demand. A read-only [List] from Kotlin would be acceptable to the compiler, but it would not accurately represent an object that Hibernate and the [add] function modify. Properties are [val]: we modify the contents of the collection, never the reference;
  • a relationship to a single entity, which is required, is declared as [lateinit var category: Category] (in [Product]; the same applies to [CustomerOrder.client] and [OrderLine.order]). The type is not nullable, because a registered product always has a category; however, at the time of its creation, it does not yet have one: [Category.add] will populate it. [lateinit] expresses exactly that: the property will be initialized later, and reading it before then would throw a [UninitializedPropertyAccessException], which is more descriptive than a [NullPointerException]. The Java course had relied on [null] up until then. We could also have written [var category: Category? = null], at the cost of having to use [?.] or [!!] each time;
  • the modifier [internal set] placed under these properties reserves the modification of a product’s category (of an order’s customer, of an order’s line item) for the module—that is, for the Gradle subproject [relations]: only the function [add] uses it. In Java, the method [setCategory] was visible only within the package; Kotlin does not have “package” visibility, and [internal] is the closest equivalent;
  • A product’s tags are passed to its constructor via a [vararg] parameter, which is not a property (there is no [val] or [var]): it is used only in the block [init], which adds them to the set. In this block, [tags] refers to the parameter and [this.tags] to the property; the block [init] is placed after the property declaration, because initializations are executed in the order they appear in the text. The operator [+=] adds all elements of an array to a mutable collection;
  • the parameterless constructor added by the [jpa] plugin (the one Hibernate uses to create the entities it reads) does not execute property initializations: the [tags] collection for a product read by Hibernate is therefore not created by [mutableSetOf()]. This is not a problem, because Hibernate itself populates all associations for the entities it reads using its lazy-loaded collections;
  • entities remain ordinary classes, not data classes. Relationships provide yet another reason for this: the functions [toString], [equals], and [hashCode] generated for a data class all use the properties of its primary constructor; if they included associations, they would iterate over the lazy collections (triggering queries or a [LazyInitializationException] outside the session), and two entities that reference each other would call each other indefinitely ([StackOverflowError]);
  • Finally, the [allopen] plugin is essential here: for a lazy relationship to a single entity, Hibernate places a proxy—an object of a subclass of the entity generated at runtime—in the property, which requires that the class and its accessors be non-final. We’ll see this proxy in action in the program.

The [Shop] object configures Hibernate for the [hbshop] database and creates an initial dataset there:

package relations

import org.hibernate.SessionFactory
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import tools.SqlLog
import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.time.LocalDate

// the [hbshop] database: Hibernate configuration and first data set
object Shop {

    // a SessionFactory for the [hbshop] database and its six entities
    fun createSessionFactory(): SessionFactory =
        HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("shop")
            .managedClasses(
                Category::class.java, Product::class.java, Tag::class.java,
                Client::class.java, CustomerOrder::class.java, OrderLine::class.java,
            )
            .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbshop?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
            .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
            .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
            .createEntityManagerFactory()

    // (re)creation of the tables and of a first data set, without an SQL log
    fun initialize(sessionFactory: SessionFactory) = SqlLog.withoutLog {
        sessionFactory.schemaManager.drop(false)
        sessionFactory.schemaManager.create(false)
        sessionFactory.inTransaction { session ->
            // two tags
            val promo = Tag("promo")
            val novelty = Tag("new")
            // three categories and their products: a graph of objects
            val cycles = Category("cycles")
            cycles.add(Product("bike", BigDecimal(500), promo))
            val pump = Product("pump", BigDecimal(10))
            cycles.add(pump)
            val archery = Category("archery")
            val bow = Product("bow", BigDecimal(600), novelty)
            archery.add(bow)
            archery.add(Product("arrows - set of 6", BigDecimal(100), promo, novelty))
            val diving = Category("diving")
            // the persistence is propagated to the products and to the tags (cascade)
            session.persist(cycles)
            session.persist(archery)
            session.persist(diving)
            // a client and their order of two lines
            val order = CustomerOrder(LocalDate.of(2026, 9, 28))
            order.add(OrderLine(pump, 2))
            order.add(OrderLine(bow, 1))
            val martin = Client("Martin")
            martin.add(order)
            session.persist(martin)
        }
    }
}
  • Line 11: Like [BaseArticles], a [object] replaces the Java utility class;
  • lines 16–18: the six entities, declared by [managedClasses];
  • line 26: the function is an expression: the result of [SqlLog.withoutLog], to which the processing to be executed without a log (SQL) is passed;
  • lines 31–42: an object graph: three categories, their products, and the products’ tags;
  • lines 44–46: it is sufficient to persist the categories: thanks to cascading, Hibernate traverses the associations and persists all the entities it reaches, in the correct order (the categories before the products that reference them), populating the foreign keys and the association table;
  • lines 48–53: a customer, their order, and its two line items, persisted in a single operation.

Unlike other ORM entries, Hibernate does not require cascade deletion in the database ([ON DELETE CASCADE]): this can be achieved using the [@OnDelete(action = OnDeleteAction.CASCADE)] annotation;
  • the association table has two columns—foreign keys to the two linked tables—which together form its primary key.

The schema is exactly the same as the one used in the Java course: the annotations, written in Kotlin, are identical.

docs.text:
package relations

import org.hibernate.LazyInitializationException
import org.hibernate.Session
import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.time.LocalDate

// relationships between entities: lazy loading, join fetch, entity graph, joins

// the results of the projection queries
data class ProductCategory(val product: String, val category: String)

data class OrderAmount(val id: Int, val client: String, val amount: BigDecimal)

data class CategoryStatistics(val category: String, val count: Long, val averagePrice: Double)

fun main() {
    Shop.createSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
        // 1 - creation of the tables and of a first data set, without a log
        Shop.initialize(sessionFactory)

        // 2 - a client, their order and its lines, added in one go
        println("--- addition of a client, an order and its two lines")
        sessionFactory.inTransaction { session ->
            val bike = session.product("bike")
            val arrows = session.product("arrows - set of 6")
            val order = CustomerOrder(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 1))
            order.add(OrderLine(bike, 1))
            order.add(OrderLine(arrows, 3))
            val client = Client("Dupont")
            client.add(order)
            session.persist(client)
            println("client no. ${client.id}, order no. ${order.id}")
        }

        // 3 - lazy loading: the relationships are read on demand
        println("--- lazy loading")
        sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
            val orders = session
                .createSelectionQuery("from CustomerOrder order by id", CustomerOrder::class.java)
                .resultList
            for (order in orders) {
                // the client and the lines are only read here, when first used
                println("order no. ${order.id} : client=${order.client.name}, " +
                        "${order.lines.size} line(s)")
            }
            // the [client] property contains a proxy: an object of a subclass of Client
            println("class of the client: ${orders[0].client.javaClass.name}")
        }

        // 4 - a relationship that is not loaded is no longer accessible once the session is closed
        println("--- after the session is closed")
        val detachedOrder = sessionFactory.fromSession { it.find(CustomerOrder::class.java, 1) }
        try {
            println("${detachedOrder.lines.size} line(s)")
        } catch (e: LazyInitializationException) {
            println("${e.javaClass.simpleName} : ${e.message}")
        }

        // 5 - join fetch: the orders, their client, their lines and their products in one query
        println("--- join fetch")
        sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
            val orders = session.createSelectionQuery(
                """
                from CustomerOrder c
                join fetch c.client
                join fetch c.lines l
                join fetch l.product
                order by c.id""", CustomerOrder::class.java
            ).resultList
            for (order in orders) {
                println("order no. ${order.id} of ${order.date} for ${order.client.name}")
                for (line in order.lines) {
                    val product = line.product
                    println("  %d x %s at %.2f euros".format(line.quantity, product.name, product.price))
                }
            }
        }

        // 6 - an entity graph: what must be loaded with the entity, described outside the query
        println("--- entity graph")
        val category = sessionFactory.fromSession { session ->
            val graph = session.createEntityGraph(Category::class.java)
            graph.addAttributeNodes(Category::products.name)
            session.find(graph, 2)
        }
        // the session is closed, but the products have been loaded
        println("${category.name} : ${category.products.joinToString(", ") { it.name }}")

        // 7 - the many-to-many relationship in a query
        println("--- the products on promotion")
        sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
            session.createSelectionQuery(
                """
                select p.name, p.category.name from Product p join p.tags e
                where e.label = :label order by p.name""", ProductCategory::class.java
            )
                .setParameter("label", "promo")
                .resultList
                .forEach { (product, category) -> println("$product ($category)") }
        }

        // 8 - a computation across the relationships, done by the DBMS
        println("--- amount of the orders")
        sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
            session.createSelectionQuery(
                """
                select c.id, c.client.name, sum(l.quantity * l.product.price)
                from CustomerOrder c join c.lines l
                group by c.id, c.client.name order by c.id""", OrderAmount::class.java
            )
                .resultList
                .forEach { (id, client, amount) ->
                    println("order no. %d (%s) : %.2f euros".format(id, client, amount))
                }
        }

        // 9 - a grouping: number of products and average price per category
        println("--- products per category")
        sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
            session.createSelectionQuery(
                """
                select p.category.name, count(*), avg(p.price) from Product p
                group by p.category.name order by p.category.name""", CategoryStatistics::class.java
            )
                .resultList
                .forEach { (category, count, averagePrice) ->
                    println("%s : %d product(s), average price %.2f euros".format(category, count, averagePrice))
                }
        }
    }
}

// the product with the given name: an extension function of the session
fun Session.product(name: String): Product =
    createSelectionQuery("from Product where name = :name", Product::class.java)
        .setParameter("name", name)
        .singleResult
