Comments:

  • Lines 11–15: The data classes that will receive the projection results. Their types correspond to those returned by the DBMS: [Long] for [count], [Double] for [avg];
  • lines 135–138: the product with the given name, read by an extension function of the Hibernate interface [Session]: inside it, [createSelectionQuery] is called on the session itself ([this], implicit). It is called as a session method: [session.product("bike")] (line 25), where the Java code previously defined a static method [product(session, "bike")];
  • lines 24–33: a customer, their order, and its two lines are persisted with a single call to [persist]. SQL shows the order of insertions: first the customer, then the order—whose foreign key [client_id] receives the generated key from the customer (2)—and finally the lines, whose foreign key [order_id] receives the key from the order. [inTransaction] receives a Kotlin lambda where Hibernate expects a Java functional interface ([Consumer<Session>]): this is the conversion SAM from Chapter 7;
  • lines 39–45: lazy loading. The query reads only the orders: the customer and the lines for each order are read only when the program uses them, via additional queries (two for the first order, two for the second). For the customer, Hibernate has placed a proxy in the [client] property—an object of a subclass of [Client] generated by Hibernate (using Byte Buddy)—which contains only the identifier and reads the client on the first call to an accessor ([order.client.name], i.e., [getName()]). Line 48 shows this: the object’s class is [relations.Client$HibernateProxy]. This is why an entity must not be a final class, nor its accessors final methods: in Kotlin, where classes and members are final by default, it is the [allopen] plugin that makes them non-final. For the rows, the list is a Hibernate collection, loaded on first use ([size]);
  • Lines 53–57: The command is read by a session that is immediately closed ([fromSession], which returns the result of the lambda). These lines were not loaded, and once the session is closed, they can no longer be loaded: accessing the collection triggers a [LazyInitializationException], one of the most common exceptions in applications that use Hibernate. Nothing in the property’s [MutableList<OrderLine>] type signals this risk to the Kotlin compiler: type safety ends where on-demand loading begins. You must load what you’ll need while the session is open;
  • lines 63–69: preloading via a query. [join fetch] instructs Hibernate to load, along with the orders, their customers, their lines, and the product of each line: a single query with joins. The output shows both orders and their lines. The join with the rows produces one SQL row per order line; Hibernate derives a single order for each ID: the rendered list does indeed contain two orders. The query text, spanning multiple lines, is a raw string;
  • lines 82–88: an “entity graph” (Jakarta Persistence) describes, outside of any query, the associations to be loaded with an entity: here, the products in the category, identified by the property reference [Category::products.name] rather than by the string ["products"]. [session.find(graph, 2)] (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) reads category 2 along with its products in a single query (an outer join, [left join]). Once the session is closed, the products remain accessible. To load an association later, while the session is open, use [Hibernate.initialize(category.products)]. Note the call to [addAttributeNodes] (plural) rather than [addAttributeNode]: the latter, which is generic, returns a *[AttributeNode<Y>]*, and Kotlin cannot infer the type *[Y]* when the result is not used (“cannot infer type for type parameter 'Y'”);
  • Lines 95–100: associations are used in queries: [join p.tags e] traverses the many-to-many relationship (two joins, with the association table and the label table), and [p.category.name] is translated into an implicit join with the category table. The label text is passed via a named parameter (the Java course wrote it as a literal in the query); each result is unpacked into the lambda’s parameters: [{ (product, category) -> ... \}];
  • lines 108–114: a calculation involving two relations—the amount of each order—entirely performed by the DBMS: joins, [sum] and [group by];
  • lines 123–128: a grouping. [group by p.category.name] groups products by category name; for each group, the number of products ([count], of type [Long]) and the average price ([avg], of type [Double]) are calculated by the DBMS. The category [diving], which has no product, does not appear: the join with the category table is an inner join ([join]).

docs.title: 11.8.3. The N+1 Query Problem
docs.text: The lazy loading in the example illustrates a problem that affects any user of a ORM, known as the “N+1 queries” problem: one query to read the N orders, then one query per order to read its customer (and another for its line items). With a thousand orders, this results in a thousand and one round trips to the server, when a single one would have sufficed. The problem is all the more insidious because it’s invisible in the code: [order.client.name] doesn’t look like a query, and Kotlin’s property syntax hides it even better than the Java call [getClient().getName()]. The solutions are those shown in the example: [join fetch], an entity graph, or better yet, a projection onto a data class that retrieves only the necessary data. Hibernate also offers batch loading ([@BatchSize(size = 20)] applied to a collection, or to the referenced entity class, in this case [Client]), which, for example, retrieves the customers for twenty orders in a single query. The SQL log helps identify the problem: the same query being repeated numerous times.

docs.title: 11.9.1. The Problem
docs.text:
Until now, tables were created by Hibernate after being deleted. This is impossible for a live application: its database contains data that must be preserved when the model evolves (a new column, a new table). It must be possible to migrate the database from one schema version to the next, in a safe and reproducible manner, both on the developer’s machine and on the production server. This is referred to as schema migration.

Hibernate does not support schema migrations: it can create a schema, validate it, and make limited updates to it. The standard practice, as described in JVM (in both Java and Kotlin), is to delegate migrations to versioned SQL scripts, applied by a dedicated tool—most commonly Flyway or Liquibase—and to have Hibernate verify that the resulting schema matches the entities.

docs.title: 11.9.2. Schema Management by Hibernate
docs.text:
The [hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto] property (or the [schemaToolingAction] method in the configuration, which is used by the program below) specifies what Hibernate should do with the schema when creating the [SessionFactory]:

ValueConstant [Action]Effect[none][NONE]none (default value)[create-only][CREATE_ONLY]table creation[create][CREATE]Deleting and then creating tables[create-drop][CREATE_DROP]such as [create], and deletion of tables upon closing [SessionFactory]: for testing[drop][DROP]Delete the tables[validate][VALIDATE]Check that the tables and columns of the entities exist, with compatible types; throw an exception otherwise[update][UPDATE]Create any missing tables and columns

Jakarta Persistence defines a related property, [jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.database.action], with the values [none], [create], [drop-and-create], and [drop]. The same actions are available programmatically, as we did with [SchemaManager] from [SessionFactory] ([create], [drop], [validate], [truncate]).

The [update] option is tempting: Hibernate compares the entities to the database schema and adds what’s missing. It has limitations that make it unsuitable for a production application:

  • it only adds: it never deletes a column or table that has become unnecessary, does not modify the type or length of an existing column, and cannot rename (renaming a property creates a new empty column, while the old one remains with its data);
  • it cannot transform data (fill a new required column, split a column into two);
  • what it does depends on the state of the database it encounters: it is impossible to know in advance which commands will be executed, or in what order, and no record of this is kept.

We therefore reserve [create], [create-drop], and [update] for development and testing, and we use [validate] (or [none]) in production, with the schema managed by scripts.

docs.title: 11.9.3. Versioned SQL scripts
docs.text:
The principle behind script-based migrations is simple:

  • each schema change is described by an SQL script, numbered sequentially: [V1__create_clients.sql], [V2__add_phone.sql]... Once a script has been applied to a database, it is never modified again: any correction is the subject of a new script;
  • the database contains a history table that lists the versions that have been applied to it;
  • When the application starts (or during deployment), a tool compares the available scripts with the history and applies, in order, those that have not yet been applied.

The scripts are part of the application’s source code: they are stored and managed along with the rest of the code (in a Git repository, for example). To understand how this works, the [clients] subproject implements a small versioned script runner, modeled after Flyway; we will then introduce Flyway itself.

docs.title: 11.9.4. The [clients] subproject
docs.text:
The [clients] subproject uses the [hbclients] database. It has two programs: [clients.MainKt], which runs by default, and [clients.GenerateScriptKt], which is specified as needed by the [main] property, as in the previous chapters. Its [build.gradle.kts] is the same as that of the [relations] subproject, with one exception:

application {
    // the program run by [gradlew -q :clients:run]: clients.MainKt by default,
    // or the one given by the [main] property: gradlew -q :clients:run -Pmain=clients.GenerateScriptKt
    mainClass = providers.gradleProperty("main").orElse("clients.MainKt")
}

The entity is a customer:

package clients

import jakarta.persistence.Column
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.Table

// a client
@Entity
@Table(name = "clients")
class Client(
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 50)
    var name: String,
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 100)
    var email: String,
    // version 2: the phone, optional (type String? and a column that accepts NULL)
    @Column(length = 20)
    var phone: String? = null,
) {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
        protected set

    override fun toString() = "[$id, $name, $email, ${phone ?: "no phone"}]"
}

In the first version of the application, the customer does not have a phone number: lines 18–20 do not yet exist. We will add them in the second version. The phone number is optional, which Kotlin expresses using the nullable type [String?] and the default value [null] (so we can create a customer without a phone number: [Client("Durand", "durand@example.com")]). Hibernate, however, does not recognize Kotlin types: it is the absence of ***[nullable = false] in *[@Column] that makes the column optional (conversely, a non-nullable Kotlin [String] only produces a [NOT NULL] column if explicitly requested, as is the case with [name] and [email]). The [toString] function (line 27) uses the Elvis operator to display the absence of a phone number.

The scripts are located in the [src/main/resources/db/migration] folder of the subproject, which Gradle copies to the classpath (into the [build/resources/main] folder). These are the scripts from the Java course: an SQL script does not depend on the application’s programming language. The first one creates the table:

-- version 1: the clients table
create table clients (
    id integer not null auto_increment,
    name varchar(50) not null,
    email varchar(100) not null,
    primary key (id)
) engine=InnoDB;

The second adds the phone number column:

-- version 2: the (optional) phone of the clients
alter table clients
    add column phone varchar(20);

The [Migrations] class applies the scripts using JDBC (Chapter 10), independently of Hibernate:

package clients

import java.nio.file.Path
import java.sql.Connection
import java.sql.DriverManager
import java.sql.SQLException
import kotlin.io.path.listDirectoryEntries
import kotlin.io.path.name
import kotlin.io.path.readLines

// a small runner of versioned SQL scripts, modeled on Flyway: the scripts
// [db/migration/V<version>__<description>.sql] are applied only once, in the order of the versions,
// and the [migration_history] table of the database records those that have been
class Migrations(
    private val url: String,
    private val user: String,
    private val password: String,
) {
    // a migration script
    data class Script(val version: Int, val description: String, val path: Path) {
        override fun toString() = "V$version ($description)"
    }

    private companion object {
        // the name of a script: V1__create_clients.sql
        val NAME = Regex("""V(\d+)__(\w+)\.sql""")

        // the history table
        const val CREATE_HISTORY = """
            create table if not exists migration_history (
                version integer not null primary key,
                description varchar(100) not null,
                applied_on datetime not null default current_timestamp
            ) engine=InnoDB"""
    }

    // a connection to the database
    private fun connection(): Connection = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, password)

    // the scripts of the [db/migration] folder of the classpath, in version order
    fun scripts(): List<Script> {
        val folder = Migrations::class.java.getResource("/db/migration") ?: return emptyList()
        return Path.of(folder.toURI()).listDirectoryEntries()
            .mapNotNull { file ->
                // the files whose name does not follow the convention are ignored (null)
                NAME.matchEntire(file.name)?.destructured?.let { (version, description) ->
                    Script(version.toInt(), description.replace('_', ' '), file)
                }
            }
            .sortedBy { it.version }
    }

    // the versions already applied to the database (the history table is created if needed)
    fun appliedVersions(): Set<Int> = connection().use { cnx ->
        cnx.createStatement().use { statement ->
            statement.execute(CREATE_HISTORY)
            statement.executeQuery("select version from migration_history").use { rows ->
                sortedSetOf<Int>().apply {
                    while (rows.next()) add(rows.getInt(1))
                }
            }
        }
    }

    // the scripts that remain to be applied
    fun pending(): List<Script> {
        val applied = appliedVersions()
        return scripts().filter { it.version !in applied }
    }

    // application of the pending scripts, up to version [target] included; the applied scripts are returned
    fun migrate(target: Int = Int.MAX_VALUE): List<Script> =
        pending().takeWhile { it.version <= target }.onEach { applyScript(it) }

    // application of a script and addition of its version to the history, in a transaction
    private fun applyScript(script: Script) {
        // the statements of the script, separated by semicolons, without the comment lines
        val statements = script.path.readLines()
            .filterNot { it.trim().startsWith("--") }
            .joinToString("\n")
            .split(";")
            .filter { it.isNotBlank() }
        connection().use { cnx ->
            cnx.autoCommit = false
            try {
                cnx.createStatement().use { statement -> statements.forEach { statement.execute(it) } }
                cnx.prepareStatement("insert into migration_history(version, description) values (?, ?)")
                    .use { history ->
                        history.setInt(1, script.version)
                        history.setString(2, script.description)
                        history.executeUpdate()
                    }
                cnx.commit()
            } catch (e: SQLException) {
                // beware: with MySQL, a schema modification statement cannot be rolled back
                cnx.rollback()
                throw e
            }
        }
    }
}
  • lines 14–17: the database is described by the private properties of the primary constructor;
  • lines 20–21: a script is described by a nested data class, [Migrations.Script]: its version, description, and path; its [toString] method is overridden for display;
  • lines 24–34: the class constants, in a private companion object. Line 26: a script’s name follows the Flyway convention: [V]—the version number, two underscores, and a description. The regular expression is written as a raw string, where the backslash does not need to be doubled (["""V(\d+)__(\w+)\.sql"""]; in Java: ["V(\\d+)__(\\w+)\\.sql"]). The history table (one row per applied version, with its description and the date it was applied) is created by a command written as a raw string, a constant [const val];
  • lines 41–50: the list of scripts. [getResource("/db/migration")] returns the URL from the directory in the classpath, or [null] if it does not exist: the Elvis operator then immediately returns an empty list ([?: return emptyList()]). The directory is listed by the [listDirectoryEntries] extension function of [kotlin.io.path] (Chapter 5). Each file is checked against the regular expression by [matchEntire], which returns [null] if the name does not match: [mapNotNull] filters out these files, and the expression’s groups are retrieved via destructuring ([destructured], Chapter 5). This code assumes that the directory is a real directory (which is the case when the program is run by Gradle from the [build/resources/main] directory); Flyway can also read scripts from a [.jar] archive. The scripts are sorted by version number ([sortedBy]): alphabetical sorting would place [V10] before [V2];
  • Lines 54–59: The versions that have already been applied, retrieved from the history table, which is created as needed ([create table if not exists]). The three JDBC resources (connection, statement, results) are closed by three nested [use] resources. The function returns a sorted set ([sortedSetOf], a Java [TreeSet]), populated by [apply];
  • lines 66–68: the remaining scripts to be applied: the [!in] operator checks for the absence of a version in the set;
  • lines 72–73: application of the pending scripts, up to a given version (all by default: [target: Int = Int.MAX_VALUE]). [takeWhile] retains the scripts as long as their version does not exceed the target; [onEach] applies each of them and returns the list itself: the function fits into a single expression, whereas Java would have written a loop using [break];
  • lines 76–97: applying a script: its commands (comment lines removed by [filterNot], the text split at semicolons), then adding its version to the history table, within a transaction ([cnx.autoCommit = false], the Kotlin property corresponding to [setAutoCommit]). One caveat, noted in the comment on line 95: under MySQL, a schema modification command ([CREATE TABLE], [ALTER TABLE]) implicitly commits the current transaction and cannot be rolled back. If an error occurs in the middle of a script, the database may remain in an intermediate state. This is why it is advisable to use short scripts, each performing a single operation.

Note that no function in the class declares the exceptions it may throw: the Java version had to specify [throws SQLException, IOException, URISyntaxException] on most of its methods, as well as on the [main] method that calls them. Kotlin does not have controlled exceptions (Chapter 3): a [SQLException] simply propagates up to whoever wants to handle it.

The main program applies the migrations, then asks Hibernate to validate the schema:

package clients

import jakarta.persistence.PersistenceException
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import org.hibernate.tool.schema.Action

// the clients database; MySQL creates it if it does not exist
const val URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbclients?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true"

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    // the targeted version: the last one by default, or the one passed as an argument
    val target = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: Int.MAX_VALUE

    // the state of the migrations
    val migrations = Migrations(URL, "root", "")
    println("applied versions: ${migrations.appliedVersions()}")
    println("pending migrations: ${migrations.pending()}")

    // application of the pending migrations
    for (script in migrations.migrate(target)) {
        println("migration applied: $script")
    }

    // Hibernate checks that the database schema matches the entities (validate)
    try {
        HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("clients")
            .managedClass(Client::class.java)
            .jdbcUrl(URL)
            .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
            .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
            .schemaToolingAction(Action.VALIDATE)
            .createEntityManagerFactory()
            .use { sessionFactory ->
                println("the database schema matches the entities")
                // the new column is usable
                sessionFactory.inTransaction { session ->
                    session.persist(Client("Dupont", "dupont@example.com", "01 23 45 67 89"))
                }
                sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
                    session.createSelectionQuery("from Client", Client::class.java)
                        .resultList
                        .forEach(::println)
                }
            }
    } catch (e: PersistenceException) {
        // the validation error is the cause of the exception
        val cause = e.cause ?: e
        println("${cause.javaClass.simpleName} : ${cause.message}")
    }
}
  • line 9: the database’s URL, a top-level constant in the [clients] package, which the second program will also use;
  • line 13: You can specify, as an argument, the version up to which to apply the migrations; by default, all are applied. [args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: Int.MAX_VALUE] combines the safe call and the Elvis operator;
  • lines 16–22: the status of the migrations, followed by their application;
  • lines 27–34: [SessionFactory] is created with the action [VALIDATE]: Hibernate verifies that the database schema matches the entity [Client]. If this is not the case, the creation of [SessionFactory] fails with a [PersistenceException], the cause of which is the validation error (lines 46–49). [e.cause ?: e] captures the cause, or the exception itself if it has none;
  • lines 37–43: the new column is used.

docs.title: 11.9.5. Generating Scripts with Hibernate
docs.text:
The SQL scripts are written by hand. However, Hibernate can help write them: it can generate—without executing it—the script to create the schema, or, by comparing the entities to an existing database, the script to update it. This is what the program [GenerateScript.kt] does:

package clients

import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import java.io.StringWriter

// generation by Hibernate of the SQL script that creates (create) or updates (update) the database schema
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    // the action: create (by default) or update
    val action = args.firstOrNull() ?: "create"
    val script = StringWriter()
    // a SessionFactory that writes the script without executing it; it is only created for that:
    // it is closed immediately
    HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("clients")
        .managedClass(Client::class.java)
        .jdbcUrl(URL)
        .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
        .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_ACTION, action)
        .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_CREATE_TARGET, script)
        .property(AvailableSettings.HBM2DDL_DELIMITER, ";")
        .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
        .createEntityManagerFactory()
        .close()
    // the script, without the 4-space indentation of its lines
    script.toString().trim().lines()
        .map { it.removePrefix("    ").trimEnd() }
        .forEach(::println)
}
  • line 10: the action, passed as an argument: [create] or [update];
  • lines 14–23: [SessionFactory] is created solely to generate the script: it is closed immediately after creation, without even being stored in a variable (the Java course declared it in a [try] statement with resources, using the anonymous Java variable [_] from Java 22);
  • lines 18–21: the script generation properties, already encountered in the subproject [model]. This time, Hibernate connects to the database: for the action [update], it needs to know its schema;
  • lines 25–27: the script, with the 4-space indentation removed from its lines by [removePrefix], which only removes the prefix if it is present.

Note that the two programs in the subproject each have a top-level [main] function in the same package: this is permitted for the [main] function, as each is compiled into its own file class ([clients.MainKt], [clients.GenerateScriptKt]).

The creation script, generated from the current version of the entity, is used to create a new database all at once (for testing, for example):

> gradlew -q :clients:run -Pmain=clients.GenerateScriptKt
create table clients (
    id integer not null auto_increment,
    phone varchar(20),
    name varchar(50) not null,
    email varchar(100) not null,
    primary key (id)
) engine=InnoDB;

With the first version of the entity (without a phone number), it would have produced, in the same column order, the script [V1__create_clients.sql].

docs.title: 11.9.6. Apply the migrations
docs.text:
Let’s assume the database does not yet exist. We apply only the first migration, passing version 1 as an argument (option [--args] of task [run]):

> gradlew -q :clients:run --args="1"
applied versions: []
pending migrations: [V1 (create clients), V2 (add phone)]
migration applied: V1 (create clients)
SchemaManagementException : Schema validation: missing column [phone] in table [clients]
  • No version is applied; two scripts are pending (the Kotlin list is displayed the same way as the Java list, in square brackets). The history table was created by function [appliedVersions], and the database [hbclients] by MySQL ([createDatabaseIfNotExist=true]);
  • the script [V1] is applied;
  • Hibernate detects that the [phone] column of the entity does not exist in the table: this is normal, since the database is at version 1 and the entity is at version 2. With the version 1 entity, the validation would have succeeded.

The application is evolving: we’re adding the phone number to the entity. To write the script for version 2, we ask Hibernate to compare the entity to the database, which is still at version 1:

> gradlew -q :clients:run -Pmain=clients.GenerateScriptKt --args="update"
alter table clients
   add column phone varchar(20);

This is, apart from the formatting, the same as the script [V2__add_phone.sql]. We now apply all pending migrations:

> gradlew -q :clients:run
applied versions: [1]
pending migrations: [V2 (add phone)]
migration applied: V2 (add phone)
the database schema matches the entities
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> insert into clients (email, name, phone)
    SQL> values (?, ?, ?)
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = dupont@example.com
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = Dupont
    SQL> -- parameter 3 = 01 23 45 67 89
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)
    SQL> select c1_0.id, c1_0.email, c1_0.name, c1_0.phone
    SQL> from clients c1_0
[1, Dupont, dupont@example.com, 01 23 45 67 89]
  • Version 1 is applied, version 2 is pending, and it is applied;
  • Validation succeeds;
  • the new column is ready for use: the customer is saved with their phone number, then retrieved.

The history table now contains both versions:

> mysql -uroot -t hbclients -e "SELECT * FROM migration_history"
+---------+----------------+---------------------+
| version | description    | applied_on          |
+---------+----------------+---------------------+
|       1 | create clients | 2026-10-04 10:55:57 |
|       2 | add phone      | 2026-10-04 10:56:18 |
+---------+----------------+---------------------+

Running the program again does not apply any changes: both versions appear in the history (however, it does add a second customer named Dupont, which we are not showing):

> gradlew -q :clients:run
applied versions: [1, 2]
pending migrations: []
the database schema matches the entities

docs.title: 11.9.7. Flyway
docs.text:
Flyway is the most widely used migration tool for JVM (Spring Boot runs it automatically when an application starts if it is present in the classpath). It works exactly according to the same principle as our executor, but is more comprehensive: [V<version>__<description>.sql] scripts are searched for by default in the [db/migration] folder of the classpath, the [flyway_schema_history] history table is used, and pending scripts are applied in version order. In particular, it adds a checksum for each script, which detects changes to a script that has already been applied; “repeatable” scripts ([R__description.sql], reapplied with each change, for views for example); migrations written in the application’s language (Java or Kotlin classes); a lock that prevents two instances of the application from migrating the database at the same time, and a Gradle plugin (tasks [flywayMigrate], [flywayInfo]).

To use it in the [clients] subproject, simply add the dependencies [org.flywaydb:flyway-core] and [org.flywaydb:flyway-mysql] (in their latest versions) to [build.gradle.kts], keep both scripts as is—since they already follow its convention—and replace the use of the [Migrations] class with a single line: [Flyway.configure().dataSource(URL, "root", "").load().migrate()].

Liquibase, the other commonly used tool, describes schema changes in XML, YAML, or SQL files (the “changelogs”), and can generate the SQL specific to each DBMS. In both cases, Hibernate is configured with [validate] or [none], and no longer modifies the schema.

docs.title: 11.10. Hibernate and Virtual Threads
docs.text:
A database query is an I/O operation: while the server is processing the request, the waiting thread does nothing. Chapters 8 and 9 presented two ways to avoid wasting threads during these waits: JDK virtual threads and Kotlin coroutines. Hibernate’s API, like the JDBC it uses, is blocking: [getResultList] (the [resultList] property in Kotlin) does not yield control until the lines have been read. With virtual threads, this is no longer a drawback: a virtual thread blocked on I/O frees up the system thread that was executing it, and you can create thousands of them. So you write ordinary blocking code, executed by virtual threads. With coroutines, we similarly entrust this blocking code to a dispatcher designed for I/O, [Dispatchers.IO] (Chapter 9), using [withContext]: the coroutine waiting for the result is suspended, without blocking its thread.

One rule must be followed in both cases: a session is not thread-safe. It is never shared among multiple threads or multiple coroutines: each thread, each task, and each coroutine opens its own session with [SessionFactory], which is itself shared. With coroutines, this rule requires special attention: a coroutine may resume execution after a suspension on a different thread than the one where it started; a session opened before a suspended call and used after it would therefore switch threads. The simplest approach is to open and close the session within the [withContext] block, which contains no suspension points. Hibernate does not always detect concurrent use of the same session; the resulting errors are unpredictable.

The [async] subproject enforces this rule. In addition to the [articles] library, it depends on kotlinx-coroutines:

// Hibernate, virtual threads and coroutines
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    // no [jpa] or [allopen] plugin: the module does not define any entity (Article is compiled in [articles])
    application
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // the [Article] entity and the [hbarticles] database (Hibernate, MySQL and the SQL log included)
    implementation(project(":articles"))
    // coroutines (chapter 9)
    implementation("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-core:1.11.0")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
    // the program run by [gradlew -q :async:run]
    mainClass = "async.MainKt"
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}
  • line 14: the [Article] entity and the [hbarticles] database, as in the previous examples;
  • line 16: the coroutines library (Chapter 9);
  • lines 32–35: the programs launched by Gradle write their output to UTF-8, so that accented characters display correctly on Windows (Chapter 2).

The program:

package async

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import jakarta.persistence.QueryTimeoutException
import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture
import java.util.concurrent.Executors
import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers
import kotlinx.coroutines.async
import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking
import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory

// Hibernate (a blocking API) with virtual threads, then with coroutines
fun main() {
    BaseArticles.createSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
        // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
        BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory)

        // 1 - two queries executed at the same time by two virtual threads, each one with its session
        println("--- two queries in parallel")
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { executor ->
            val lowPrices = executor.submit<List<Article>> {
                sessionFactory.fromSession { s ->
                    s.createSelectionQuery("from Article where price < 200 order by price", Article::class.java)
                        .resultList
                }
            }
            val hql = "select count(*) from Article where currentStock < minimumStock"
            val outOfStock = executor.submit<Long> {
                sessionFactory.fromSession { s ->
                    s.createSelectionQuery(hql, Long::class.java).singleResult
                }
            }
            // get() waits for the end of each task
            lowPrices.get().forEach { println(it) }
            println("${outOfStock.get()} article(s) out of stock")
        }

        // 2 - a transaction executed by a virtual thread, followed by a processing of its result
        println("--- CompletableFuture")
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { executor ->
            val processing = CompletableFuture
                .supplyAsync({
                    sessionFactory.fromTransaction { session ->
                        session.createSelectionQuery("from Article where name = 'bow'", Article::class.java)
                            .singleResult
                            .apply { price = BigDecimal.valueOf(550) }
                    }
                }, executor)
                .thenAccept { bow -> println("new price of the bow: ${bow.price}") }
            processing.join()
        }

        // 3 - coroutines: each one executes a suspending function that opens its own session
        println("--- coroutines")
        runBlocking {
            // two child coroutines of runBlocking, executed at the same time
            val cheap = async {
                countArticles(sessionFactory, "select count(*) from Article where price < 200")
            }
            val expensive = async {
                countArticles(sessionFactory, "select count(*) from Article where price >= 200")
            }
            // await() suspends the main coroutine until the result of each child coroutine
            println("${cheap.await()} article(s) under 200 euros")
            println("${expensive.await()} article(s) at 200 euros or more")
        }

        // 4 - a stream: the entities are processed as they are read
        println("--- getResultStream")
        sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
            session.createSelectionQuery("from Article where price >= 300", Article::class.java)
                .resultStream
                .use { articles -> articles.forEach { println("read: ${it.name}") } }
        }

        // 5 - a query that is too long is interrupted after the set timeout (in seconds)
        println("--- timeout exceeded")
        try {
            sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
                session.createNativeQuery("select sleep(5)", Int::class.java)
                    .setTimeout(1)
                    .singleResult
            }
        } catch (e: QueryTimeoutException) {
            println("${e::class.simpleName} : ${e.message}")
        }
    }
}

// a counting query executed in a session specific to the coroutine; the blocking work is
// handed to the [IO] dispatcher: the calling coroutine is suspended, its thread is not blocked
suspend fun countArticles(sessionFactory: SessionFactory, hql: String): Long =
    withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        sessionFactory.fromSession { session ->
            session.createSelectionQuery(hql, Long::class.java).singleResult
        }
    }

Results:

> gradlew -q :async:run
--- two queries in parallel
    SQL> select count(*)
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.currentStock<a1_0.minimumStock
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.price<200
    SQL> order by a1_0.price
[2, pump, 10.00, 10, 2]
[4, arrows - set of 6, 100.00, 12, 20]
[6, diver's oxygen tanks, 120.00, 10, 5]
1 article(s) out of stock
--- CompletableFuture
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.name='bow'
    SQL> update articles
    SQL> set currentStock=?, minimumStock=?, name=?, price=?
    SQL> where id=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 4
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = 1
    SQL> -- parameter 3 = bow
    SQL> -- parameter 4 = 550
    SQL> -- parameter 5 = 3
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)
new price of the bow: 550
--- coroutines
    SQL> select count(*)
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.price<200
    SQL> select count(*)
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.price>=200
3 article(s) under 200 euros
3 article(s) at 200 euros or more
--- getResultStream
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.price>=300
read: bike
read: bow
read: diving suit
--- timeout exceeded
    SQL> select sleep(5)
    SQL> -- failure: Statement cancelled due to timeout or client request
QueryTimeoutException : JDBC exception executing SQL [Statement cancelled due to timeout or client request] [select sleep(5)]

Comments:

  • line 23: an executor that creates a virtual thread per task (Chapter 8). A [ExecutorService] is [AutoCloseable]: the function [use] closes it at the end of the block, and its closure waits for all tasks to finish;
  • Lines 24–33: Two tasks submitted to the executor. Each opens its own session ([fromSession]) and executes a query; both queries run simultaneously, on two connections from the pool. Their order in the log (lines 3–9 of the results) may therefore vary from one execution to another. The result type is specified in [submit] ([submit<List<Article>>]): otherwise, the lambda might be interpreted as a [Runnable]—which returns nothing—rather than as a [Callable];
  • Line 33: the type of the result of the count query. [Long::class.java] here refers to the Java primitive type [long]; Hibernate accepts it and returns the value as a [java.lang.Long], which Kotlin treats as a [Long];
  • lines 36–38: [get()] waits for each task to complete and returns its result (lines 10–13);
  • lines 44–53: a [CompletableFuture] (Chapter 9) whose first step—a complete transaction—is executed by a virtual thread ([supplyAsync(..., executor)]), and the second step displays its result. The function [apply] modifies the read record and returns it: this is the value of the lambda, and thus the result of the transaction. The record returned by the transaction is detached (its session is closed): we can read its properties but not load its associations;
  • lines 58–68: the same idea using coroutines. [runBlocking] creates a main coroutine; [async] launches two child coroutines, which call the suspension function [countArticles]. Both requests run simultaneously (lines 30–35), and [await] suspends the main coroutine until each one returns (lines 36–37);
  • lines 95–96: the suspension function delegates the blocking work to the [Dispatchers.IO] dispatcher, whose threads are designed to wait for I/O operations. The session is opened and closed by [fromSession] within the [withContext] block: it is used by only one coroutine, and on a single thread. This is the approach to use when calling Hibernate from suspended code. One could also use a dispatcher built on virtual threads ([Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher()], Chapter 9);
  • lines 73–76: the property [resultStream] (the method [getResultStream]) returns a Java stream: entities are processed as they are read, without forming a list (lines 42–44). A stream is [AutoCloseable]: [use] closes it, which releases the JDBC cursor. It could also be converted to a Kotlin sequence ([asSequence()], Chapter 5). This is useful for processing a large number of lines. With MySQL, note that by default the driver reads all lines of the result before returning the first one; for truly progressive reading, you must instruct it to use a cursor (parameter [useCursorFetch=true] of URL and batch size set by [setFetchSize]);
  • Lines 83–87: A maximum execution time, in seconds, set by [setTimeout]. The query (a native SQL query, which we’ll discuss later) takes five seconds; after one second, the JDBC driver interrupts it, and Hibernate launches a [QueryTimeoutException] (lines 46–48).

The duration of the last request warrants a note. In Chapter 9, we canceled coroutines ([job.cancel()], [withTimeout]) and tasks ([Future.cancel]). These cancellations would have no effect on the request here: canceling a coroutine is cooperative, and a coroutine blocked in the JDBC driver does not check whether it has been canceled; as for interrupting a thread blocked in the driver, it does not interrupt the request currently in progress on the server. A [withTimeout(1000) { countArticles(...) }] would indeed launch a [TimeoutCancellationException]... but only once the request is complete, after five seconds: the [withContext] block of [countArticles] does not yield control until it has finished its blocking operation. To limit the duration of a request, you must therefore address the JDBC driver via [setTimeout].

For applications that require a truly non-blocking API, there is Hibernate Reactive, a variant of Hibernate that relies on reactive drivers (those from Vert.x) rather than JDBC, and whose methods return [CompletionStage] or objects from the Mutiny library; A [CompletionStage] is expected in a coroutine with the [await] extension function from kotlinx-coroutines. Virtual threads and the [Dispatchers.IO] dispatcher eliminate this complexity in most cases: this is the approach taken in this course.

docs.title: 11.11.1. Transactions
docs.text:
Chapter 10 introduced transactions: a set of operations that either all succeed or all fail. With Hibernate:

  • every write operation is performed within a transaction, opened by [session.beginTransaction()] and closed by [commit] or [rollback]. The methods [inTransaction] and [fromTransaction] of [SessionFactory] handle this for us: they commit the transaction if the lambda completes normally, and roll it back if it throws an exception, which is then rethrown;
  • all commands sent during the transaction (immediate commands via [INSERT], explicit synchronizations via [flush], and synchronization via [commit]) are either committed or rolled back together;
  • An error from the DBMS is propagated as a Hibernate exception, derived from [JDBCException], which encapsulates the driver’s [SQLException]: [ConstraintViolationException] for a constraint violation (primary key, uniqueness, foreign key, [NOT NULL]), [SQLGrammarException] for an error in the SQL statement, and so on. These are uncaught exceptions, in both Java and Kotlin (which, as a reminder, does not have caught exceptions: Chapter 3); we only catch those that we know how to handle.

The subproject [transactions] illustrates the two ways to handle a transaction:

package transactions

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import java.math.BigDecimal
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory
import org.hibernate.exception.ConstraintViolationException

// the two ways of managing a transaction: inTransaction, and a transaction managed by the code
fun main() {
    BaseArticles.createSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
        // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
        BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory)

        // 1 - inTransaction: commit if everything succeeds, rollback in case of an exception
        println("--- two additions, the second of which violates the uniqueness of the name")
        try {
            sessionFactory.inTransaction { session ->
                session.persist(Article("racket", BigDecimal.valueOf(80), 5, 2))
                session.persist(Article("bike", BigDecimal.valueOf(450), 3, 1))
            }
        } catch (e: ConstraintViolationException) {
            println("${e::class.simpleName} : constraint [${e.constraintName}] violated")
        }
        display(sessionFactory, "racket")

        // 2 - a transaction managed by the code: several writes, committed or rolled back together
        println("--- transaction rolled back")
        sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
            val transaction = session.beginTransaction()
            try {
                // sale of two bikes: the UPDATE is sent by flush
                val bike = session
                    .createSelectionQuery("from Article where name = 'bike'", Article::class.java)
                    .singleResult
                bike.currentStock -= 2
                session.flush()
                // addition of an article whose name already exists: error
                session.persist(Article("pump", BigDecimal.valueOf(12), 5, 1))
                // commit of the whole (not reached here)
                transaction.commit()
            } catch (e: ConstraintViolationException) {
                println("${e::class.simpleName} : ${e.sqlException.message}")
                // rollback of all the operations of the transaction
                transaction.rollback()
            }
        }
        // the sale of the bikes has been rolled back
        display(sessionFactory, "bike")
    }
}

// display of an article read from the database, with a new session
fun display(sessionFactory: SessionFactory, name: String) {
    val article = sessionFactory.fromSession { session ->
        session.createSelectionQuery("from Article where name = :name", Article::class.java)
            .setParameter("name", name)
            .singleResultOrNull
    }
    println("article [$name] in the database: ${article ?: "missing"}")
}

Results:

> gradlew -q :transactions:run

    SQL> insert into articles (currentStock, minimumStock, name, price)
    SQL> values (?, ?, ?, ?)
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 5
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = 2
    SQL> -- parameter 3 = racket
    SQL> -- parameter 4 = 80
    SQL> insert into articles (currentStock, minimumStock, name, price)
    SQL> values (?, ?, ?, ?)
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 3
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = 1
    SQL> -- parameter 3 = bike
    SQL> -- parameter 4 = 450
    SQL> -- failure: Duplicate entry 'bike' for key 'articles.uk_articles_name'
    SQL> -- transaction rolled back (ROLLBACK)
ConstraintViolationException : constraint [articles.uk_articles_name] violated
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.name=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = racket
article [racket] in the database: missing
--- transaction rolled back
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.name='bike'
    SQL> update articles
    SQL> set currentStock=?, minimumStock=?, name=?, price=?
    SQL> where id=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 8
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = 5
    SQL> -- parameter 3 = bike
    SQL> -- parameter 4 = 500.00
    SQL> -- parameter 5 = 1
    SQL> insert into articles (currentStock, minimumStock, name, price)
    SQL> values (?, ?, ?, ?)
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 5
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = 1
    SQL> -- parameter 3 = pump
    SQL> -- parameter 4 = 12
    SQL> -- failure: Duplicate entry 'pump' for key 'articles.uk_articles_name'
ConstraintViolationException : Duplicate entry 'pump' for key 'articles.uk_articles_name'
    SQL> -- transaction rolled back (ROLLBACK)
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.name=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = bike
article [bike] in the database: [1, bike, 500.00, 10, 5]

Comments:

  • Lines 18–20: Two items are added to a transaction managed by [inTransaction]; the second item has the same name as an existing item. Both [INSERT] processes are executed immediately (lines 4–15); the second violates the uniqueness constraint on the [name] column: MySQL rejects it (line 16), [persist] launches a [ConstraintViolationException], [inTransaction] rolls back the transaction (line 17) and rethrows the exception;
  • lines 22–23: the exception is caught; the [constraintName] property (the [getConstraintName] method) returns the name of the violated constraint (line 18). This demonstrates the value of having named the constraint;
  • line 25: the racket, which had been successfully inserted, is not in the database (line 23): rolling back the transaction deleted it;
  • Lines 29–45: A transaction managed by the code, in a session opened by [openSession] and closed by [use] ([Session] is [AutoCloseable]). Two bicycles are sold ([bike.currentStock -= 2]: the operator [-=] is applied to a property [var] just as it is to a variable), and the change is sent to the DBMS via an explicit [flush] (lines 29–36); then an item is added whose name already exists: the insertion fails (line 43);
  • line 41: the commit is never reached;
  • lines 42–45: in the [catch], the transaction is rolled back (line 45 of the results). The [sqlException] property returns the original exception from the JDBC driver, and its message is that of MySQL (line 44);
  • line 49: the sale of bicycles, although sent to the DBMS by [flush], was canceled: the bicycle inventory is still 10 (line 50);
  • lines 54–60: a function that re-reads a record with a new session to view the actual state of the database rather than the entities from the current working session. The property [singleResultOrNull] sets [null] if the query finds nothing; the Elvis operator ([?:]) then displays “missing.”

After an exception, a session should no longer be used: its persistence context may contain entities in a state that is inconsistent with the database. We roll back the transaction, close the session, and start over if necessary with a new session. This is what [inTransaction] does, and what our code does when exiting the [use] block, which closes the session.

The transaction isolation level is that of the JDBC connection: [REPEATABLE_READ], the default value for MySQL, as shown in the first example. You can change this for the entire [SessionFactory] using the [jdbcTransactionIsolation] method in the configuration.

docs.title: 11.11.2. Optimistic Concurrency
docs.text:
Two users are reading the same item, which has a stock of 10. The first user sells one item and updates the stock to 9. The second user, who read the stock value before this update, sells three items and updates the stock to 7: the first user’s sale is lost. This is the problem of lost updates.

One solution would be to lock the row for the entire duration of each user’s operation (“pessimistic” concurrency): this blocks other users, sometimes for a long time. With Hibernate, optimistic concurrency is generally preferred: nothing is locked, but a check is performed at the time of saving to ensure that the row has not been modified since it was read. The standard way to do this is to add a version number to the entity—a property annotated with [@Version]. Hibernate increments this number each time the row is modified, and adds the condition “the version still has the value read” to the [WHERE] clause via the commands [UPDATE] and [DELETE]. If the transaction does not modify any rows, it means another user has already accessed the data: Hibernate executes a [OptimisticLockException].

The subproject [concurrency] uses its own database, [hbconcurrency], and its own entity, [Article], stripped down to the essentials:

// an article whose modifications are controlled by a version number
@Entity
@Table(name = "articles")
class Article(
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    var name: String,
    var currentStock: Int,
) {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
        protected set

    // the version number: incremented by Hibernate at each modification of the row
    @Version
    var version: Int = 0
        protected set
}
  • lines 15–17: the version number, of the form [Int] (you can also use [Long], or a date in the form [Instant]). The application never modifies this itself: its modifier is protected ([protected set]), just like that of the identifier; Hibernate, which accesses the field directly, is not affected by this. The initial value [0] is that of an article created by the application; for an article read from the database, the parameterless constructor added by the plugin [jpa] does not perform this initialization (as we have seen), but Hibernate immediately assigns the read value to the property.

Since the entity is defined in the subproject itself, its build file applies the [jpa] and [allopen] plugins, and depends directly on Hibernate and the [tools] library:

// optimistic concurrency: an entity with a version number, in its own [hbconcurrency] database
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    // the module defines its own entity: the [jpa] and [allopen] plugins
    kotlin("plugin.jpa")
    kotlin("plugin.allopen")
    application
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // the compact SQL log (and Logback)
    implementation(project(":tools"))
    // Hibernate and the MySQL JDBC driver
    implementation("org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-core:7.4.5.Final")
    runtimeOnly("com.mysql:mysql-connector-j:9.7.0")
}

// the classes annotated this way are opened by the [allopen] plugin
allOpen {
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.Entity")
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.MappedSuperclass")
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.Embeddable")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
    // the program run by [gradlew -q :concurrency:run]
    mainClass = "concurrency.MainKt"
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}
  • lines 5–6: the two entity plugins, configured by the [allOpen] block (lines 23–26);
  • lines 16–19: the compact SQL log, Hibernate, and the JDBC driver for MySQL;
  • lines 42–45: the programs launched by Gradle write their output to UTF-8, so that accented characters display correctly on Windows (Chapter 2).

The program simulates the two users with two sessions:

package concurrency

import jakarta.persistence.OptimisticLockException
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import tools.SqlLog

// optimistic concurrency: two users modify the same article
fun main() {
    HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("concurrency")
        .managedClass(Article::class.java)
        .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbconcurrency?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
        .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
        .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
        .createEntityManagerFactory()
        .use { sessionFactory ->
            // the [articles] table is recreated with a single article, without a log
            SqlLog.withoutLog {
                sessionFactory.schemaManager.drop(false)
                sessionFactory.schemaManager.create(false)
                sessionFactory.inTransaction { session -> session.persist(Article("bike", 10)) }
            }

            // two users, two sessions: each one reads the same article
            sessionFactory.openSession().use { session1 ->
                sessionFactory.openSession().use { session2 ->
                    println("--- the two users read the bike")
                    val bike1 = session1.find(Article::class.java, 1)
                    val bike2 = session2.find(Article::class.java, 1)

                    // user 1 sells 1 bike
                    println("--- user 1 sells 1 bike")
                    val transaction1 = session1.beginTransaction()
                    bike1.currentStock -= 1
                    transaction1.commit()
                    println("stock saved by user 1: ${bike1.state()}")

                    // user 2 sells 3 bikes from outdated data (stock = 10, version 0)
                    println("--- user 2 sells 3 bikes")
                    val transaction2 = session2.beginTransaction()
                    bike2.currentStock -= 3
                    try {
                        session2.flush()
                        transaction2.commit()
                    } catch (e: OptimisticLockException) {
                        println("${e::class.simpleName} : ${e.message}")
                        transaction2.rollback()
                    }
                }
            }

            // resolution: user 2 reads the article again, with a new session, and starts over
            println("--- user 2 reads the bike again and starts over")
            sessionFactory.inTransaction { session ->
                val bike = session.find(Article::class.java, 1)
                println("stock read again: ${bike.state()}")
                bike.currentStock -= 3
                session.flush()
                println("stock saved by user 2: ${bike.state()}")
            }
        }
}

// the state of an article, for display: an extension function
fun Article.state() = "$currentStock (version $version)"

Results:

> gradlew -q :concurrency:run
--- the two users read the bike
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.version
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.id=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 1
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.version
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.id=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 1
--- user 1 sells 1 bike
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> update articles
    SQL> set currentStock=?, name=?, version=?
    SQL> where id=? and version=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 9
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = bike
    SQL> -- parameter 3 = 1
    SQL> -- parameter 4 = 1
    SQL> -- parameter 5 = 0
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)
stock saved by user 1: 9 (version 1)
--- user 2 sells 3 bikes
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> update articles
    SQL> set currentStock=?, name=?, version=?
    SQL> where id=? and version=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 7
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = bike
    SQL> -- parameter 3 = 1
    SQL> -- parameter 4 = 1
    SQL> -- parameter 5 = 0
OptimisticLockException : Unexpected row count (expected row count 1 but was 0) [update articles set currentStock=?,name=?,version=? where id=? and version=?] for entity [concurrency.Article with id '1']
    SQL> -- transaction rolled back (ROLLBACK)
--- user 2 reads the bike again and starts over
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.version
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.id=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 1
stock read again: 9 (version 1)
    SQL> update articles
    SQL> set currentStock=?, name=?, version=?
    SQL> where id=? and version=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 6
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = bike
    SQL> -- parameter 3 = 2
    SQL> -- parameter 4 = 1
    SQL> -- parameter 5 = 1
stock saved by user 2: 6 (version 2)
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)

Comments:

  • lines 10–15: the Hibernate configuration for the [hbconcurrency] database and its single entity;
  • lines 18–21: the table is recreated with a single item, the bicycle, version 0. The function [withoutLog] from the library [tools] receives the action to be executed in the form of a lambda, written without parentheses since it is its only parameter (Chapter 7);
  • lines 28–29: Each user reads the bicycle in their own session; the two sessions are opened by two nested [use] functions and closed in the reverse order of their opening. The [version] column is read along with the others (lines 3–10);
  • lines 33–35: the [UPDATE] order from the first user (lines 13–20) writes the new version (1) and contains the condition [version=?] with the read version (0). The row is modified; the entity’s [version] property is set to 1 (line 22);
  • lines 41–44: the second user’s request contains the same condition, with the version they read, 0, whereas the version of the row in the database is now 1. No rows are modified, and Hibernate throws a [OptimisticLockException] (line 33). We explicitly synchronize the session ([flush]) before the [commit] to trigger this exception as-is; if it were raised during the [commit], it would be encapsulated within a [RollbackException];
  • Lines 54–59: The resolution depends on the application: abort, notify the user, or, as here, re-read the item using a new session (the session that received the exception must no longer be used), and repeat the operation. The restocked inventory is 9 in version 1 (line 41), and the sale of the three bicycles results in an inventory of 6 in version 2 (line 50);
  • line 65: an extension function (Chapter 4) that formats an item’s status for display. It is defined within the program, without modifying the entity.

Two variants:

  • without a version column, Hibernate can check the old values of the columns themselves: with the annotations [@OptimisticLocking(type = OptimisticLockType.DIRTY)] and [@DynamicUpdate] on the entity, the [WHERE] clause of [UPDATE] contains the value read from each modified column ([where id=? and currentStock=?]). This is useful for an existing database that cannot be modified;
  • pessimistic concurrency remains possible when conflicts are frequent: [session.find(Article::class.java, 1, LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)] reads the row with a [select ... for update] order, which locks it until the end of the transaction.

docs.title: 11.12. The native SQL
docs.text:
Hibernate generates the SQL from HQL or the Criteria API, but it is still possible to write the SQL for a query yourself, to use a feature specific to the DBMS or to optimize a complex query: this is referred to as a native query. The [rawsql] subproject lists the available methods:

package rawsql

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.sql.Connection

// native SQL queries: written by hand, passed as they are to the DBMS
fun main() {
    BaseArticles.createSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
        // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
        BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory)
        sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
            // 1 - an SQL query written by hand that returns entities
            println("--- createNativeQuery: entities")
            val minPrice = BigDecimal.valueOf(200)
            val expensive = session
                .createNativeQuery(
                    """
                    select * from articles
                    where price > :minPrice order by name""".trimIndent(), Article::class.java
                )
                .setParameter("minPrice", minPrice)
                .resultList
            expensive.forEach { println(it) }

            // 2 - a value passed as a parameter: no SQL injection possible
            println("--- SQL injection attempt with a parameter")
            val name = "x' or '1'='1"
            var nb = session
                .createNativeQuery("select count(*) from articles where name = :name", Long::class.java)
                .setParameter("name", name)
                .singleResult
            println("$nb article(s) found")
            // the same query built with a string template: never do this
            println("--- the same attempt with a string template")
            val sql = "select count(*) from articles where name = '$name'"
            nb = session.createNativeQuery(sql, Long::class.java).singleResult
            println("$nb article(s) found")

            // 3 - results that are not entities
            println("--- createNativeQuery: values")
            val names = session
                .createNativeQuery(
                    "select name from articles where currentStock < minimumStock", String::class.java
                )
                .resultList
            println("out of stock: ${names.joinToString(", ")}")
            val value = session
                .createNativeQuery("select sum(price * currentStock) from articles", BigDecimal::class.java)
                .singleResult
            println("value of the stock: %.2f euros".format(value))

            // 4 - an update statement
            println("--- createNativeMutationQuery")
            val nbRows = session.fromTransaction { _ ->
                session
                    .createNativeMutationQuery(
                        """
                        update articles set price = price * :coefficient
                        where name = :name""".trimIndent()
                    )
                    .setParameter("coefficient", BigDecimal("0.9"))
                    .setParameter("name", "bow")
                    .executeUpdate()
            }
            println("$nbRows row(s) modified")

            // 5 - the JDBC connection of the session, for ordinary JDBC code
            println("--- doWork: the JDBC connection")
            session.doWork { connection: Connection ->
                val query = "select name, price from articles where name = 'bow'"
                connection.createStatement().use { statement ->
                    statement.executeQuery(query).use { rows ->
                        while (rows.next()) {
                            val price = rows.getBigDecimal("price")
                            println("${rows.getString("name")} : %.2f euros".format(price))
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

Results:

> gradlew -q :rawsql:run
--- createNativeQuery: entities
    SQL> select *
    SQL> from articles
    SQL> where price > ?
    SQL> order by name
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 200
[1, bike, 500.00, 10, 5]
[3, bow, 600.00, 4, 1]
[5, diving suit, 300.00, 8, 2]
--- SQL injection attempt with a parameter
    SQL> select count(*)
    SQL> from articles
    SQL> where name = ?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = x' or '1'='1
0 article(s) found
--- the same attempt with a string template
    SQL> select count(*)
    SQL> from articles
    SQL> where name = 'x' or '1'='1'
6 article(s) found
--- createNativeQuery: values
    SQL> select name
    SQL> from articles
    SQL> where currentStock < minimumStock
out of stock: arrows - set of 6
    SQL> select sum(price * currentStock)
    SQL> from articles
value of the stock: 12300.00 euros
--- createNativeMutationQuery
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> update articles
    SQL> set price = price * ?
    SQL> where name = ?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 0.9
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = bow
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)
1 row(s) modified
--- doWork: the JDBC connection
bow : 540.00 euros

Comments:

  • Lines 17–24: [createNativeQuery] executes a query (SQL) that returns rows from an entity's table, and the second parameter ([Article::class.java]) instructs Hibernate to materialize them as entities managed by the session. The column names in the result must match those in the model: [select *] is appropriate here. The query is written as a raw string (["""]), from which [trimIndent] removes the common indentation (Chapter 5). It is passed as-is to the DBMS (lines 3–6), except that the parameter named [:minPrice] becomes a JDBC parameter ([?]);
  • lines 29–34: an attempt to inject SQL. The value of [name] is passed as a parameter: it is compared as-is to the [name] column, and no item matches (line 16);
  • lines 37–38: the same query constructed using a string template (['$name']). Templates are so convenient in Kotlin that it’s tempting to use them to build a query: this is a serious mistake. The value of [name] becomes SQL code, the condition always evaluates to true (line 20), and the query returns six items (line 21): this is a successful SQL injection. As in Chapter 10, a native query must contain only constant text, with values passed as parameters;
  • Lines 43–52: Queries that return single values ([String], [BigDecimal]): The second parameter of [createNativeQuery] is then the type of the value. For multiple columns, you can specify a data class (whose constructor receives the columns in order) or use [Array<Any>::class.java];
  • lines 56–65: [createNativeMutationQuery] prepares an update statement, executed by [executeUpdate], which returns the number of rows modified. It runs within a transaction: the session’s [fromTransaction] method opens it, commits it, and returns the result of the lambda. The lambda receives the transaction as a parameter; since it does not use it, this parameter is named [_];
  • lines 71–77: [doWork] provides access to the session’s JDBC connection ([java.sql.Connection]) for standard JDBC code (Chapter 10): calling a stored procedure, use of a driver feature... It includes the function [use], which closes the statement ([Statement]) and the [ResultSet]. The price of the bow has indeed been reduced by 10% (line 40).

A note on line 71: the type of the lambda parameter ([connection: Connection]) is explicitly specified here, which is not standard practice in Kotlin. Without it, the compiler rejects the program:

error: type annotation class 'org.checkerframework.checker.nullness.qual.UnknownKeyFor' of the inferred type is inaccessible. Check the module classpath for missing or conflicting dependencies.

The Hibernate interface [Work], which the lambda implements, carries type annotations from the Checker Framework library on its parameter type; these annotations are used by Hibernate developers to verify the usage of [null] in their code. This library is not part of Hibernate’s dependencies; therefore, its annotations are unknown to the compiler, which refuses to infer a type that carries them. By specifying the parameter’s type ourselves, we avoid the inference—and the error. This type of issue sometimes arises when using a Java library from Kotlin: the Java code itself ignores these annotations.

A native query is not portable from one DBMS to another, and Hibernate cannot validate it before execution: it is reserved for cases where HQL is insufficient. HQL, in fact, covers a large part of SQL (joins of all kinds, subqueries, windowing functions, [union]...), and allows you to call a DBMS function that it does not recognize.

docs.title: 11.13. Bulk updates, read-only mode, and batches
docs.text:
Tracking changes comes at a cost: to increase the price of 100 items, you must read all 100 items, modify them one by one, and the session synchronization will send 100 [UPDATE] commands. Hibernate offers several ways to efficiently process large numbers of rows. The [bulkupdate] subproject introduces them:

package bulkupdate

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import java.math.BigDecimal

// bulk processing: HQL update/delete statements, read-only, stateless session and batches
fun main() {
    BaseArticles.createSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
        // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
        BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory)
        sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
            var transaction = session.beginTransaction()

            // 1 - HQL update: a single UPDATE statement, no entity loaded into memory
            println("--- restocking the articles that are out of stock")
            var nbRows = session
                .createMutationQuery(
                    """
                    update Article set currentStock = minimumStock * 2
                    where currentStock < minimumStock""".trimIndent()
                )
                .executeUpdate()
            println("$nbRows article(s) modified")

            println("--- 10 % increase of the prices below 150 euros")
            nbRows = session
                .createMutationQuery("update Article set price = price * 1.1 where price < 150")
                .executeUpdate()
            println("$nbRows article(s) modified")

            // 2 - HQL delete: a single DELETE statement
            println("--- deletion of the articles over 550 euros")
            nbRows = session
                .createMutationQuery("delete from Article where price > 550")
                .executeUpdate()
            println("$nbRows article(s) deleted")
            transaction.commit()

            // 3 - read-only: the entities read are not tracked
            println("--- read-only")
            transaction = session.beginTransaction()
            val articles = session
                .createSelectionQuery("from Article order by id", Article::class.java)
                .setReadOnly(true)
                .resultList
            articles.forEach { println(it) }
            // the modification of a read-only entity is ignored
            articles.first().price = BigDecimal.ZERO
            println("session modified: ${session.isDirty}")
            transaction.commit()

            // 4 - an HQL update statement does not modify the entities already loaded by the session
            println("--- HQL update and loaded entities")
            transaction = session.beginTransaction()
            val pump = session.find(Article::class.java, 2)
            session.createMutationQuery("update Article set price = 9.5 where id = :id")
                .setParameter("id", pump.id)
                .executeUpdate()
            println("price in memory: ${pump.price}")
            session.refresh(pump)
            println("price after refresh: ${pump.price}")
            transaction.commit()
        }

        // 5 - a stateless session (StatelessSession) and statements sent in batches
        println("--- StatelessSession and batches of 3 statements")
        sessionFactory.inStatelessTransaction { session ->
            session.jdbcBatchSize = 3
            val articles = session
                .createSelectionQuery("from Article order by id", Article::class.java)
                .resultList
            for (article in articles) {
                article.currentStock += 1
                // each modification is requested explicitly: the entities are not tracked
                session.update(article)
            }
        }
    }
}

--- read-only

    SQL> from articles a1_0
