Comments:

  • Lines 17–23: A [update] command written as HQL, prepared by [createMutationQuery], and executed by [executeUpdate]. It becomes a single SQL [UPDATE] statement (lines 4–6), executed by the DBMS on all affected lines, without any entity being loaded into memory. The new value may depend on the line itself ([minimumStock * 2]). Such a command is executed within a transaction (lines 2 and 18);
  • lines 27–29: a 10% increase in low prices. The constants for the HQL query ([1.1], [150]) are written directly into the text of the SQL command (lines 10–11);
  • lines 34–36: a [delete] HQL statement removes the bow, the only item priced over 550 euros (lines 14–16);
  • lines 43–50: a read-only operation ([setReadOnly(true)]). The entities being read are managed by the session, but the session does not retain their original state or monitor them: this is faster and more memory-efficient for data that is read without being modified (display, calculations). The trade-off is that any modification to such an entity is ignored (line 49): the session has nothing to synchronize ([session.isDirty] is equal to [false], line 29) and [commit] does not send any commands. You can also set an entire session to read-only ([session.isDefaultReadOnly = true]);
  • lines 56–62: a trap. A command like [update] HQL operates directly on the database: it does not modify entities already loaded by the session. The pump managed by the session retains its old price (line 37) until it is read again with [session.refresh(pump)] (lines 38–42);
  • Lines 68–76: A stateless session ([StatelessSession]), opened here with a transaction via [inStatelessTransaction]. It has no persistence context: no first-level cache, no change tracking, no lazy loading, and no cascades. Each operation is explicitly requested ([insert], [update], [delete], [get]) and executed as is. This is the tool for bulk processing: importing a large file, recalculating all rows in a table;
  • line 69: the SQL commands will be sent to the DBMS in batches (see Chapter 10) of three: the JDBC driver transmits three commands in a single exchange with the server. In Kotlin, the [getJdbcBatchSize]/[setJdbcBatchSize] pair is used as a property. The log shows the first three [UPDATE] entries, followed by the execution of the batch (line 58), and concludes with the final batch of two commands (line 63). An application sets the batch size for all its sessions using the [hibernate.jdbc.batch_size] property (typically between 10 and 50). Note that inserts into a table whose key is generated by [IDENTITY] cannot be grouped into batches.

For bulk processing with a regular session, you must prevent its persistence context from accumulating entities: synchronize and flush the session regularly, for example every fifty records ([session.flush(); session.clear()]). With Kotlin, the [chunked] function for sequences and collections (Chapter 5) conveniently splits the data into chunks of this size.

docs.title: 11.14.1. The [SessionFactory] in the container
docs.text:
The previous examples created their own sessions. In a layered application (Chapter 6), and in all Spring applications, the [SessionFactory] is an object in the dependency injection container, just like the layers that use it. To this end, the Spring Framework provides, in its [spring-orm] library:

  • the [LocalSessionFactoryBean] class, which constructs the [SessionFactory] from a data source ([DataSource], Chapter 10) and a list of entities;
  • the [HibernateTransactionManager] class, a transaction manager that opens a Hibernate session for each transaction, associates it with the current thread, and closes it at the end of the transaction;
  • the [@Transactional] annotation (library [spring-tx]): when applied to a method, or to a class for all its public methods, it instructs Spring to execute the method within a transaction, which is committed if the method completes normally and rolled back if it throws an uncaught exception. These are known as declarative transactions. A note regarding Kotlin: by default, Spring does not roll back the transaction for a controlled exception as defined by Java (a [IOException], for example). Kotlin does not distinguish these exceptions from others, but Spring does: a Kotlin function that throws a [IOException] within a transactional method will have its transaction committed! We therefore write [@Transactional(rollbackFor = [Exception::class])] to ensure the transaction is rolled back in all cases.

Inside a transactional method, ***[sessionFactory.currentSession]*** (the *[getCurrentSession] method) resets the current transaction session. A [dao] layer can then be a singleton that receives the [SessionFactory] (thread-safe) and asks it, in each method, for the current session: the rule “one session per unit of work, never shared between threads” is effortlessly enforced. Be careful with coroutines, however: the current session is associated with the thread, and a suspension function that switches threads in the middle of a transaction would lose its session. Therefore, we retain the blocking transactional methods and call them from a coroutine within a [withContext(Dispatchers.IO)] block, as shown in the example [async]*.

docs.title: 11.14.2. The [injection] subproject
docs.text:
The [injection] subproject depends on Spring and HikariCP, in addition to the [articles] library:

// Hibernate and dependency injection: Spring ORM and declarative transactions
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    // makes the classes annotated by Spring open (@Configuration, @Transactional...)
    kotlin("plugin.spring")
    application
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // the [Article] entity and the [hbarticles] database (Hibernate, MySQL and the SQL log included)
    implementation(project(":articles"))
    // Spring: container, declarative transactions, Hibernate integration
    implementation("org.springframework:spring-context:7.0.9")
    implementation("org.springframework:spring-orm:7.0.9")
    // the HikariCP connection pool
    implementation("com.zaxxer:HikariCP:7.0.2")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
    // the program run by [gradlew -q :injection:run]
    mainClass = "injection.MainKt"
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}
  • Line 5: The [all-open] plugin configured for Spring (Chapter 6). It makes the classes annotated with [@Configuration], as well as [@Transactional] and a few others ([@Component], [@Service], [@Async]....), as well as their methods. We’ll see why this is essential;
  • line 15: the [Article] entity and the [hbarticles] database (including Hibernate, MySQL, and the SQL log);
  • Lines 17–18: the Spring container and Hibernate integration; [spring-orm] includes [spring-tx], the transaction library;
  • line 19: the HikariCP connection pool (Chapter 10);
  • lines 36–39: Programs launched by Gradle write their output to UTF-8 so that accented characters display correctly on Windows (Chapter 2).

The Spring configuration is written in Kotlin, using the annotations [@Configuration] and [@Bean] from Chapter 6:

package injection

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource
import java.util.Properties
import javax.sql.DataSource
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration
import org.springframework.orm.jpa.hibernate.HibernateTransactionManager
import org.springframework.orm.jpa.hibernate.LocalSessionFactoryBean
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.EnableTransactionManagement

// the Spring configuration: connection pool, SessionFactory, transaction manager, [dao] layer
@Configuration
@EnableTransactionManagement
class Config {

    // the HikariCP connection pool (chapter 10)
    @Bean(destroyMethod = "close")
    fun dataSource() = HikariDataSource().apply {
        jdbcUrl = BaseArticles.URL
        username = BaseArticles.USER
        password = BaseArticles.PASSWORD
    }

    // the SessionFactory, built by Spring with the connection pool
    @Bean
    fun sessionFactory(dataSource: DataSource) = LocalSessionFactoryBean().apply {
        setDataSource(dataSource)
        setAnnotatedClasses(Article::class.java)
        hibernateProperties = Properties().apply { put(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, "true") }
    }

    // the transaction manager: one Hibernate session per transaction
    @Bean
    fun transactionManager(sessionFactory: SessionFactory) = HibernateTransactionManager(sessionFactory)

    // the [dao] layer: a singleton that receives the SessionFactory
    @Bean
    fun articlesDao(sessionFactory: SessionFactory) = ArticlesDao(sessionFactory)
}
  • line 18: enables the [@Transactional] annotation: Spring will replace every object with a method bearing this annotation with a proxy that opens and commits the transaction around the call;
  • lines 22–26: the HikariCP connection pool from Chapter 10, configured in a [apply] block: The modifiers [setJdbcUrl], [setUsername], and [setPassword] are used as properties. The attribute [destroyMethod] specifies the method to be called when the container is shut down. The inferred return type of the function is [HikariDataSource]: this is the type under which Spring registers the bean;
  • lines 31–34: [SessionFactory]. A *[LocalSessionFactoryBean] is a factory for *[SessionFactory]*: Spring registers the object it produces in the container, and it is a *[SessionFactory] that is obtained by requesting this bean. It receives the connection pool (which replaces Hibernate’s built-in pool), the entities, and the Hibernate properties. We write [setDataSource(dataSource)] rather than [dataSource = dataSource], which would assign the parameter to itself (and would be rejected, since a parameter is read-only);
  • line 39: the transaction manager;
  • line 43: the [dao] layer, which receives the [SessionFactory].

The [dao] layer:

package injection

import articles.Article
import org.hibernate.Session
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional

// the [dao] layer: each public method runs in a transaction opened by Spring
@Transactional
class ArticlesDao(
    // the SessionFactory, shared by all the threads
    private val sessionFactory: SessionFactory
) {

    // do two requests for the current session, in the same transaction, return the same session?
    fun sameSession() = sessionFactory.currentSession === sessionFactory.currentSession

    // the session of the transaction
    fun session(): Session = sessionFactory.currentSession

    // the articles to restock; a read-only transaction
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    fun articlesOutOfStock(): List<String> {
        val hql = "select name from Article where currentStock < minimumStock"
        return sessionFactory.currentSession.createSelectionQuery(hql, String::class.java).resultList
    }

    // the article with the given name
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    fun article(name: String): Article =
        sessionFactory.currentSession
            .createSelectionQuery("from Article where name = :name", Article::class.java)
            .setParameter("name", name)
            .singleResult

    // the sale of a quantity of an article: an exception rolls back the transaction
    fun sell(name: String, quantity: Int) {
        val article = article(name)
        article.currentStock -= quantity
        // check throws an IllegalStateException if the condition is false
        check(article.currentStock >= 0) { "insufficient stock for the article [$name]" }
    }
}
  • line 9: all public methods of the class are transactional;
  • line 12: the [SessionFactory], received by the primary constructor;
  • line 16: within the same transaction, do two requests from the current session return the same session? The [===] operator compares the references (Chapter 3);
  • line 19: the transaction’s session, returned to the caller (for the following experiment: this is not done in a real application);
  • lines 22–25: a read-only transaction ([readOnly = true]): Spring sets the session to read-only and does not synchronize it;
  • lines 37–41: the sale of a quantity of an item. If the inventory becomes negative, the Kotlin function [check] (Chapter 3) throws a [IllegalStateException], an unhandled exception: Spring rolls back the transaction. The call to the [article] method (line 38) is an internal call within the object, which does not go through the proxy: it executes within the [sell] transaction.

The proxy created by Spring for the [ArticlesDao] class is a subclass of it, generated at runtime by the CGLIB library, which redefines each public method to wrap it in a transaction. Without the [plugin.spring] plugin, the Kotlin class would be final, and Spring would not be able to derive from it. If you compile the subproject without this plugin (by manually declaring the [Config] class and its [open] functions to work around the first error, which we already encountered in Chapter 6), the container refuses to start:

Exception in thread "main" org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'articlesDao' defined in injection.Config: Could not generate CGLIB subclass of class injection.ArticlesDao: Common causes of this problem include using a final class or a non-visible class
Caused by: org.springframework.aop.framework.AopConfigException: Could not generate CGLIB subclass of class injection.ArticlesDao: Common causes of this problem include using a final class or a non-visible class
Caused by: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Cannot subclass final class injection.ArticlesDao

A more insidious pitfall awaits anyone who manually opens the class ([open class ArticlesDao]) without opening its methods: the proxy is then created, but it cannot override the methods that remain final. Calling these methods directly executes the code of the [ArticlesDao]... class on the proxy object, whose fields have not been initialized (Spring creates it without calling the class’s constructor). The result, obtained by compiling the subproject in this way, is confusing:

--- sessions and transactions
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "org.hibernate.SessionFactory.getCurrentSession()" because "this.sessionFactory" is null

The property [sessionFactory], which is of a non-nullable type, is set to [null]! The plugin prevents these two errors: with it, the class and all its methods are open.

The main program:

package injection

import articles.BaseArticles
import org.hibernate.HibernateException
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory
import org.springframework.beans.factory.getBean
import org.springframework.context.annotation.AnnotationConfigApplicationContext

// Hibernate in the Spring container: current session and declarative transactions
fun main() {
    // the Spring container, configured by the [Config] class
    AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Config::class.java).use { context ->
        // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
        val sessionFactory = context.getBean<SessionFactory>()
        BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory)
        val dao = context.getBean<ArticlesDao>()

        // 1 - during a transaction, the current session is always the same
        println("--- sessions and transactions")
        println("one transaction: same session = ${dao.sameSession()}")
        // 2 - two transactions: two sessions, closed at the end of their transaction
        val session1 = dao.session()
        val session2 = dao.session()
        println("two transactions: same session = ${session1 === session2}, " +
                "first session open = ${session1.isOpen}")
        // 3 - outside a transaction, there is no current session
        try {
            sessionFactory.currentSession
        } catch (e: HibernateException) {
            println("${e::class.simpleName} : ${e.message}")
        }

        // 4 - transactional methods of the [dao] layer
        println("--- articles out of stock")
        println("out of stock: ${dao.articlesOutOfStock()}")
        println("--- sale of 2 bikes")
        dao.sell("bike", 2)
        println("--- sale of 50 pumps")
        try {
            dao.sell("pump", 50)
        } catch (e: IllegalStateException) {
            println("${e::class.simpleName} : ${e.message}")
        }
        println("--- state of the database")
        println(dao.article("bike"))
        println(dao.article("pump"))
    }
}

Results:

> gradlew -q :injection:run
--- sessions and transactions
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)
one transaction: same session = true
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)
two transactions: same session = false, first session open = false
HibernateException : Could not obtain transaction-synchronized Session for current thread
--- articles out of stock
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> select a1_0.name
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.currentStock<a1_0.minimumStock
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)
out of stock: [arrows - set of 6]
--- sale of 2 bikes
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.name=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = bike
    SQL> update articles
    SQL> set currentStock=?, minimumStock=?, name=?, price=?
    SQL> where id=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 8
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = 5
    SQL> -- parameter 3 = bike
    SQL> -- parameter 4 = 500.00
    SQL> -- parameter 5 = 1
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)
--- sale of 50 pumps
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.name=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = pump
    SQL> -- transaction rolled back (ROLLBACK)
IllegalStateException : insufficient stock for the article [pump]
--- state of the database
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.name=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = bike
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)
[1, bike, 500.00, 8, 5]
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.name=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = pump
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)
[2, pump, 10.00, 10, 2]

Comments:

  • Line 12: the Spring container, configured by the [Config] class. It is closed at the end of the [use] block, which closes the [SessionFactory] and the connection pool;
  • line 14: the [SessionFactory] constructed by Spring, obtained via Spring’s [getBean<T>()] extension function (Chapter 6); it is used to recreate the product table;
  • line 20: a transaction (lines 3–4): within the same transaction, the current session remains the same (line 5);
  • lines 22–25: two calls, two transactions (lines 6–9), two different sessions; the first is closed, since its transaction is complete (line 10). The property [isOpen] is the session’s method [isOpen()];
  • lines 28–29: outside a transaction, there is no current session: [getCurrentSession] launches a [HibernateException] (line 11). This is the classic error of a method that omitted the annotation [@Transactional];
  • line 35: a read-only transaction (lines 13–17);
  • line 37: the sale of two bicycles. The transaction is committed, and session synchronization sends the [UPDATE] (lines 20–33);
  • lines 40–41: the sale of fifty pumps triggers an exception: Spring rolls back the transaction (line 40), and [UPDATE] is never sent, since the session was not synchronized;
  • lines 45–46: database state: the bicycle inventory has changed to 8, while the pump inventory remains at 10 (lines 49 and 56).

In a Spring Boot application, all of this happens automatically: Spring Boot creates the connection pool, the factory (in its Jakarta Persistence form, a [EntityManagerFactory]), and the transaction manager from the [application.properties] file. Spring Data JPA is often used on top of Hibernate; it generates the [dao] layer from a simple interface: [interface ArticleRepository : JpaRepository<Article, Int>] provides [findAll], [findById], [save], [delete]..., and a declared method [fun findByPriceLessThan(price: BigDecimal): List<Article>] is automatically translated into a query. Spring Data adds a few extension functions for Kotlin, such as [findByIdOrNull], which returns a [Article?] rather than a [Optional<Article>].

docs.title: 11.15.1. The Architecture
docs.text:
Version 6 of the tax calculation application (Chapter 10) read the tax brackets from a MySQL database using JDBC. Version 7 does the same using Hibernate. As with version 6, only the [dao] layer changes: the [business] and [ui] layers from version 5 (Chapter 6) are reused as-is, thanks to the composite architecture.

Version 7 consists of two subprojects from the structure in Chapter 11, stored in the [TaxV7] folder:

11-hibernate/
  settings.gradle.kts                   the subprojects and the included build (chapter 6)
  TaxV7/
    tax-dao-hibernate/                  library: the Hibernate [dao] layer
      build.gradle.kts
      src/main/kotlin/tax/dao/
        Bracket.kt                      the entity
        HibernateTax.kt                 the implementation of ITaxDao
        CreateDatabase.kt               the creation of the [hbtaxes] database
      src/main/resources/
        logback.xml
    tax-ui-hibernate/                   executable: integration of the layers
      build.gradle.kts
      src/main/kotlin/tax/ui/
        MainHibernate.kt
      tax-hibernate.properties
      tax-hibernate-error.properties

The [TaxV7] folder does not have a build file: like the [TaxV5] folder in Chapter 6, it is simply a collection of subprojects. The modules for version 5 ([tax-dao], [tax-business], [tax-ui], in version 5.0) are provided by the build from Chapter 6, included via the line [includeBuild("../06-architectures")] in the file [settings.gradle.kts]: Gradle replaces any [examples.tax:tax-xxx:5.0] dependency with the corresponding subproject from this build, which it compiles as needed. There is nothing to install beforehand, unlike with Maven, where you first had to enter [mvn install] in the version 5 folder.

docs.title: 11.15.2. The [dao] layer
docs.text:
The [tax-dao-hibernate] subproject depends on the [dao] layer from version 5, which contains the application entities ([TaxBracket], [TaxException]) and the [ITaxDao] interface:

// TaxV7: the tax-dao-hibernate subproject, a library (the [dao] layer written with Hibernate)
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    // the [Bracket] entity: the [jpa] and [allopen] plugins
    kotlin("plugin.jpa")
    kotlin("plugin.allopen")
    // the library plugin: it adds the [api] configuration
    `java-library`
    // [gradlew -q :TaxV7:tax-dao-hibernate:run] creates the [hbtaxes] database
    application
}

// the coordinates of the library: examples.tax:tax-dao-hibernate:7.0
group = "examples.tax"
version = "7.0"

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // the [dao] layer of version 5 (chapter 6): entities, ITaxDao interface, HardwiredTax
    api("examples.tax:tax-dao:5.0")
    // Hibernate, the MySQL JDBC driver and Logback
    implementation("org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-core:7.4.5.Final")
    runtimeOnly("com.mysql:mysql-connector-j:9.7.0")
    runtimeOnly("ch.qos.logback:logback-classic:1.5.38")
}

// the classes annotated this way are opened by the [allopen] plugin
allOpen {
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.Entity")
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.MappedSuperclass")
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.Embeddable")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
    // the creation of the [hbtaxes] database
    mainClass = "tax.dao.CreateDatabaseKt"
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}
  • lines 5–6: entity plugins: the subproject defines the entity [Bracket];
  • line 8: the subproject is a library that exposes some of its dependencies through the configuration [api];
  • line 10: the [application] plugin, used to create the database (line 47);
  • line 23: the [dao] layer of version 5. This is a dependency on [api]: the class [HibernateTax] implements the interface [ITaxDao] from this library, which its users must therefore also see;
  • lines 25–27: Hibernate, the JDBC driver for MySQL, and Logback. Hibernate is a dependency of [implementation]: it is used internally by the library but does not appear in its public interface;
  • lines 31–34: the standard configuration for the [allopen] plugin;
  • lines 50–53: Programs launched by Gradle write their output to UTF-8 so that accented characters display correctly on Windows (Chapter 2).

The [TaxBracket] data class in version 5 cannot be a Hibernate entity: it is a data class (we’ve seen why this isn’t a good idea for an entity), it is immutable, and it has no identifier. We do not modify it, because it is part of the contract between the layers, shared by all versions. We create an entity, specific to the [dao] layer, whose role is to represent a row in the table:

// a tax bracket as it is stored in the database: a Hibernate entity
@Entity
@Table(name = "brackets")
class Bracket(
    @Column(name = "limits", nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    private var limit: BigDecimal,

    @Column(name = "coeffr", nullable = false, precision = 6, scale = 4)
    private var coeffR: BigDecimal,

    @Column(name = "coeffn", nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    private var coeffN: BigDecimal,
) {
    // the primary key, which does not exist in the TaxBracket class
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private var id: Int? = null
}
  • row 3: the table [brackets];
  • rows 6–12: the three columns, declared in the primary constructor, with appropriate [decimal] types: the limit and the coefficient [coeffN] are amounts with two decimal places, and [coeffR] is a rate with four decimal places. The column names are in lowercase. The properties are private: the entity is used only to populate the table ([CreateDatabase]) and to write queries; the rest of the application never sees it. Hibernate, which accesses the fields directly, does not require them to be public;
  • lines 15–17: the primary key, which is also used to sort the brackets.

The class [HibernateTax] implements the interface [ITaxDao]:

package tax.dao

import tax.entities.TaxException
import tax.entities.TaxBracket
import jakarta.persistence.PersistenceException
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration

// a [dao] layer that reads the tax brackets from a database with Hibernate
class HibernateTax(url: String, user: String, password: String) : ITaxDao {

    companion object {
        // error codes specific to this implementation
        const val ACCESS_ERROR = 1
        const val EMPTY_TABLE = 2
    }

    // tax brackets, read once and for all at construction
    override val taxBrackets: List<TaxBracket> = try {
        // a short-lived SessionFactory, just long enough to read the table
        HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("tax")
            .managedClass(Bracket::class.java)
            .jdbcUrl(url)
            .jdbcCredentials(user, password)
            .createEntityManagerFactory()
            .use { sessionFactory ->
                // the rows of the table are projected to the TaxBracket class of the application
                val hql = "select b.limit, b.coeffR, b.coeffN from Bracket b order by b.id"
                sessionFactory.fromSession { session ->
                    session.createSelectionQuery(hql, TaxBracket::class.java).resultList
                }
            }
    } catch (e: PersistenceException) {
        // Hibernate or DBMS error: it is wrapped in a TaxException
        throw TaxException("Error while reading the tax brackets from the database",
            e, ACCESS_ERROR)
    }

    init {
        // the [business] layer needs at least one bracket
        if (taxBrackets.isEmpty()) {
            throw TaxException("The tax brackets table is empty", code = EMPTY_TABLE)
        }
    }
}
  • lines 11–14: the error codes for this implementation, as with [FileTax] and [JsonTax];
  • line 9: the [dao] layer receives the URL from the database, along with the user and their password. These are simply constructor parameters ([val] is not written: they do not become properties, since they are used only for construction). It reads the brackets once and for all during construction: it will be a singleton;
  • line 18: the property [taxBrackets] of the interface [ITaxDao], initialized by an expression [try] (Chapter 3): its value is that of the block [try]; if an error occurs, [catch] throws an exception;
  • Lines 20–25: A short-lived [SessionFactory]—just long enough to read the table—immediately closed by [use]. Since the layer accesses the database only once, there is no need to keep it; a [dao] layer that accessed the database on every call would instead receive a [SessionFactory] created once and for all, as in the previous example;
  • Lines 27–29: Reading the table in primary key order. The query is a projection onto the data class [TaxBracket]: Hibernate requests only the three relevant columns from the DBMS and directly creates the application objects by calling the constructor of *[TaxBracket] with the three values, without going through *[Bracket] entities. The value returned by [fromSession], and then by [use], is the list that was read: this is the value of the property;
  • Lines 32–35: An error from Hibernate or the DBMS (database inaccessible, table missing, etc.) manifests as a [PersistenceException] (the base class for Jakarta Persistence exceptions, from which Hibernate’s exceptions are derived). As in other implementations, it is encapsulated within a *[TaxException]. The exception can occur as early as the creation of the *[SessionFactory]* (line 24), which connects to the server: it is also contained within the ***[try]** block;
  • lines 38–41: an empty table is also an error: the [business] layer requires at least one row. The [init] block executes after the property is initialized, which precedes it in the class. The error code is passed via a named argument ([code = EMPTY_TABLE]), since the exception has no cause (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 11.15.3. The database
docs.text:
The database [hbtaxes] is created by the program [CreateDatabase.kt]. To avoid rewriting the pay scale brackets, it reuses those from class [HardwiredTax] in version 5:

package tax.dao

import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import org.hibernate.tool.schema.Action

// creation of the [hbtaxes] database: the [brackets] table, filled with the brackets of HardwiredTax
fun main() {
    HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("tax")
        .managedClass(Bracket::class.java)
        .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbtaxes?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
        .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
        // display of the SQL statements, without formatting
        .showSql(true, false, false)
        // the table is dropped then recreated when the SessionFactory is created
        .schemaToolingAction(Action.CREATE)
        .createEntityManagerFactory()
        .use { sessionFactory ->
            // the brackets of the tax scale, those of version 5, numbered from 1 by the DBMS
            sessionFactory.inTransaction { session ->
                for ((limit, coeffR, coeffN) in HardwiredTax().taxBrackets) {
                    session.persist(Bracket(limit, coeffR, coeffN))
                }
            }
        }
}
  • line 10: the database [hbtaxes], created by MySQL if it does not exist;
  • line 13: displays the SQL statements, without formatting;
  • line 15: the table is deleted and then recreated when [SessionFactory] is created;
  • lines 19–21: one [Bracket] entity per bracket of the [HardwiredTax] class, persisted in a transaction. The [for] loop breaks down each [TaxBracket] into its three components ([(limit, coeffR, coeffN)]) using the functions [component1], [component2], and [component3], which are generated for a data class (Chapter 4).

The subproject also contains a file named [logback.xml], used by [CreateDatabase.kt] and by the application, which only allows the following errors to pass through:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- Logback configuration: only Hibernate errors are displayed -->
<configuration>
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%-5level %logger{0} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>
    <!-- the DBMS errors are passed to the application by exceptions: they are not logged -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error" level="OFF"/>
    <root level="ERROR">
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>
  • line 10: Errors from the DBMS, which Hibernate logs before throwing an exception, are not displayed: the application reports them itself;
  • Line 11: The other logs record only errors.

Execution:

> gradlew -q :TaxV7:tax-dao-hibernate:run
Hibernate: drop table if exists brackets
Hibernate: create table brackets (coeffn decimal(10,2) not null, coeffr decimal(6,4) not null, id integer not null auto_increment, limits decimal(10,2) not null, primary key (id)) engine=InnoDB
Hibernate: insert into brackets (coeffn,coeffr,limits) values (?,?,?)
Hibernate: insert into brackets (coeffn,coeffr,limits) values (?,?,?)
Hibernate: insert into brackets (coeffn,coeffr,limits) values (?,?,?)
Hibernate: insert into brackets (coeffn,coeffr,limits) values (?,?,?)
Hibernate: insert into brackets (coeffn,coeffr,limits) values (?,?,?)
Hibernate: insert into brackets (coeffn,coeffr,limits) values (?,?,?)
Hibernate: insert into brackets (coeffn,coeffr,limits) values (?,?,?)

We check the table contents:

> mysql -uroot -t hbtaxes -e "SELECT id, limits, coeffr, coeffn FROM brackets"
+----+----------+--------+---------+
| id | limits   | coeffr | coeffn  |
+----+----------+--------+---------+
|  1 |  4962.00 | 0.0000 |    0.00 |
|  2 |  8382.00 | 0.0680 |  291.09 |
|  3 | 14753.00 | 0.1910 | 1322.92 |
|  4 | 23888.00 | 0.2830 | 2668.39 |
|  5 | 38868.00 | 0.3740 | 4846.98 |
|  6 | 47932.00 | 0.4260 | 6883.66 |
|  7 |     0.00 | 0.4810 | 9505.54 |
+----+----------+--------+---------+

We see the pay scale brackets, with the last one having a zero limit (it is not used by layer [business], which selects the last bracket when no other applies).

To create the database on your own system:

  • run MySQL (in Laragon; see the appendix; user [root] with no password);
  • navigate to the [11-hibernate] folder and enter the command [gradlew -q :TaxV7:tax-dao-hibernate:run] (or run [CreateDatabase.kt] in IntelliJ IDEA, with the green triangle placed in front of its function [main]). Gradle compiles the Version 5 modules at the same time, in the adjacent folder [06-architectures].

The database [hbtaxes] is then created, with its table [brackets] populated. If the command fails, verify that MySQL is running and that the URL for [CreateDatabase.kt] corresponds to your server (port 3306, username [root], empty password). Alternatively, if you prefer, you can create the table and its rows using a SQL script, as described in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 11.15.4. Integrating the Layers
docs.text:
The [tax-ui-hibernate] subproject combines the following layers:

// TaxV7: the tax-ui-hibernate subproject, the integration of the layers
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    application
}

group = "examples.tax"
version = "7.0"

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // the [business] and [ui] layers of version 5, unchanged (composite build)
    implementation("examples.tax:tax-business:5.0")
    implementation("examples.tax:tax-ui:5.0")
    // the new [dao] layer, which brings Hibernate, the JDBC driver and Logback
    implementation(project(":TaxV7:tax-dao-hibernate"))
    // the Spring dependency injection container
    implementation("org.springframework:spring-context:7.0.9")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
    // the main program: gradlew -q :TaxV7:tax-ui-hibernate:run [--args="file.properties"]
    mainClass = "tax.ui.MainHibernateKt"
}

tasks.named<JavaExec>("run") {
    // the program reads the keyboard
    standardInput = System.`in`
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}
  • lines 16–17: the layers [business] and [ui] from version 5. The [tax-ui] subproject contains the main program for version 5; it is used here as a library, specifically for its [Dialog] object;
  • line 19: the new layer [dao], which includes Hibernate, the driver JDBC, and Logback;
  • line 21: the Spring container;
  • line 34: the main class;
  • lines 37–39: the program reads from the keyboard (Chapter 6);
  • lines 42–45: the programs launched by Gradle write their output to UTF-8, so that accented characters display correctly on Windows (Chapter 2).

The configuration file [tax-hibernate.properties], located in the subproject folder, specifies the database:

# configuration of the [Tax] application, version 7: the database of the tax brackets
jdbc.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbtaxes
jdbc.user=root
jdbc.password=

The file [tax-hibernate-error.properties] references a database named [hbtaxesmissing], which does not exist:

# a database that does not exist
jdbc.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbtaxesmissing
jdbc.user=root
jdbc.password=

The main program is the one from version 5, in which only the composition of the [dao] layer changes:

package tax.ui

import tax.dao.HibernateTax
import tax.dao.ITaxDao
import tax.entities.TaxException
import tax.business.ITaxBusiness
import tax.business.TaxBusiness
import java.util.Properties
import kotlin.io.path.Path
import kotlin.io.path.bufferedReader
import kotlin.system.exitProcess
import org.springframework.beans.factory.getBean
import org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext
import org.springframework.context.support.registerBean

// version 7: the [dao] layer reads the tax brackets from a database with Hibernate
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    // the configuration file: tax-hibernate.properties by default, or the one passed as an argument
    val configFile = args.firstOrNull() ?: "tax-hibernate.properties"

    // integration of the layers
    val business: ITaxBusiness = try {
        // reading the configuration, in the current folder
        val config = Properties()
        Path(configFile).bufferedReader().use { config.load(it) }
        val url = config.getProperty("jdbc.url")
            ?: throw TaxException("Database URL [jdbc.url] missing from the file $configFile")
        val user = config.getProperty("jdbc.user", "root")
        val password = config.getProperty("jdbc.password", "")

        // the Spring container: the layers are registered in it
        val context = GenericApplicationContext()
        // the [dao] layer: HibernateTax, with the database of the configuration
        context.registerBean<ITaxDao> { HibernateTax(url, user, password) }
        // the [business] layer of version 5: the container will pass it the [dao] layer
        context.registerBean<TaxBusiness>()

        // starting the container: it creates the [dao] layer, then the [business] layer
        context.refresh()
        context.getBean<ITaxBusiness>()
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        // display of the error and end of the program
        Dialog.displayError(e)
        exitProcess(1)
    }

    // the dialog with the user, that of version 5
    Dialog.run(business)
}
  • The file is not named [Main.kt]: it would be compiled into a class named [tax.ui.MainKt], which already exists in the [tax-ui] module of version 5, on which we depend. The file [MainHibernate.kt] generates a class named [tax.ui.MainHibernateKt];
  • lines 26–29: the required URL database, the username, and the password, read from the configuration. [getProperty] returns [null] for a missing key: the Elvis operator ([?:]) then evaluates to [TaxException] ([throw] is a Kotlin expression);
  • line 34: the [dao] layer is a [HibernateTax], created by a lambda that passes it the parameters from the database;
  • line 36: the [business] layer in version 5: the container will pass the [dao] layer to its constructor;
  • line 48: the dialog for version 5.

docs.title: 11.15.5. Executions
docs.text:
The user’s input, redirected to the program to obtain these results, was placed after the questions:

> gradlew -q :TaxV7:tax-ui-hibernate:run
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2 60000
Tax=4282 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 3 60000
Tax=2959 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: n 0 60000
Tax=11519 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop:

The control values from previous versions are retained: 4,282 euros for a married couple with two children and a combined income of 60,000 euros, 2,959 euros with three children, and 11,519 euros for a single person without children.

With the configuration file [tax-hibernate-error.properties], which refers to a nonexistent database:

> gradlew -q :TaxV7:tax-ui-hibernate:run --args="tax-hibernate-error.properties"
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'tax.dao.ITaxDao': Instantiation of supplied bean failed
----------------------------------------
tax.entities.TaxException: Error while reading the tax brackets from the database
----------------------------------------
org.hibernate.service.spi.ServiceException: Unable to create requested service [org.hibernate.engine.jdbc.env.spi.JdbcEnvironment] due to: Error calling Driver.connect() [Unknown database 'hbtaxesmissing']
----------------------------------------
org.hibernate.exception.SQLGrammarException: Error calling Driver.connect() [Unknown database 'hbtaxesmissing']
----------------------------------------
java.sql.SQLSyntaxErrorException: Unknown database 'hbtaxesmissing'
----------------------------------------
  • line 12: the original exception, thrown by the JDBC driver;
  • lines 8 and 10: the Hibernate exceptions that encapsulate it: the error occurred during the creation of [SessionFactory], when Hibernate connected to the server to determine its version;
  • line 6: the [dao] layer wrapped the error in a [TaxException];
  • line 4: the Spring container, which was creating the [dao] layer, itself encapsulated the exception in a [BeanCreationException], which was displayed by the main program.

Changing the DBMS is equivalent to changing the URL in the database and the dependency on the JDBC driver: Hibernate automatically selects the SQL dialect from the DBMS encountered, and the code for the [HibernateTax] class, written in HQL, remains unchanged. Only the database creation—which depends on the column types—needs to be redone, which the program [CreateDatabase.kt] does without any modifications other than to its own URL.

docs.title: 11.16. Conclusion: JDBC, JdbcClient, jOOQ—Exposed or Hibernate?
docs.text:
We now have two ways to access a database: JDBC (Chapter 10) and Hibernate (this chapter). There are other, intermediate approaches that are widely used:

  • JdbcClient, from the Spring Framework ([spring-jdbc] library), adds to JDBC a flexible API that executes a hand-written SQL query and automatically transforms the result rows into objects: [jdbcClient.sql("select * from articles where price > :price").param("price", 200).query(Article::class.java).list()]. You write the SQL; Spring handles the parameters and copies the columns into the objects (including data classes, whose constructors receive the columns). This is a “micro-ORM”;
  • jOOQ generates, from the database schema, classes that allow you to write a SQL in Java or Kotlin that is verified by the compiler: [dsl.selectFrom(ARTICLES).where(ARTICLES.PRICE.gt(price)).fetch()]. You retain full control over the SQL, with the safety of type checking;
  • Exposed, from JetBrains, is the database access library written in Kotlin and for Kotlin. Tables are described there using Kotlin objects ([object Articles : Table("articles")], with columns such as [val price = decimal("price", 10, 2)]), without code generation, and queries are written in a dedicated language (“ DSL”), which resembles SQL and is verified by the compiler: [Articles.selectAll().where { Articles.price greater minPrice }]. Exposed also offers a second API, a lightweight version of ORM (entity classes linked to tables), and relies on JDBC or, optionally, on non-blocking drivers (R2DBC) that can be used from coroutines. It takes advantage of everything we’ve covered about Kotlin: extension functions, lambdas with receivers, infix functions ([greater]), and nullable types for optional columns.
StrengthsWeaknessesJDBCFull control over SQL; performance; no dependenciesa lot of repetitive code (parameters, reading columns), streamlined in Kotlin by [use] and extension functions; SQL in strings, not checked by the compilerJdbcClientSQL hand-written, without copy-and-paste code; performance similar to JDBCNo change tracking or generation of [INSERT]/[UPDATE]; SQL not verifiedjOOQSQL verified by the compiler; all features of the DBMSCode generation with every schema change; no change tracking; paid license required for certain commercial DBMS versionsExposedDesigned for Kotlin; queries verified by the compiler, without code generation; lightweightKotlin-specific; less widespread than Hibernate, and less documentation; the schema is described manually in the codeHibernateobject-oriented model; change tracking; relationships; HQL and Criteria API; Jakarta Persistence standard; independent of the DBMSan additional layer to understand (sessions, states, lazy loading); generated SQL code to monitor; less suitable for complex bulk processing; some adaptations for Kotlin ([jpa] and [allopen] plugins, no data classes for entities)

The following guidelines can be suggested:

  • Hibernate (often via Spring Data JPA) is suitable for most business applications: a model of interconnected entities, operations for reading and updating entities, and a schema that evolves with the application. It is the default choice for Spring Boot applications, in both Kotlin and Java;
  • JDBC, JdbcClient, jOOQ or Exposed are suitable when you want precise control over the SQL being executed: complex statistical queries, stored procedures, processing very large volumes, or an existing database with a schema that is poorly suited to an object-oriented model. Exposed is a natural choice for an application written entirely in Kotlin, particularly outside of Spring (using the Ktor web framework from JetBrains, for example);
  • these approaches can be combined: an application can use Hibernate for the bulk of its operations and hand-written SQL code—in the form of native queries—with [JdbcClient] or JDBC ([doWork]), for a few critical queries.

In any case, ORM does not eliminate the need to understand SQL and how the DBMS works: the log of executed SQL commands, which we have displayed throughout this chapter, is the primary tool for verifying what Hibernate is actually doing.

To learn more, the Hibernate documentation is comprehensive, and its introductory guide is the best place to start: Hibernate ORM - documentation. The Jakarta Persistence specification is published by the Eclipse Foundation: Jakarta Persistence. Spring’s guide on using JPA in Kotlin summarizes the concepts covered in this chapter (plugins, entities, nullability): Building web applications with Spring Boot and Kotlin. Exposed is presented on its GitHub page, which links to its documentation: JetBrains Exposed.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The PDF in the document is HERE.

The code in this document is HERE.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s IA Claude. It is the Kotlin port of the course “Learning the Java 25 Language Through Examples” (October 2026), which itself is a port of the course “Learning the C# 14 Language with .NET 10 (October 2026), a rewrite of the course “Learning the C# Language, Version 3.0, with the .NET 3.5 Framework” written by Serge Tahé in May 2008. It retains the outline, examples, and main thread of that course, and rewrites them in today’s Kotlin:

  • The document uses Kotlin 2.4 (version 2.4.20, September 2026), with JDK 25, the latest long-term support (LTS) version of Java (LTS). Kotlin is a language for the Java Virtual Machine: it produces the same intermediate code as Java and directly uses all of its libraries. Readers of the Java course will therefore find the same classes from JDK (files, networking, threads, dates, etc.) and the same frameworks (JUnit, Spring, Jackson, Hibernate, Spring Boot), used from another language;
  • where the two languages differ, this document does more than just translate. Kotlin offers its own solutions to issues that Java handles differently: null safety built into the type system, properties, data classes, extension functions, operator overloading, functional types, default parameter values and named arguments, and the [when] expression. Conversely, Kotlin does not have checked exceptions or [static] members. These differences are presented in detail, often by comparing Kotlin code with Java code;
  • the chapter on asynchronous programming takes on a different character: whereas Java uses [CompletableFuture] classes and virtual threads, Kotlin offers coroutines, along with [suspend] functions, the [launch] and [async] constructors, and structured concurrency. This is Kotlin’s answer to the C# [async] / [await] from the original course;
  • the libraries are the ones currently used on the JVM: [JUnit 6] and [kotlin.test] for testing, [Spring Framework 7] for dependency injection, [Jackson 3] for JSON, [kotlinx.coroutines] for coroutines, the driver [MySQL Connector/J] for JDBC, [Hibernate 7] for object-relational mapping, and [Spring Boot 4] for web services; the projects are built using [Gradle], whose scripts are themselves written in Kotlin.

This document is not a comprehensive course. Like the materials from which it is derived, it is intended for readers who are already familiar with programming and wish to learn the basics of Kotlin. It uses examples: more than two hundred programs (more than three hundred Kotlin files), most of them short, with line-by-line comments.

docs.title: 1.1. Kotlin from 2011 to 2026
docs.text:
Kotlin was introduced in July 2011 by the company JetBrains, the publisher of IDE, IntelliJ, and IDEA, which was seeking a language that was more concise and safer than Java for writing its own tools, yet compatible with it: A Kotlin program is compiled into bytecode, executed by the Java Virtual Machine (the JVM), and can call Java code as well as be called by it. The name comes from an island in the Gulf of Finland, near Saint Petersburg, where the team that designed it worked.

Key milestones:

  • 2016: Kotlin 1.0, the first stable version, with the accompanying compatibility commitment;
  • 2017: Google announced official support for Kotlin for developing Android apps; in 2019, Android became “Kotlin first”: Kotlin is the recommended language for new Android apps;
  • 2018: Kotlin 1.3, which stabilized coroutines, Kotlin’s answer to asynchronous programming (Chapter 9);
  • The language is developed by JetBrains; the Kotlin Foundation, founded in 2017 by JetBrains and Google, oversees its evolution, with each stage subject to public proposals (the “KEEP,” Kotlin Evolution and Enhancement Process);
  • 2024: Kotlin 2.0, featuring a new compiler called K2, which is faster and better at tracking types in the code (smart type casting);
  • Kotlin also targets platforms other than JVM: JavaScript, WebAssembly, and native code (Kotlin/Native, iOS). This document covers only Kotlin on JVM;
  • since version 2.0, a new language version (2.1.0, 2.2.0, 2.3.0, 2.4.0…) is released approximately every six months; in between, a tooling release (2.x.20) provides improvements to the tools and the standard library without changing the language. This document uses version 2.4.20, released in September 2026. New features are often introduced first as experimental; they must then be explicitly enabled (via a compiler option or the [@OptIn] annotation) before they become stable in a subsequent release.

The following table summarizes the main new language features presented in this document and indicates the chapter in which they appear:

VersionYearMajor New FeaturesChapterKotlin 1.02016null safety, properties, data classes, extension functions, lambdas, [when], operator overloading3, 4, 7Kotlin 1.12017type aliases [typealias], bound references [object::function], coroutines (experimental)4, 7Kotlin 1.32018Stable coroutines, [main] function with no parameters2, 3, 9Kotlin 1.42020Functional interfaces [fun interface], conversions SAM of Kotlin interfaces7Kotlin 1.52021Unsigned types ([UInt]…) and stable classes [value class], sealed interfaces3, 4Kotlin 1.92023[..<] operator, [entries] property of enums, [data object]3, 12Kotlin 2.02024K2 compiler: more accurate smart type conversions4Kotlin 2.22025Liveness conditions in [when] ([is Int if x > 0 ->]), interpolation with multiple [$]3, 5Kotlin 2.32025Java 25 support2Kotlin 2.42026In version 2.4.20, the [kotlinr] launcher replaces the [kotlin] command2

In terms of libraries and tools, the new features include: the build tool [Gradle] and its Kotlin scripts ([build.gradle.kts]), the Kotlin standard library collections and their higher-order functions, sequences, coroutines, and streams ([Flow]), as well as major Java ecosystem frameworks used from within Kotlin: JUnit, Spring, Jackson, Hibernate, and Spring Boot.

docs.title: 1.2. Document Contents
docs.text:
The document includes the following chapters:

  • Chapter 2: Setting up the development environment (JDK 25, IntelliJ IDEA, the compiler [kotlinc], Gradle);
  • Chapter 3: Language Fundamentals (types, null safety, operators, [if] and [when], loops, exceptions, enumerations, function parameters);
  • Chapter 4: Classes, properties, inheritance, sealed classes, operator overloading, interfaces, generics, data classes, extension functions;
  • Chapter 5: Commonly Used Kotlin Classes: Strings, Arrays, Collections, Sequences, Text and Binary Files, JSON with Jackson, Regular Expressions;
  • Chapter 6: Layered architectures, unit testing with JUnit 6, and dependency injection with Spring;
  • Chapter 7: Functional types, lambda expressions, and events;
  • Chapter 8: Execution threads, synchronization, and virtual threads;
  • Chapter 9: Asynchronous Programming with Coroutines;
  • Chapter 10: Database Access with JDBC;
  • Chapter 11: Hibernate;
  • Chapter 12: Web Programming (TCP/IP, clients and servers TCP, HTTP with [HttpClient], SMTP);
  • Chapter 13: Web Services with Spring Boot;
  • Chapter 14: Going Further;
  • Appendices: Installing Laragon and MySQL, dependencies used by Gradle projects.

docs.title: 1.3. The Common Thread: Tax Calculation
docs.text:
A single problem is revisited throughout this document: calculating the income tax for a taxpayer who has only their salary to report. The tax bracket used is the original one (2003 income): it is no longer current, but it suffices for our purpose, which is to write the same application in several different ways. It is implemented in nine versions:

VersionChapterContent13A single program: validated input, calculation, display24Classes and interfaces: [TaxBracket], [ITax], [AbstractTax], [HardwiredTax]35calculation data read from a text file or a JSON file46A layered architecture ([dao], [business], [ui]) within a single program56One Gradle subproject per layer, unit tests, and integration of layers via dependency injection610A [dao] layer that reads data from a MySQL database using JDBC711a [dao] layer written with Hibernate812A TCP tax calculation server and its client913a REST web service for tax calculation, a console client, and a web client

Starting with version 5, subsequent versions reuse the layers from version 5 and replace only the layer that has changed: this is the whole point of the layered architecture presented in Chapter 6.

docs.title: 1.4. Examples
docs.text:
The code in this document is organized in a single folder named [kotlin-oct-2026], with one subfolder per chapter. Each subfolder is a Gradle project (or a Gradle build consisting of multiple projects) that can be opened as-is in IntelliJ and IDEA:

kotlin-oct-2026/
├── 02-installation/       Hello.kt, first Gradle projects
├── 03-basics/             Basics01.kt to Basics31.kt, Tax1.kt
├── 04-classes/            Classes01.kt to Classes26.kt, multi-file programs, TaxV2
├── 05-classes-kotlin/     strings, arrays, collections, sequences, files, JSON, regex, TaxV3
├── 06-architectures/      DemoTests, TaxV4, TaxV5 (layers, tests, dependency injection)
├── 07-lambdas/            Lambdas01.kt to Lambdas13.kt
├── 08-threads/            Threads01.kt to Threads31.kt
├── 09-async/              Async01.kt to Async33.kt (coroutines)
├── 10-jdbc/               SQL scripts, jdbc subproject (Jdbc01 to Jdbc10), TaxV6
├── 11-hibernate/          Hibernate subprojects, TaxV7
├── 12-internet/           Internet01.kt to Internet19.kt, TaxV8
└── 13-web-services/       Spring Boot web services and their clients (WsTax, ClientWsTax: version 9)

Each small program is a Kotlin file, stored in a package that bears its name ([src/main/kotlin/basics04/Basics04.kt], package [basics04]). You can run it in IntelliJ IDEA by clicking the green triangle next to its function [main], or from the command line using Gradle ([gradlew -q run -Pmain=basics04.Basics04Kt], Chapter 2). Programs that require an external library (Jackson, JUnit, Spring, the MySQL driver, Hibernate, Spring Boot) must declare it in their project’s [build.gradle.kts] file: Gradle downloads it from the Maven Central repository during the first build.

All programs in this document were compiled without errors or warnings by the Kotlin 2.4.20 compiler, using the option that treats all warnings as errors ([allWarningsAsErrors]), and then run on JDK 25. The results reproduced in this document are those from these executions. Those of Chapters 2 to 4 were obtained with the French language and country settings (fr-FR), as on a French Windows machine: formatted floating-point numbers are displayed with a decimal comma, and dates are in French; those of the following chapters were obtained with English settings. Two notes:

  • error messages from the Kotlin compiler and JDK (exception messages) are in English: they have no French translation;
  • the examples were run on Linux. For the most part, this makes no difference: Kotlin on JVM is cross-platform. The few differences (file paths with / instead of \, terminal commands, [./gradlew] instead of [gradlew]) are noted where they appear.

The results of multithreaded, asynchronous, or network programs, as well as the measured durations, may vary from one run to another: the comments focus on what is reproducible.
