docs.text:
The primary sources for this document are:

  • the official Kotlin documentation: the website https://kotlinlang.org/docs (language guide, tutorials, “What’s New” pages for each version) and the standard library documentation: https://kotlinlang.org/api/core/kotlin-stdlib/;
  • the coroutines guide: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/coroutines-guide.html;
  • language evolution proposals (KEEP): https://github.com/Kotlin/KEEP;
  • the Java documentation for API and SE 25, for the classes in JDK: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/;
  • the Gradle documentation (https://docs.gradle.org) and the documentation for each library: JUnit (https://docs.junit.org), Spring (https://spring.io/projects), Hibernate (https://hibernate.org/orm/documentation/), Jackson (https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson);
  • two reference books: “Kotlin in Action” by Sebastian Aigner, Roman Elizarov, Svetlana Isakova, and Dmitry Jemerov (Manning, 2nd edition) and “Effective Kotlin” by Marcin Moskała; for threads, “Java Concurrency in Practice” by Brian Goetz et al. (Addison-Wesley) remains an excellent read.

docs.title: 6.1. Introduction
docs.text:
Let’s revisit the latest version of the tax calculation application (version 3, Chapter 5). Stripped down to its essentials, its main program had the following structure (simplified diagram):

// creation of an ITax object; the class depends on the file extension
val tax: ITax = try {
    when (fileName.substringAfterLast('.').lowercase()) {
        "json" -> JsonTax(fileName)
        else -> FileTax(fileName)
    }
} catch (e: TaxException) {
    println("The following error occurred: [Code=${ErrorCode.decode(e.code)}, ...]")
    exitProcess(1)
}
// input loop
while (true) {
    print("Tax calculation parameters in the format: ...")
    val parameters = readlnOrNull()?.trim() ?: ""
    ...
    // the parameters are correct: we calculate the tax
    println("Tax=${tax.calculate(married == "y", nbChildren, salary)} euros")
}

This program combines three types of processing found in most applications:

  • retrieving data stored in files, databases, etc.: lines 1–9;
  • user interaction: lines 13–14 (input) and 17 (output);
  • the use of a business algorithm, the tax calculation: line 17. This calculation was previously performed by the abstract class [AbstractTax], the parent class of [FileTax] and [JsonTax]: in version 3, data reading and calculation are still combined within a single object.

Practical experience has shown that isolating these different processing steps into separate classes improves application maintainability. The architecture of an application structured in this way is as follows:

This architecture is called “three-tier architecture.” The term “tier” normally refers to a part of the application that runs on a different machine. When the parts are on the same machine, the term “layered architecture” is used instead:

  • The [business] layer contains the application’s business rules. For our application, these are the rules used to calculate a taxpayer’s tax. This layer requires data to function:
    • tax brackets, which change every year;
    • the number of children, the taxpayer’s marital status, and annual income;
  • the data access layer, or [dao] (DAO = Data Access Object), provides data already stored in files or databases. This includes the tax brackets, as in version 3 of the application;
  • the user interface layer, or [ui] (UI = User Interface), provides the data entered by the user and displays the results to the user. This applies here to the number of children, marital status, and the taxpayer’s annual income.

In general:

  • the [dao] layer handles access to persistent data (files, databases) or non-persistent data (network, sensors, etc.);
  • the [ui] layer handles interactions with the user, if there is one;
  • the three layers are made independent of one another through the use of interfaces.

We will revisit the [Tax] application, which we have already examined several times, to give it a layered architecture. First, we need to define the interfaces for the application’s various layers.

docs.title: 6.2. The Interfaces of the [Tax] Application
docs.text:
Remember that an interface defines a set of function signatures and properties. The classes that implement the interface provide their implementation.

Let’s return to the layered architecture of our application:

In this type of architecture, the user often takes the initiative. The user makes a request in [1] and receives a response in [8]. This is called the request-response cycle. Let’s take the example of calculating a taxpayer’s tax. This will require several steps:

  • The [ui] layer asks the user for their marital status, number of children, and annual salary. This is the [1] operation described above;
  • Once this is done, layer [ui] asks layer [business] to calculate the tax. To do this, it sends the data it received from the user to that layer. This is operation [2];
  • The [business] layer needs certain information to complete its task: the tax brackets. It requests this information from layer [dao] via the path [3, 4, 5, 6]: [3] is the initial request, and [6] is the response to that request;
  • With all the data it needed, layer [business] calculates the tax;
  • The [business] layer can now respond to the request made by the [ui] layer in [2]. This is the [7] path;
  • the [ui] layer formats this result and then presents it to the user. This is the path [8];
  • One could imagine that the user might run tax simulations and want to save them. They would use the same path, [1-8], to do so.

As seen in this description, a layer uses the resources of the layer to its right, never those of the layer to its left. Consider two adjacent layers:

The layer [A] makes requests to the layer [B]. In the simplest cases, a layer is implemented by a single class. But an application evolves over time, and the layer [B] may successively have different implementation classes: [B1], [B2], and so on. If the [B] layer is the [dao] layer, it may have an initial implementation, [B1], that retrieves data from a file. A few years later, you might want to store this data in a database: in that case, you create a second implementation class, [B2]. If, in the initial application, the [A] layer worked directly with the [B1] class, we would be forced to partially rewrite the code for the [A] layer. For example, suppose we wrote something like the following in the [A] layer:

val b1: B1 = B1(...)
...
b1.getData(...)
  • Line 1: An instance of the [B1] class is created;
  • line 3: data is requested from this instance.

If the new implementation class [B2] has functions with the same signature as the class [B1], you’ll need to change all instances of [B1] to [B2]. This is the best-case scenario, and it is quite unlikely if you have not paid attention to these signatures. In practice, it is common for the classes [B1] and [B2] to have different function signatures, meaning that a significant portion of the [A] layer must be rewritten.

This issue can be mitigated by inserting an interface between the [A] and [B] layers. This locks down, within an interface, the function signatures that the [B] layer exposes to the [A] layer. The previous diagram becomes the following:

The [A] layer no longer communicates directly with the [B] layer but with its interface, [IB]. In the code for the [A] layer, the implementation class [Bi] of the [B] layer now appears only once, when the object that implements the [IB] interface is created. After that, the [IB] interface—and not its implementation class—is used. The previous code becomes:

val ib: IB = B1(...)
...
ib.getData(...)
  • Line 1: An instance of [ib] that implements the [IB] interface is created by instantiating the [B1] class. The variable's type is explicitly declared: without it, type inference would assign the type [B1] to [ib];
  • Line 3: Data is requested from the [ib] instance.

Now, if we replace the implementation [B1] of the layer [B] with an implementation [B2], and both implementations conform to the same interface [IB], only line 1 of the [A] layer needs to be modified. This is a major advantage that, on its own, justifies the systematic use of interfaces between two layers.

We can go even further and make the [A] layer completely independent of the [B] layer. In the code above, line 1 poses a problem because it hard-codes the class name [B1]. Ideally, the [A] layer should receive an implementation of the [IB] interface without having to specify a class name. This would be consistent with the diagram above: the [A] layer interfaces with the [IB] interface, and there is no reason why it would need to know the name of the class that implements that interface.

This is what dependency injection (DI) enables. The previous architecture evolves as follows:

A cross-cutting component—the dependency injection container—creates the objects that implement the layers and connects them to one another: it passes the [A] layer a reference to the object that implements the [B] layer. The code for the [A] layer then takes the following form:

// layer [A] receives layer [B] through its constructor
class A(private val ib: IB) {

    fun work() {
        ...
        ib.getData(...)
    }
}
  • Line 2: The [A] layer receives, via its primary constructor, a [ib] instance that implements the [IB] interface. The keyword ***[val]*** preceding the parameter makes it a private property of the class: where Java requires a field, a constructor, and an assignment, Kotlin requires only a single line. It is not the *[A]* layer that creates this instance, but the container;
  • Line 6: Data is requested from the [ib] instance.

The implementation class [B1] no longer appears anywhere in the code of the [A] layer. When the implementation [B1] is replaced by a new implementation [B2], nothing will change in the code of the [A] layer: the only thing that will change is the single location in the application where the container is told which class implements [IB]. This location can even read the name of the implementation to use from a configuration file.

In the JVM, dependency injection was popularized in the early 2000s by the Spring framework, whose configuration was then written in XML files. The Spring Framework, now in version 7, remains the industry standard, and it treats Kotlin as a first-class language: it provides Kotlin extensions to its API, and Kotlin is one of the two languages used in its documentation. It forms the basis of Spring Boot, which we will use in Chapter 13, “Web Services.” We’ll use its container in version 5 of the application (there are others: CDI, the Jakarta EE standard, Google Guice, or, specific to Kotlin, Koin and Kodein). The combination of “interfaces and dependency injection” significantly improves application maintainability by making the layers independent of one another.

Let’s return to the layered architecture of our application. In simple cases, we can start with the [business] layer to discover the application’s interfaces. To function, the application needs data:

  • already available in files, databases, or via the network. This data is provided by the [dao] layer;
  • not yet available. In that case, it is provided by the [ui] layer, which obtains it from the user.

What interface should the [dao] layer provide to the [business] layer? The [dao] layer must provide the tax brackets to the [business] layer. In our application, the [dao] layer uses existing data but does not create new data. Its interface could be as follows:

package dao

import entities.TaxBracket

// the interface of the [dao] layer
interface ITaxDao {

    // the tax brackets: a read-only property
    val taxBrackets: List<TaxBracket>
}
  • Line 1: The interface is located in the [dao] package. As we will see, we will store the [ITaxDao.kt] file in a [dao] folder;
  • Line 9: The [ITaxDao] interface declares the [taxBrackets] property, which provides the tax brackets to the [business] layer. A Kotlin interface can declare properties, not just functions: an interface property [val] is abstract; each implementing class specifies how it obtains its value. Whereas Java exposed read-only data via a method [getTaxBrackets()], following the JavaBeans convention, Kotlin declares it for what it is: a read-only property. From Java’s perspective, this property is actually a method [getTaxBrackets()];
  • brackets are rendered as a [List<TaxBracket>] list rather than an array. In Kotlin, [List] is a read-only interface: it has no [add], [set], or [remove], which belong to the [MutableList] interface (Chapter 5). The recipient of the list cannot therefore modify it, whereas the elements of an array can always be modified by the recipient;
  • line 3: imports the type [TaxBracket], defined in the package [entities]:
package entities

import java.math.BigDecimal

// a tax bracket: a data class whose properties are read-only
data class TaxBracket(val limit: BigDecimal, val coeffR: BigDecimal, val coeffN: BigDecimal)

A tax bracket is represented by a data class ([data class], Chapter 4), the Kotlin equivalent of a Java record. The compiler generates the properties [limit], [coeffR], and [coeffN], as well as the functions [equals], [hashCode], [toString], [copy], and [component1]…[component3] (for destructuring). We write [TaxBracket(limit, coeffR, coeffN)] to create a bracket. Properties are declared as [val]: a bracket cannot be changed once created (a data class can have [var] properties, but this is not common practice). All three properties are of type [BigDecimal], the Java class for exact decimal numbers, which Kotlin uses directly: a [Double] cannot exactly represent 0.068 or 291.09. Since a *[BigDecimal] is itself immutable, a bracket is completely immutable. A class with [var] properties would have allowed it to be modified; we’ll see that this inability eliminates a side effect of an older way of writing the [business]* layer.

What interface should the [business] layer present to the [ui] layer? Let’s review the interactions between these two layers:

  • The [ui] layer asks the user for their marital status, number of children, and annual salary. This is operation [1] in the schema;
  • Once this is done, the [ui] layer asks the [business] layer to calculate the tax. To do this, it sends the data it received from the user to the [business] layer. This is operation [2].

The interface for layer [business] might look like this:

package business

// the interface of the [business] layer
interface ITaxBusiness {

    fun calculateTax(married: Boolean, nbChildren: Int, salary: Int): Int
}
  • Line 1: Everything related to the [business] layer is placed in the [business] package;
  • Line 6: The [ITaxBusiness] interface declares only one function, which calculates a taxpayer’s tax based on their marital status, number of children, and annual salary. An interface function without a body is abstract, and, like any Kotlin member without a visibility modifier, is public: there is no need to write [public abstract]. The result is [Int]: the tax in euros, without the cents.

We will now examine an initial implementation of this layered architecture.

docs.title: 6.3.1. The Project
docs.text:
Version 4 is a program consisting of several source files that does not use any external libraries. Kotlin does not have a simple equivalent to Java’s source code launcher ([java Main.java]), which compiles a multi-file program in memory and executes it: a multi-file Kotlin program is compiled before it is executed. We therefore create a Gradle project, [TaxV4], which is one of the subprojects of the chapter’s Gradle build (Chapter 2). The [06-architectures] folder contains all the projects in the chapter; its [settings.gradle.kts] file lists them:

// chapter 6: a Gradle build grouping all the projects of the chapter

// Gradle downloads the JDK requested by jvmToolchain(25) itself if it does not find it on the machine
plugins {
    id("org.gradle.toolchains.foojay-resolver-convention") version "1.0.0"
}

rootProject.name = "architectures"

// the subprojects, designated by their path: [TaxV5:tax-dao] is the TaxV5/tax-dao folder
include("DemoTests", "TaxV4", "TaxV5:tax-dao", "TaxV5:tax-business", "TaxV5:tax-ui")
  • lines 3–6: the plugin that allows Gradle to download JDK 25 itself if it cannot find it on the machine (Chapter 2);
  • line 8: the name of the root project;
  • line 11: the five subprojects in this chapter. A subproject is identified by its path, whose elements are separated by colons: [TaxV5:tax-dao] is the subproject of the [TaxV5/tax-dao] folder. We will discuss [DemoTests] and the three subprojects of version 5 later on.

The file [build.gradle.kts] in the root project declares the plugins used by the subprojects, along with their versions, without applying them:

// chapter 6: root project. The plugins are declared here, with their version, without being applied:
// the subprojects apply them
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.20" apply false
    kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.4.20" apply false
}
  • line 4: the Kotlin plugin for JVM, version 2.4.20. The reference to [apply false] makes it available to the subprojects, which will apply it without repeating its version;
  • line 5: a Kotlin compiler plugin that version 5 will need for Spring. We’ll explain this when the time comes.

The [TaxV4] subproject has the following directory structure. Each layer occupies a folder:

TaxV4/
  build.gradle.kts           the build file of the subproject
  TaxData.txt                the tax brackets
  TaxDataInvalid.txt         an incorrect bracket file
  src/main/kotlin/
    Main.kt                  integration of the layers
    entities/
      TaxBracket.kt
      ErrorCode.kt
      TaxException.kt
    dao/
      ITaxDao.kt
      HardwiredTax.kt
      FileTax.kt
    business/
      ITaxBusiness.kt
      TaxBusiness.kt
    ui/
      Dialog.kt
  • The [entities] folder contains types that are common to the [ui], [business], and [dao] layers: the data class [TaxBracket], the exception [TaxException], and the enumeration [ErrorCode] of its error codes;
  • the [dao] file contains the interface and classes of the [dao] layer. We will use two implementations of the [ITaxDao] interface: the [HardwiredTax] class, whose data is hard-coded (version 2), and the [FileTax] class, which reads data from a text file (version 3). Reading a JSON file—the other option in version 3—will be covered in version 5;
  • the folder [business] contains the interface and the class for the layer [business];
  • the folder [ui] contains the class for the layer [ui];
  • The file [Main.kt] creates the layers and links them together;
  • the file [TaxData.txt] contains the tax brackets read by the [FileTax] implementation of the [dao] layer. It is located at the root of the subproject, which is the current directory of the program launched by Gradle.

In Java, folder names matter: a class in the [dao] package must be located in a folder named [dao]. Kotlin is more flexible: the package is the one declared by the [package] directive in the file, regardless of the folder in which it is located. However, the convention—followed by IntelliJ, IDEA, and this course—is still to organize files into folders that mirror the packages: a file from the [tax.dao] package in a [tax/dao] folder (in a project where all packages start with the same root, the folders for that common root are simply omitted). The [.class] files produced by the compiler, on the other hand, are always organized by package: this is how the virtual machine locates the classes based on their full names.

The file [Main.kt] does not have a [package] directive: it belongs to the root package, which has no name. Its function [main] is compiled into the class [MainKt], the name that the subproject’s build file assigns to the plugin [application]:

// TaxV4: the layered [Tax] application, in a single project, without an external library
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    application
}

group = "examples.architectures"
version = "4.0"

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

kotlin {
    // the code is compiled and run with JDK 25
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        // a compiler warning is treated as an error
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        // function parameter names are kept in the bytecode
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
    // the main function of the Main.kt file, which has no package: its class is MainKt
    mainClass = "MainKt"
}

tasks.named<JavaExec>("run") {
    // the running program can read the keyboard
    standardInput = System.`in`
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}
  • lines 2–4: the subproject applies the Kotlin plugin, without a version (which is provided by the root project), and the [application] plugin, which adds the [run] task;
  • lines 7–8: the project details;
  • lines 14–21: the compiler configuration, the same as in the previous chapters;
  • lines 25–27: the main class, [MainKt], without a package name. There is only one program in this subproject: the [main] property from the previous chapters is unnecessary;
  • lines 30–32: the program reads from the keyboard;
  • lines 35–38: The programs launched by Gradle write their output to UTF-8 so that accented characters display correctly on Windows (Chapter 2).

Unlike Java, Kotlin allows you to import a declaration of the root package from another package by naming it without a prefix ([import declarationName]). The convention is still to place only the main program there, which is not imported by anyone.

Run the program from the chapter’s folder using [gradlew -q :TaxV4:run]: the path [:TaxV4] refers to the subproject, and the task [run] runs with the subproject folder as the current directory. IntelliJ IDEA opens the [06-architectures] folder as a Gradle project and runs [Main.kt] by clicking the green triangle next to its [main] function.

docs.title: 6.3.2. Application entities
docs.text:
We refer to entities as types that span multiple layers. These are generally the classes that encapsulate the data from the [dao] layer. These entities typically extend all the way up to the [ui] layer. The application entities are the data class [TaxBracket], which has already been presented, and the exception [TaxException], along with the enumeration of its error codes:

package entities

// the error codes of the [dao] layer: each one corresponds to a bit, so they can be combined
enum class ErrorCode {
    ACCESS, LINE, FIELD1, FIELD2, FIELD3;

    // the bit of the code: 1 for ACCESS, 2 for LINE, 4 for FIELD1, 8 for FIELD2, 16 for FIELD3
    val bit: Int
        get() = 1 shl ordinal

    companion object {
        // the names of the codes present in a combination of bits, for example "FIELD2, FIELD3" for 24
        fun names(code: Int): String =
            entries.filter { (code and it.bit) != 0 }.joinToString(", ") { it.name }
    }
}
  • line 4: an enumeration ([enum class]). As in Java, the values of an enumeration are objects—unique instances of the [ErrorCode] class—and an enumeration can have properties and methods;
  • line 5: the five error codes. The semicolon that terminates the list is required when other members follow it. The property [ordinal], inherited from the class [Enum], returns the position of the value in the list: 0 for [ACCESS], 4 for [FIELD3];
  • lines 8–9: Each code is associated with a bit. [bit] is a computed property: it has no field; its accessor, [get()], calculates it each time it is read. Kotlin does not have shift operators: [1 shl ordinal] (“shift left”) is equivalent to Java’s [1 << ordinal], and is equal to 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16. These powers of 2 can be combined with the infix function [or] (Java’s [|]): the code [FIELD2.bit or FIELD3.bit] (8 + 16 = 24) means that fields 2 and 3 of a row are incorrect. The exception’s error code remains a simple integer, which all implementations of the [dao] layer can use;
  • Lines 11–14: The function [names] converts the code names contained in a bit string— “FIELD2, FIELD3” for 24. It does not use any specific value from the enum: it is placed in the companion object and is called as a static Java method, [ErrorCode.names(24)]. The property [entries] (Kotlin 1.9) is the list of enum values; it replaces the function [values()], which creates a new array on every call. [(code and it.bit) != 0] is true if the bit corresponding to the value of [it] is present in [code] ([and] is the Java equivalent of [&]). The values retrieved by [filter] are then assembled by [joinToString], using the separator [", "] and a lambda that returns the name ([name]) of each value. The body of the function is an expression: the function has no curly braces, and its result follows the [=] sign.
package entities

// the exception thrown by the [dao] layer
// Kotlin has no checked exceptions: no method has to declare it
class TaxException(
    message: String,
    // the original exception, if there is one
    cause: Throwable? = null,
    // error code (a combination of ErrorCode bits)
    val code: Int = 0,
) : RuntimeException(message, cause)
  • line 5: an application-specific exception derives from the class [RuntimeException]. In Kotlin, the question of choosing between checked and unchecked exceptions does not arise: the language has no checked exceptions (Chapter 3), no function declares the exceptions it throws, and no caller is required to catch them. Deriving from *[RuntimeException]* rather than *[Exception]* remains the standard practice, as this ensures that an exception is viewed consistently from Java code;
  • lines 6–10: The primary constructor has three parameters. [message] and [cause] are simple parameters passed to the parent class’s constructor (line 11); [code], declared as [val], is also a read-only property of the exception. The cause—the original exception, if there is one—will be accessible via the property [cause], inherited from [Throwable];
  • lines 8–10: Thanks to the default parameter values, this single constructor replaces the two constructors in the Java version—one with a message and a code, the other with the cause as well. With named arguments, we write [TaxException(message, code = 2)] when there is no cause, and [TaxException(message, e, 1)] when there is one;
  • line 10: the comma after the last parameter (“trailing comma”) is allowed; it makes it easier to add a parameter;
  • An exception is serializable (the class [Throwable] implements the interface [Serializable]). The Java version declared a [serialVersionUID] field to avoid a warning from [javac -Xlint:all]; the Kotlin compiler does not issue this warning, so we do not declare this field.

In this version, only the [FileTax] class in the [dao] layer throws [TaxException].

docs.title: 6.3.3. The [dao] layer
docs.text:
Let’s review the interface of the [dao] layer:

package dao

import entities.TaxBracket

// the interface of the [dao] layer
interface ITaxDao {

    // the tax brackets: a read-only property
    val taxBrackets: List<TaxBracket>
}

We implement this interface in two different ways. First, with the [HardwiredTax] class:

package dao

import entities.TaxBracket

// a [dao] layer whose data are "hard-coded"
class HardwiredTax : ITaxDao {

    // tax brackets (2004 tax scale on 2003 income): a read-only list
    override val taxBrackets: List<TaxBracket> = listOf(
        bracket("4962", "0", "0"),
        bracket("8382", "0.068", "291.09"),
        bracket("14753", "0.191", "1322.92"),
        bracket("23888", "0.283", "2668.39"),
        bracket("38868", "0.374", "4846.98"),
        bracket("47932", "0.426", "6883.66"),
        bracket("0", "0.481", "9505.54"),
    )
}

// a bracket built from strings: the BigDecimals are exact
private fun bracket(limit: String, coeffR: String, coeffN: String) =
    TaxBracket(limit.toBigDecimal(), coeffR.toBigDecimal(), coeffN.toBigDecimal())
  • Line 6: The class [HardwiredTax] implements the interface [ITaxDao]. In Kotlin, the colon is used for both class inheritance and interface implementation: there is no [implements] keyword. Note that the interface is named without parentheses, whereas a parent class is named with its constructor arguments ([RuntimeException(message, cause)]): an interface does not have a constructor;
  • Lines 9–16: the implementation of the interface’s property. The keyword [override] is required: the compiler verifies that the property does indeed implement a member of the interface, similar to Java’s optional annotation [@Override]. The property is initialized in its declaration by [listOf], which creates a read-only list. Again, a comma after the last element is allowed;
  • Lines 20–22: A private function that creates a bracket from three strings. It is declared at the file level, outside the class: [private] makes it visible only within the file [HardwiredTax.kt]. The extension function [toBigDecimal] from the standard library converts a string to [BigDecimal]; this is the constructor [BigDecimal(String)]. A [BigDecimal] constructed from a string is exact: ["0.068".toBigDecimal()] is exactly 0.068, whereas a [BigDecimal] constructed from a [Double] inherits its imprecision: [0.068.toBigDecimal()], which is derived by converting [Double] to a string, does indeed yield 0.068, but [(0.1 + 0.2).toBigDecimal()] yields 0.30000000000000004. The type of the function’s result, [TaxBracket], is inferred from the expression following the sign [=].

The [ITaxDao] interface is also implemented by the [FileTax] class, which reads tax brackets from a text file. The [TaxData.txt] file is as follows:

4962:0:0
8382:0.068:291.09
14753:0.191:1322.92
23888:0.283:2668.39
38868:0.374:4846.98
47932:0.426:6883.66
0:0.481:9505.54

Each line describes a tax bracket in the format [limit:coeffR:coeffN]. Numbers are written with a decimal point, regardless of the system language; this ensures the file is readable on all machines. The values are those from the 2004 tax schedule for 2003 income, retained as-is: this is an exercise. The class [FileTax] is as follows:

package dao

import entities.ErrorCode.ACCESS
import entities.ErrorCode.FIELD1
import entities.ErrorCode.FIELD2
import entities.ErrorCode.FIELD3
import entities.ErrorCode.LINE
import entities.TaxException
import entities.TaxBracket
import java.io.IOException
import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException
import kotlin.io.path.Path
import kotlin.io.path.exists
import kotlin.io.path.readLines

// a [dao] layer that reads the tax brackets from a text file
// one line per bracket: limit:coeffR:coeffN (decimal point)
class FileTax(val fileName: String) : ITaxDao {

    // tax brackets, read when the object is constructed
    override val taxBrackets: List<TaxBracket>

    init {
        // reading the file (relative to the current folder): a list of lines
        val lines = try {
            val path = Path(fileName)
            if (!path.exists()) {
                throw NoSuchFileException(fileName, null, "The file [$fileName] does not exist")
            }
            path.readLines()
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            // file access error: it is wrapped in a TaxException
            throw TaxException("Error while reading the file $fileName", e, ACCESS.bit)
        }
        // one bracket per non-empty line; the lines are numbered from 1
        taxBrackets = lines.withIndex()
            .filter { it.value.isNotBlank() }
            .map { (index, line) -> bracket(index + 1, line.trim()) }
    }

    // the bracket described by a line, or a TaxException if the line is incorrect
    private fun bracket(lineNumber: Int, line: String): TaxBracket {
        // line split into fields separated by : (possibly surrounded by spaces)
        val fields = line.split(SEPARATOR)
        if (fields.size != 3) {
            throw TaxException("Line no. $lineNumber is incorrect: [$line]", code = LINE.bit)
        }
        // conversions of the 3 fields: null for an incorrect field
        val (limit, coeffR, coeffN) = fields.map(::number)
        if (limit == null || coeffR == null || coeffN == null) {
            // each incorrect field adds its bit to the code
            var code = 0
            if (limit == null) code = code or FIELD1.bit
            if (coeffR == null) code = code or FIELD2.bit
            if (coeffN == null) code = code or FIELD3.bit
            throw TaxException("Line no. $lineNumber is incorrect: [$line]", code = code)
        }
        // the three fields are correct: here, they are of type BigDecimal and not BigDecimal?
        return TaxBracket(limit, coeffR, coeffN)
    }

    companion object {
        // the field separator and the form of a number (regular expressions)
        private val SEPARATOR = Regex("""\s*:\s*""")
        private val NUMBER = Regex("""\d+(\.\d+)?""")

        // a positive or zero number written with digits and a decimal point; null if incorrect
        private fun number(field: String): BigDecimal? =
            if (NUMBER.matches(field)) field.toBigDecimal() else null
    }
}
  • Lines 3–7: Kotlin does not have static imports ([import static] from Java): the standard [import] directive imports classes, enum values, and functions alike. We then write [FIELD1] instead of [ErrorCode.FIELD1];
  • lines 13–15: the functions in the [kotlin.io.path] package (Chapter 5), which complement the Java functions API and NIO;
  • line 19: the primary constructor takes the name of the tax bracket file. Declared as [val], this parameter is also a public, read-only property, [fileName]: it replaces the field and method [getFileName] from the Java version;
  • line 22: the interface property. It is not initialized in its declaration: the compiler verifies that it is assigned a value—only once—in the following [init] block;
  • lines 24–39: the [init] block is executed when the object is constructed. It reads the file and then extracts the brackets from it;
  • lines 26–34: In Kotlin, [try] is an expression: its value is either that of the last expression in the [try]*** block—in this case, the list of lines in the file—or that of the [catch] block. The block [catch] throws an exception: its type is [Nothing], the type of expressions that never return a value, and the variable [lines] has the type [List<String>]*;
  • line 27: the function [Path] in [kotlin.io.path] creates the file path; it is equivalent to [Path.of]. A relative path is relative to the current directory;
  • Lines 28–29: If the file does not exist, a [NoSuchFileException] ([java.nio.file] package) is thrown with an explicit message. Its three-parameter constructor takes the file name, the name of a possible second file (here, [null]), and the reason for the error. Without this check, the read operation would itself throw a [NoSuchFileException], whose message would consist solely of the file name;
  • Line 31: The [readLines] extension function reads the entire file using UTF-8 and returns a list of its lines. It opens and closes the file itself. For a large file, we would prefer a stream-based read using [useLines];
  • Lines 32–34: All input/output errors stem from [IOException]: file missing ([NoSuchFileException]), insufficient permissions ([AccessDeniedException]), file not in UTF-8 format ([MalformedInputException]), etc. The error is wrapped in a [TaxException] with code [ACCESS]; the original exception is retained as the cause (second argument);
  • lines 37–39: Reading the lines and parsing them are separate operations, which was not the case in Java. [withIndex] associates each line with its index (starting at 0) in an [IndexedValue] object with properties [index] and [value]; [filter] removes empty lines or lines consisting of spaces ([isNotBlank]) without losing the indices of the others; [map] transforms each of the remaining lines into a bracket. The lambda function [map] unpacks its parameter [IndexedValue] into its two components, [(index, line)]. The line number, [index + 1], and the line with its leading and trailing spaces removed ([trim]) are passed to the function [bracket]. The result of [map] is a read-only [List];
  • line 43: the function that returns the bracket described by a line, or throws a [TaxException] if the line is invalid. This exception is not an [IOException]: it is passed back to the caller as-is;
  • line 45: the line is split by [split] using the regular expression [SEPARATOR]: the separator is a colon, which may be surrounded by spaces. Note: In Kotlin, ***[split(":")]** with a string splits the string itself without interpreting it as a regular expression; you must pass a *[Regex] object for this;
  • Lines 46–47: A line that does not have three fields is invalid. The error code is passed via a named argument, [code = LINE.bit]: there is no cause, and the parameter [cause] retains its default value, [null];
  • line 50: conversion of the three fields. [fields.map(::number)] applies the function [number] to each field ([::number] is a function reference; see Chapter 7) and returns a list of three [BigDecimal?] values, which the destructuring assignment distributes into three variables;
  • lines 51–57: if a field is incorrect, each incorrect field adds its bit to the error code using the infix function [or], and a [TaxException] is thrown. Its message provides the line number and the line’s content;
  • line 60: at this point, the compiler knows that [limit], [coeffR], and [coeffN] are not [null]; otherwise, the previous [if] would have thrown an exception. Through smart casting, these variables of type [BigDecimal?] are treated as [BigDecimal], the type expected by the constructor of [TaxBracket]: neither [!!] nor any conversion is necessary;
  • lines 65–66: the two regular expressions are created once and for all in the companion object, rather than on each call. They are written as raw strings (["""..."""]), where the backslash does not need to be doubled: [\s*] matches zero or more spaces;
  • Lines 69–70: Converting a field to [BigDecimal]. [NUMBER.matches(field)] verifies that the entire string matches the regular expression [\d+(\.\d+)?]: one or more digits, optionally followed by a period and more digits. Thus, “0,191” is rejected, as is any negative number. The function [toBigDecimal] is not dependent on the user’s language: it always expects a decimal point. In case of an error, the function returns [null], hence its type [BigDecimal?]. We could have used [toBigDecimalOrNull], which returns [null] for an invalid string, but it also accepts “-1” or “1e3”.

docs.title: 6.3.4. The [business] layer
docs.text:
Let’s review the interface for this layer:

package business

// the interface of the [business] layer
interface ITaxBusiness {

    fun calculateTax(married: Boolean, nbChildren: Int, salary: Int): Int
}

Its implementation, [TaxBusiness], is as follows:

package business

import dao.ITaxDao
import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.math.MathContext

// the [business] layer receives the [dao] layer through its constructor
class TaxBusiness(dao: ITaxDao) : ITaxBusiness {

    // the tax brackets, requested once and for all from the [dao] layer
    private val brackets = dao.taxBrackets

    // tax calculation
    override fun calculateTax(married: Boolean, nbChildren: Int, salary: Int): Int {
        // checking the parameters
        require(nbChildren >= 0) { "nbChildren ($nbChildren) must be positive or zero" }
        require(salary >= 0) { "salary ($salary) must be positive or zero" }
        // number of shares: the + and * operators of BigDecimal are exact
        var shares = nbChildren.toBigDecimal() * HALF + (if (married) 2 else 1).toBigDecimal()
        if (nbChildren >= 3) {
            shares += HALF
        }
        // taxable income and family quotient
        val income = ALLOWANCE * salary.toBigDecimal()
        val qf = income.divide(shares, MathContext.DECIMAL128)
        // the bracket: the first one whose limit is greater than or equal to QF,
        // the last one if none fits (its limit is not used)
        val bracket = brackets.dropLast(1).firstOrNull { qf <= it.limit } ?: brackets.last()
        // tax (integer part)
        return (income * bracket.coeffR - shares * bracket.coeffN).toInt()
    }

    private companion object {
        // a half-share and the coefficient that gives the taxable income from the salary
        val HALF = BigDecimal("0.5")
        val ALLOWANCE = BigDecimal("0.72")
    }
}
  • Line 8: The class [TaxBusiness] implements the interface [ITaxBusiness]. The [business] layer must collaborate with the [dao] layer: it therefore receives, via its primary constructor, a [dao] reference to the object that implements the [ITaxDao] interface. This parameter is not declared as [val]: it is used only during object construction and does not become a property;
  • Line 11: Upon object construction, the [business] layer requests the tax brackets from the [dao] layer once and for all and stores them in a private, read-only property. Its type, [List<TaxBracket>], is inferred. Note that the [business] layer knows the [dao] layer only through its [ITaxDao] interface: it does not know whether the tax brackets come from the code, a file, or, later, a database;
  • line 14: the implementation of the interface’s function, with the required keyword [override];
  • lines 16–17: the [business] layer does not trust its callers. The function [require] from the standard library (Chapter 3) throws an [IllegalArgumentException] if the condition is false; the exception message is calculated by the lambda, which is executed only in the event of an error. The message identifies the incorrect parameter;
  • lines 19–21: the number of shares. [nbChildren.toBigDecimal()] converts the integer to [BigDecimal]. A Java class such as [BigDecimal] does not have arithmetic operators, but the Kotlin standard library adds them via extension functions labeled [operator] (Chapter 4): [a + b], [a - b], and [a * b] call [add], [subtract] and [multiply], and [shares += HALF] is written in Java as [shares = shares.add(HALF)]. Since a [BigDecimal] is immutable, each operation returns a new object: this is why [shares] is a variable ([var]). The number of children is multiplied by 0.5 rather than divided by 2, for the reason given below: 3 children equal 1.5 shares;
  • lines 24–25: taxable income and the family quotient. Division by the number of shares can result in an infinite number of decimal places (division by 3, for example): without any specified limit, the [divide] method would then throw an [ArithmeticException]. [MathContext.DECIMAL128] limits the result to 34 significant digits;
  • Line 28: We look for the first income bracket whose threshold is greater than or equal to the family quotient, among all brackets except the last one ([dropLast(1)]). [firstOrNull] returns the first element that satisfies the condition, or [null] if there is none; the Elvis operator [?:] then replaces [null] with the last bracket, [brackets.last()], whose limit (0) is not used. The [BigDecimal] classes implement the [Comparable] interface: Kotlin translates [qf <= it.limit] to [qf.compareTo(it.limit) <= 0]. This line replaces the [for] loop and the [break] from the Java version;
  • line 30: the tax. The function [toInt()] of a [BigDecimal] (the Java method [intValue()]) returns the integer part of the result;
  • lines 33–36: two constants, stored in a private companion object. They cannot be declared as [const]: only primitive types and strings can be.

A note on the [/] operator. The standard library also defines the [/] operator for [BigDecimal], but it calls [divide(other, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)]: the result has the same number of decimal places as the dividend. Thus, [3.toBigDecimal() / BigDecimal.TWO] evaluates to 2, not 1.5, whereas [3.toBigDecimal().divide(BigDecimal.TWO)] does indeed evaluate to 1.5. That is why the code above avoids this operator: it multiplies by 0.5 and explicitly calls [divide] with a [MathContext]. With the [BigDecimal] functions, it’s always best to know exactly what a division operation does.

A common approach in the past was to modify, before the search, the limit of the last bracket (something like [brackets[brackets.size - 1].limit = qf + 1]) so that the search loop would always stop. This instruction modified the array provided by the [dao] layer: a side effect on data shared by all layers. We could no longer write this here: the [limit] property of a [TaxBracket] is read-only, and the list containing the brackets is also read-only. Modern code simply takes the last bracket when no limit is suitable, without modifying the data it receives.

docs.title: 6.3.5. The [ui] layer
docs.text:
In versions 2 and 3, the user interface was written in the main program, following the creation of the calculation object. The only difference was how this object was created. We now isolate this user interface in the [ui] layer, which knows the [business] layer only through its interface:

package ui

import business.ITaxBusiness

// the console dialog with the user: it only knows the interface of the [business] layer
object Dialog {

    // the question asked to the user
    private const val QUESTION =
        "Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: "

    // help displayed in case of incorrect input
    private val SYNTAX = """
        syntax: Married NbChildren Salary
        Married: y for married, n for not married
        NbChildren: number of children
        Salary: annual salary in euros
        """.trimIndent()

    // one or more spaces
    private val SPACES = Regex("""\s+""")

    // dialog loop: input of the parameters, calculation, display
    fun run(business: ITaxBusiness) {
        while (true) {
            // we ask for the tax calculation parameters; null at end of stream is treated as nothing
            print(QUESTION)
            val parameters = readlnOrNull()?.trim() ?: ""
            // anything to do?
            if (parameters.isEmpty()) {
                break
            }
            // checking the number of parameters
            val fields = parameters.split(SPACES)
            if (fields.size != 3) {
                println(SYNTAX)
                continue
            }
            // married
            val married = fields[0].lowercase()
            if (married != "y" && married != "n") {
                println("$SYNTAX\nIncorrect Married argument: type y or n")
                continue
            }
            // number of children: -1 if the field is not an integer
            val nbChildren = fields[1].toIntOrNull() ?: -1
            if (nbChildren < 0) {
                println("$SYNTAX\nIncorrect NbChildren argument: type a positive or zero integer")
                continue
            }
            // salary
            val salary = fields[2].toIntOrNull() ?: -1
            if (salary < 0) {
                println("$SYNTAX\nIncorrect Salary argument: type a positive or zero integer")
                continue
            }
            // the parameters are correct: we ask the [business] layer for the calculation
            println("Tax=${business.calculateTax(married == "y", nbChildren, salary)} euros")
        }
    }
}
  • Line 6: The dialog has no state of its own. In Java, we created a class named [final] with a private constructor, containing only static members. Kotlin uses the object declaration ([object], Chapter 4) for this purpose: [Dialog] is both a class and its sole instance, created upon first use. Its functions are called like static methods: [Dialog.run(business)];
  • lines 9–10: the question asked of the user, a private constant ([const val]);
  • lines 13–18: the help message is a raw string, delimited by three quotation marks. It can span multiple lines; [trimIndent] (Chapter 5) removes the common indentation from the lines, as well as the first and last lines if they are empty: the text does not begin or end with a line break. The result of [trimIndent] is calculated at runtime: the string cannot be declared as [const];
  • line 24: the function [run] receives the layer [business] in the form of its interface [ITaxBusiness]. It knows nothing about the class that implements it or the layer [dao];
  • Lines 27–28: The question is displayed by [print], without a line break, and then [readlnOrNull] reads a line from the keyboard. This returns [null] at the end of the input stream; the safe call to [?.trim()] then also returns [null], which the Elvis operator replaces with the empty string: the end of the stream terminates the dialog just like an empty line;
  • line 34: the entered line is split by spaces; the regular expression [\s+] (one or more spaces) ignores multiple spaces;
  • lines 40–41: In Kotlin, the operator [] (and [!=]) compares the contents of strings: it calls [equals]*. It is the *[=] operator that compares references. The Java pitfall, where [==] compares references, does not exist;
  • lines 46–54: the number of children and the salary must be positive integers or zero. [toIntOrNull] returns [null] if the field is not an integer, and the Elvis operator then replaces [null] with -1. A negative number and an invalid input are thus rejected by the same check. The [integer] method in the Java version, along with its [try]/[catch] variants of [NumberFormatException], has become obsolete;
  • line 58: the parameters are correct: the calculation is requested from the [business] layer. The call is written directly into the string template, between [${...}].

docs.title: 6.3.6. Integrating the Layers
docs.text:
All that remains is to create the layers and link them together. This is the role of the main program [Main.kt]:

import dao.FileTax
import dao.HardwiredTax
import dao.ITaxDao
import entities.ErrorCode
import entities.TaxException
import business.ITaxBusiness
import business.TaxBusiness
import ui.Dialog
import kotlin.system.exitProcess

// integration of the layers: this is the only place where the implementation classes are named
// argument: "hardwired" for HardwiredTax,
// otherwise the name of the file read by FileTax (TaxData.txt by default)
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    val source = args.firstOrNull() ?: "TaxData.txt"
    val business: ITaxBusiness = try {
        // creation of the [dao] layer
        val dao: ITaxDao = if (source == "hardwired") HardwiredTax() else FileTax(source)
        // creation of the [business] layer, which receives the [dao] layer
        TaxBusiness(dao)
    } catch (e: TaxException) {
        // display of the error and stop of the program with exit code 1
        val origin = e.cause?.let { ", original exception: ${it.message}" } ?: ""
        println("The following error occurred: [Code=${ErrorCode.names(e.code)}, " +
            "Message=${e.message}$origin]")
        exitProcess(1)
    }

    // the [ui] layer: the dialog with the user
    Dialog.run(business)
}
  • lines 1–9: the file does not contain a [package] directive; its imports specify the classes from the other four packages;
  • line 14: the function [main] receives command-line arguments in the array [args]. The argument selects the implementation of the layer [dao]: [hardwired] for class [HardwiredTax], otherwise the name of the file read by class [FileTax], with [TaxData.txt] as the default;
  • line 15: [firstOrNull] returns the first argument, or [null] if there is none, which the Elvis operator replaces with the default file name;
  • line 16: the variable [business] is initialized with an expression [try]. Its type is declared: it is the interface [ITaxBusiness], not the class [TaxBusiness] that inference would yield;
  • Line 18: Creation of the layer [dao]. [if] is an expression: its value is one or the other of the two implementations. This is the only place in the program where the classes [HardwiredTax] and [FileTax] are named;
  • line 20: creation of the layer [business], which receives the layer [dao]. This is the last expression in the block [try], and therefore its value;
  • Lines 21–26: Creating the [dao] layer may throw a [TaxException]. An error is then displayed, along with the message from the original exception (if any), and the program terminates with exit code 1. The error code is displayed in plain text using the [ErrorCode.names] function. If [e.cause] is not [null], [let] constructs the description of the original exception; otherwise, the Elvis operator returns an empty string;
  • line 26: the function [exitProcess] from the standard library calls [System.exit]. Its return type is [Nothing]: the compiler knows that it never returns control, and therefore that the [catch] block does not produce any value. The expression [try] thus has the type [ITaxBusiness]. The Java version had to add a [return] statement—which is never executed—after [System.exit(1)], so that the compiler would recognize that the variable [business] was initialized;
  • Line 30: The layers are ready: the [ui] layer interacts with the user.

With the [HardwiredTax] implementation. The program arguments are passed via the [--args] option of the [run] task:

With a file that does not exist:

The error code is [ACCESS], and the message from the original exception, [NoSuchFileException], is displayed: it consists of the file name, followed by the reason provided to its constructor. The program exits with exit code 1: Gradle then reports the failure of task [run] with a few additional lines, which we will not reproduce here.

With the following file, [TaxDataInvalid.txt], where line 3 is written with decimal commas:

docs.title: 6.3.8. Conclusion
docs.text:
The layered architecture and the use of interfaces have brought a certain degree of flexibility to our application. This is evident in the way the main program creates the layers [dao] and [business]:

        // creation of the [dao] layer
        val dao: ITaxDao = if (source == "hardwired") HardwiredTax() else FileTax(source)
        // creation of the [business] layer, which receives the [dao] layer
        TaxBusiness(dao)

Changing the implementation of the [dao] layer affects only line 2. Once the layers are created, the code for the [ui] layer is the same in both cases: the [business] layer is manipulated there through its [ITaxBusiness] interface, not through its implementation class.

The same flexibility is evident in the [business] layer: it is built based on a reference to the interface of the [dao] layer. Changing the implementation of the latter therefore has no impact on the [business] layer. This is why our single [TaxBusiness] class was able to work without modification with two different implementations of the [dao] layer.

docs.title: 6.4. Sample Application - Version 5
docs.text:
This new version is based on the previous one, with the following changes:

  • The layers [dao] and [business] are each placed in a Gradle subproject that produces a library (a JAR file) and are tested using the unit test framework JUnit;
  • The [dao] layer receives a third implementation, [JsonTax], which reads the tax brackets from a JSON file using the Jackson library;
  • The integration of the layers is handled by Spring’s dependency injection container, and the implementation of the [dao] layer is selected from a configuration file.

In large projects, multiple developers work on the same application. Layered architectures facilitate this way of working: because the layers communicate with each other through well-defined interfaces, a developer working on one layer does not have to worry about the work of other developers on other layers. All that is required is that everyone adheres to the interfaces.

Thus, to test the [business] layer, the developer needs an implementation of the [dao] layer. Until that implementation is complete, the developer can use a dummy implementation of the [dao] layer, provided it adheres to the [ITaxDao] interface. This is another advantage of the layered architecture: a delay in the [dao] layer does not prevent the [business] layer from being tested. The mock implementation also has the advantage of being much simpler to set up than the actual [dao] layer, which may require a DBMS, network connections, etc.

Once the [dao] layer is complete and tested, it is provided to the developers of the [business] layer in the form of a library (a JAR file) rather than source code to be copied. Ultimately, the application is delivered as a main program (the one from the [ui] layer) and class libraries (the other layers).

docs.title: 6.4.1. The Gradle subprojects for version 5
docs.text:
Version 5 consists of three subprojects of the chapter’s Gradle build, one per layer, located in the [TaxV5] folder. The tests do not form a separate project: the Gradle convention (the same as Maven’s) places a subproject’s tests in its [src/test/kotlin] folder. They are compiled and run by Gradle but are not part of the subproject’s JAR file. This results in the following directory structure:

TaxV5/
  tax-dao/                         subproject: entities and [dao] layer (jar)
    build.gradle.kts
    TaxData.txt
    TaxData.json
    TaxDataInvalid.txt             an incorrect bracket file, for the tests
    src/main/kotlin/tax/entities/
      TaxBracket.kt
      TaxException.kt
    src/main/kotlin/tax/dao/
      ITaxDao.kt
      HardwiredTax.kt
      FileTax.kt
      JsonTax.kt
    src/test/kotlin/tax/dao/
      DaoTests.kt                  JUnit tests
      TrialDao.kt                  trial program
  tax-business/                    subproject: [business] layer (jar)
    build.gradle.kts
    src/main/kotlin/tax/business/
      ITaxBusiness.kt
      TaxBusiness.kt
    src/test/kotlin/tax/business/
      BusinessTests.kt             JUnit tests
      TrialBusiness.kt             trial program
  tax-ui/                          subproject: [ui] layer and integration of the layers
    build.gradle.kts
    tax.properties                 configuration files
    tax-json.properties
    tax-hardwired.properties
    tax-error.properties
    tax-beans.xml                  Spring XML configuration
    tax-beans-error.xml
    TaxData.txt
    TaxData.json
    src/main/kotlin/tax/ui/
      Dialog.kt
      Main.kt
      MainXml.kt
      TaxConfig.kt
      MainConfig.kt

The packages are now prefixed with [tax]: [tax.entities], [tax.dao], [tax.business], [tax.ui]. The subprojects [tax-dao] and [tax-business] will in fact be reused by other projects (Chapters 10 through 13), and two libraries used by the same program must not define two classes with the same fully qualified name. In professional projects, packages are prefixed with the organization’s reverse domain name ([org.springframework], [tools.jackson]…), which ensures unique names.

The [TaxV5] folder itself does not have a build file: it is a simple grouping folder, which Gradle treats as an empty project, [:TaxV5], the parent of the three subprojects [:TaxV5:tax-dao], [:TaxV5:tax-business], and [:TaxV5:tax-ui] declared in the [settings.gradle.kts] file in this chapter. Whereas Maven requires a parent project to group modules, Gradle only needs this file. Each subproject has its own [build.gradle.kts] file, which we’ll cover along with its layer. These files repeat a few lines (the Maven Central repository, compiler configuration, and test setup); in a larger project, we would factor these lines into a convention plugin ([buildSrc] folder) and consolidate the library versions into a version catalog ([gradle/libs.versions.toml]).

The application is built and tested using the following command, entered in the chapter’s folder:

> gradlew build

Gradle compiles each subproject, compiles and runs its tests, and then creates its JAR file in the subproject's [build/libs] folder—for example, [TaxV5/tax-dao/build/libs/tax-dao-5.0.jar]. Subprojects are processed in the order dictated by their dependencies: [tax-dao], then [tax-business], then [tax-ui]. If a test fails, the build stops. The command [gradlew :TaxV5:tax-business:build] builds only the subproject [tax-business]… and those on which it depends: Gradle knows that [tax-business] needs [tax-dao], and compiles the latter first if it has changed (without running its tests). Unlike with Maven, there is no local repository that needs to be kept up to date by a [install] command: within a build, the subprojects are visible to each other directly.

The applications in Chapters 10 through 13 will reuse the layers from Version 5 without copying their source code. Their [settings.gradle.kts] file will include the build from Chapter 6 as a composite build:

// the build of chapter 6, whose subprojects replace the libraries with the same coordinates
includeBuild("../06-architectures")

and their [build.gradle.kts] files will declare dependencies on [examples.tax:tax-business:5.0] and, for the [Dialog] object, [examples.tax:tax-ui:5.0], just as they would for Jackson or Spring:

dependencies {
    implementation("examples.tax:tax-business:5.0")
    implementation("examples.tax:tax-ui:5.0")
}

Gradle recognizes the subprojects with these coordinates (group [examples.tax], subproject name, version [5.0]) in the included build and uses them in place of a downloaded library: it builds them as needed, and a change to version 5 is immediately reflected in subsequent versions. This is why the three subprojects declare the group [group = "examples.tax"] and the version [version = "5.0"].

docs.title: 6.4.2. The [dao] layer
docs.text:
The [tax-dao] subproject contains the [dao] layer and the application entities. Its [build.gradle.kts] file is as follows:

// TaxV5: the tax-dao subproject, a library (the entities and the [dao] layer)
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    // the library plugin: it adds the [api] configuration
    `java-library`
}

// the coordinates of the library: examples.tax:tax-dao:5.0
group = "examples.tax"
version = "5.0"

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // Jackson for reading the JSON file: a dependency internal to the library
    implementation("tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind:3.1.5")
    // the tests
    testImplementation(kotlin("test"))
    testImplementation(platform("org.junit:junit-bom:6.0.3"))
    testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter")
    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        // parameter names are kept: Jackson and JUnit use them
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

tasks.test {
    useJUnitPlatform()
    testLogging {
        events("passed", "skipped", "failed")
    }
}

// gradlew -q :TaxV5:tax-dao:trial : runs the trial program, stored with the tests
tasks.register<JavaExec>("trial") {
    classpath = sourceSets["test"].runtimeClasspath
    mainClass = "tax.dao.TrialDaoKt"
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}
  • Lines 2–5: The subproject applies the Kotlin plugin and the [java-library] plugin, which is the libraries plugin. The latter, provided by Gradle, is written with grave accents because its name contains a hyphen. It adds the [api] dependency configuration, which the [tax-business] subproject will use;
  • lines 9–10: the library’s coordinates, [examples.tax:tax-dao:5.0];
  • line 18: the Jackson 3 library, which reads the JSON file. It is declared by [implementation]: this is an internal detail of the [dao] layer, whose types do not appear in its public interface. A project that depends on [tax-dao] will have Jackson available at runtime, but will not be able to use its classes in its own code;
  • lines 20–23: the test dependencies, which we will present along with the tests. The configurations [testImplementation] and [testRuntimeOnly] are used only to compile and run the tests: they are not part of the dependencies of the generated library;
  • lines 26–31: the compiler configuration. The parameter names retained in the compiled code are used by Jackson to map the properties of JSON to the constructor parameters of [TaxBracket], and by JUnit to display the parameterized tests;
  • lines 35–38: the configuration of the task [test], which we will present along with the tests;
  • lines 43–45: an additional task, [trial], of type [JavaExec] (execution of a Java class), which launches the test program presented below. This program is stored with the tests: its classpath ([classpath]) is therefore that of the tests, [sourceSets["test"].runtimeClasspath], which includes the main classes, the test classes, and all dependencies;
  • Lines 48–51: Programs launched by Gradle write their output to UTF-8 so that accented characters display correctly on Windows (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 6.4.2.1. The entities
docs.text:
The data class [TaxBracket] is from version 4 (package [tax.entities]). The enumeration [ErrorCode] is removed, and the exception [TaxException] becomes the exception for the entire application, regardless of which layer invokes it:

package tax.entities

// the exception of the [Tax] application, whatever the layer that throws it
// Kotlin has no checked exceptions: no function has to declare it
class TaxException(
    message: String,
    // the original exception, if there is one
    cause: Throwable? = null,
    // error code, specific to the class that throws the exception (0: no code)
    val code: Int = 0,
) : RuntimeException(message, cause)
  • line 10: the error code remains a simple integer: each implementation of the [dao] layer defines its own codes. Its default value, 0, means “no code”;
  • Lines 6–10: thanks to the default values, this single constructor accepts the four call forms for which the Java version had four constructors: [TaxException(message)], [TaxException(message, cause)], [TaxException(message, code = 2)], and [TaxException(message, cause, 2)]. When the code is provided without a context, it must be named: without the name, the compiler would attempt to pass the integer to the [cause] parameter. One could also implement the class with a secondary constructor ([constructor(message: String, code: Int) : this(message, null, code)]), but the named argument makes the call more readable.

docs.title: 6.4.2.2. The [FileTax] implementation
docs.text:
The [ITaxDao] interface and the [HardwiredTax] class are those from version 4. The [FileTax] class differs only in the way its error codes are written:

    companion object {
        // error codes specific to this implementation: powers of 2, which can be combined
        const val ACCESS = 1
        const val LINE = 2
        const val FIELD1 = 4
        const val FIELD2 = 8
        const val FIELD3 = 16
  • lines 3–7: The error codes, which were previously in the [ErrorCode] enumeration in the entity package, have become constants in the [FileTax] class: These are, in fact, codes specific to this implementation of the [ITaxDao] interface ([JsonTax] has its own). Kotlin does not have static members: the class constants are declared in its companion object, using the keyword [const], which makes them compile-time constants (the equivalent of a Java field named [static final]). They are written as [FIELD1] within the class and [FileTax.FIELD1] outside of it. The imports of [ErrorCode] values from version 4 are no longer necessary.

Earlier in the class:

        } catch (e: IOException) {
            // file access error: it is wrapped in a TaxException
            throw TaxException("Error while reading the file $fileName", e, ACCESS)
        }
        // one bracket per non-empty line; the lines are numbered from 1
        taxBrackets = lines.withIndex()
            .filter { it.value.isNotBlank() }
            .map { (index, line) -> bracket(index + 1, line.trim()) }
    }

    // the bracket described by a line, or a TaxException if the line is incorrect
    private fun bracket(lineNumber: Int, line: String): TaxBracket {
        // line split into fields separated by : (possibly surrounded by spaces)
        val fields = line.split(SEPARATOR)
        if (fields.size != 3) {
            throw TaxException("Line no. $lineNumber is incorrect: [$line]", code = LINE)
        }
        // conversions of the 3 fields: null for an incorrect field
        val (limit, coeffR, coeffN) = fields.map(::number)
        if (limit == null || coeffR == null || coeffN == null) {
            // each incorrect field adds its code
            var code = 0
            if (limit == null) code = code or FIELD1
            if (coeffR == null) code = code or FIELD2
            if (coeffN == null) code = code or FIELD3
            throw TaxException("Line no. $lineNumber is incorrect: [$line]", code = code)
  • line 3: the file access error is encapsulated in a [TaxException], with the cause and code [ACCESS];
  • line 16: a line that does not have three fields throws an exception with code [LINE];
  • Lines 22–25: The codes are integers that are combined directly with the infix function [or].

docs.title: 6.4.2.3. The [JsonTax] Implementation
docs.text:
Like version 3 of Chapter 5, the third implementation of the [dao] layer reads the tax brackets from a JSON file using the Jackson library. The [TaxData.json] file is as follows:

[
  { "limit": 4962, "coeffR": 0, "coeffN": 0 },
  { "limit": 8382, "coeffR": 0.068, "coeffN": 291.09 },
  { "limit": 14753, "coeffR": 0.191, "coeffN": 1322.92 },
  { "limit": 23888, "coeffR": 0.283, "coeffN": 2668.39 },
  { "limit": 38868, "coeffR": 0.374, "coeffN": 4846.98 },
  { "limit": 47932, "coeffR": 0.426, "coeffN": 6883.66 },
  { "limit": 0, "coeffR": 0.481, "coeffN": 9505.54 }
]

The [JsonTax] class is as follows:

package tax.dao

import tax.entities.TaxException
import tax.entities.TaxBracket
import java.io.IOException
import java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException
import kotlin.io.path.Path
import kotlin.io.path.exists
import kotlin.io.path.readText
import tools.jackson.core.JacksonException
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper

// a [dao] layer that reads the tax brackets from a JSON file
class JsonTax(val fileName: String) : ITaxDao {

    // tax brackets, read when the object is constructed
    override val taxBrackets: List<TaxBracket>

    init {
        // reading the file (relative to the current folder)
        val json = try {
            val path = Path(fileName)
            if (!path.exists()) {
                throw NoSuchFileException(fileName, null, "The file [$fileName] does not exist")
            }
            path.readText()
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            throw TaxException("Error while reading the file $fileName", e, ACCESS)
        }
        // deserialization of the JSON array into an array of TaxBracket (null for the JSON text null)
        val message = "The file $fileName is not a valid JSON file of tax brackets"
        val brackets = try {
            JsonMapper.builder().build().readValue(json, Array<TaxBracket>::class.java)
        } catch (e: JacksonException) {
            throw TaxException(message, e, FORMAT)
        }
        taxBrackets = brackets?.toList() ?: throw TaxException(message, code = FORMAT)
    }

    companion object {
        // error codes specific to this implementation
        const val ACCESS = 1
        const val FORMAT = 2
    }
}
  • Line 14: As with [FileTax], the class receives the file name, which becomes the [fileName] property;
  • Lines 21–28: The file is read, as in [FileTax]. The extension function [readText] reads the entire file, as in UTF-8, into a string. An I/O error results in a [TaxException] with code [ACCESS];
  • Lines 32–35: Deserialization (Chapter 5). [JsonMapper.builder().build()] creates the Jackson object that converts JSON into objects, and its method [readValue] reads the JSON text as an array of [TaxBracket]. The array type is written as [Array<TaxBracket>::class.java]: [::class] specifies the Kotlin class ([KClass]) of the type, and [.java] specifies the corresponding Java class, which is the one Jackson expects. To create each bracket, Jackson calls the constructor of the data class [TaxBracket], mapping the JSON properties and [limit], [coeffR], and [coeffN] to the names of its parameters, which are preserved thanks to the [javaParameters] compiler option. The numbers JSON are converted to [BigDecimal], the parameter type, without going through a [Double]: the conversion is exact. A syntax or content error causes a [JacksonException], encapsulated in a [TaxException] with code [FORMAT];
  • line 37: [readValue] is a Java method: Kotlin does not know if it can return [null], and assigns its result a platform type—denoted as [Array<TaxBracket>!] in compiler messages—which can be treated as either nullable or non-nullable. It actually returns [null] if the file contains the JSON text [null]: the safe call [?.toList()] and the Elvis operator transform this case into a [TaxException] with code [FORMAT]. Otherwise, [toList] converts the array into a read-only list;
  • Lines 42–43: the error codes for this implementation.

Chapter 5 mentioned the existence of the [jackson-module-kotlin] module, which informs Jackson about Kotlin’s specific features (default parameter values, nullable types), and the kotlinx.serialization library from JetBrains. Our simple data class does not need them.

docs.title: 6.4.2.4. A Test Program
docs.text:
Before writing automated tests, let’s perform an initial visual test of the [dao] layer. The [TrialDao.kt] program displays the brackets provided by the three implementations. We’ve placed it in the test sources of the subproject ([src/test/kotlin]): it will not be included in the [dao] layer’s JAR file:

package tax.dao

import tax.entities.TaxException

// trial program: the tax brackets provided by the three implementations of the [dao] layer
fun main() {
    try {
        val daos = listOf(HardwiredTax(), FileTax("TaxData.txt"), JsonTax("TaxData.json"))
        for (dao in daos) {
            println("--- ${dao::class.simpleName}")
            dao.taxBrackets.forEach(::println)
        }
    } catch (e: TaxException) {
        // display of the error
        val origin = e.cause?.let { ", original exception: ${it.message}" } ?: ""
        println("The following error occurred: [Code=${e.code}, Message=${e.message}$origin]")
    }
}
  • line 6: a high-level, parameterless [main] function in the [tax.dao] package: its class is [tax.dao.TrialDaoKt]. Placed in the same package as the tested classes, the program uses them without importing them;
  • line 8: a list of the three implementations of the [ITaxDao] interface. The compiler infers the most specific type common to all three elements: [List<ITaxDao>];
  • line 10: [dao::class] returns the actual class of the object, whose name (without the package) is [simpleName];
  • line 11: each bracket is passed to the function [println] (function reference [::println]), which displays it using its function [toString], generated by the compiler for a data class;
  • lines 13–16: handling a potential [TaxException].

The program runs with the [tax-dao] subproject folder as the current folder, via the [trial] task declared in the build file:

> gradlew -q :TaxV5:tax-dao:trial
--- HardwiredTax
TaxBracket(limit=4962, coeffR=0, coeffN=0)
TaxBracket(limit=8382, coeffR=0.068, coeffN=291.09)
TaxBracket(limit=14753, coeffR=0.191, coeffN=1322.92)
TaxBracket(limit=23888, coeffR=0.283, coeffN=2668.39)
TaxBracket(limit=38868, coeffR=0.374, coeffN=4846.98)
TaxBracket(limit=47932, coeffR=0.426, coeffN=6883.66)
TaxBracket(limit=0, coeffR=0.481, coeffN=9505.54)
--- FileTax
TaxBracket(limit=4962, coeffR=0, coeffN=0)
TaxBracket(limit=8382, coeffR=0.068, coeffN=291.09)
TaxBracket(limit=14753, coeffR=0.191, coeffN=1322.92)
