docs.title: 6.4.3. The [business] layer
docs.text:
The file [build.gradle.kts] from the subproject [tax-business] is as follows:

// TaxV5: the tax-business subproject, a library (the [business] layer)
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    `java-library`
}

// the coordinates of the library: examples.tax:tax-business:5.0
group = "examples.tax"
version = "5.0"

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // the [business] layer uses the [dao] layer, which is part of its API:
    // the constructor of TaxBusiness receives an ITaxDao
    api(project(":TaxV5:tax-dao"))
    // the tests
    testImplementation(kotlin("test"))
    testImplementation(platform("org.junit:junit-bom:6.0.3"))
    testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter")
    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

tasks.test {
    useJUnitPlatform()
    testLogging {
        events("passed", "skipped", "failed")
    }
}

// gradlew -q :TaxV5:tax-business:trial : runs the trial program, stored with the tests
tasks.register<JavaExec>("trial") {
    classpath = sourceSets["test"].runtimeClasspath
    mainClass = "tax.business.TrialBusinessKt"
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}
  • Line 18: The layer [business] uses the layer [dao]. The notation [project(":TaxV5:tax-dao")] refers to another subproject in the structure by its path. The dependency is declared by [api] and not by [implementation]: the interface [ITaxDao] appears in the public API of the layer [business], since the constructor of [TaxBusiness] receives an [ITaxDao]. A project that depends on [tax-business] should therefore be able to use the types from [tax-dao] in its code: with [api], it receives them automatically, without having to declare the dependency on [tax-dao] itself. Jackson, declared by [implementation] in [tax-dao], is only included at runtime;
  • lines 42–44: the [trial] task in this subproject;
  • lines 47–50: the programs launched by Gradle write their output to UTF-8, so that accented characters display correctly on Windows (Chapter 2).

The [ITaxBusiness] interface and the [TaxBusiness] class are those from version 4 (package [tax.business]). The test program [TrialBusiness.kt], located in the subproject’s test sources, performs some tax calculations:

package tax.business

import tax.dao.FileTax
import tax.entities.TaxException

// trial program: a few tax calculations with the FileTax [dao] layer
fun main() {
    try {
        // the brackets file is that of the tax-dao subproject (path relative to the current folder)
        val business: ITaxBusiness = TaxBusiness(FileTax("../tax-dao/TaxData.txt"))
        println("Tax(true,2,60000)=${business.calculateTax(true, 2, 60000)} euros")
        println("Tax(false,3,60000)=${business.calculateTax(false, 3, 60000)} euros")
        println("Tax(false,3,6000)=${business.calculateTax(false, 3, 6000)} euros")
        println("Tax(false,3,600000)=${business.calculateTax(false, 3, 600000)} euros")
    } catch (e: TaxException) {
        // display of the error
        val origin = e.cause?.let { ", original exception: ${it.message}" } ?: ""
        println("The following error occurred: [Code=${e.code}, Message=${e.message}$origin]")
    }
}
  • line 10: creation of layers [dao] and [business]. The layer [dao] is implemented by the class [FileTax]. Since the program runs in the [tax-business] folder, the relative path [../tax-dao/TaxData.txt] refers to the data file for the [tax-dao] subproject;
  • Lines 11–14: Repeated calls to the single function of the [ITaxBusiness] interface.

Results:

> gradlew -q :TaxV5:tax-business:trial
Tax(true,2,60000)=4282 euros
Tax(false,3,60000)=4282 euros
Tax(false,3,6000)=0 euros
Tax(false,3,600000)=179275 euros

A married couple with 2 children and a single person with 3 children have the same number of shares (3): their taxes are equal.

docs.title: 6.4.4.1. The Principle
docs.text:
The tests performed so far relied on visual verification: we checked that the screen displayed the expected results. This method is impractical when there are many tests to run: humans are prone to fatigue, and their ability to verify results diminishes as the day goes on. The tests must therefore be automated and require no human intervention.

An application evolves over time. With each update, we must verify that it does not “regress”—that is, that it continues to pass the functionality tests performed during its initial development. These tests are called non-regression tests. A moderately large application may require hundreds of tests: in fact, every function in every class of the application is tested. These are called unit tests.

Test frameworks have been developed to automate these tests. For JVM, the reference framework is JUnit, created in the late 1990s by Kent Beck and Erich Gamma. It can be used in both Kotlin and Java. We use version 6, released in September 2025 (here, version 6.0.3); its API, the one from the [org.junit.jupiter.api] package, is the same as JUnit 5, also known as JUnit Jupiter. Kotlin adds its test library, kotlin.test: a set of assertions written for Kotlin ([assertEquals], [assertFailsWith], [assertIs]…), which delegate their work to the test framework being used, in this case JUnit. The tests are run by the command [gradlew test] from the command line: this is what allows them to be launched automatically, for example, whenever code changes are pushed to a continuous integration server. IntelliJ and IDEA also run them and display their results in a tree structure. Kotest is another testing framework, written for Kotlin, that operates on the same principle.

docs.title: 6.4.4.2. A First Example
docs.text:
Let’s examine the principle behind JUnit tests using an example. The [DemoTests] subproject contains only tests, located in the [src/test/kotlin/demotests] folder. Its [build.gradle.kts] file is as follows:

// DemoTests: a project that only contains JUnit tests
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
}

group = "examples.architectures"
version = "1.0"

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // the Kotlin assertions (kotlin.test), plugged into JUnit
    testImplementation(kotlin("test"))
    // JUnit: the bill of materials (BOM) sets the version of all its modules
    testImplementation(platform("org.junit:junit-bom:6.0.3"))
    // the test API and the JUnit Jupiter engine that runs them
    testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter")
    // the JUnit platform launcher, used by Gradle
    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        // parameter names are kept: JUnit displays them for parameterized tests
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

tasks.test {
    // gradlew test: the tests are run by the JUnit platform
    useJUnitPlatform()
    testLogging {
        // a report for each test
        events("passed", "skipped", "failed")
        // the output of the tests (println) is shown
        showStandardStreams = true
        // on failure: the full message of the assertion, without the call stack
        exceptionFormat = org.gradle.api.tasks.testing.logging.TestExceptionFormat.FULL
        showStackTraces = false
    }
}
  • Lines 2–3: the Kotlin plugin; that’s all—the project has no main program;
  • line 15: the kotlin.test library. The notation [kotlin("test")] refers to the artifact [org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-test], in the Kotlin plugin version. When the task [test] uses the platform JUnit (line 35), the Kotlin plugin automatically adds the adapter that links the assertions from kotlin.test to those of JUnit;
  • Line 17: JUnit consists of several modules (API, the engine, the parameterized tests, the platform, etc.), which must have compatible versions. Its bill of materials (BOM), [junit-bom], specifies the versions of all these modules: the following dependencies are declared as versionless;
  • line 19: the artifact [junit-jupiter] combines the test artifact API ([@Test], [@BeforeEach]…), the parameterized test artifact, and the Jupiter engine that executes them;
  • line 21: the JUnit platform launcher, through which Gradle starts the tests. It is only required at runtime ([testRuntimeOnly]);
  • line 29: the compiler preserves the names of the function parameters, which JUnit displays for parameterized tests;
  • Lines 33–43: the configuration of the [test] task. [useJUnitPlatform()] instructs it to run the tests using the JUnit platform. By default, Gradle displays only failed tests and a summary; [events("passed", "skipped", "failed")] instructs it to report on each test—whether it passed, was skipped, or failed— [showStandardStreams = true] instructs it to display the output of the tests on the screen, and lines 42–43 instruct it to display, for a failed test, the full error message without the call stack (by default, Gradle displays only the exception name and the error location).

The test class [Tests1] is as follows:

package demotests

import kotlin.test.Test
import kotlin.test.assertEquals
import org.junit.jupiter.api.AfterAll
import org.junit.jupiter.api.AfterEach
import org.junit.jupiter.api.BeforeAll
import org.junit.jupiter.api.BeforeEach

// the tested function
private fun sum(a: Int, b: Int) = a + b

// a test class
class Tests1 {

    // the init block is part of the constructor
    init {
        println("constructor")
    }

    // executed before each test
    @BeforeEach
    fun before() {
        println("before")
    }

    // executed after each test
    @AfterEach
    fun after() {
        println("after")
    }

    // a test that succeeds
    @Test
    fun `two and two make four`() {
        println("test1")
        assertEquals(4, sum(2, 2))
    }

    // a test that fails
    @Test
    fun `two and two make five`() {
        println("test2")
        assertEquals(5, sum(2, 2), "2 + 2 is not equal to 5")
    }

    // the functions executed only once, before the first test and after the last one:
    // for JUnit, they must be static methods
    companion object {
        @BeforeAll
        @JvmStatic
        fun beforeAll() {
            println("before all the tests")
        }

        @AfterAll
        @JvmStatic
        fun afterAll() {
            println("after all the tests")
        }
    }
}
  • Lines 3–4: the [Test] annotation and the [assertEquals] assertion for kotlin.test. With JUnit, [kotlin.test.Test] is a type alias ([typealias]) for the annotation [org.junit.jupiter.api.Test]: it is the same annotation. Assertions are high-level functions that are imported as classes;
  • lines 5–8: test lifecycle annotations specific to JUnit;
  • line 11: the function being tested. In a real project, it would be in the project’s main source code ([src/main/kotlin]);
  • line 14: a test class is an ordinary class, without any annotations;
  • lines 17–18: the block [init], executed when the object is constructed. It is used only to display a message on the screen: we want to see when the object is created;
  • line 22: the annotation [@BeforeEach] designates a function executed before each test;
  • line 28: the annotation [@AfterEach] designates a function executed after each test;
  • lines 34–35: The annotation [@Test] denotes a test function. A test function returns nothing, is not private, and—with one exception we’ll discuss—has no parameters. Its name is written with grave accents: Kotlin thus allows you to give a function a name that contains spaces and accented characters, which is discouraged in regular code but common practice for tests—the test name clearly states what it verifies. In JVM, this name cannot contain certain characters ([. ; [ ] / < > :] and the backslash). Java achieves the same effect with the annotation [@DisplayName];
  • Line 37: The [assertEquals(expected, actual)] function checks that the resulting value equals the expected value. If it does not, it throws an [AssertionFailedError] exception and the test fails. Here, the assertion must pass;
  • line 44: this assertion must fail. The third parameter is the message displayed in case of failure: as in JUnit, the message is the last parameter of the assertions in kotlin.test;
  • lines 49–59: the annotations [@BeforeAll] and [@AfterAll] designate functions that are executed only once, before the first test and after the last test in the class. JUnit requires that they be static methods. Kotlin does not have static members: these functions are placed in the class’s companion object and annotated with [@JvmStatic], which instructs the compiler to additionally generate a true static method in the class [Tests1]. Without [@JvmStatic], these functions would simply be methods of the companion object’s class: JUnit, which searches for annotated functions in the [Tests1] class, would not find them, and they would never be executed.

The tests are run using the command [gradlew test], which runs the tests for all subprojects, or [gradlew :DemoTests:test], which runs only those for the [DemoTests] subproject. Below we reproduce the test reports and their output, in the order in which they were executed, but not the other Gradle messages:

> gradlew :DemoTests:test
Tests1 STANDARD_OUT
    before all the tests
    constructor

Tests1 > two and two make five() STANDARD_OUT
    before
    test2
    after

Tests1 > two and two make five() FAILED
    org.opentest4j.AssertionFailedError: 2 + 2 is not equal to 5 ==> expected: <5> but was: <4>

Tests1 STANDARD_OUT
    constructor

Tests1 > two and two make four() STANDARD_OUT
    before
    test1
    after

Tests1 > two and two make four() PASSED

Tests1 STANDARD_OUT
    after all the tests

Tests2 > booleans, null and references() PASSED

Tests2 > reals equal within a tolerance() PASSED

Tests2 > exceptions() PASSED

Tests2 > sum of two integers(int, int, int) > [1] a = "1", b = "1", sum = "2" PASSED

Tests2 > sum of two integers(int, int, int) > [2] a = "2", b = "3", sum = "5" PASSED

Tests2 > sum of two integers(int, int, int) > [3] a = "-1", b = "1", sum = "0" PASSED

Tests2 > even numbers(int) > [1] n = 2 PASSED

Tests2 > even numbers(int) > [2] n = 4 PASSED

Tests2 > even numbers(int) > [3] n = 6 PASSED

Tests2 > strings and collections() PASSED

Tests3 STANDARD_OUT
    preparing the data

Tests3 > the square of 7() PASSED

Tests3 > the sum of the squares() PASSED

14 tests completed, 1 failed
  • Lines in the form [Tests1 > two and two make four() PASSED] are the test reports: the class, the test, and then the result, [PASSED] (passed) or [FAILED] (failed). The tests for the classes [Tests2] and [Tests3], shown below, all passed. The execution order of the classes and functions is fixed but intentionally non-obvious: the tests must not depend on their execution order;
  • Gradle groups the outputs under a line that lists their author followed by the notation [STANDARD_OUT]: the class ([Tests1 STANDARD_OUT]) for code written outside a test, and the test itself for code written within the test;
  • The line [before all the tests]: the function [@BeforeAll] is executed once, before the first test of the class [Tests1];
  • Next come the outputs from test [two and two make five]: the constructor has been executed (line [constructor], written before the test begins, is placed under [Tests1 STANDARD_OUT]), followed by function [before], the test, and finally function [after];
  • followed by the output of test [two and two make four]. Note that the constructor has been executed again: JUnit creates a new instance of the test class for each test. The tests are thus independent of one another: one test cannot be affected by the state left by another test (the class [Tests3] will show how to request, instead, a single instance for all tests in the class);
  • The test [two and two make five] failed. The error message contains the message passed to [assertEquals], the expected value, and the actual value: This is [AssertionFailedError], a child of JUnit, to which kotlin.test delegated the verification. The messages from JUnit are in English. Without the settings [exceptionFormat] and [showStackTraces] in the file [build.gradle.kts], Gradle would only display the location of the failed assertion ([org.opentest4j.AssertionFailedError at Tests1.kt:44], line 44 of the file [Tests1.kt]). Gradle finally reports that the [test] task failed (“14 tests completed, 1 failed”): the [gradlew test] command then ends with a build failure (“BUILD FAILED”) and a non-zero exit code, which allows a script to detect the failure. Gradle also generates a detailed HTML test report in the [build/reports/tests/test] folder of the subproject;
  • line [after all the tests], the last line of class [Tests1]: the function [@AfterAll] is executed once, after the last test in the class.

To run only a subset of the tests, use the [--tests] option of task [test]: [gradlew :DemoTests:test --tests demotests.Tests2] runs only the tests in class [Tests2] (the name may contain the wildcard character [*]). By default, JUnit runs the tests sequentially; parallel execution can be specified in a [junit-platform.properties] configuration file.

docs.title: 6.4.4.3. Additional assertions
docs.text:
The kotlin.test library has many assertions, and JUnit adds more. The [Tests2] class provides a few examples:

package demotests

import kotlin.test.Test
import kotlin.test.assertContains
import kotlin.test.assertEquals
import kotlin.test.assertFailsWith
import kotlin.test.assertFalse
import kotlin.test.assertIs
import kotlin.test.assertNotEquals
import kotlin.test.assertNotNull
import kotlin.test.assertNotSame
import kotlin.test.assertNull
import kotlin.test.assertSame
import kotlin.test.assertTrue
import org.junit.jupiter.api.assertAll
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.CsvSource
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.ValueSource

// a few other assertions of kotlin.test and JUnit
class Tests2 {

    // booleans, null, references
    @Test
    fun `booleans, null and references`() {
        val yes = 1 < 2
        val no = 1 > 2
        assertTrue(yes)
        assertFalse(no)
        val obj1 = Any()
        val obj2: Any? = null
        val obj3 = obj1
        assertNotNull(obj1)
        assertNull(obj2)
        assertSame(obj1, obj3)
        assertNotSame(obj1, Any())
    }

    // reals: equality within a tolerance
    @Test
    fun `reals equal within a tolerance`() {
        val d1 = 0.1 + 0.2
        val d2 = 0.3
        assertNotEquals(d2, d1)
        assertEquals(d2, d1, absoluteTolerance = 1e-6)
    }

    // strings and collections: all the assertions are checked, even if one of them fails
    @Test
    fun `strings and collections`() {
        val message = "Line no. 3 is incorrect"
        val numbers = listOf(1, 2, 3)
        assertAll(
            { assertTrue(message.startsWith("Line")) },
            { assertContains(message, "incorrect") },
            { assertEquals(3, numbers.size) },
            { assertContains(numbers, 2) },
            { assertEquals(listOf(1, 2, 3), numbers) },
        )
    }

    // exceptions: the test succeeds if the expected exception is thrown
    @Test
    fun exceptions() {
        val numbers = listOf(1, 2, 3)
        assertFailsWith<IndexOutOfBoundsException> { numbers[3] }
        val e = assertFailsWith<NumberFormatException> { "x".toInt() }
        assertNotNull(e.message)
        // assertIs checks the type of an object... and casts it
        val obj: Any = "abc"
        assertIs<String>(obj)
        assertEquals(3, obj.length)
    }

    // a parameterized test: one execution per line of values
    @ParameterizedTest
    @CsvSource("1, 1, 2", "2, 3, 5", "-1, 1, 0")
    fun `sum of two integers`(a: Int, b: Int, sum: Int) {
        assertEquals(sum, a + b)
    }

    // a parameterized test with a single parameter: one execution per value
    @ParameterizedTest
    @ValueSource(ints = [2, 4, 6])
    fun `even numbers`(n: Int) {
        assertEquals(0, n % 2)
    }
}
  • lines 28–29: check whether a Boolean expression is true or false;
  • lines 33–34: check whether a reference is non-null or null. [obj2] must be declared with a nullable type, [Any?];
  • lines 35–36: check whether two references refer to the same object (the [===] operator);
  • lines 42–45: calculations on real numbers [Double] are approximated: [0.1 + 0.2] is not exactly equal to [0.3]. We are therefore comparing two real numbers to within a tolerance, in this case one millionth. The parameter [absoluteTolerance] is named: the call clearly specifies what the third number is;
  • lines 53–58: the function [assertAll] of JUnit receives lambda expressions, each containing an assertion: all assertions are executed, even if one of them fails, and the failures are reported together. Without [assertAll], the first failure stops the test. This high-level function, from the [org.junit.jupiter.api] package, is part of the extensions that JUnit provides for Kotlin: it accepts Kotlin lambdas ([{ ... }]) rather than [Executable] objects. [assertContains] checks whether a string contains a substring, or whether a collection contains an element. Kotlin lists are compared using [==] (function [equals]): two lists are equal if they have the same elements in the same order, and [assertEquals] suffices where Java used [assertIterableEquals];
  • Line 66: [assertFailsWith<Type> { action }] executes the action—a lambda—and checks that it throws an exception of type [Type] or a derived type. The type is a reified type parameter ([reified], Chapter 4): it is written between angle brackets, without [::class]. Here, the [numbers[3]] read operation throws an [ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException], a class derived from [IndexOutOfBoundsException]: the assertion succeeds;
  • lines 67–68: [assertFailsWith] throws the exception, which then allows its properties to be verified. Its type is the one requested, [NumberFormatException]: no type conversion is necessary. kotlin.test has no equivalent to [assertThrowsExactly], which requires the exact type of the exception; one can use the one from JUnit, or subsequently verify [e::class];
  • lines 70–72: [assertIs<Type>(obj)] verifies that the object is of the specified type or a derived type. It also informs the compiler that, after the assertion, [obj] is of that type: through smart type casting, the next line uses the property [length] of a [String] on a variable declared as [Any];
  • Lines 76–79: a parameterized test. The annotation [@ParameterizedTest] replaces [@Test]; the function has parameters, and the annotation [@CsvSource] provides sets of values, one string per set, with the values separated by commas. In Kotlin, if the parameter [value] of an annotation is an array, it is written as a list of arguments. JUnit converts the values to the parameter type. The test is executed once per set of values;
  • Lines 84–86: For a single-parameter test, the annotation [@ValueSource] directly provides the list of values ([ints], [strings], [doubles]…). An array passed to a named annotation parameter is written in square brackets: [ints = [2, 4, 6]].

In the previous results, each set of values for a parameterized test resulted in a report, numbered in square brackets and accompanied by the names and values of the parameters: [Tests2 > sum of two integers(int, int, int) > [1] a = "1", b = "1", sum = "2" PASSED]. The test is first identified by the function name followed by the types of its parameters, as seen from Java ([int] for a Kotlin [Int]). The values provided by [@CsvSource] are displayed exactly as they are written in the annotation, enclosed in quotation marks, before their conversion; those from [@ValueSource], which are already integers, are displayed without quotation marks ([even numbers(int) > [1] n = 2]).

Let’s summarize the main assertions of kotlin.test (package [kotlin.test]):

FunctionChecks that[assertEquals(expected, actual)]the two values are equal (function [equals], so this also applies to lists)[assertEquals(real1, real2, absoluteTolerance)]the two real numbers are equal within the tolerance[assertNotEquals(v1, v2)]The two values are different[assertSame(o1, o2)], [assertNotSame(o1, o2)]The two references may or may not refer to the same object[assertNull(o)], [assertNotNull(o)]The reference is null (or not); [assertNotNull] returns the value, which is not nullable[assertTrue(b)], [assertFalse(b)]the Boolean expression is true (or false)[assertIs<Type>(o)]the object is of type [Type] or a derived type (and the cast)[assertContains(c, e)]the collection, array, or string [c] contains [e][assertContentEquals(t1, t2)]both arrays (or sequences) have the same elements, in the same order[assertFailsWith<Type> { action }]The action throws an exception of type [Type] or a derived type[assertFails { action }]The action throws an exception, regardless of its type[fail(message)](always fails)

All of these functions accept an optional parameter [message]: the message displayed in case of failure. The function [assertAll] exists only within JUnit. The assertions in JUnit (class [org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions]) remain usable in Kotlin; kotlin.test has the advantage of being more concise, taking advantage of reified types and smart type casting, and not depending on the test framework.

docs.title: 6.4.4.4. One instance per test class
docs.text:
The functions [@BeforeAll] of the class [Tests1] were supposed to be placed in the companion object. JUnit offers another solution, as shown by the class [Tests3]:

package demotests

import kotlin.test.Test
import kotlin.test.assertEquals
import org.junit.jupiter.api.BeforeAll
import org.junit.jupiter.api.TestInstance

// a single instance of the class for all its tests: @BeforeAll can then be an ordinary function
@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)
class Tests3 {

    // data that is expensive to prepare, shared by the tests; lateinit: initialized later
    private lateinit var squares: List<Int>

    // executed only once, before the first test
    @BeforeAll
    fun prepare() {
        println("preparing the data")
        squares = (0..10).map { it * it }
    }

    @Test
    fun `the square of 7`() {
        assertEquals(49, squares[7])
    }

    @Test
    fun `the sum of the squares`() {
        assertEquals(385, squares.sum())
    }
}
  • Line 9: The annotation [@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)] instructs JUnit to create a single instance of the class for all its tests, rather than one instance per test. The functions [@BeforeAll] and [@AfterAll] can then be ordinary functions of the class;
  • line 13: data shared by the tests. The modifier [lateinit] allows a property [var] to be declared as non-nullable without initializing it: it will receive its value later, before it is first read (a premature read would throw an [UninitializedPropertyAccessException]);
  • lines 16–19: The function, executed once before the first test, prepares the data: the list of squares of integers from 0 to 10;
  • lines 23–29: two tests use this data.

The previous results show that the setup was performed only once. This mode is useful when the setup is resource-intensive (connecting to a database, reading a large file); in such cases, tests must take care not to modify the shared state. It can also be selected for the entire project in the file [junit-platform.properties] ([junit.jupiter.testinstance.lifecycle.default = per_class]), which is often done in Kotlin projects.

docs.title: 6.4.4.5. Tests for the [dao] layer
docs.text:
Let’s return to the [Tax] application. The [DaoTests] class, which tests the [dao] layer, is located in the [src/test/kotlin/tax/dao] folder of the [tax-dao] subproject. It belongs to the same package as the classes being tested. The test sources for a subproject also include its [internal] declarations, which are visible in the single module that declares them. The test dependencies have been declared in the subproject’s build file, just as in that of [DemoTests]. The invalid data file [TaxDataInvalid.txt] is placed in the subproject folder: this is the current folder while the tests are running.

package tax.dao

import tax.entities.TaxException
import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException
import kotlin.test.Test
import kotlin.test.assertEquals
import kotlin.test.assertFailsWith
import kotlin.test.assertIs
import kotlin.test.assertTrue
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.ValueSource

// tests of the [dao] layer
class DaoTests {

    // the same test for the three implementations
    @ParameterizedTest
    @ValueSource(strings = ["HardwiredTax", "FileTax", "JsonTax"])
    fun `tax brackets`(implementation: String) {
        val brackets = createDao(implementation).taxBrackets
        // a few checks: compareTo ignores the scale of BigDecimals (0.191 and 0.1910 are equal)
        assertEquals(7, brackets.size)
        val (limit, coeffR, coeffN) = brackets[2]
        assertEquals(0, BigDecimal("14753").compareTo(limit))
        assertEquals(0, BigDecimal("0.191").compareTo(coeffR))
        assertEquals(0, BigDecimal("1322.92").compareTo(coeffN))
    }

    // the three implementations give the same brackets
    @Test
    fun `the three implementations give the same brackets`() {
        val reference = HardwiredTax().taxBrackets
        assertEquals(reference, FileTax("TaxData.txt").taxBrackets)
        assertEquals(reference, JsonTax("TaxData.json").taxBrackets)
    }

    // missing file
    @Test
    fun `missing file`() {
        val e = assertFailsWith<TaxException> { FileTax("TaxDataMissing.txt") }
        assertEquals(FileTax.ACCESS, e.code)
        assertIs<NoSuchFileException>(e.cause)
    }

    // file whose line 3 is incorrect (decimal commas)
    @Test
    fun `incorrect line`() {
        val e = assertFailsWith<TaxException> { FileTax("TaxDataInvalid.txt") }
        assertEquals(FileTax.FIELD2 or FileTax.FIELD3, e.code)
        assertTrue(e.message!!.startsWith("Line no. 3"))
    }

    // missing JSON file
    @Test
    fun `missing JSON file`() {
        val e = assertFailsWith<TaxException> { JsonTax("TaxDataMissing.json") }
        assertEquals(JsonTax.ACCESS, e.code)
    }

    private companion object {
        // factory of a [dao] layer from the name of its class
        fun createDao(implementation: String): ITaxDao = when (implementation) {
            "HardwiredTax" -> HardwiredTax()
            "FileTax" -> FileTax("TaxData.txt")
            "JsonTax" -> JsonTax("TaxData.json")
            else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown implementation: $implementation")
        }
    }
}
  • lines 61–67: a function that creates a layer named [dao] based on the name of its class, using an expression [when]: each branch returns, after the arrow [->], the value of the expression. It is placed in a private companion object, but could just as easily have been a private function of the class or the file;
  • lines 18–27: the same test is performed for all three implementations, using the annotation [@ValueSource]. It verifies that there are 7 brackets and checks the value of bracket #2 (the third one). The destructuring declaration [val (limit, coeffR, coeffN) = brackets[2]] distributes the three properties of the bracket into three variables, using the functions [component1] through [component3] generated for a data class. The [BigDecimal] functions are compared with [compareTo] rather than with [equals]: the [equals] method of a [BigDecimal] takes into account the number of decimal places written (its scale, “scale”) and treats 0.191 and 0.1910 as different, whereas [compareTo] compares only the values. Note: In Kotlin, [a == b] calls [equals], and therefore has this issue with the [BigDecimal] methods; it is the operators [<], [<=]… that call [compareTo];
  • Lines 32–35: All three implementations yield exactly the same brackets. [assertEquals] compares the lists using its function [equals], which compares the elements one by one; the function [equals] of a data class, generated by the compiler, compares their properties. The comparison succeeds because all three sources write the numbers in the same way;
  • lines 40–43: a missing file throws a [TaxException] from the [ACCESS] code, which encapsulates a [NoSuchFileException]. [assertFailsWith] also accepts classes derived from the requested type, but a Kotlin class is final by default: [TaxException] has no derived classes, and the test correctly verifies the exact type of the exception. [assertIs] checks the type of the cause;
  • lines 48–51: the file [TaxDataInvalid.txt] throws a [TaxException], whose code combines the codes [FIELD2] and [FIELD3], and whose message begins with “Line no. 3.” The [message] property of an exception is of type [String?]: the operator [!!] asserts that it is not [null] (otherwise, it would throw a [NullPointerException], which would also cause the test to fail);
  • Lines 56–58: the same check for the [JsonTax] implementation.

docs.title: 6.4.4.6. Tests for the [business] layer
docs.text:
The [BusinessTests] class in the [tax-business] subproject tests the [business] layer:

package tax.business

import tax.dao.HardwiredTax
import tax.dao.ITaxDao
import tax.entities.TaxBracket
import java.math.BigDecimal
import kotlin.test.Test
import kotlin.test.assertEquals
import kotlin.test.assertFailsWith
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.CsvSource

// tests of the [business] layer
class BusinessTests {

    // the [dao] layer and the tested [business] layer: JUnit creates one instance of the class per test
    private val dao = HardwiredTax()
    private val business: ITaxBusiness = TaxBusiness(dao)

    // calculations whose result is known
    @ParameterizedTest
    @CsvSource(
        "true, 2, 60000, 4282",
        "false, 3, 60000, 4282",
        "true, 3, 60000, 2959",
        "false, 0, 60000, 11519",
        "false, 3, 6000, 0",
        "false, 3, 600000, 179275",
    )
    fun `tax calculation`(married: Boolean, nbChildren: Int, salary: Int, tax: Int) {
        assertEquals(tax, business.calculateTax(married, nbChildren, salary))
    }

    // the calculation does not modify the brackets provided by the [dao] layer
    @Test
    fun `the brackets are unchanged`() {
        val before = dao.taxBrackets.toList()
        business.calculateTax(true, 2, 600000)
        assertEquals(before, dao.taxBrackets)
    }

    // negative parameters are rejected
    @Test
    fun `negative parameters are rejected`() {
        assertFailsWith<IllegalArgumentException> { business.calculateTax(true, -1, 60000) }
        assertFailsWith<IllegalArgumentException> { business.calculateTax(true, 2, -60000) }
    }

    // the [business] layer tested with a fake [dao] layer: a single bracket, a 10% tax
    // ITaxDao has only one property: an anonymous object is enough to implement it
    @Test
    fun `with a fake dao layer`() {
        val fakeDao = object : ITaxDao {
            override val taxBrackets =
                listOf(TaxBracket(BigDecimal.ZERO, "0.1".toBigDecimal(), BigDecimal.ZERO))
        }
        val fakeBusiness: ITaxBusiness = TaxBusiness(fakeDao)
        // taxable income = 0.72 x 100000 = 72000; tax = 10% of 72000
        assertEquals(7200, fakeBusiness.calculateTax(false, 0, 100000))
    }
}
  • Lines 17–18: The [business] layer being tested is built on the [dao] and [HardwiredTax] layers, which do not depend on any files. The properties are initialized when the object is created; since JUnit creates a new instance of the class for each test, each test has brand-new layers;
  • lines 21–31: calculations whose results are known, provided by [@CsvSource]. These are the application’s control values, already obtained by previous versions: they must remain accurate in all future versions. The strings [true] and [false] are converted to [Boolean]. The test name, [tax calculation], contains a space: this is allowed between grave accents;
  • Lines 36–39: The tax calculation does not modify the tax brackets provided by layer [dao]. A copy of the brackets ([toList]) is saved before a calculation that uses the last bracket, and then a comparison is made. The test tracks the old defect described above: if someone were to reintroduce it, this test would flag it. Note that a Kotlin [List] is read-only for the compiler, but the actual object may be a mutable list: code that would cast it to [MutableList] could modify it;
  • lines 44–46: Negative parameters are rejected by a *[IllegalArgumentException], the one thrown by *[require];
  • lines 53–55: a dummy [dao] layer, such as the one the developer of the [business] layer would use before the actual [dao] layer is ready: a single tax bracket, a 10% tax on taxable income. The [ITaxDao] interface is implemented without writing a class, using an object expression ([object : ITaxDao { ... }]): an object of an anonymous class that implements the interface, the equivalent of Java’s anonymous classes. The Java version, whose interface had only one abstract method, used a lambda expression; our interface declares a property, and a lambda can only implement a Kotlin functional interface ([fun interface], Chapter 7), which declares only one abstract function. The type of the redefined property, [List<TaxBracket>], is inferred;
  • lines 57–59: the [business] layer works with the dummy [dao] layer. The [business] layer is thus tested on its own, independently of the actual implementations of the [dao] layer.

docs.title: 6.4.4.7. Running the Tests
docs.text:
The command [gradlew test], entered in the chapter’s folder, runs the tests for all subprojects; [gradlew :TaxV5:tax-dao:test] runs only the tests for the [tax-dao] subproject. Here are the test reports for this subproject (we have included only these lines):

> gradlew :TaxV5:tax-dao:test
DaoTests > missing JSON file() PASSED

DaoTests > incorrect line() PASSED

DaoTests > missing file() PASSED

DaoTests > the three implementations give the same brackets() PASSED

DaoTests > tax brackets(String) > [1] implementation = "HardwiredTax" PASSED

DaoTests > tax brackets(String) > [2] implementation = "FileTax" PASSED

DaoTests > tax brackets(String) > [3] implementation = "JsonTax" PASSED

and those for subproject [tax-business]:

> gradlew :TaxV5:tax-business:test
BusinessTests > negative parameters are rejected() PASSED

BusinessTests > tax calculation(boolean, int, int, int) > [1] married = "true", nbChildren = "2", salary = "60000", tax = "4282" PASSED

BusinessTests > tax calculation(boolean, int, int, int) > [2] married = "false", nbChildren = "3", salary = "60000", tax = "4282" PASSED

BusinessTests > tax calculation(boolean, int, int, int) > [3] married = "true", nbChildren = "3", salary = "60000", tax = "2959" PASSED

BusinessTests > tax calculation(boolean, int, int, int) > [4] married = "false", nbChildren = "0", salary = "60000", tax = "11519" PASSED

BusinessTests > tax calculation(boolean, int, int, int) > [5] married = "false", nbChildren = "3", salary = "6000", tax = "0" PASSED

BusinessTests > tax calculation(boolean, int, int, int) > [6] married = "false", nbChildren = "3", salary = "600000", tax = "179275" PASSED

BusinessTests > with a fake dao layer() PASSED

BusinessTests > the brackets are unchanged() PASSED

All 16 tests passed: each set of values in a parameterized test counts as one test, and JUnit displays them along with the names and values of their parameters (these names are available via the compiler option [javaParameters]). We now consider the layers [dao] and [business] to be operational. The JAR files generated by [gradlew build] (or [gradlew jar]) contain only the layer code: the test classes, compiled in the [build/classes/kotlin/test] folder, are not included. Finally, note that [gradlew build] runs the tests: a regression causes the build to fail. Gradle only repeats the necessary work: if neither the code nor the tests of a subproject have changed since the last successful run, its tests are not rerun (the task is called “UP-TO-DATE”); the option [--rerun] ([gradlew :TaxV5:tax-dao:test --rerun]) forces them to run.

docs.title: 6.4.5. The [ui] layer
docs.text:
The file [build.gradle.kts] from the subproject [tax-ui] is as follows:

// TaxV5: the tax-ui subproject (the [ui] layer and the integration of the layers)
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
    // makes the classes annotated by Spring, such as @Configuration, open (non final)
    kotlin("plugin.spring")
    application
}

// the coordinates of the project: examples.tax:tax-ui:5.0 (the Dialog class is reused)
group = "examples.tax"
version = "5.0"

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // the [ui] layer uses the [business] layer and, through its API, the [dao] layer
    implementation(project(":TaxV5:tax-business"))
    // Spring's dependency injection container
    implementation("org.springframework:spring-context:7.0.9")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
    // the program run by [gradlew run] is designated by the [main] property:
    // gradlew -q :TaxV5:tax-ui:run -Pmain=tax.ui.MainConfigKt
    mainClass = providers.gradleProperty("main").orElse("tax.ui.MainKt")
}

tasks.named<JavaExec>("run") {
    // the running program can read the keyboard
    standardInput = System.`in`
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}
  • Lines 2–6: the Kotlin plugin, the Kotlin compiler plugin [plugin.spring]—whose role we’ll explore when configuring Spring using an annotated class—and the plugin [application];
  • line 19: the [ui] layer uses the [business] layer and, through the latter’s [api] dependency, the [dao] layer;
  • line 21: Spring’s dependency injection container, the artifact [spring-context], which brings along the other Spring modules it needs ([spring-core], [spring-beans], etc.);
  • lines 32–35: the subproject has several main programs; the property [main] selects the one to be executed by [gradlew run] and [tax.ui.MainKt] by default;
  • lines 43–46: Programs launched by Gradle write their output to UTF-8 so that accented characters display correctly on Windows (Chapter 2).

The [Dialog] object is from version 4 ([tax.ui] package), enhanced with a function that displays an exception and all the exceptions it encapsulates:

    // display of an exception and of all those it wraps
    fun displayError(exception: Throwable) {
        val separator = "-".repeat(40)
        println("Exception chain:\n$separator")
        generateSequence(exception) { it.cause }.forEach { e ->
            println("${e::class.qualifiedName}: ${e.message}")
            println(separator)
        }
    }
}
  • line 2: the parameter is of type [Throwable], the parent class of all exceptions;
  • line 3: a string of 40 dashes, created by the function [repeat];
  • line 5: each exception provides access, via its [cause] property, to the exception it encapsulates, all the way down to the last one, whose cause is [null]. The function [generateSequence] (Chapter 5) generates this string as a sequence: it starts with the initial value, [exception], and calculates each subsequent element from the previous one using the lambda [{ it.cause }]; the sequence stops at the first [null]. The [for] loop in the Java version, with its variable modified on each iteration, becomes a simple enumeration;
  • line 6: for each exception, the full name of its class (including the package) and its message are displayed.

The [Dialog] object is public: subsequent versions of the application, which will change the [dao] layer, will be able to reuse the [ui] layer by depending on the [tax-ui] subproject and calling [Dialog.run(business)].

docs.title: 6.4.6. Integrating Layers via Dependency Injection
docs.text:
In version 4, the main program created the layers [dao] and [business] by naming their implementation classes:

        val dao: ITaxDao = if (source == "hardwired") HardwiredTax() else FileTax(source)
        // creation of the [business] layer, which receives the [dao] layer
        TaxBusiness(dao)

Apart from these lines, nothing in the application changes when a layer’s implementation changes, since each layer communicates with the next through an interface. We can take layer independence a step further by entrusting their creation to a dependency injection container and placing the choice of the [dao] layer’s implementation in a configuration file. Changing the implementation of this layer then simply involves modifying that file, without recompiling the application.

In the example above, the main program of the [ui] layer starts the Spring container, [0]. The Spring container creates the [dao] layer [1], then the [business] layer [2], to which it passes the [dao] layer. Finally, the [ui] layer requests the [business] layer from the container and receives a reference to it: [3].

docs.title: 6.4.6.1. The configuration file
docs.text:
The choice of the [dao] layer implementation is specified in the [tax.properties] file in the [tax-ui] folder:

# configuration of the [Tax] application: implementation of the [dao] layer
dao.implementation=FileTax
dao.file=TaxData.txt
  • Line 1: A comment begins with the character [#];
  • line 2: the class that implements the [dao] layer: [HardwiredTax], [FileTax], or [JsonTax];
  • line 3: the data file, for implementations that read one.

A “properties” file is the traditional configuration format for JVM: one property per line, in the form [key=value], read by the Java class [java.util.Properties]. Keys are often prefixed to form groups, such as the prefix [dao.] here. The subproject contains three other configuration files, which the program uses if their names are passed as arguments:

tax-json.properties      : dao.implementation=JsonTax, dao.file=TaxData.json
tax-hardwired.properties : dao.implementation=HardwiredTax
tax-error.properties     : dao.implementation=FileTax, dao.file=TaxDataMissing.txt

The files [TaxData.txt] and [TaxData.json] have been copied into the [tax-ui] folder: their paths are relative to the current folder, and [gradlew run] runs the program in the subproject folder.

docs.title: 6.4.6.2. The Main Program
docs.text:
The main program [Main.kt] for the subproject [tax-ui] is as follows:

package tax.ui

import tax.dao.FileTax
import tax.dao.HardwiredTax
import tax.dao.ITaxDao
import tax.dao.JsonTax
import tax.entities.TaxException
import tax.business.ITaxBusiness
import tax.business.TaxBusiness
import java.util.Properties
import kotlin.io.path.Path
import kotlin.io.path.bufferedReader
import kotlin.system.exitProcess
import org.springframework.beans.factory.getBean
import org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext
import org.springframework.context.support.registerBean

// integration of the layers by the Spring container GenericApplicationContext
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    // the configuration file: tax.properties by default, or the one passed as an argument
    val configFile = args.firstOrNull() ?: "tax.properties"

    // integration of the layers
    val business: ITaxBusiness = try {
        // reading the configuration, in the current folder
        val config = Properties()
        Path(configFile).bufferedReader().use { config.load(it) }
        val implementation = config.getProperty("dao.implementation", "HardwiredTax")
        val file = config.getProperty("dao.file", "")

        // the Spring container: the layers are registered in it
        val context = GenericApplicationContext()
        // the [dao] layer: the implementation is chosen by the configuration
        context.registerBean<ITaxDao> {
            when (implementation) {
                "HardwiredTax" -> HardwiredTax()
                "FileTax" -> FileTax(file)
                "JsonTax" -> JsonTax(file)
                else -> throw TaxException("Unknown implementation [$implementation] of the [dao] layer")
            }
        }
        // the [business] layer: the container will pass the [dao] layer to its constructor
        context.registerBean<TaxBusiness>()

        // starting the container: it creates the [dao] layer, then the [business] layer
        context.refresh()
        context.getBean<ITaxBusiness>()
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        // display of the error and stop of the program
        Dialog.displayError(e)
        exitProcess(1)
    }

    // the dialog with the user
    Dialog.run(business)
}
  • Lines 14–16: Spring provides extension functions for Kotlin, which make its API more natural in this language. [getBean] and [registerBean] are imported as top-level functions from their packages;
  • line 19: the [main] function from the [tax.ui] package, compiled into the [tax.ui.MainKt] class;
  • line 21: the name of the configuration file: [tax.properties] by default, or the one passed as an argument;
  • line 24: as in version 4, the [business] layer is the value of an expression [try];
  • lines 26–29: reading the configuration. The [bufferedReader] extension function of [kotlin.io.path] opens the file in UTF-8, and [use] closes it at the end of the block, even in the event of an exception ([try] with a Java resource). [Properties.load] reads the lines from [key=value]. A missing file throws a [NoSuchFileException], which is intercepted further down. [getProperty] returns the value of a key, or the default value provided as the second parameter if the key does not exist;
  • line 32: the Spring container. Spring refers to an object created and managed by the container as a “bean,” and to the container itself as the “application context.” [GenericApplicationContext] is a container that is configured programmatically;
  • Lines 34–39: the [dao] layer entry. The extension function [registerBean<ITaxDao> { ... }] specifies that the bean of type [ITaxDao] will be created by the following lambda—a parameterless “supplier” that returns the object. The bean’s type is a reified type parameter: we write [registerBean<ITaxDao>] where Java writes [registerBean(ITaxDao.class, ...)]. The bean is a singleton, Spring’s default scope: it will be created only once, and all requests will return the same object; there is only one [dao] layer in the application. The supplier selects the class based on the configuration, using the expression [when]. An unknown implementation results in a [TaxException]. Note that the lambda uses the variables [implementation] and [file] from the function [main]: it “captures” them (Chapter 7) and will use them when the container calls it;
  • Line 43: The [business] layer record: The container will create the [TaxBusiness] object itself. To do this, it examines the constructor of the [TaxBusiness] class, sees that it expects an [ITaxDao], and passes it the bean of that type registered above: this is dependency injection, in this case via the constructor. The [dao] layer is a dependency of the [business] layer;
  • line 46: [refresh()] starts the container. Spring then creates all the singleton beans in the order they were registered: the [dao] layer, followed by the [business] layer. A creation error therefore occurs on this line;
  • Line 47: The container is asked for a bean of type [ITaxBusiness]. The container finds the bean [TaxBusiness], which implements this interface. The extension function [getBean<T>()] replaces the Java call [getBean(ITaxBusiness.class)], and its result is of the requested type. [getBean] throws an exception if no bean has this type, or if multiple beans do. Note that the [ui] layer retrieves the [business] layer without specifying the class that implements it. This is the last expression in the [try] block, and thus the value of the variable [business];
  • lines 48–51: Any error reading the configuration ([IOException]) or creating layers (Spring exceptions and our [TaxException]) is displayed along with the exception stack trace, and the program terminates. Kotlin does not support multiple catch blocks ([catch (IOException | RuntimeException e)] in Java); catching [Exception], the parent class of both, achieves the same result here;
  • Line 55: the user interface, identical to that of version 4.

Early versions of Spring read the full names of the classes to be instantiated from a XML file and created them using reflection; we’ll see an example of this later. Here, we chose instead to define the possible implementations in the provider: the configuration file simply selects from among them, and the compiler verifies that the classes exist and have the required constructors. In both cases, the code for the [ui] and [business] layers never specifies the class that implements the [dao] layer. It’s also worth noting that the layer classes know nothing about Spring: none of them import any Spring classes; only the main program does.

docs.title: 6.4.6.3. Executions
docs.text:
From the chapter folder, with the file [tax.properties] (implementation [FileTax]):

Tax=2959 euros

Tax=11519 euros

With the implementation [JsonTax]:

> gradlew -q :TaxV5:tax-ui:run --args="tax-json.properties"

Tax=4282 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop:

With the implementation [HardwiredTax]:

> gradlew -q :TaxV5:tax-ui:run --args="tax-hardwired.properties"
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2 60000
Tax=4282 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop:

We switched to the [dao] implementation without changing a single line of code or recompiling the application.

With the file [tax-error.properties], which refers to a nonexistent data file:

> gradlew -q :TaxV5:tax-ui:run --args="tax-error.properties"
Oct 04, 2026 12:25:44 PM org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext refresh
WARNING: Exception encountered during context initialization - cancelling refresh attempt: org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'tax.dao.ITaxDao': Instantiation of supplied bean failed
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'tax.dao.ITaxDao': Instantiation of supplied bean failed
----------------------------------------
tax.entities.TaxException: Error while reading the file TaxDataMissing.txt
----------------------------------------
java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException: TaxDataMissing.txt: The file [TaxDataMissing.txt] does not exist
----------------------------------------
  • the first two lines: before propagating the exception, Spring writes a warning to its log. Since there is no logging library in the project, this log is handled by the standard logging mechanism of JDK ([java.util.logging]), which writes the date, the throwing class, then the message level, and the message itself (in English) to the error output;
  • the original exception—the last one displayed, of type [NoSuchFileException]—was thrown by the class [FileTax];
  • the [dao] layer encapsulated it within a [TaxException];
  • Spring itself encapsulated the [TaxException] within a [BeanCreationException], whose message specifies the bean that could not be created: the one of type [ITaxDao], which the function [registerBean] named after the full type name, [tax.dao.ITaxDao]. It is this exception that was propagated up to the main program through the call to [refresh].

The key takeaway from this chain is that it is often the most severe exception—the last one displayed—that is the most significant.

Finally, with a configuration file that doesn’t exist, the error occurs even before the container is created:

> gradlew -q :TaxV5:tax-ui:run --args="tax-missing.properties"
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException: tax-missing.properties
----------------------------------------

The message from [NoSuchFileException], thrown by the JDK, contains only the file name.

docs.title: 6.4.6.4. A variation: the XML configuration
docs.text:
Early versions of Spring described beans in a XML file, and many applications still do. The [tax-ui] subproject contains an example of this, the [tax-beans.xml] file:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- XML configuration of the Spring container: the beans of the [Tax] application -->
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
       xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
       xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
           https://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans.xsd">

    <!-- the [dao] layer: the implementation class and the argument of its constructor -->
    <bean id="dao" class="tax.dao.FileTax">
        <constructor-arg value="TaxData.txt"/>
    </bean>

    <!-- the [business] layer: its constructor receives the [dao] bean -->
    <bean id="business" class="tax.business.TaxBusiness">
        <constructor-arg ref="dao"/>
    </bean>
</beans>
  • lines 3–6: the root element [beans] and Spring’s XML namespace. The [xsi:schemaLocation] attribute associates the schema describing the allowed elements with this namespace; Spring finds it in its own JAR files, without needing network access;
  • Lines 9–11: the [dao] layer bean. The [id] attribute gives it a name, the [class] attribute provides the full name of the class to be instantiated, and the [constructor-arg] element specifies the value ([value]) to be passed to its constructor: the name of the data file. Changing the implementation involves modifying these lines;
  • lines 14–15: the [business] layer bean. Its constructor receives a reference ([ref]) to the bean named [dao]: this is dependency injection, described in the XML file.

The main program [MainXml.kt] uses this configuration:

package tax.ui

import tax.business.ITaxBusiness
import kotlin.system.exitProcess
import org.springframework.beans.factory.getBean
import org.springframework.context.support.GenericXmlApplicationContext

// integration of the layers by the Spring container, configured by an XML file
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    // the XML file: tax-beans.xml by default, or the one passed as an argument (in the current folder)
    val xmlFile = args.firstOrNull() ?: "tax-beans.xml"
    try {
        // creating and starting the container; use closes it at the end of the block
        GenericXmlApplicationContext("file:$xmlFile").use { context ->
            // the [business] layer, and the dialog with the user
            val business = context.getBean<ITaxBusiness>()
            Dialog.run(business)
        }
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        // display of the error and stop of the program
        Dialog.displayError(e)
        exitProcess(1)
    }
}
  • line 11: the name of the XML file: [tax-beans.xml] by default, or the one passed as an argument;
  • line 14: [GenericXmlApplicationContext] is a container configured by the XML files. Its constructor reads the specified files, registers the beans they describe, and starts the container. The prefix [file:] refers to a file in the file system, relative to the current directory; the prefix [classpath:] would refer to a resource located in the JAR file. The container implements the [AutoCloseable] (and [Closeable]) interface: the [use] function closes it at the end of the block, which releases the beans;
  • line 16: the [business] layer is obtained as before, without specifying its class name;
  • Lines 19–22: error handling.

Results:

> gradlew -q :TaxV5:tax-ui:run -Pmain=tax.ui.MainXmlKt
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2 60000
Tax=4282 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop:

The XML file no longer chooses from among the implementations specified in the code: it names the class itself, which Spring creates via reflection. This is more flexible, since an implementation can be added without modifying the main program; however, the compiler no longer performs any checks. The file [tax-beans-error.xml] differs from the previous one only by a typo in the name of the [dao] layer class ([tax.dao.FileTaxes]). The error only appears at runtime:

> gradlew -q :TaxV5:tax-ui:run -Pmain=tax.ui.MainXmlKt --args="tax-beans-error.xml"
Oct 04, 2026 12:25:55 PM org.springframework.context.support.GenericXmlApplicationContext refresh
WARNING: Exception encountered during context initialization - cancelling refresh attempt: org.springframework.beans.factory.CannotLoadBeanClassException: Cannot find class [tax.dao.FileTaxes] for bean with name 'dao' defined in URL [file:tax-beans-error.xml]
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
org.springframework.beans.factory.CannotLoadBeanClassException: Cannot find class [tax.dao.FileTaxes] for bean with name 'dao' defined in URL [file:tax-beans-error.xml]
----------------------------------------
java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: tax.dao.FileTaxes
----------------------------------------

Spring’s [CannotLoadBeanClassException] specifies the bean, the class that cannot be found, and the file that describes it; it encapsulates the virtual machine’s [ClassNotFoundException]. Note that the XML configuration required no adaptation to Kotlin: for Spring, the [FileTax] and [TaxBusiness] classes are ordinary Java classes with a public constructor.

docs.title: 6.4.6.5. An alternative: configuration using an annotated class
docs.text:
Modern Spring applications typically describe their beans in an annotated configuration class. The [tax-ui] subproject contains an example of this, the [TaxConfig] class:

package tax.ui

import tax.dao.FileTax
import tax.dao.HardwiredTax
import tax.dao.ITaxDao
import tax.dao.JsonTax
import tax.entities.TaxException
import tax.business.ITaxBusiness
import tax.business.TaxBusiness
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration
import org.springframework.context.annotation.PropertySource

// the configuration of the Spring container written as an annotated Kotlin class
@Configuration
// the properties of the tax.properties file of the current folder are accessible through ${...}
@PropertySource("file:tax.properties")
class TaxConfig {

    // the [dao] layer: the implementation is chosen by the configuration
    @Bean
    fun dao(
        @Value("\${dao.implementation}") implementation: String,
        @Value("\${dao.file:}") file: String,
    ): ITaxDao = when (implementation) {
        "HardwiredTax" -> HardwiredTax()
        "FileTax" -> FileTax(file)
        "JsonTax" -> JsonTax(file)
        else -> throw TaxException("Unknown implementation [$implementation] of the [dao] layer")
    }

    // the [business] layer: Spring passes to the function the [dao] layer created by the dao function
    @Bean
    fun business(dao: ITaxDao): ITaxBusiness = TaxBusiness(dao)
}
  • line 16: the [@Configuration] annotation indicates that the class describes beans;
  • line 18: the annotation [@PropertySource] instructs Spring to read the file [tax.properties] from the current directory (prefix [file:]) itself;
  • Lines 22–30: An annotated function [@Bean] creates a bean whose name is the name of the function ([dao]) and whose type is the function’s return type. Spring calls the function, providing its parameters. The annotation [@Value] requests the value of a property: [${dao.implementation}] is the value of the key [dao.implementation], and [${dao.file:}] is the value of the key [dao.file], with the empty string (placed after the colon) as the default value. Note: In a Kotlin string, [${...}] is a placeholder, which the compiler would replace with the value of the expression it contains; so the character [$] must be escaped with a backslash, ["\${dao.implementation}"], to ensure that the string passed to Spring actually contains [${dao.implementation}]. The body of the function is an expression [when];
  • lines 34–35: the bean from the [business] layer. The function expects an [ITaxDao]: Spring passes it the bean created by the [dao] function. This time, it is injection via a function parameter.

To ensure that a singleton bean is created only once—even if a function [@Bean] calls another function—Spring derives a subclass of the configuration class at runtime, which overrides its functions [@Bean]: therefore, neither the class nor these functions should be final. However, in Kotlin, classes and their methods are final by default (Chapter 4). You would need to write [open class TaxConfig] and [open fun dao(...)]… This is the role of the compiler plugin [plugin.spring], applied in the subproject’s build file: it automatically makes the classes annotated with [@Configuration], [@Component], [@Service], [@Transactional]…, and their members, open. It is a Spring-specific specialization of the [all-open] plugin, which opens the selected annotated classes. Here’s what happens when you compile the same code without this plugin:

> gradlew -q :TaxV5:tax-ui:run -Pmain=tax.ui.MainConfigKt      (without the plugin.spring plugin)
Oct 04, 2026 12:26:36 PM org.springframework.context.annotation.AnnotationConfigApplicationContext refresh
WARNING: Exception encountered during context initialization - cancelling refresh attempt: org.springframework.beans.factory.parsing.BeanDefinitionParsingException: Configuration problem: @Configuration class 'TaxConfig' may not be final. Remove the final modifier to continue.
Offending resource: tax.ui.TaxConfig
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
org.springframework.beans.factory.parsing.BeanDefinitionParsingException: Configuration problem: @Configuration class 'TaxConfig' may not be final. Remove the final modifier to continue.
Offending resource: tax.ui.TaxConfig
----------------------------------------

Spring rejects the final class as soon as the container starts, with an explicit error message.

The main program [MainConfig.kt] uses this configuration:

package tax.ui

import tax.business.ITaxBusiness
import kotlin.system.exitProcess
import org.springframework.beans.factory.getBean
import org.springframework.context.annotation.AnnotationConfigApplicationContext

// integration of the layers by the Spring container, configured by the TaxConfig class
fun main() {
    try {
        // creating and starting the container; use closes it at the end of the block
        AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(TaxConfig::class.java).use { context ->
            // the [business] layer, and the dialog with the user
            val business = context.getBean<ITaxBusiness>()
            Dialog.run(business)
        }
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        // display of the error and stop of the program
        Dialog.displayError(e)
        exitProcess(1)
    }
}
  • Line 12: [AnnotationConfigApplicationContext] is a container configured by annotated classes. Its constructor registers the beans described by the class [TaxConfig] and starts the container. The class is passed as its Java class, [TaxConfig::class.java]; the function [use] shuts down the container at the end of the block;
  • line 14: the [business] layer is obtained as before;
  • Lines 17–20: error handling.

Results:

> gradlew -q :TaxV5:tax-ui:run -Pmain=tax.ui.MainConfigKt
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2 60000
Tax=4282 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop:

With an incorrect configuration (in this case, a [tax.properties] file whose content would be that of [tax-error.properties]), the exception chain now includes one additional level: Spring reports the failure of the [dao] function via a [BeanInstantiationException], encapsulated within the [BeanCreationException]:

> gradlew -q :TaxV5:tax-ui:run -Pmain=tax.ui.MainConfigKt
Oct 04, 2026 12:26:13 PM org.springframework.context.annotation.AnnotationConfigApplicationContext refresh
WARNING: Exception encountered during context initialization - cancelling refresh attempt: org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'dao' defined in tax.ui.TaxConfig: Failed to instantiate [tax.dao.ITaxDao]: Factory method 'dao' threw exception with message: Error while reading the file TaxDataMissing.txt
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'dao' defined in tax.ui.TaxConfig: Failed to instantiate [tax.dao.ITaxDao]: Factory method 'dao' threw exception with message: Error while reading the file TaxDataMissing.txt
----------------------------------------
org.springframework.beans.BeanInstantiationException: Failed to instantiate [tax.dao.ITaxDao]: Factory method 'dao' threw exception with message: Error while reading the file TaxDataMissing.txt
----------------------------------------
tax.entities.TaxException: Error while reading the file TaxDataMissing.txt
----------------------------------------
java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException: TaxDataMissing.txt: The file [TaxDataMissing.txt] does not exist
----------------------------------------

Spring can also automatically discover which classes to instantiate: with the [@ComponentScan] annotation on the configuration class, it creates a bean for each class in a package annotated with [@Component] (or [@Service], [@Repository]). We did not do this here, as it would have required annotating the layer classes, thereby making them dependent on Spring. Spring Boot, in Chapter 13, makes extensive use of this mechanism. Finally, it’s worth noting that Spring also offers a dedicated language for declaring beans programmatically in Kotlin ([BeanRegistrarDsl]), which is even more concise than the calls to [registerBean] in our program [Main.kt].

Dependency injection deserves a chapter all its own. We’ve only used the essentials: registering beans ([registerBean], XML file, [@Bean]), starting the container ([refresh]), and obtaining a bean ([getBean]). The container can also create a new object for each request (scope [prototype]), one object per request (HTTP), or one per session in a web application (scopes [request] and [session]). You can learn more about this topic in the Spring documentation: The IoC Container, and its pages dedicated to Kotlin: Kotlin.

docs.title: 6.5. Conclusion
docs.text:
This chapter has given the [Tax] application the architecture it will retain until the end of the course:

  • a [dao] layer that provides tax brackets through the [ITaxDao] interface;
  • a [business] layer that calculates the tax and knows the [dao] layer only through its interface;
  • a layer [ui] that interacts with the user and knows the layer [business] only through its interface [ITaxBusiness];
  • a main program—the only one that knows the implementation classes—which creates the layers and links them, in this case using Spring’s dependency injection container and a configuration file;
  • automated unit tests, written using JUnit and kotlin.test, which verify each layer independently of the others and ensure the application’s non-regression.

The benefits of this architecture will become fully apparent in the following chapters, where the subprojects [tax-dao], [tax-business], and [tax-ui] from Version 5 will be reused as-is, through a composite build, as ordinary dependencies:

  • Version 6 (Chapter 10, “Database Access with JDBC”): A new implementation of the [dao] layer reads tax brackets from a MySQL database. The [business] and [ui] layers remain unchanged;
  • Version 7 (Chapter 11, “Hibernate”): Another implementation of the [dao] layer uses the ORM Hibernate layer to access the same database;
  • Version 8 (Chapter 12, “Internet Programming”): The [business] layer is installed on a TCP server, which calculates taxes for remote clients whose [ui] layer is from Version 5; The layers are thus distributed across multiple machines, restoring the original meaning of the term “tier”;
  • Version 9 (Chapter 13, “Web Services”): The [business] layer is exposed by a web service REST/JSON written with Spring Boot, whose console client uses the [HttpClient] class from JDK.

Each time, the work will be limited to writing the new layer and modifying the program that integrates the layers: that is the whole point of a layered architecture.

docs.title: 2. Setting Up the Development Environment
docs.text:
The Kotlin developer’s work environment consists of three independent components:

  • the JDK (“Java Development Kit”): Kotlin, as we use it in this document, is compiled into bytecode and executed by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), just like a Java program. JDK provides this virtual machine, the [java] command that runs programs, the standard Java libraries SE (which Kotlin uses directly: files, networking, dates, threads, etc.), and tools such as [javap] or [jar];
  • a project build tool, in this case Gradle: it downloads the Kotlin compiler and the libraries a project needs, compiles the project, runs its tests, and packages it;
  • an editor or an IDE (Integrated Development Environment): [IntelliJ IDEA], designed by the company that created Kotlin, is the natural choice; [VS Code] with the Kotlin extension is another option. IDE is based on JDK and can read Gradle projects.

The Kotlin compiler itself is not included in this list: Gradle downloads it for each project, and IntelliJ IDEA bundles it. However, you can install it separately using the command [kotlinc] to compile a single file: we’ll do this for our first program, but it’s optional.

This document uses the commands [java], [kotlinc], and [gradlew] for all operations: they work the same way on Windows, Linux, and macOS, regardless of the editor you choose.

docs.title: 2.1.1. Installation
docs.text:
There are several distributions of JDK, all built from the OpenJDK source code and equivalent for our purposes. We recommend Eclipse Temurin, a free and open-source distribution from the Eclipse Foundation, which can be downloaded at https://adoptium.net: There, select version 25—LTS—the operating system, and the package type (on Windows, a [.msi] installer). On Windows, you can also install it from a terminal (PowerShell or command prompt) using the [winget] package manager:

winget install EclipseAdoptium.Temurin.25.JDK

You must select JDK (which contains everything) and not just JRE alone (which only allows you to run pre-compiled programs). When installing on Windows, check the options that add JDK to [PATH] and set the [JAVA_HOME] environment variable: Gradle, the [kotlinc] compiler, and the IDE files use this to locate the JDK file. On Linux, JDK is available in the repositories of major distributions (for example, [sudo apt install openjdk-25-jdk] on Ubuntu).

After installation, open a new terminal to verify that the [java] command is available and displays the version of JDK:

> java --version
openjdk 25.0.4 2026-07-21 LTS
OpenJDK Runtime Environment Temurin-25.0.4+7 (build 25.0.4+7-LTS)
OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM Temurin-25.0.4+7 (build 25.0.4+7-LTS, mixed mode, sharing)

These results were obtained using JDK Temurin 25.0.4, which was used to write this document. The exact version depends on the installation date: bugfix updates are released quarterly. All JDK and 25.0.x versions are suitable for this document. Multiple JDK instances can coexist on the same computer: the first one found in the [PATH] directory responds to the [java] command.

The JDK also contains the Java compiler [javac] ([javac --version] displays [javac 25.0.4]). We won’t need it: the Kotlin compiler generates the bytecode itself. But it’s there, and a Gradle project can easily mix Kotlin and Java files, which work together.

docs.title: 2.1.2. The commands for JDK
docs.text:
Here are the commands from JDK that we’ll use:

CommandRole[java -jar program.jar]Runs the program contained in a [.jar] archive whose manifest specifies the main class[java -cp classes MyClass]executes the function [main] of a compiled class, searched for in the class path ([-cp], “class path”)[javap -cp classes MyClass]displays the members of a compiled class: we’ll use this to see what the Kotlin compiler has produced[jar]creates or reads a [.jar] archive (a ZIP file of compiled classes)

JDK also provides the interactive interpreter [jshell], but it only accepts Java statements. To test a Kotlin expression without writing a program, use the IntelliJ and IDEA tools described below instead.

docs.title: 2.2.1. Installation
docs.text:
This installation is optional: Gradle projects do not require it, and IntelliJ IDEA includes its own compiler. It allows you to compile and run a standalone Kotlin file from a terminal without creating a project.

The compiler can be downloaded from the Kotlin project's released versions page, specifically GitHub (https://github.com/JetBrains/kotlin/releases): In the “Assets” section of version 2.4.20, download the archive [kotlin-compiler-2.4.20.zip]. Unzip it into a folder, for example [C:\Program Files\kotlinc], and add its subfolder [bin] to [PATH] (Windows: “Edit system environment variables”). You can also use a package manager: [scoop install kotlin] on Windows (with Scoop), or SDKMAN! on Linux and macOS ([sdk install kotlin 2.4.20]). The compiler requires a JDK, which it locates via the [JAVA_HOME] variable or the [PATH] variable.

Verify the installation in a new terminal:

> kotlinc -version
info: kotlinc-jvm 2.4.20 (JRE 25.0.4+7-LTS)

The compiler version (2.4.20) is followed by the version of the JVM that runs it (JDK 25).

docs.title: 2.2.2. Compiler Commands
docs.text:
The [bin] directory contains two main commands, [kotlinc] (the compiler) and [kotlinr] (the launcher, “runner”):

CommandRole[kotlinc File.kt -d classes]compiles one or more source files and places the resulting [.class] files in the [classes] folder[kotlinc File.kt -include-runtime -d prog.jar]compiles and produces an executable archive named [.jar], which also contains the Kotlin standard library[kotlinr -cp classes MyClass]as [java -cp classes MyClass], adding the Kotlin standard library to the classpath[kotlinr script.main.kts]runs a Kotlin script (file [.main.kts]), with no visible compilation step

A Kotlin script is a sequence of instructions executed from top to bottom, without a function [main]. For example, the following script [essai.main.kts]:

val s = "Kotlin " + 2.4
println(s.length)

runs as follows:

> kotlinr essai.main.kts
10

Prior to Kotlin 2.4.20, the launcher was called [kotlin]; it was renamed to [kotlinr] in Kotlin 2.4.20 to avoid a naming conflict with another command, [kotlin], which belongs to the “Kotlin Toolchain” tool. The old name still works in version 2.4.20 of the compiler (it is not officially deprecated), but the Kotlin documentation now recommends [kotlinr].
