Without any arguments, the command [kotlinc] used to launch an interactive interpreter (a “REPL,” equivalent to [jshell]). This feature has now been deprecated:

> kotlinc
error: Kotlin REPL is deprecated and should be enabled explicitly for now; please use the '-Xrepl' option

To try out a few lines of Kotlin, you should instead use a scratch file created with IntelliJ IDEA (“File / New / Scratch File,” Kotlin language), which displays the results next to each line.

docs.title: 2.3.1. The Role of Gradle
docs.text:
A real-world application uses libraries that are not part of JDK or the Kotlin standard library: a database driver, a testing framework, Hibernate, Spring, coroutines… They are distributed as [.jar] archives via a public repository, Maven Central (https://central.sonatype.com). A build tool reads the project description to determine which libraries it needs, downloads them (along with the libraries on which they depend), and then compiles, tests, and packages the project.

The two major build tools in the Java world are Maven (used by the Java course on which this document is based) and Gradle. Kotlin can be used with both, but Gradle is the de facto standard in the Kotlin ecosystem: it is used by Android and by Kotlin projects created by IntelliJ IDEA, and its build files are written... in Kotlin. This document uses Gradle 9.8.

docs.title: 2.3.2. The Gradle wrapper: no installation required
docs.text:
There is no need to install Gradle. Each project in this document comes with the Gradle wrapper—a small launcher consisting of three files located in the project root:

  • [gradlew]: the launch script for Linux and macOS ([./gradlew]);
  • [gradlew.bat]: the same script for Windows ([gradlew]);
  • the [gradle/wrapper] folder, which contains the launcher program ([gradle-wrapper.jar]) and its configuration ([gradle-wrapper.properties]).

The file [gradle-wrapper.properties] specifies the Gradle version to use:

distributionUrl=https\://services.gradle.org/distributions/gradle-9.8.0-bin.zip

The first time it is run, [gradlew] downloads this version of Gradle and stores it on the computer; on subsequent runs, it uses it directly. Each project thus uses the version of Gradle with which it was written, regardless of which version may be installed on the computer. Gradle only needs a JDK to run, which it finds either through the [JAVA_HOME] variable or the [PATH] variable.

In this document, commands are written in the Windows format ([gradlew build]); on Linux or macOS, they are written as [./gradlew build]. In PowerShell, you must also write [.\gradlew build].

If you still want to use the command [gradle] (to create a project with [gradle init], for example), download the [gradle-9.8.0-bin.zip] archive from https://gradle.org/releases, unzip it, and add its [bin] subfolder to [PATH]; or use [scoop install gradle] or [sdk install gradle]. Then verify the installation:

> gradle --version
------------------------------------------------------------
Gradle 9.8.0
------------------------------------------------------------

Build time:    2026-09-24 13:40:00 UTC
Revision:      a927be5e08efe79e0b87ada06c762dde6bb9f8b8

Kotlin:        2.4.10
Groovy:        4.0.33
Ant:           Apache Ant(TM) version 1.10.17 compiled on April 6 2026
Launcher JVM:  25.0.4 (Eclipse Adoptium 25.0.4+7-LTS)
Daemon JVM:    /home/claude/tools/jdk-25.0.4+7 (no Daemon JVM specified, using current Java home)
OS:            Linux 6.18.44-fc-v64 amd64

These results were obtained on Linux. The line [Kotlin:] provides the version of Kotlin integrated into Gradle, which is used to read the [.gradle.kts] build files: it is independent of the version of the Kotlin compiler used to compile our programs (2.4.20), which is set by each project. The line [Launcher JVM] indicates the JDK that runs Gradle.

docs.title: 2.3.3. Gradle Commands
docs.text:
The [gradlew] command is followed by one or more tasks; it is entered in the project’s root directory, the one containing the [settings.gradle.kts] file:

CommandRole[gradlew build]compiles the source code for [src/main/kotlin], runs the tests, and creates the project archive [.jar] in [build/libs][gradlew run]compiles and then runs the project’s main class ([application] plugin)[gradlew test]compiles, then runs the unit tests for [src/test/kotlin] (Chapter 6)[gradlew clean]deletes the [build] folder[gradlew tasks]displays the list of available tasks in the project[gradlew installDist]creates an installable version of the program in [build/install]: its archives and launch scripts[gradlew bootRun]runs a Spring Boot application (Chapter 13)

The tasks are interdependent: running [run] also triggers the compilation, and Gradle only re-runs the parts that have changed since the previous build. The [-q] (“quiet”) option suppresses Gradle messages and displays only those from the executed program; the [-Pname=value] option sets a property that the build file can read: we’ll use it to choose which program to run. The arguments for the program launched by [run] are passed via the [--args="a b"] option.

The first command run in a project is slow: Gradle starts a background process (the Gradle “daemon”), which remains active for a few hours to speed up subsequent commands and downloads what the project needs.

docs.title: 2.3.4. Maven Central and the Gradle Cache
docs.text:
The libraries downloaded by Gradle are stored locally in the Gradle cache, in the [%USERPROFILE%\.gradle\caches] folder (Linux and macOS: [~/.gradle/caches]). They are downloaded only once and are then reused by all projects. Therefore, an Internet connection is required when building a project for the first time. The same [.gradle] folder contains, within [wrapper/dists], the Gradle versions downloaded by the wrapper.

A library is identified by its coordinates—three names separated by colons: the group (often a reverse domain name, such as [org.hibernate.orm]), the library name, and its version, for example, [tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind:3.1.5]. These coordinates are what you enter in a project’s build file, and they can be found by searching for the library on the Maven Central website.

docs.title: 2.3.5. The Kotlin syntax: DSL
docs.text:
The project’s build file is named [build.gradle.kts]. The extension [.kts] indicates that it is a Kotlin script: the file is written in a dedicated language (“DSL,” “Domain Specific Language”) built using Kotlin syntax. Gradle also supports [build.gradle] files written in Groovy, which are found in older projects; since Gradle 8.2, Kotlin DSL has been the default format. Here is a typical excerpt:

plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.20"
    application
}

dependencies {
    implementation("tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind:3.1.5")
}

Even without knowing Kotlin yet, you can read this text as a configuration:

  • a name followed by a block enclosed in curly braces ([plugins { ... }], [dependencies { ... }]) is a section of the configuration. In Kotlin, this is a function call that takes a code block as a parameter (a lambda, Chapter 7);
  • [kotlin("jvm")] and [implementation("...")] are function calls; the strings are enclosed in double quotes;
  • [version = "1.0"] assigns a value to a project property.

One advantage of this format is that IntelliJ IDEA recognizes it as Kotlin code: it offers code completion and flags errors as you type.

docs.title: 2.4.1. IntelliJ IDEA
docs.text:
IntelliJ IDEA, from the company JetBrains, is the recommended editor for this document. JetBrains is also the company that developed Kotlin (the first stable version of the language was released in 2016) and continues to develop it: Kotlin support is built into IntelliJ IDEA, with no extensions required, and it is the version that most closely tracks the language’s evolution. Its basic features, which are more than sufficient for this document, are free.

IntelliJ IDEA recognizes Gradle projects: select “File / Open,” then choose the folder containing the [settings.gradle.kts] file; IntelliJ launches Gradle to read the project (you can monitor the process in the “Build” window), downloads the libraries, and then displays a “Gradle” view that provides access to all the project’s tasks. You can then run a program by clicking the green triangle in the margin next to its function [main] ([Ctrl-Shift-F10]), or run a test by clicking the same triangle next to the test function. You specify the JDK to use in “File / Project Structure / SDK”; for a Gradle project, it is generally the project’s [jvmToolchain(25)] declaration (see below) that specifies the JDK for compilation.

IntelliJ IDEA also offers Kotlin-specific features: automatic conversion of a Java file to Kotlin (“Code / Convert Java File to Kotlin File,” or simply by pasting Java code into a Kotlin file), display of the bytecode generated by the compiler (“Tools / Kotlin / Show Kotlin Bytecode”), and the draft files mentioned earlier.

docs.title: 2.4.2. VS Code
docs.text:
VS Code is a free, cross-platform editor. To program in Kotlin, install the Kotlin extension published by JetBrains (go to the “Extensions” menu, search for “Kotlin,” and select the one whose editor is JetBrains). This official extension is new: it uses the same code-analysis engine as IntelliJ and IDEA and can import Gradle projects, but it does not yet offer all the features of IDE or JetBrains, and its functionality changes from one version to the next. Check the extension’s page to see what it supports at the time of installation. For the purposes of this document, it is suitable for reading and editing programs; you can always run them from the built-in terminal (“Terminal / New Terminal”) using the [gradlew] commands provided in the text.

In VS Code, open a chapter folder ("File / Open Folder"), for example, the [kotlin-oct-2026/03-basics] folder.

docs.title: 2.4.3. Android Studio
docs.text:
Kotlin is also the language recommended by Google for Android apps. Android Studio, built on IntelliJ IDEA, is dedicated to this type of app, which is not covered in this document.

In the remainder of this document, operations are described using the commands [java], [kotlinc], and [gradlew], which produce the same results regardless of the editor.

docs.title: 2.5. A Sample Program: The Hello.kt File
2.5.1. The program
docs.text:
A Kotlin program can be a simple file containing a function named [main], without a class declaration. Let’s create the following file, [Hello.kt] (in the [02-installation] examples folder):

// first Kotlin program: a top-level main function
fun main() {
    println("1st try with Kotlin 2.4")
}

Comments:

  • line 1: a comment. Everything following [//] until the end of the line is ignored by the compiler;
  • line 2: the function [main], the program’s entry point. The keyword [fun] introduces a function. It is declared at the file level (“top-level function”), outside of any class; it does not need to be declared as [public] (this is the default visibility in Kotlin) nor does it need to receive any program arguments;
  • Line 3: the program’s only statement: it prints a line of text to the screen. The function [println] (and [print], which does not wrap to the next line) is part of the Kotlin standard library; This is the equivalent of [System.out.println] in Java. Note the absence of a semicolon at the end of the statement: it is optional in Kotlin and is not written.

The program is a bit simpler than its equivalent in the Java course ([void main() { IO.println(...); }]), but the real difference lies elsewhere: the high-level function [main] has existed in Kotlin since its first release, whereas Java has only supported it since Java 25.

docs.title: 2.5.2. Compilation and Execution
docs.text:
We compile the program with [kotlinc], specifying an executable archive named [.jar], and then run it using the [java] command from JDK:

> kotlinc Hello.kt -include-runtime -d hello.jar
> java -jar hello.jar
1st try with Kotlin 2.4
  • [-d hello.jar]: the compilation destination. If it ends with [.jar], the compiler produces an archive; otherwise, it is a folder in which it stores the [.class] files;
  • [-include-runtime]: The archive also contains the Kotlin standard library ([kotlin-stdlib]), which Kotlin programs need at runtime, and a manifest that specifies the main class. The program can thus be run by [java -jar] on any machine equipped with JDK (or JRE), even if Kotlin is not installed on that machine. On the other hand, the archive is over 5 MB in size, consisting mainly of the standard library;
  • compilation takes a few seconds: the Kotlin compiler, itself a Java program, must first start up. Gradle and IntelliJ IDEA avoid this overhead by keeping a compiler active between compilations.

There is no equivalent in Kotlin to the Java command [java Hello.java], which compiles and executes a source file in a single step; the closest equivalent is the [.main.kts] script presented above.

docs.title: 2.5.3. What the Compiler Produces
docs.text:
The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) recognizes only classes: a function cannot exist outside of a class. The Kotlin compiler therefore wraps the high-level functions in a file into a class that it generates, naming it after the file: the file name followed by [Kt]. For [Hello.kt], the generated class is [HelloKt]. The command [javap] in JDK displays its members:

> javap -cp hello.jar HelloKt
Compiled from "Hello.kt"
public final class HelloKt {
  public static final void main();
  public static void main(java.lang.String[]);
}
  • The class [HelloKt] is [public final];
  • it contains our function [main], which has become a static method with no parameters;
  • and a second method, [main(String[])], added by the compiler: this is the method [public static void main(String[] args)] that the virtual machine knows how to invoke. It simply calls the first one. We will return to this mechanism in Chapter 3.

It is this class name that identifies the program to be executed: the manifest for [hello.jar] contains the line [Main-Class: HelloKt], and one can also write [java -cp hello.jar HelloKt].

Unlike in Java, there are no restrictions on the filename: it does not have to be a valid identifier or match the name of a class it contains. A file named [first-try.kt] is accepted, and its generated class is named [First_tryKt] (the compiler capitalizes the first letter and replaces characters prohibited in an identifier with [_]). By convention, however, files are given names that start with a capital letter and contain no hyphens, such as [Hello.kt] or [Basics01.kt].

On Windows, accented characters written as [println] display correctly in the terminal: the virtual machine converts the text to the terminal’s encoding. Source files must be saved in UTF-8, the default encoding for VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA, and the one that the Kotlin compiler always assumes. The situation is different when the program is launched by Gradle ([gradlew run], or the green triangle in a Gradle project): its output is no longer a console but a pipe to Gradle, and the virtual machine then encodes it in the historical Windows encoding (windows-1252), so that IntelliJ IDEA, which waits for UTF-8, displays a placeholder character (a diamond containing a question mark) in place of each accented character. The course projects resolve this issue in their [build.gradle.kts] file (see the next section). For the built-in terminal of IntelliJ IDEA (PowerShell), you can also switch the console to UTF-8 by typing [chcp 65001] at the start of the session, or once and for all by specifying [powershell.exe -NoExit -Command "[Console]::OutputEncoding = [Text.Encoding]::UTF8"] as the interpreter in “File / Settings / Tools / Terminal / Shell path.”

The command [kotlinc] is suitable for single-file programs that use only the standard library. As soon as a program requires an external library, you must download it—along with the libraries it depends on—and pass it to the compiler and then to the virtual machine: this involves creating a Gradle project. This is what we will do for all the examples in this document.

docs.title: 2.6.1. Project Structure
docs.text:
A Gradle project is a folder containing a build file named [build.gradle.kts] and source files organized according to a standard directory structure. The root of a Gradle build also contains a file named [settings.gradle.kts], which provides the build’s name and a list of the projects it groups together, as well as the wrapper. The [02-installation] folder in the examples is a build that groups two projects, [FirstProgram] and [TwoHands]:

02-installation/
├── gradlew
├── gradlew.bat
├── gradle/
│   └── wrapper/
│       ├── gradle-wrapper.jar
│       └── gradle-wrapper.properties
├── settings.gradle.kts
├── build.gradle.kts
├── Hello.kt
├── FirstProgram/
│   ├── build.gradle.kts
│   └── src/
│       └── main/
│           └── kotlin/
│               └── first/
│                   └── Main.kt
└── TwoHands/
    ├── build.gradle.kts
    └── src/
        └── main/
            └── kotlin/
                └── twohands/
                    ├── P1.kt
                    └── P2.kt
  • [src/main/kotlin] contains the program’s source files; [src/main/resources] would contain the data or configuration files to be placed alongside the compiled classes; [src/test/kotlin] would contain the tests (Chapter 6);
  • Under [src/main/kotlin], the folder structure mirrors that of the packages (Chapter 4): the file [Main.kt] from the package [first] is located in the folder [first]. Kotlin does not enforce this correspondence, unlike Java, but recommends it, and we will always follow it;
  • The file [Hello.kt] does not belong to any project: it is placed there to be compiled by [kotlinc], and Gradle ignores it.

A standalone project (not grouped with others) has the same structure, with its own [settings.gradle.kts] and wrapper files: this is the case for the project in Chapter 3. You can create this directory structure manually, or let IDE create it (IntelliJ: “File / New / Project,” select “Kotlin” as the language and “Gradle” as the build system, with the Kotlin DSL).

We’ll look at the root files in the next section. The [build.gradle.kts] file in the [FirstProgram] project is as follows:

// the [FirstProgram] project: a Kotlin program executed by the JVM
plugins {
    // the Kotlin plugin for the JVM (its version is declared in the root project)
    kotlin("jvm")
    // the [application] plugin: run and installDist tasks
    application
}

// the project coordinates
group = "examples.installation"
version = "1.0"

// the repository where libraries are looked up
repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // no library apart from the Kotlin standard library, added by the plugin
}

kotlin {
    // the code is compiled and run with JDK 25
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        // a compiler warning is treated as an error
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        // function parameter names are kept in the bytecode
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
    // the class containing the main function run by [gradlew run]
    mainClass = "first.MainKt"
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}

Comments:

  • line 1: a comment. The build file is written in Kotlin: comments are written just as they would be in a program;
  • lines 2–7: the plugins applied to the project. These provide Gradle with the tasks we need:
    • Line 4: The Kotlin plugin for JVM. It adds tasks that compile the files in [src/main/kotlin] and automatically adds the Kotlin standard library to the project's dependencies. The notation [kotlin("jvm")] is a shorthand for the plugin’s full identifier, [org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm]. Its version is not specified here because the project is part of a multi-project build where the root project sets this version for all of them (see the next section). In a standalone project, you would write [kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.20"]: this version determines the version of the Kotlin compiler used;
    • line 6: the [application] plugin, which adds the tasks [run] (run the program) and [installDist] (prepare an installable version);
  • lines 10–11: the project, group, and version identifiers, which identify the project by its name ([FirstProgram], the name of its folder). These are also the identifiers that another project could use to reference this one, similar to how a library from Maven Central is referenced (Chapter 6);
  • lines 14–15: the repository where Gradle looks for the project’s libraries, in this case Maven Central;
  • lines 18–20: the libraries used by the project. This project does not use any, apart from the standard Kotlin library that the Kotlin plugin adds automatically;
  • line 24: the project’s toolchain: the code is compiled for Java 25 and run by [gradlew run] with a JDK 25, even though Gradle itself is run by a different JDK. Gradle searches for this JDK among those installed on the machine. If it does not find any, it fails with the error message [Cannot find a Java installation on your machine ... matching: {languageVersion=25 ...}], unless the build declares the [foojay-resolver-convention] plugin—which all projects in the course do (see the next section): Gradle then downloads a JDK 25 on its own. In IntelliJ IDEA, you can also install this JDK via “File / Project Structure / SDK / Add SDK / Download JDK";
  • line 27: A compiler warning is treated as an error and stops the compilation. The Kotlin compiler flags many issues (unused variables, unnecessary type casting, superfluous [!!] operators, etc.): we want programs that produce none of these;
  • line 29: The compiler preserves the names of function parameters in the bytecode. Some libraries use this, for example, Jackson to create an object from a JSON document (Chapter 5) or Spring (Chapter 13);
  • lines 33–35: the class whose function [main] is executed by [gradlew run]. The name is that of the class generated by the compiler for the [Main.kt] file in the [first] package: [first.MainKt];
  • lines 38–41: All tasks that execute a Java program ([JavaExec]), such as [run], receive two options from the virtual machine: the program’s screen output ([System.out], [System.err]) is encoded in UTF-8. Without them, accented characters written by the program would be corrupted in the console of IntelliJ and IDEA under Windows (see the note on accents above). [tasks.withType<JavaExec>()] refers to all tasks of this type, and [configureEach { … }] configures each of them. All course projects that run a program contain this configuration.

This project does not use any libraries. A project that uses a library declares it in the [dependencies] section using its coordinates, as we will do starting in Chapter 5:

dependencies {
    implementation("tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind:3.1.5")
}

The term [implementation] indicates that the library is required to compile and run the program. You’ll also encounter [runtimeOnly] (required only for execution, such as a database driver) and [testImplementation] (required only for testing). Gradle will then download [jackson-databind] and the libraries it depends on.

The file [Main.kt] contains the program:

package first

// the main program of the [FirstProgram] project
fun main() {
    println("1st try with a Gradle / Kotlin 2.4 project")
}
  • line 1: the file belongs to the [first] package. The full name of the class generated for this file is therefore [first.MainKt];
  • Lines 4–6: the function [main], in the same form as in [Hello.kt]. A Kotlin file can contain any number of functions and classes, whether public or not: the file name does not depend on its contents.

docs.title: 2.6.2. Compilation and Execution
docs.text:
The command [gradlew build], entered in the [02-installation] folder, compiles the build projects (and would run their tests if they had any): Gradle downloads the Kotlin plugin, the compiler, and the standard library as needed, then compiles the files in [src/main/kotlin] and places the resulting classes in the [build/classes/kotlin/main] folder for each project, preserving the package structure ([FirstProgram/build/classes/kotlin/main/first/MainKt.class]).

The [gradlew run] command compiles a project and then runs it. In a build involving multiple projects, the project is specified by its path, preceded by a colon: [:FirstProgram:run] is the task [run] of the project [FirstProgram]. With the option [-q], only the program output is displayed:

> gradlew -q :FirstProgram:run
1st try with a Gradle / Kotlin 2.4 project

You can also navigate to the project folder and type [..\gradlew -q run]: Gradle traces back to the [settings.gradle.kts] file in the root directory and executes the [run] task from the project in the current folder. On the other hand, typing [gradlew run] at the root directory would execute the [run] task for all projects that have one.

Once the project has been compiled, you can also run the class directly using the command [java], specifying the location of the classes (in the [FirstProgram] folder):

> java -cp build/classes/kotlin/main first.MainKt
1st try with a Gradle / Kotlin 2.4 project

This works here because this program does not actually use anything from the Kotlin standard library at runtime: the compiler replaces the call to [println] with a direct call to [System.out.println]. However, a program that uses, for example, a list ([listOf(1, 2, 3)]) fails in this way with the error [java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: kotlin/collections/CollectionsKt]: the class [CollectionsKt] from the standard library cannot be found. You must then add the [kotlin-stdlib-2.4.20.jar] archive to the classpath (it is in the Gradle cache; the [lib] folder of the [kotlinc] compiler also contains it, under the name [kotlin-stdlib.jar]): [java -cp "build/classes/kotlin/main;path/kotlin-stdlib-2.4.20.jar" first.MainKt] on Windows (the separator is [:] on Linux and macOS). The command-line compiler’s [kotlinr -cp build/classes/kotlin/main first.MainKt] command does this for us.

The easiest way is to have Gradle build the program and everything it needs using the [installDist] task from the [application] plugin:

> gradlew -q :FirstProgram:installDist

It creates the [FirstProgram/build/install/FirstProgram] folder, which contains a [lib] folder (the project archive, the Kotlin standard library, and, if applicable, the project’s other libraries) and a [bin] folder with two launch scripts, [FirstProgram] (Linux, macOS) and [FirstProgram.bat] (Windows), which call [java] with the correct classpath. In this form, a program is delivered so that it can be copied to another computer running JDK:

> FirstProgram\build\install\FirstProgram\bin\FirstProgram
1st try with a Gradle / Kotlin 2.4 project

The [build] folder can be safely deleted ([gradlew clean]): it is recreated by the next compilation. The command [gradlew build] also produces the project’s archive [build/libs/FirstProgram-1.0.jar], which contains only its own classes.

docs.title: 2.7.1. The multi-project build
docs.text:
A Gradle build can group together multiple projects, called its subprojects (or modules). The [settings.gradle.kts] file in the root directory lists them. The one in the [02-installation] folder is as follows:

// chapter 2: a Gradle build grouping the two projects of the folder

// Gradle downloads the JDK requested by jvmToolchain(25) itself if it does not find it on the machine
plugins {
    id("org.gradle.toolchains.foojay-resolver-convention") version "1.0.0"
}

rootProject.name = "installation"

// the subprojects, designated by their folder name
include("FirstProgram", "TwoHands")
  • Lines 3–6: a plugin for the build itself (not for a project), [foojay-resolver-convention]: When a project requests a JDK via [jvmToolchain(25)] that Gradle cannot find on the machine, Gradle downloads it from the foojay.io service and stores it in its cache. The first run takes a little longer, but the student no longer needs to have the correct JDK installed. The [plugins] block must be the first in the file. All builds in the course declare this plugin;
  • line 8: the build name (the root project). Without this line, it would be the folder name;
  • line 11: the subprojects, identified by their folder names. A subproject can be nested deeper: [include("TaxV5:tax-dao")] refers to the project in the [TaxV5/tax-dao] folder (Chapter 6).

The root project also has a file named [build.gradle.kts]:

// chapter 2: root project. The Kotlin plugin is declared here, with its version, without being applied:
// the subprojects apply it
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.20" apply false
}
  • Lines 3–4: The Kotlin plugin is declared, along with its version, but it is not applied to the root project ([apply false]), which does not contain any code to compile. This declaration makes the plugin available to subprojects, which apply it via [kotlin("jvm")] without repeating the version: all subprojects thus use the same version of Kotlin, which can be changed in a single location. If each subproject declared the plugin version on its own, Gradle would load it multiple times, which the Kotlin plugin advises against.

In the [02-installation] folder, the [gradlew build] command compiles both projects; a IDE that opens this folder sees both projects at once. In Chapter 6, we’ll see that a subproject can depend on another ([implementation(project(":TaxV5:tax-dao"))]), and in Chapters 10 through 13, we’ll see that a build can even reuse projects from another build ([includeBuild]).

docs.title: 2.7.2. A project with multiple main functions
docs.text:
A project can contain multiple files, each with a [main] function: each is a possible entry point, and the class to be executed is chosen at runtime. The [TwoHands] project contains two files from the [twohands] package. The [P1.kt] file:

package twohands

// a first entry point of the [TwoHands] project
fun main() {
    println("main of the P1.kt file")
}

and the file [P2.kt], which is identical except for the name. Both functions are named [main] and belong to the same package: there is no conflict because they are located in two different classes, [twohands.P1Kt] and [twohands.P2Kt]. The [java] command executes the class specified to it (in the [TwoHands] folder, once the project has been compiled):

> java -cp build/classes/kotlin/main twohands.P1Kt
main of the P1.kt file
> java -cp build/classes/kotlin/main twohands.P2Kt
main of the P2.kt file

For the [gradlew run] command, the project’s [build.gradle.kts] file specifies the class to be executed:

application {
    // the program run by [gradlew run] is designated by the [main] property;
    // by default, it is the main function of the P2.kt file:
    // gradlew -q :TwoHands:run -Pmain=twohands.P1Kt
    mainClass = providers.gradleProperty("main").orElse("twohands.P2Kt")
}
  • Line 5: The class being executed is specified by the Gradle property [main], which is provided on the command line via the option [-Pmain=...]. The [providers.gradleProperty("main")] function reads this property; [orElse(...)] specifies the value to use if it has not been provided: in this case, the [twohands.P2Kt] class.

The rest of the file is the same as that of [FirstProgram], with the addition of a configuration for the [run] task ([standardInput = System.in]), which transmits keyboard input to the program: without it, a program launched by [gradlew run] cannot read the keyboard.

Results:

> gradlew -q :TwoHands:run
main of the P2.kt file
> gradlew -q :TwoHands:run -Pmain=twohands.P1Kt
main of the P1.kt file

This allows you to select the program to run without modifying the [build.gradle.kts] file. With IntelliJ and IDEA, the issue doesn’t arise: each [main] function has its own green triangle in the margin.

docs.title: 2.7.3. One package per program
docs.text:
The projects in the following chapters all use this mechanism, since each one contains many small programs. To prevent these programs from interfering with one another, this document follows a simple convention: each program has its own package, which bears its name in lowercase and is stored in a folder with the same name. Thus, the program [Basics04.kt] from Chapter 3 is the file [03-basics/src/main/kotlin/basics04/Basics04.kt], which begins with the line [package basics04]; its class is [basics04.Basics04Kt], and it is executed as follows:

gradlew -q run -Pmain=basics04.Basics04Kt

There are two reasons for this convention:

  • All programs in a project are compiled together. If they were in the same package, two programs could not declare a function or class with the same name (a function [display], a class [Person]…): the compiler would report a duplicate declaration. With one package per program, each has its own namespace;
  • a program consisting of multiple files is simply a package containing multiple files: in Chapter 4, the package [persons] contains the class [Person] in [Person.kt] and the main program in [Main.kt], which is executed by [-Pmain=persons.MainKt].

The text of each chapter provides, before the results of a program, the exact command that executes it. We will revisit this structure in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 2.8. Examples in this document
docs.text:
To run the examples in this document:

  • download the [kotlin-oct-2026] folder (link at the beginning of the document). It contains one folder per chapter ([02-installation], [03-basics], [04-classes]…), and each of these folders is a Gradle build, complete with its wrapper: a single project, or multiple subprojects grouped together by its [settings.gradle.kts] file;
  • Open a chapter’s folder in IntelliJ IDEA (“File / Open”); then run a program by clicking the green triangle next to its function [main];
  • or, in a terminal located in the chapter’s folder, run a program using [gradlew -q run -Pmain=package.ClassKt] (with the subproject path preceding [run] if there are multiple subprojects); the text for each chapter provides the exact command.

The first [gradlew] command in a chapter requires Internet access: Gradle then downloads its own distribution, the Kotlin plugin, and the project’s libraries, which it subsequently stores in its cache.

Chapters 10 and 11 use a database named MySQL; the installation of MySQL with [Laragon] is described in the appendix.

docs.title: 3. The Basics of the Kotlin Language
3.1. Introduction
docs.text:
We’ll start by treating Kotlin as a traditional programming language. We’ll cover classes in the next chapter. A program consists of two things:

  • data;
  • the instructions that manipulate them.

We generally strive to separate data from instructions:

All the examples in this chapter are part of the Gradle project in the [03-basics] folder of the course code. As noted in Chapter 2, “Setting Up the Development Environment,” each program is contained in a file located within a package named after the program in lowercase: the program [Basics04.kt] is located in the folder [src/main/kotlin/basics04] and begins with the line [package basics04]. You can run it by clicking the green triangle next to IntelliJ IDEA, located in the margin next to the [main] function, or from the command line, from the project folder, using the command [gradlew -q run -Pmain=basics04.Basics04Kt] ([./gradlew] on Linux and macOS). The [-q] (“quiet”) option suppresses Gradle messages: only the program’s output remains. We will explain the name [basics04.Basics04Kt] in the next section. The examples run using French language and formatting conventions (the “locale” fr-FR), just as they would on a French Windows machine. We’ll see that this only affects numbers and dates formatted with a specific format: simply converting a floating-point number to a string always uses a decimal point.

docs.title: 3.2.1. The high-level main function
docs.text:
The program [Basics01.kt] is as follows:

// minimal program: a top-level main function, written outside any class
package basics01

fun main() {
    println("Hello world!")
    // the Java form remains usable: the out field of the System class, then its println method
    System.out.println("Hello world!")
    // listOf (package kotlin.collections) can be used without an import
    val words = listOf("Hello", "the", "world")
    println(words)
}

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=basics01.Basics01Kt
Hello world!
Hello world!
[Hello, the, world]

Comments:

  • Line 2: the program's package. A package groups related declarations, just as a folder groups files. The full name of everything declared in this file begins with [basics01.]. In Kotlin, unlike in Java, the file’s directory is not dictated by the package name; however, it is common practice—which we follow—to make them match;
  • Line 4: The function [main] is the program’s entry point. The keyword [fun] declares a function; [main()] has no parameters and returns no value. The function is written directly in the file, outside of any class: it is a top-level function. The body of the function is enclosed in curly braces;
  • line 5: the function [println] prints a line to the screen. It is also a top-level function, declared in the [kotlin.io] package of the Kotlin standard library;
  • line 7: the Java version of the same operation. [System] is a class of JDK, [out] is one of its fields, representing standard output (the screen), and [println] is a method of this object. Kotlin directly uses all Java classes: this is one of its major advantages. The Kotlin function [println] is, in fact, just a shorthand for [System.out.println]; this is the one we will use;
  • Line 9: [words] is a list of strings; lists will be covered in Chapter 5. The keyword [val] declares a variable whose value will not change; we did not specify its type: the compiler infers it from the value, in this case [List<String>]. The function [listOf] belongs to the package [kotlin.collections], which can be used without an import statement (see below);
  • Line 10: A list is displayed with its elements enclosed in square brackets;
  • statements do not end with a semicolon: a line break is sufficient. The semicolon is only used to write multiple statements on a single line. Lines beginning with // are comments, which are ignored by the compiler.

With two command-line arguments, which are passed to Gradle via the [--args] option:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=basics01.Basics01Kt --args="a0 a1"
Hello world!
Hello world!
[Hello, the, world]

The arguments are ignored because the [main()] function has no parameters to receive them. To use them, declare the function as [fun main(args: Array<String>)]: the [args] string array will then contain the command-line arguments. We’ll come back to this in the “Main Program Arguments” section.

docs.title: 3.2.2. The main function and its arguments
docs.text:
The program [Basics02.kt] is as follows:

// the main function with a parameter: the command-line arguments
package basics02

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    println("Hello world!")
    println("Number of arguments received: ${args.size}")
    // contentToString builds a string with the elements of an array
    println("Arguments: ${args.contentToString()}")
}

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=basics02.Basics02Kt --args="a0 a1"
Hello world!
Number of arguments received: 2
Arguments: [a0, a1]

Comments:

  • Line 4: The [main] function receives command-line arguments in the [args] parameter. In Kotlin, a parameter’s type is written after its name, separated by a colon: [args: Array<String>] reads as “[args], of type array of strings.” This is equivalent to [String[] args] in Java;
  • line 6: the number of elements in the array is [args.size] (the Java equivalent of [args.length]). In the string, [${args.size\}] is replaced by the value of the expression enclosed in curly braces: this is a string template, which we will discuss in more detail later;
  • Line 7: The function [contentToString] constructs a string using the elements of an array. It replaces the Java method [Arrays.toString] and, like the previous function, does not require any imports.

We haven't written any classes. However, the Java virtual machine (JVM), which runs the program, only recognizes classes. The Kotlin compiler therefore organizes the high-level declarations in a file into a class that it generates itself, named after the file followed by [Kt]: for the file [Basics02.kt] in the package [basics02], this is the class [basics02.Basics02Kt]. This is why the execution command refers to the program as [-Pmain=basics02.Basics02Kt]. You can verify this by compiling the file with the command-line compiler [kotlinc] (Chapter 2), then examining the generated class with the [javap] tool from the JDK package:

> kotlinc Basics02.kt -d classes
> ls classes/basics02
Basics02Kt.class
> kotlinr -cp classes basics02.Basics02Kt a0 a1
Hello world!
Number of arguments received: 2
Arguments: [a0, a1]
> javap classes/basics02/Basics02Kt.class
Compiled from "Basics02.kt"
public final class basics02.Basics02Kt {
  public static final void main(java.lang.String[]);
}
> java -cp classes basics02.Basics02Kt a0 a1
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: kotlin/jvm/internal/Intrinsics
    at basics02.Basics02Kt.main(Basics02.kt)
  • [kotlinc] generated a single intermediate code file (“bytecode”), [Basics02Kt.class], in the package directory;
  • the command [kotlinr] (the Kotlin launcher, Chapter 2) executes this class by adding the Kotlin standard library ([kotlin-stdlib.jar]) to the classpath;
  • [javap] shows that the generated class is [public final] and that the function [main] has become a method [public static] within it: exactly the method [public static void main(String[] args)] that JVM expects. For JVM, a Kotlin program is just another Java class;
  • when launched with the simple command [java], the class fails: the generated code calls on classes from the Kotlin standard library (in this case, [kotlin.jvm.internal.Intrinsics], which, among other things, checks that the parameters are not equal to [null]), which is missing from the classpath. Gradle and IntelliJ IDEA add it automatically; a standalone Kotlin program must include it (option [-include-runtime] of [kotlinc], Chapter 2, or Gradle scripts, see below).

For the program [Basics01.kt], whose function [main] has no parameters, the compiler also generates a method [main(String[])] that simply calls the first one. Gradle places the classes it compiles in the project’s [build/classes/kotlin/main] folder; you can examine them there after a compilation ([gradlew build]):

> javap -cp build/classes/kotlin/main basics01.Basics01Kt
Compiled from "Basics01.kt"
public final class basics01.Basics01Kt {
  public static final void main();
  public static void main(java.lang.String[]);
}

A comparison with Java 25 is instructive. Java 25 also allows you to write a program without declaring a class (a “compact source file,” with a method named [void main()]): the Java compiler then wraps the file’s contents in an implicit class bearing the file’s name. Kotlin has done the same thing since its first version, with two differences:

  • the generated class is named [Basics02Kt] rather than [Basics02], which leaves the name [Basics02] available for a class the programmer might want to write themselves in the same file. The annotation ***[@file:JvmName("ClassName")]***, placed at the top of the file, allows you to choose a different name;
  • high-level functions are compiled into [static] methods: no object is created to call [main], whereas the [void main()] method in a compact Java file is an instance method. Most importantly, in Kotlin, this syntax is not limited to small programs: top-level functions, variables, and constants are commonly used in all programs, alongside classes.

The function [main] can only take the two forms encountered: [fun main()] and [fun main(args: Array<String>)]. It does not need to be declared public: in Kotlin, everything is public by default.

docs.title: 3.2.3. Default imports
docs.text:
The program [Basics01.kt] uses the functions [println] and [listOf], and the program [Basics02.kt] uses the function [contentToString], without any [import] directive. This is possible because every Kotlin file automatically imports the following packages from the standard library:

import kotlin.*
import kotlin.annotation.*
import kotlin.collections.*
import kotlin.comparisons.*
import kotlin.io.*
import kotlin.ranges.*
import kotlin.sequences.*
import kotlin.text.*
// and, for the JVM:
import java.lang.*
import kotlin.jvm.*

This provides the basic types ([Int], [String]... from the [kotlin] package), lists, sets, and dictionaries ([kotlin.collections]), console input and output ([kotlin.io]), intervals ([kotlin.ranges]), string functions ([kotlin.text]), as well as classes from the Java package [java.lang] ([System], [Math], [Thread]...). Any other declarations must be imported at the top of the file, immediately after the line [package]: one directive per class or function ([import java.math.BigDecimal]) or one directive per package ([import java.time.*]). There is no equivalent to the [import module java.base;] directive from Java 25, which a compact Java file automatically receives: A Kotlin program that uses the classes [BigDecimal] or [LocalDate] from JDK must import them. A note on syntax: [import] directives, like other statements, do not end with a semicolon.

docs.title: 3.3. Kotlin Data Types
docs.text:
Kotlin uses the following data types:

  • integers, both signed and unsigned;
  • real numbers;
  • decimal numbers;
  • characters and strings;
  • Booleans;
  • objects.

docs.title: 3.3.1. Predefined data types
docs.text:
Kotlin typeCorresponding Java typeData representedLiteral suffixEncodingValue range[Char][char] / [Character]character 2 bytesUnicode character (UTF-16), from '\u0000' to '\uFFFF'[Byte][byte] / [Byte]integer 1 byte[-2⁷, 2⁷-1] or [-128, 127][Short][short] / [Short]integer 2 bytes[-2¹⁵, 2¹⁵-1] or [-32768, 32767][Int][int] / [Integer]integer 4 bytes[-2³¹, 2³¹-1] or [-2147483648, 2147483647][Long][long] / [Long]integerL8 bytes[-2⁶³, 2⁶³-1] or [-9223372036854775808, 9223372036854775807][UByte], [UShort], [UInt], [ULong](no equivalent)unsigned integerU, UL1, 2, 4, 8 bytes[0, 2⁸-1], [0, 2¹⁶-1], [0, 2³²-1], [0, 2⁶⁴-1][Float][float] / [Float]actual numberF4 bytes[1.4 10⁻⁴⁵, 3.4 10³⁸] in absolute value, 7 significant digits[Double][double] / [Double]actual number 8 bytes[4.9 10⁻³²⁴, 1.8 10³⁰⁸] in absolute value, 15 to 16 significant digits[Boolean][boolean] / [Boolean]Boolean not defined[true], [false][String][String]character string reference to a Unicode character sequence[BigDecimal] (Java class)[BigDecimal]decimal number variableexact decimal number, of any precision[Any][Object]object reference reference to an object of any type

Java distinguishes between the eight primitive types ([int], [double]...), whose values are not objects, and reference types (classes), and it associates each primitive type with a wrapper class ([Integer] for [int]...). Kotlin removes this distinction: in Kotlin, every value is an object. The type [Int] is a class that has methods; you can write [3.plus(4)] or [3.toString()], which Java does not allow for the literal 3 of type [int]. Type names all begin with a capital letter, just like class names.

This has no impact on runtime performance. The compiler translates a variable of type [Int] into a variable of the primitive type [int] or JVM whenever possible, and uses the wrapper class *[java.lang.Integer] only when an object is required: when the value is passed to a parameter of type [Any] (the Kotlin equivalent of Java’s [Object] class), stored in a list, or when it can be of type [null] (see below). Boxing and unboxing are therefore still present, but this is handled by the compiler, and the Kotlin programmer does not need to worry about it. There is no [Integer] type in Kotlin: there is only [Int]*.

The sizes in bytes are given by the constants [Int.SIZE_BYTES], [Long.SIZE_BYTES]... (and [Int.SIZE_BITS]... in bits), the range bounds by [Int.MIN_VALUE] and [Int.MAX_VALUE], etc.

Unlike Java, Kotlin has unsigned integers: [UByte], [UShort], [UInt], and [ULong], which are the same size as their signed counterparts but represent only positive or zero values. Their literals are suffixed with U ([42U]) or UL ([42UL]). They are primarily used to manipulate binary data (file bytes, addresses, colors); common calculations are performed using signed types. Kotlin also lacks a decimal type: amounts are calculated using the [BigDecimal] class from the Java package [java.math], which we’ll discuss a bit later.

The program [Basics03.kt] illustrates these various points:

// the basic types: Kotlin name, Java class and size in bytes
package basics03

import java.math.BigDecimal

fun main() {
    val integer: Int = 2
    val fl: Float = 10.5F
    val d: Double = -4.6
    val s: String = "test"
    val l: Long = 1000
    val bt: Byte = 5
    val sh: Short = -4
    val c: Char = 'A'
    val b: Boolean = true
    val dec: BigDecimal = BigDecimal("10.67")
    // in a string, $name and ${expression} are replaced by their value
    println("Type of integer[$integer] : [${typeName(integer)},${Int.SIZE_BYTES}]")
    println("Type of fl[$fl] : [${typeName(fl)},${Float.SIZE_BYTES}]")
    println("Type of d[$d] : [${typeName(d)},${Double.SIZE_BYTES}]")
    println("Type of s[$s] : [${typeName(s)}]")
    println("Type of l[$l] : [${typeName(l)},${Long.SIZE_BYTES}]")
    println("Type of bt[$bt] : [${typeName(bt)},${Byte.SIZE_BYTES}]")
    println("Type of sh[$sh] : [${typeName(sh)},${Short.SIZE_BYTES}]")
    println("Type of c[$c] : [${typeName(c)},${Char.SIZE_BYTES}]")
    println("Type of b[$b] : [${typeName(b)}]")
    println("Type of dec[$dec] : [${typeName(dec)}]")
    // the literal 3 is an object: it has methods
    println("The literal 3 : ${3::class.simpleName}, 3.plus(4)=${3.plus(4)}, 3.toString()=${3.toString()}")
    // extreme values
    println("Int : [${Int.MIN_VALUE}, ${Int.MAX_VALUE}]")
    println("Long : [${Long.MIN_VALUE}, ${Long.MAX_VALUE}]")
    println("Double : [${Double.MIN_VALUE}, ${Double.MAX_VALUE}]")
    // unsigned integers: UByte, UShort, UInt, ULong
    val u: UInt = 4_000_000_000U
    println("u=$u, UInt : [${UInt.MIN_VALUE}, ${UInt.MAX_VALUE}], ULong.MAX_VALUE=${ULong.MAX_VALUE}")
    val minusOne = -1
    println("-1 read as an unsigned integer: ${minusOne.toUInt()}")
}

// returns the Kotlin name and the Java class name of the object received
fun typeName(o: Any): String {
    return "${o::class.qualifiedName},${o.javaClass.name}"
}

Results:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=basics03.Basics03Kt
Type of integer[2] : [kotlin.Int,java.lang.Integer,4]
Type of fl[10.5] : [kotlin.Float,java.lang.Float,4]
Type of d[-4.6] : [kotlin.Double,java.lang.Double,8]
Type of s[test] : [kotlin.String,java.lang.String]
Type of l[1000] : [kotlin.Long,java.lang.Long,8]
Type of bt[5] : [kotlin.Byte,java.lang.Byte,1]
Type of sh[-4] : [kotlin.Short,java.lang.Short,2]
Type of c[A] : [kotlin.Char,java.lang.Character,2]
Type of b[true] : [kotlin.Boolean,java.lang.Boolean]
Type of dec[10.67] : [java.math.BigDecimal,java.math.BigDecimal]
The literal 3 : Int, 3.plus(4)=7, 3.toString()=3
Int : [-2147483648, 2147483647]
Long : [-9223372036854775808, 9223372036854775807]
Double : [4.9E-324, 1.7976931348623157E308]
u=4000000000, UInt : [0, 4294967295], ULong.MAX_VALUE=18446744073709551615
-1 read as an unsigned integer: 4294967295

Comments:

  • Line 4: The class [BigDecimal] is a subclass of JDK; it must be imported;
  • line 7: declaration of a variable [integer] of type [Int] initialized to 2. In Kotlin, a variable’s type is written after its name, separated by a colon. We’ll see that the type can usually be omitted;
  • line 8: the suffix F is required: the literal 10.5 is of type [Double], and the compiler refuses to assign it to a variable of type [Float];
  • line 11: the literal 1000 is accepted for a variable of type [Long], because the compiler knows that it is a constant that fits within the type. The same applies to lines 12–13 for the types [Byte] and [Short]. However, as we will see, Kotlin never implicitly converts a variable from one numeric type to another;
  • line 16: a [BigDecimal] number is an object; here, it is created from a string, which guarantees an exact value. Kotlin does not have a [new] operator: an object is created by calling its class constructor as a function;
  • line 18: In a string, [$integer] is replaced by the value of the variable [integer], and [${typeName(integer)\}] by the value of the expression written between the curly braces. These string templates are the standard way to construct a string in Kotlin; we’ll return to this in the next section. [Int.SIZE_BYTES] is the size in bytes of a [Int];
  • Line 18: The function [typeName] (lines 42–43) expects a parameter of type [Any]. The parameter is therefore an object, and the value [integer] is wrapped in a [java.lang.Integer] object. The function displays two names: [o::class.qualifiedName] is the full type name for Kotlin ([kotlin.Int]), and [o.javaClass.name] is the name of the object’s class for JVM ([java.lang.Integer]). We can see that [kotlin.Int], [kotlin.Double], [kotlin.String]... are represented at runtime by Java classes;
  • line 21: the size of a string in memory is not accessible: [String] does not have a constant [SIZE_BYTES];
  • line 26: the size of a boolean is not defined by JVM: [Boolean] does not have a constant [SIZE_BYTES];
  • line 27: [BigDecimal] is a Java class: its two names are identical;
  • line 29: the literal 3 is an object of type [Int]: [3::class.simpleName] is the short name of its type, and its methods can be called [plus] and [toString]. We will see in Chapter 4 that the + operator is simply another way of writing the method [plus];
  • lines 31–33: the constants [MIN_VALUE] and [MAX_VALUE] specify the bounds of the value domain. Note: For real numbers, [Double.MIN_VALUE] is the smallest strictly positive value (4.9 × 10⁻³²⁴) and not the largest negative number, which is [-Double.MAX_VALUE];
  • line 35: a 32-bit unsigned integer. The value 4,000,000,000 exceeds the range of [Int], but not that of [UInt], which extends up to 2³²-1;
  • lines 37–38: -1 is encoded as 32 bits set to 1; the [toUInt] function interprets them as an unsigned integer, which is equal to 2³²-1;
  • Lines 42–43: A high-level function from the file. The return type is specified after the list of parameters: [: String]. It returns ([return]), a character string. Functions are described in the section “Passing Parameters to a Function.”

Note that real numbers are displayed with a decimal point (10.5, -4.6), even though the program runs in French. Converting a number to a string—whether using a template, concatenation, or the [toString] method—does not depend on the user’s language: it always produces a decimal point. Only numeric formats such as %f, which we will discuss later, follow the conventions of the language.

docs.title: 3.3.2. Notation for Literal Data
docs.text:
DataExamples of literals[Int] integer (32 bits)145, -7, 0xFF (hexadecimal), 0b1010_1010 (binary)Integer [Long] (64 bits), suffix L100000L, 1_000_000_000_000L, 3_000_000_000 (too large for a [Int])unsigned integer [UInt], [ULong], suffix U, UL255U, 0xFFFF_FFFFU, 1ULreal [Double]134.789, -45E-18 (-45 × 10⁻¹⁸), 10.0real [Float], suffix F or f134.789F, -45E-18Fdecimal number [BigDecimal]no literal: [BigDecimal("100000.50")]character [Char]'A', 'b', '\n', '\u00e9'string [String]"today", "c:\\chap1", "$name is ${age + 10\} years old", raw string """c:\chap1"""boolean [Boolean][true], [false]date[LocalDate.of(1954, 10, 13)] (year, month, day) for 10/13/1954

In the source code, floating-point numbers are always written with a decimal point. As in Java, integers can be written in hexadecimal (prefix [0x]) or binary (prefix [0b]), and groups of digits can be separated by the _ character to improve readability: [1_000_000] is the integer one million. Kotlin differs from Java in a few ways, which eliminate just as many pitfalls:

  • an integer literal without a suffix is of type [Int] if it fits within that type, and of type [Long] otherwise: [3_000_000_000] is a [Long]. Java rejects this literal without the suffix L;
  • the suffix L must be written in uppercase: the compiler rejects [100l] with the message [use 'L' instead of 'l'], because l looks too much like the digit 1;
  • there is no octal notation. The Java pitfall, where 017 equals 15, does not exist: the compiler rejects 017 with the message [leading zeros are not allowed in integer literals];
  • there is no “D” suffix for floating-point numbers: a literal containing a decimal point or an exponent is [Double]; 10.0 is therefore written as 10.0 and not 10D;
  • Unsigned integers have their own suffixes, U and UL.

A string literal may contain escape sequences introduced by the \ character: "\n" represents the end-of-line character and not the sequence of the two characters \ and n, "\t" represents a tab, "\"" represents a double quote, "\\" the \ character itself, "\$" the $ character (see below), and "\u00e9" the Unicode character with hexadecimal code 00E9. To write the Windows path c:\chap1\paragraph3, you must therefore write "c:\\chap1\\paragraph3". Java file classes also accept the / separator on Windows: "c:/chap1/paragraph3" refers to the same file.

To construct a string from multiple values, Kotlin offers three methods:

  • string templates: In a string, [$name] is replaced by the value of the variable [name], and [${expression\}] by the value of any expression: ["in 10 years he will be ${age + 10\}"]. This is the most readable and most widely used method. It is equivalent to C#’s interpolated strings, such as [$"..."]; Java, on the other hand, does not have this feature (the “string templates” proposed as a preview in Java 21 and 22 have been removed);
  • Concatenation using the + operator: if the left operand is a string, the right operand is converted to a string, regardless of its type. Unlike in Java, the left operand must be a string: [10 + " years"] is rejected by the compiler because the type [Int] does not have a + operator that accepts a string;
  • the formats: ["format".format(value1, value2, ...)] or [String.format(format, value1, value2, ...)]. These are the Java formats, with the same specifiers, replaced in order by the following values: %s (any value converted to a string), %d (an integer), %f (a floating-point number), %.2f (a floating-point number with two decimal places), %x or %X (an integer in hexadecimal), %,d (an integer with a thousands separator), %e (scientific notation), %n (a line break), %10s (a string right-aligned to 10 characters), %-10s (left-aligned)... Numeric formats follow the conventions of the user’s language. They are used when you need to control the presentation of numbers (number of decimal places, alignment); otherwise, the template is sufficient.

Finally, Kotlin offers “raw strings”: a string delimited by three quotation marks, such as ["""..."""], can span multiple lines and contain quotation marks; most importantly, escape sequences are not interpreted in raw strings: the \ character is treated as-is, so you would write ["""c:\chap1"""]. This is very useful for writing JSON, SQL, HTML, or regular expressions (Chapter 5). Raw strings support templates. Leading spaces are preserved as-is; to indent the text with the code, apply the function [trimIndent()] to the string, which removes the spaces common to all lines as well as the first and last lines if they are empty, or the function [trimMargin()], which removes everything preceding the | character (the “margin”). Java 15 text blocks were designed based on this model; they automatically remove common indentation but interpret escape sequences.

The program [Basics04.kt] demonstrates these different notations:

// the notation of literal data
package basics04

import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.time.LocalDate
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter

fun main() {
    // integers: decimal, hexadecimal (0x), binary (0b), separator _
    val i1 = 145; val i2 = -7; val i3 = 0xFF; val i4 = 0b1010_1010
    val l1 = 100000L; val l2 = 1_000_000_000_000L; val l3 = 3_000_000_000
    println("integers: $i1 $i2 $i3 $i4 $l1 $l2 $l3")
    // unsigned integers: suffix U
    val u1 = 255U; val u2 = 0xFFFF_FFFFU
    println("unsigned: $u1 $u2")
    // reals
    val d1 = 134.789; val d2 = -45E-18; val d3 = 10.0
    val f1 = 134.789F
    val m1 = BigDecimal("100000.50")
    println("reals: $d1 $d2 $d3 $f1 $m1")
    // characters and booleans
    val c1 = 'A'; val c2 = '\u00e9'
    val b1 = true
    println("characters: $c1 $c2, boolean: $b1")
    // a date: (year, month, day)
    val birth = LocalDate.of(1954, 10, 13)
    println("date: $birth")

    // the \ character introduces an escape sequence
    val path = "c:\\chap1\\paragraph3"
    println(path)
    println("line 1\nline 2\t[tab]")
    // the $ character is written \$ in a string
    println("price: 10 \$, quotes: \"yes\"")

    // building a string: template, concatenation or format
    val name = "dupont"
    val age = 23
    println("$name is $age years old, in 10 years he will be ${age + 10}")
    println(name + " is " + age + " years old, in 10 years he will be " + (age + 10))
    println(String.format("%s is %d years old, in 10 years he will be %d", name, age, age + 10))
    // the format function applies to the format string itself
    println("d1=%.1f, i3 in hexadecimal=%X, l2=%,d".format(d1, i3, l2))
    println("i4 in binary=${i4.toString(2)}, name in upper case=${name.uppercase()}")
    println("date=${birth.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("EEEE d MMMM yyyy"))}")

    // raw string: no escape sequences, no quotes to escape
    val json = """
        {
          "name": "dupont",
          "path": "c:\chap1"
        }
        """.trimIndent()
    println(json)
    // a raw string accepts templates
    val json2 = """{ "name": "$name", "age": $age }"""
    println(json2)
    // trimMargin: the margin stops at the | character
    val text = """
        |A raw string
        |   on several lines, costing 10 ${'$'}
        """.trimMargin()
    println(text)
}
