A machine has at least two IP addresses: the loopback address 127.0.0.1 and the address it has on the network to which it is connected. It may have others if it is connected to multiple networks. Unless an address is specified, the service listens on all of these addresses. As soon as it is created, the service begins listening—that is, waiting for connection requests from clients. [ServerSocket] is also [AutoCloseable]: [use] will close it when the block ends;
  • Line 4: a *[ExecutorService]* (Chapter 8) that creates a virtual thread for each task submitted to it. Starting with Java 19, [ExecutorService] is [AutoCloseable]: the [use] function therefore also applies, and its [close] method waits for all submitted tasks to complete. Where Java declares multiple resources within a single [try], Kotlin nests the [use] blocks;
  • lines 10–17: the loop waits for a client and launches its service, repeated for each new client;
  • line 13: a client’s request is accepted. [accept] returns a so-called service [Socket]:
    • the client made its request using its own [Socket], which we’ll call [RequestSocket];
    • the server accepts this request with [accept], which creates a server-side [Socket], which we will call [ServiceSocket]. We now have a TCP connection open, with the sockets [RequestSocket] ↔ [ServiceSocket] at either end;
    • the client/server communication that takes place next occurs over this connection. The listening service is no longer involved;
  • Line 17: To allow the server to handle multiple clients at once, the service is handled by a virtual thread. The server does not wait for it; it immediately returns to wait for the next client. The lambda passed to *[submit] captures the variable [number]*, which is a copy of the client number made on line 16. In Kotlin, a lambda can capture a [var] (which Java prohibits), but that would be an error here: the lambda executes later, in another thread, while the loop may have already incremented [clientNum]. So we give each lambda its own copy, a *[val]* that will no longer change.

Without [ExecutorService], we can also start the virtual thread directly: [Thread.ofVirtual().start { serve(client, number) \}]. [ExecutorService] has the advantage, when the server shuts down, of waiting for all running services to finish.

The [serve] function, executed by the virtual thread, receives the [Socket], which is already connected to the client to be served. It contains code similar to that of the client TCP: [client.use { … \}], creation of streams, followed by a loop “reading a request via [readLine], writing the response via [println] ,” until [readLine] returns [null]—that is, until the client closes the connection. Exceptions must be caught in this function: no one is waiting for the result of the service thread, and an uncaught exception there would go unnoticed (it would only be displayed in the error output). The Kotlin compiler won’t remind you of this, since there are no checked exceptions: it’s up to the programmer to keep this in mind.

docs.title: 12.5.4. One Thread Per Client: Platform Threads or Virtual Threads?
docs.text:
Before Java 21, a server assigned each client to a platform thread—that is, an operating system thread—or to a thread from a fixed-size pool ([Executors.newFixedThreadPool]). This thread performed blocking reads and writes: for as long as the client was processing a request, its thread remained blocked in [readLine]. Each platform thread consumes memory (a reserved stack of approximately 1 MB) and processor time, as the system must switch between them. With a few dozen clients, this isn’t a problem; with thousands of simultaneous connections—a common scenario for a real-world server—the server crashes. With a thread pool limited to 10 threads, the eleventh client must wait for one of the first ten to disconnect.

To get around this limitation, for a long time we had to avoid blocking operations: the non-blocking channels in [java.nio] and their [Selector], which allow a single thread to monitor multiple connections, or the asynchronous channels in Java 7, which call a callback function at the end of each operation. These techniques are effective but difficult to program: the logic of the interaction is spread across multiple functions. They form the basis of libraries such as Netty, which are used by many servers. Kotlin has provided another solution with coroutines (Chapter 9): sequential code, written using [suspend] functions, which the compiler transforms into a state machine; this is the approach taken by Ktor.

Virtual threads (Java 21, Chapter 8) have been a game-changer. A virtual thread is managed by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) rather than by the operating system. When it performs a blocking network operation, it is “detached” from its carrier thread, which can then execute another virtual thread; it is reattached to a carrier thread when the data arrives. A few carrier threads—as many as there are processor cores—are thus sufficient to serve thousands of clients, and a client that sends nothing consumes almost nothing: just a few hundred bytes of stack. The code itself remains the simple, sequential code of the “one thread per client” model, without even having to mark the [suspend] functions: the blocking classes [Socket] and [ServerSocket] are used as-is. This is the model we’ll use in all the servers in this chapter: [ServerSocket.accept] in the main thread, with one virtual thread per client.

docs.title: 12.6. Examples of TCP clients/servers
docs.text: The programs in this section are [InternetNN.kt] files from the Gradle project [12-internet], each in its own package ([internet04], [internet05]…). They are executed by [gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet04.Internet04Kt --args="..."] (or by clicking the green triangle in IntelliJ or IDEA, in which case the arguments are entered in the execution configuration). The servers and clients are launched in separate command windows on the same machine; the ports used are in the form 271xx.

docs.title: 12.6.1. An Echo Server
docs.text:
We propose to write an echo server, which will be launched from a command window using:

gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet04.Internet04Kt --args="port"

The server runs on the port passed as an argument. It simply sends back to the client every line the client sends it, enclosed in square brackets. The program [Internet04.kt] is as follows:

package internet04

import java.io.IOException
import java.io.PrintWriter
import java.net.ServerSocket
import java.net.Socket
import java.net.SocketException
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap
import java.util.concurrent.Executors
import kotlin.concurrent.thread

// echo server: sends back to each client the lines that the client sends to it
// each client is served by a virtual thread
// call: gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet04.Internet04Kt --args="port" ; stop with Ctrl-C

private const val SYNTAX = "Syntax: internet04.Internet04Kt port"

// the service connections in progress, closed when the server stops
private val connections: MutableSet<Socket> = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()

// has the server been asked to stop?
@Volatile
private var stopping = false

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    // an argument is required: a port between 1 and 65535
    val port = args.singleOrNull()?.toIntOrNull()
    if (port == null || port !in 1..65535) {
        println(SYNTAX)
        return
    }
    try {
        // the listening service, on all the network interfaces of the machine
        ServerSocket(port).use { listener ->
            // one virtual thread per client; close() waits for the end of all the services
            Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { services ->
                // Ctrl-C: the server stops cleanly
                stopOnCtrlC(listener)
                println("Echo server started on ${listener.localSocketAddress}")
                try {
                    // loop waiting for the clients - stopped by Ctrl-C
                    var clientNum = 0
                    while (true) {
                        // (blocking) wait for a client
                        val client = listener.accept()
                        connections.add(client)
                        // the client is served by a virtual thread; we immediately go back to wait for the next one
                        val number = clientNum++
                        services.submit { serve(client, number) }
                    }
                } catch (e: SocketException) {
                    // accept fails when Ctrl-C closes the listening service
                    if (!stopping) throw e
                    println("Server stop requested")
                    // the connections in progress are closed: the services stop
                    connections.forEach { it.close() }
                }
            }
        }
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        println("The following error occurred on the server: ${e.message}")
    }
}

// Ctrl-C: closing of the listening service, then wait for the end of the main program
fun stopOnCtrlC(listener: ServerSocket) {
    val main = Thread.currentThread()
    // thread(start = false) creates the thread without starting it: the virtual machine will start it
    Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(thread(start = false) {
        stopping = true
        listener.close()
        // the virtual machine stops at the end of this thread: we wait for the end of the main thread
        main.join()
    })
}

// the service provided to a client
fun serve(client: Socket, clientNum: Int) {
    println("Start of the service to client $clientNum (${client.remoteSocketAddress})")
    try {
        // the connection and its streams are closed when leaving use
        client.use {
            // Kotlin's bufferedReader, bufferedWriter... extensions use UTF-8 by default
            val reader = client.getInputStream().bufferedReader()
            // autoFlush (true): each line written by println leaves immediately on the network
            val writer = PrintWriter(client.getOutputStream(), true, Charsets.UTF_8)
            // loop reading request / writing response
            // readLine returns null when the client closes the connection
            while (true) {
                val request = reader.readLine() ?: break
                println("<--- client $clientNum : $request")
                // echo of the request to the client, between square brackets
                writer.println("[$request]")
                println("---> client $clientNum : [$request]")
            }
        }
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        if (stopping) {
            println("Service to client $clientNum interrupted by the server stop")
        } else {
            println("The following error occurred while serving client $clientNum : ${e.message}")
        }
    } finally {
        connections.remove(client)
        println("End of the service to client $clientNum")
    }
}

The structure of the echo server conforms to the basic architecture of TCP servers described earlier, with a few additions:

  • lines 19–23: two high-level, private file properties ([private]: visible only to the file itself). The set [connections] contains the current service connections; several threads add to and remove elements from it simultaneously, so it is a set designed for concurrent access, obtained via [ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()] (Chapter 8). Its type is explicitly declared as [MutableSet<Socket>], since the element’s type cannot be inferred from a call without arguments. The boolean [stopping] indicates whether the server has been requested to shut down; it is annotated as [@Volatile] because it is modified by one thread and read by others (this is the Java keyword [volatile]);
  • lines 27–30: the port must be an integer between 1 and 65,535. [args.singleOrNull()] returns the single argument, or [null] if there is not exactly one, and [toIntOrNull] returns [null] if the string is not an integer: the auxiliary method [integer] in the Java program is unnecessary. After the check, the compiler knows that [port] is not [null] (smart type casting);
  • lines 34–36: the listener service and the [ExecutorService] method, which creates one virtual thread per client, each enclosed within its own [use] block;
  • line 38: the server shuts down. Ctrl-C does not allow the program to execute a function of its choosing, as an event handler would; instead, it shuts down the virtual machine. However, before shutting down, the virtual machine executes the “shutdown hooks” that were registered by [Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook]. Our hook (lines 66–73) is a thread created—but not started—by the [thread(start = false) { … \}] function of [kotlin.concurrent] (Chapter 8): the virtual machine will start it at shutdown. It notes that shutdown has been requested (line 70), closes the listening service (line 71), and then waits for the main thread to finish (line 73): the virtual machine shuts down as soon as the blocks are completed. Whereas the Java program had to catch the checked exceptions from [close] and [join] in order to ignore them, Kotlin imposes no such requirement;
  • line 45: closing the listener service causes a client’s wait to fail, triggering a [SocketException], which is caught on line 51. If the shutdown was not requested, this is a genuine error: it is restarted (line 53) so that it can be handled by the [catch] on line 60;
  • line 56: all active service connections are closed; the service threads, blocked in a read operation, receive a [SocketException] and terminate. Upon exiting the [use] block of the [ExecutorService], its [close] method waits for all services to finish before the [main] function terminates.

The “customer service” section:

  • Line 79: the client's address and port, property [remoteSocketAddress] (the Java method [getRemoteSocketAddress()], treated as a property by Kotlin);
  • line 82: the client’s socket is closed when the block exits, and its streams are closed along with it. The read stream is created by the [bufferedReader] extension (UTF-8 by default); the write stream is an auto-flushing [PrintWriter], as in the echo client;
  • Line 90: The client’s request is read. [readLine] returns [null] when the client closes the connection: the Elvis operator then executes [break], and the loop and the service stop. After this line, [request] is of type [String] and not [String?];
  • line 93: the request is returned to the client, enclosed in square brackets;
  • lines 97–101: a [IOException] indicates either that the server has shut down—having closed the connection during reading—or that the client has terminated the connection;
  • lines 103–105: the [finally] removes the connection from the list of all active connections and signals the end of service, regardless of the cause.

To see the server in action, we need a client. We’ll write it in the next section and present the results afterward.

docs.title: 12.6.2. A Client for the Echo Server
docs.text:
We will now write a client for the previous server. It will be called as follows:

gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet05.Internet05Kt --args="machine port"

It connects to the machine [machine] on port [port], then sends the text lines typed on the keyboard to the server, which echoes them back. The program [Internet05.kt] is as follows:

package internet05

import java.io.IOException
import java.io.PrintWriter
import java.net.Socket

// echo client: sends to the server the lines typed on the keyboard
// and displays the responses of the server
// call: gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet05.Internet05Kt --args="machine port"

private const val SYNTAX = "Syntax: internet05.Internet05Kt machine port"

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    val port = args.getOrNull(1)?.toIntOrNull()
    if (args.size != 2 || port == null || port !in 1..65535) {
        println(SYNTAX)
        return
    }
    val server = args[0]

    try {
        // connection to the service; the connection and its streams are closed when leaving use
        Socket(server, port).use { client ->
            // read and write streams on the connection
            val reader = client.getInputStream().bufferedReader()
            // autoFlush: each line written by println leaves immediately on the network
            val writer = PrintWriter(client.getOutputStream(), true, Charsets.UTF_8)
            println("Connected to the server ${client.remoteSocketAddress} from ${client.localSocketAddress}")
            // request - response loop
            while (true) {
                // the request comes from the keyboard; null if standard input is closed
                print("Request (bye to stop): ")
                val request = readlnOrNull()
                // finished?
                if (request == null || request.trim().equals("bye", ignoreCase = true)) break
                // the request is sent to the server
                writer.println(request)
                // we wait for its response
                val response = reader.readLine()
                if (response == null) {
                    println("The server closed the connection")
                    break
                }
                println("Response: $response")
            }
        }
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        println("The following error occurred: ${e::class.simpleName} (${e.message})")
    }
}

The structure of this client conforms to the basic architecture proposed for TCP clients:

  • lines 14–19: [args.getOrNull(1)] returns the second argument, or [null] if it does not exist; no exceptions are possible;
  • lines 23–27: connect to the server and create streams; these lines are already commented out;
  • line 28: the two ends of the connection are displayed: [remoteSocketAddress] (the server) and [localSocketAddress] (the client). The client’s port was chosen by the system;
  • lines 32–33: the request is typed on the keyboard. [readlnOrNull] returns [null] if standard input is closed (Ctrl-D on Linux, Ctrl-Z followed by Enter on Windows);
  • line 35: the comparison with [bye] is case-insensitive ([equals(..., ignoreCase = true)], the Java equivalent of [equalsIgnoreCase]). In the second part of the test, the compiler knows that [request] is not [null]: the operator [||] evaluates its second operand only if the first is false;
  • line 37: the request is sent to the server;
  • lines 39–42: the response is awaited; [null] indicates that the server has closed the connection;
  • lines 47–48: connection and exchange errors. [e::class.simpleName] is the short name of the exception class (Java’s [e.getClass().getSimpleName()]).

Here are the results obtained with the following configuration:

  • the server is running on port 27100 in a command window;
  • on the same machine, two clients, A and B, are launched in two other windows; client B was started while client A was still communicating with the server.

To obtain these results, the clients’ input was sent via standard input redirection; it was reinserted after the questions it answered, just as it would appear on the screen when typed on a keyboard. In client A’s window:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet05.Internet05Kt --args="localhost 27100"
Connected to the server localhost/127.0.0.1:27100 from /127.0.0.1:34252
Request (bye to stop): line1A
Response: [line1A]
Request (bye to stop): line2A
Response: [line2A]
Request (bye to stop): line3A
Response: [line3A]
Request (bye to stop): bye

Client A sent three lines, which were echoed back, then typed [bye]: it closed the connection without sending anything to the server.

In Client B’s window:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet05.Internet05Kt --args="localhost 27100"
Connected to the server localhost/127.0.0.1:27100 from /127.0.0.1:34254
Request (bye to stop): line1B
Response: [line1B]
Request (bye to stop): line2B
Response: [line2B]
Request (bye to stop): line3B
The server closed the connection

Client B sent two lines; then, before typing the third, the server was terminated with Ctrl-C. The line [line3B] was sent over a connection that had already been closed by the server: reading the response (line 8 of the results) returned [null].

In the server window:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet04.Internet04Kt --args="27100"
Echo server started on 0.0.0.0/0.0.0.0:27100
Start of the service to client 0 (/127.0.0.1:34252)
<--- client 0 : line1A
---> client 0 : [line1A]
Start of the service to client 1 (/127.0.0.1:34254)
<--- client 0 : line2A
---> client 0 : [line2A]
<--- client 1 : line1B
---> client 1 : [line1B]
<--- client 0 : line3A
---> client 0 : [line3A]
<--- client 1 : line2B
---> client 1 : [line2B]
End of the service to client 0
Server stop requested
Service to client 1 interrupted by the server stop
End of the service to client 1
  • line 2: the server is listening on port 27100 from all addresses on the machine, represented by the wildcard address 0.0.0.0;
  • Lines 3 and 6: Both clients arrived from the same machine (127.0.0.1) using different ports, which were assigned by the system. These ports are what distinguish the two connections, both of which terminate at port 27100 on the server;
  • Line 6: Client 1 (B) is being served while Client 0 (A) is still being served, and lines 7–14 show that their requests are processed as they arrive: the server is indeed serving multiple clients simultaneously;
  • line 15: the server detected that client A closed the connection;
  • Lines 16–18: Ctrl-C was pressed in the server window. The attempt to wait for a new client failed, and then service to client 1—who was waiting for a line—was interrupted when their connection closed. The server shut down properly.

A note on Ctrl-C. When launched by [gradlew run], the server is not the program that receives Ctrl-C: it is Gradle, which in turn shuts down the server process in its own way. Depending on the system and the version of Gradle, the program’s shutdown blocks may not necessarily be executed, and the last three lines would not be visible. The results above were obtained by sending the termination signal (the one triggered by Ctrl-C) directly to the server’s Java process—which is what Ctrl-C does in the window of a program launched by the command [java]. In IntelliJ and IDEA, the stop button (the red square) also first attempts to shut down the program normally.

Here’s what happens when you try to connect to a port on which no service is listening:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet05.Internet05Kt --args="localhost 27199"
The following error occurred: ConnectException (Connection refused)

The creator of [Socket] launched a [ConnectException]: the machine responded, but no program is listening on port 27199. The message comes from the operating system; it is different on Windows.

Finally, if you start the server on a port that is already in use—for example, in a second window while the first server is still running—the creation of [ServerSocket] fails:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet04.Internet04Kt --args="27100"
The following error occurred on the server: Address already in use

docs.title: 12.6.3. A generic TCP client
docs.text:
We will write a generic TCP client, which will be launched as follows:

gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet06.Internet06Kt --args="machine port"

It will function similarly to the [telnet] and PuTTY clients: it will allow communication with any TCP text-based server.

In the previous application, the communication protocol was known: the client sent a single line, and the server responded with a single line. Each service has its own specific protocol, and the following situations may also arise:

  • the client must send multiple lines of text before receiving a response (a HTTP request);
  • a server’s response may consist of multiple lines of text (the response [EHLO] from a server SMTP, a document HTML);
  • the server may speak first (the welcome message from servers SMTP and POP).

The cycle of “sending a single line to the server / receiving a single line sent by the server” is therefore not always suitable. To handle protocols more complex than the echo protocol, the generic TCP client performs two activities in parallel, in two threads:

  • a virtual thread reads the lines of text typed on the keyboard and sends them to the server;
  • the main thread reads the lines of text sent by the server. As soon as it receives one, it displays it on the console. It does not stop until the connection is closed.

The program [Internet06.kt] is as follows:

package internet06

import java.io.IOException
import java.io.Writer
import java.net.Socket

// generic TCP client
// - connects to the service (machine, port)
// - a virtual thread sends to the server each line typed on the keyboard
// - the main thread continuously displays the lines sent by the server
// call: gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet06.Internet06Kt --args="machine port"

private const val SYNTAX = "Syntax: internet06.Internet06Kt machine port"

// end requested on the keyboard (bye)?
@Volatile
private var end = false

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    val port = args.getOrNull(1)?.toIntOrNull()
    if (args.size != 2 || port == null || port !in 1..65535) {
        println(SYNTAX)
        return
    }
    val server = args[0]

    // connection to the service
    val client = try {
        Socket(server, port)
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        println("Unable to connect to the service ($server, $port) : ${e.message}")
        return
    }
    try {
        client.use {
            val reader = client.getInputStream().bufferedReader()
            val writer = client.getOutputStream().writer()
            println("Type your commands (bye to stop):")
            // reading the keyboard commands is handed to a virtual thread
            Thread.ofVirtual().start { input(client, writer) }
            // the main thread displays the lines of the server until the connection is closed
            reader.lineSequence().forEach { response -> println("<-- $response") }
            println("[the server closed the connection]")
        }
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        // a connection closed by the input thread (bye) is not an error
        if (!end) {
            println("The following error occurred while reading: ${e.message}")
        }
    }
    // end of the main thread: the virtual input thread, if it is still waiting for the keyboard, is abandoned
}

// sends to the server the lines typed on the keyboard, until bye
fun input(client: Socket, writer: Writer) {
    try {
        // the sequence of typed lines, stopped by the end of standard input (null) or by bye
        generateSequence { readlnOrNull() }
            .takeWhile { command -> !command.trim().equals("bye", ignoreCase = true) }
            .forEach { command ->
                // the lines sent end with \r\n, as required by HTTP, SMTP, POP, FTP...
                writer.write("$command\r\n")
                writer.flush()
            }
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        println("The following error occurred while writing: ${e.message}")
    } finally {
        // the connection is closed: the read in progress in the main thread ends
        end = true
        client.close()
    }
}
  • Lines 28–32: The client connects to the server. [try] is an expression: its value is that of the created [Socket]; if the operation fails, the [catch] block displays the error and exits the [main] function via [return]. The variable [client] is thus a [val], initialized once and for all (in Java, it had to be declared before the [try]);
  • lines 35–37: the socket, which is closed upon exiting the [use] block, and its streams. The write stream is a simple [OutputStreamWriter], created by the [writer()] extension, whose methods launch a [IOException] in the event of an error;
  • line 40: keyboard input is handled by a virtual thread, created and started by [Thread.ofVirtual().start] (Java 21), which executes the function [input] (lines 55–70). The Kotlin lambda is converted to [Runnable], the interface expected by [start] (conversion SAM, Chapter 7);
  • line 42: Meanwhile, the main thread displays each line sent by the server, preceded by [<--]. The [lineSequence] extension makes the sequence of lines in the stream lazy: each line is read when [forEach] requests it—that is, as soon as it arrives from the network—and the sequence ends at the end of the stream, when the server closes the connection (line 43);
  • lines 45–48: when the user types [bye], the input thread closes the connection (line 70); the current read operation in the main thread then ends with a [SocketException]. This is not an error: the property [end], set by the input thread (line 69), confirms this;
  • Line 51: When the server closes the connection, the main thread terminates, even though the input thread may still be waiting for a line of input from the keyboard. This isn’t a problem: a virtual thread is always a “daemon thread,” and the virtual machine stops when all non-daemon threads have terminated—in this case, only the main thread. Unlike what would be necessary with an ordinary thread, there’s no need to stop the input thread;
  • lines 58–63: the input thread reads the lines typed on the keyboard and sends them to the server. [generateSequence { readlnOrNull() \}] is the sequence of typed lines, which ends when the function returns [null] (end of standard input); [takeWhile] stops it at the first line, [bye], which is not sent. The [while] loop in the Java program is thus replaced by a sequence of operations on a sequence, evaluated lazily, line by line, as the user types. The sent lines end with \r\n, as required by the protocols we want to explore, and are immediately transmitted to the network by [flush].

We can now manually send a HTTP request to our test web server ([Internet03.kt]), which is running in another window. The lines preceded by [<--] are those sent by the server; the others were typed on the keyboard (again, sent via redirection and then reinserted in their proper places):

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet06.Internet06Kt --args="localhost 27110"
Type your commands (bye to stop):
GET /hello?name=Serge HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:27110
Connection: close

<-- HTTP/1.1 200 OK
<-- Date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:55:26 GMT
<-- Transfer-encoding: chunked
<-- Content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
<--
<-- c
<-- Hello Serge!
<-- 0
<--
[the server closed the connection]
  • lines 3–5: the request, typed on the keyboard: we are requesting the document [/hello?name=Serge]. The header [Connection: close] instructs the server to close the connection once its response has been sent;
  • Line 6: The blank line terminates the request. It triggers the server’s response;
  • line 7: the document was found;
  • line 9: The server did not specify the size of the document ([Content-length]); it sends it in chunks, each preceded by its size in hexadecimal;
  • line 10: this time, the document is plain text;
  • lines 12–14: a single chunk of 0xc = 12 bytes, the text [Hello Serge!], followed by a zero-size chunk that marks the end of the document;
  • line 16: as requested, the server closed the connection. The client detected this and stopped on its own, without waiting for the user to type [bye].

Let’s try again without the header [Connection: close], requesting the site’s root:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet06.Internet06Kt --args="localhost 27110"
Type your commands (bye to stop):
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:27110

<-- HTTP/1.1 200 OK
<-- Date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:55:32 GMT
<-- Content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
<-- Content-length: 173
<--
<-- <!DOCTYPE html>
<-- <html lang="en">
<-- <head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Test server</title></head>
<-- <body><h1>Welcome to the test server of the Kotlin course</h1></body>
<-- </html>
bye
  • line 9: the document is announced along with its size, 173 bytes. The client thus knows where it ends;
  • Lines 15–16: The document has been received in its entirety, but the server has not closed the connection: in HTTP/1.1, it remains open by default for further requests. The server waits for a new request; the user then enters [bye] to close the connection.

When the server is unavailable, the connection fails:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet06.Internet06Kt --args="localhost 27199"
Unable to connect to the service (localhost, 27199) : Connection refused

The reader can use this generic TCP client with the echo server, or, if they have a SMTP or POP3 server that accepts unencrypted connections (such as a locally installed test server), to reproduce the sample dialogs shown above.

docs.title: 12.6.4. A generic TCP server
docs.text:
We will now focus on a server:

  • that displays on the screen the lines sent by its clients;
  • which sends back as responses the lines of text typed on the keyboard by a user. The user, therefore, acts as the server.

The program is launched in a command window via [gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet07.Internet07Kt --args="port"], where [port] is the port to which clients must connect. Clients are served one after another, not in parallel: the console cannot be used for two clients simultaneously. Clients that connect during this time have their connections established by the system but must wait for the program to accept them. Three activities occur in parallel:

  • a virtual thread reads the lines typed on the keyboard for the entire duration of the program;
  • for each client, a virtual thread reads the lines sent by the client and displays them;
  • the main thread accepts clients and sends the lines typed on the keyboard to the current client. The user signals with the command [bye] that they are closing the connection with the client.

The main thread must therefore wait for two types of events: a line typed on the keyboard, or the client’s departure. The other two threads signal these events to the main thread by placing them in a blocking queue ([BlockingQueue], Chapter 8), from which the main thread retrieves them one by one. The server stops only when the user presses Ctrl-C on the keyboard or when standard input is closed. The program [Internet07.kt] is as follows:

package internet07

import java.io.IOException
import java.io.Writer
import java.net.ServerSocket
import java.net.Socket
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue
import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue

// generic TCP server
// - displays the lines sent by the client
// - sends it as responses the lines typed on the keyboard by the user
// the clients are served one after the other (a single console)
// call: gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet07.Internet07Kt --args="port" ; stop with Ctrl-C

private const val SYNTAX = "Syntax: internet07.Internet07Kt port"

// the events awaited by the main program
sealed interface Event

// a line typed on the keyboard
data class Input(val line: String) : Event

// end of standard input (Ctrl-D, Ctrl-Z)
data object EndOfInput : Event

// client no. [clientNum] has closed the connection
data class ClientLeft(val clientNum: Int) : Event

// the queue of events, fed by two virtual threads: the keyboard and the reading of the client
private val events: BlockingQueue<Event> = LinkedBlockingQueue()

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    val port = args.singleOrNull()?.toIntOrNull()
    if (port == null || port !in 1..65535) {
        println(SYNTAX)
        return
    }
    try {
        // the listening service
        ServerSocket(port).use { listener ->
            println("Generic server started on ${listener.localSocketAddress}")
            // a virtual thread reads the keyboard for the whole duration of the program
            Thread.ofVirtual().start(::readKeyboard)
            // service loop - the server is stopped by Ctrl-C
            var clientNum = 0
            while (true) {
                // wait for a client
                println("Waiting for the next client...")
                val client = listener.accept()
                println("Client ${client.remoteSocketAddress}")
                // a virtual thread displays the lines sent by the client
                val number = clientNum++
                val reception = Thread.ofVirtual().start { receive(client, number) }
                println("Type your responses (bye to close the connection with the client):")
                // the connection with the client is closed when leaving use
                val goOn = try {
                    client.use {
                        // the events are processed until the end of the connection with this client
                        serve(client.getOutputStream().writer(), number)
                    }
                } catch (e: IOException) {
                    println("The following error occurred while writing: ${e.message}")
                    true
                }
                // we wait for the end of the reception thread
                reception.join()
                // end of standard input: the server stops
                if (!goOn) return
            }
        }
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        println("The following error occurred on the server: ${e.message}")
    }
}

// the dialog with client no. [clientNum]; returns false if standard input has been closed
fun serve(writer: Writer, clientNum: Int): Boolean {
    while (true) {
        // we wait either for a line typed on the keyboard, or for the departure of the client
        when (val event = events.take()) {
            is ClientLeft if event.clientNum == clientNum -> {
                println("[the client closed the connection]")
                return true
            }
            // departure of a previous client, already handled: it is ignored
            is ClientLeft -> {}
            EndOfInput -> return false
            is Input if event.line.trim().equals("bye", ignoreCase = true) -> {
                println("[connection closed by the server]")
                return true
            }
            is Input -> {
                // the response is sent to the client
                writer.write("${event.line}\r\n")
                writer.flush()
            }
        }
    }
}

// reads the keyboard and puts each typed line in the queue of events
fun readKeyboard() {
    generateSequence { readlnOrNull() }.forEach { line -> events.add(Input(line)) }
    events.add(EndOfInput)
}

// displays the lines sent by the client until the connection is closed
fun receive(client: Socket, clientNum: Int) {
    try {
        client.getInputStream().bufferedReader().lineSequence().forEach { request -> println("<-- $request") }
    } catch (_: IOException) {
        // the connection was closed by the server during the read
    }
    // the departure of the client is signaled to the main program
    events.add(ClientLeft(clientNum))
}
  • lines 19–28: the three types of events, which implement a sealed interface ([sealed], Chapter 4): all of its implementations are known to the compiler, since they must be located in the same package and the same module. [Input] and [ClientLeft] are data classes (the records of the Java program). [EndOfInput], which contains no data, is a data object ([data object]): there is only one instance of it, whose method [toString] simply returns [EndOfInput];
  • line 31: the event queue. [LinkedBlockingQueue] can be used concurrently by multiple threads without any special precautions;
  • Line 41: the listening service, on all of the machine's network interfaces;
  • Line 44: the virtual keyboard-reading thread, which executes the function [readKeyboard] (lines 103–105), passed by its reference [::readKeyboard] (Chapter 7). It places each line read into the queue, then triggers the [EndOfInput] event when standard input is closed. It is launched only once: when a client closes the connection, the current keyboard read operation will be used by the next client. Launching a new read operation for each client would cause two read operations to compete for the same keys;
  • line 47: infinite loop waiting for clients. The user will stop the server with Ctrl-C;
  • line 50: waiting for a client. When a client arrives, the [Socket] returned by [accept] represents the server side of the open connection with that client;
  • line 54: Reading the lines sent by the client is handled by a virtual thread, which executes the function [receive] (lines 109–116). When the connection is closed, this function places a [ClientLeft] event containing the client’s number into the queue;
  • Lines 57–64: Communication with the client is handled by the [serve] function. The connection is closed upon exiting the [use] block. [try] and [use] are expressions: [goOn] receives the Boolean value returned by [serve] or, in the event of a write error, the value of the last expression in the [catch] or [true] block;
  • line 67: wait for the end of the receive thread with [join];
  • line 69: if standard input has been closed, the server shuts down;
  • lines 78–96: the function [serve] retrieves events from the queue (line 81) and processes them using an expression [when]. The subject of [when] is declared within its parentheses ([val event = ...]), which limits its scope to [when]. Since the interface is sealed, the compiler verifies that all cases are handled: if the last branch, [is Input], is removed, the compilation fails with the message “'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Input' branch or an 'else' branch.” The previous branch, which includes a guard, does not count: it does not cover all possible inputs. The branches:
    • line 82: [is ClientLeft] checks the event type; within the branch, [event] is treated as a [ClientLeft] (smart type conversion), from which the property [clientNum] can be read. The guard [if event.clientNum == clientNum] (Kotlin 2.2) verifies that this is the current client: it serves the same purpose as the [when] clause in Java patterns;
    • line 87: a [ClientLeft] event for another client originates from a connection closed by the server itself (command [bye]): it is ignored (empty block);
    • line 88: end of standard input. Since [EndOfInput] is a unique object, it is compared directly, without [is];
    • lines 89–91: the command [bye] closes the connection with the current client;
    • lines 93–96: any other line typed is sent to the client, terminated by \r\n.

Kotlin does not have an equivalent to Java’s record patterns ([case ClientLeft(int number)]), which deconstruct the object within the pattern: we check the type with [is], then read the object’s properties, which are automatically cast. A destructuring declaration ([val (number) = event]) would be possible with a data class, but it is unnecessary here.

Let’s use this server to simulate a web server queried by a client HTTP, in this case [curl]. The generic server is running on port 27101. In another window, we ask [curl] for URL and [http://localhost:27101/example.html]. [curl] then connects to port 27101 on the machine [localhost] and requests the document [/example.html]. Here is the server window, where the response typed by the user (sent via redirection) has been reinserted in its place:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet07.Internet07Kt --args="27101"
Generic server started on 0.0.0.0/0.0.0.0:27101
Waiting for the next client...
Client /127.0.0.1:58112
Type your responses (bye to close the connection with the client):
<-- GET /example.html HTTP/1.1
<-- Host: localhost:27101
<-- User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
<-- Accept: */*
<--
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: generic tcp server
Connection: close
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<html><head><title>Generic server</title></head>
<body><h1>Response of the generic server</h1></body></html>
bye
[connection closed by the server]
Waiting for the next client...
  • line 4: a client has arrived;
  • Lines 6–10: We see the request HTTP sent by [curl], ending with a blank line. A browser would send many more headers (supported languages and formats, compression, cookies, etc.): the reader can test this by requesting the same URL from their browser;
  • Lines 11–17: The user at the keyboard is the actual server here, and they craft the response manually. They stick to the bare minimum: a status line, three headers, a blank line, and the document HTML. They do not specify the document size ([Content-Length]) but indicate that they will close the connection after sending it ([Connection: close]). This is sufficient: when the client sees the connection close, it will know that the response is complete;
  • lines 18–19: the user typed [bye]: the server closes the connection with the client;
  • line 20: the server waits for a new client. We stop it with Ctrl-C.

And here is what [curl] displayed:

> curl -sv http://localhost:27101/example.html
* Host localhost:27101 was resolved.
* IPv6: ::1
* IPv4: 127.0.0.1
*   Trying 127.0.0.1:27101...
* Connected to localhost (127.0.0.1) port 27101
> GET /example.html HTTP/1.1
> Host: localhost:27101
> User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
> Accept: */*
>
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< Server: generic tcp server
< Connection: close
< Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
<
{ [111 bytes data]
* Closing connection
<html><head><title>Generic server</title></head>
<body><h1>Response of the generic server</h1></body></html>

[curl] received exactly what was typed into the server window (lines 12–16 and 19–20) and detected that the connection was closed (line 18). A browser would have displayed the received page HTML, with the title [Generic server] in the tab.

docs.title: 12.6.5. A web client
docs.text:
In the previous example, we saw the HTTP headers sent by [curl]. We’re going to write a web client that takes a URL as a parameter and displays on the screen everything the server sends it. We’ll assume that the server supports the HTTP/1.1 protocol. Our client will send the following request:

GET /document HTTP/1.1
Host: machine:port
User-Agent: web-client-kotlin-course
Connection: close
  • the first line specifies the desired document;
  • the header [Host] identifies the server being queried;
  • the header [User-Agent] identifies our client;
  • the header [Connection] indicates that we want the server to close the connection after responding to us: we will read its response until the end of the stream;
  • the empty line terminates the request.

If, in the first line, we replace [GET] with [HEAD], the server will send us only the HTTP headers from its response, and not the document.

Our web client will be called as follows: [gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet08.Internet08Kt --args="URL command"], where [URL] is the desired URL and [command] is one of the two keywords [GET] or [HEAD]. The program [Internet08.kt] is as follows:

package internet08

import java.io.IOException
import java.net.Socket
import java.net.URI
import java.net.URISyntaxException

// web client: requests a URL with an HTTP/1.1 request written "by hand"
// and displays everything the server sends back (HTTP headers and document)
// call: gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet08.Internet08Kt --args="URL GET|HEAD"

private const val SYNTAX = "Syntax: internet08.Internet08Kt http://machine[:port][/document] GET|HEAD"

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    if (args.size != 2) {
        println(SYNTAX)
        return
    }
    // checking the URL: it must be absolute and use the http scheme
    val uri = parse(args[0])
    if (uri == null) {
        println("Incorrect URL [${args[0]}]. $SYNTAX")
        return
    }
    // checking the command
    val command = args[1].uppercase()
    if (command != "GET" && command != "HEAD") {
        println("The second parameter must be GET or HEAD. $SYNTAX")
        return
    }

    // connection to the web server: port 80 is the default port of HTTP
    val port = if (uri.port == -1) 80 else uri.port
    try {
        Socket(uri.host, port).use { client ->
            val reader = client.getInputStream().bufferedReader()
            val writer = client.getOutputStream().bufferedWriter()
            // the request: command line, HTTP headers, empty line; HTTP requires the end of line \r\n
            val request = listOf(
                "$command ${pathAndQuery(uri)} HTTP/1.1",
                "Host: ${uri.rawAuthority}",
                "User-Agent: web-client-kotlin-course",
                "Connection: close",
            ).joinToString(separator = "\r\n", postfix = "\r\n\r\n")
            writer.write(request)
            // the request leaves on the network in one go
            writer.flush()
            // the response is read until the server closes the connection
            reader.lineSequence().forEach(::println)
        }
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        println("The following error occurred: ${e::class.simpleName} (${e.message})")
    }
}

// a correct absolute http URL, or null
fun parse(url: String): URI? {
    val uri = try {
        URI(url)
    } catch (_: URISyntaxException) {
        return null
    }
    return uri.takeIf { it.isAbsolute && it.scheme == "http" && it.host != null }
}

// the path of the document and the possible parameters, for example /hello?name=Serge
fun pathAndQuery(uri: URI): String {
    val path = uri.rawPath.ifEmpty { "/" }
    return if (uri.rawQuery == null) path else "$path?${uri.rawQuery}"
}

A new feature of this program is the use of the [URI] class ([java.net] package). The program receives a URL (Uniform Resource Locator), a specific form of URI (Uniform Resource Identifier), in the form [http://server:port/path?param1=val1&param2=val2]. The [URI] class breaks this string down into its various components:

  • lines 57–63: the [URI(String)] constructor parses the string and invokes a [URISyntaxException] if it is not a valid URI; the static method [URI.create] does the same thing by launching a [IllegalArgumentException]. [try] is an expression whose value is the constructed URI; in the event of an error, the [catch] block exits the function by returning [null]. The unused exception parameter is named [_]. We then verify that URI is absolute (it begins with a schema), that the schema is [http] (our client cannot perform the TLS negotiation from [https]) and that it refers to a machine: [uri.takeIf { condition \}] returns [uri] if the condition is true, and [null] otherwise. The return type, [URI?], clearly indicates that the function may fail. Once the object [URI] is constructed, we have access to the various elements of URI, which Kotlin presents as properties (the [getXxx] methods in Java). Thus, if the [uri] object was constructed from the string [http://localhost:27110/hello?name=Serge], we have:
    • [uri.scheme]: http;
    • [uri.host]: localhost;
    • [uri.port]: 27110 (-1 if the port is not specified in URL; in that case, it is the schema's default port—80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS);
    • [uri.rawAuthority]: localhost:27110;
    • [uri.rawPath]: /hello;
    • [uri.rawQuery]: name=Serge;
    • The properties [path], [query]… return the same elements, but decoded (we’ll see later what the encoding of a URL is): To build a query, you must use the “raw” versions ([rawXxx]);
    • properties that can take the value [null] ([host], [rawQuery]…) are treated by Kotlin as having a platform type ([String!]): the compiler does not know whether the Java method can return [null], and it is up to the programmer to test this, as shown here;
  • lines 67–69: the path and parameters, as they must appear in the request; an empty path refers to the root [/] of the site: [ifEmpty { "/" \}] returns the string if it is not empty, ["/"] otherwise;
  • line 26: the command, in uppercase, must be [GET] or [HEAD];
  • lines 33–35: connection to the server specified by URL, on port 80 if URL does not specify one;
  • line 37: the write stream is a [BufferedWriter] without automatic flushing, created by the [bufferedWriter()] extension;
  • lines 39–44: the query HTTP, constructed as a list of its lines, joined by [joinToString]: each line is followed by \r\n (the separator), and the last by \r\n\r\n (the suffix), which adds the final empty line. HTTP requires these \r\n line endings to be written explicitly. Note the comma after the last element in the list, which is allowed by Kotlin and makes it easier to add a line;
  • line 47: the request is sent all at once, after it has been fully written;
  • line 49: the response is displayed until the server closes the connection. The function reference [::println] is passed to [forEach] instead of the lambda [{ println(it) \}].

Let’s retrieve only the headers from the root of our test server:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet08.Internet08Kt --args="http://localhost:27110/ HEAD"
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:55:48 GMT
Content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-length: 173

We receive the status line and the headers, followed by a blank line, but not the document. The header [Content-length] indicates the size the document would have had with the command [GET]. With the command [GET] and a document sent in chunks:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet08.Internet08Kt --args="http://localhost:27110/hello?name=Serge GET"
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:55:49 GMT
Transfer-encoding: chunked
Content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

c
Hello Serge!
0

The quotation marks surrounding the arguments of [--args] also protect the character [?] from URL, to which certain command interpreters assign a specific meaning. The document ([Hello Serge!]) is defined by the sizes of its chunks, as we have already seen. Our client displays the raw response; a true HTTP client, on the other hand, must reconstruct the document from the chunks.

A non-existent document:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet08.Internet08Kt --args="http://localhost:27110/unknown GET"
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:55:49 GMT
Content-length: 0

A URL that is being redirected:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet08.Internet08Kt --args="http://localhost:27110/old GET"
HTTP/1.1 302 Temporary Redirect
Date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:55:49 GMT
Content-length: 0
Location: /hello?name=visitor
  • Line 2: The 302 code indicates a redirect—the requested document is temporarily located at a different address. The message following the code is arbitrary: the server for JDK writes [Temporary Redirect]; other servers might write [Found] (the message from RFC) or [Moved Temporarily];
  • Line 5: This address is provided by the [Location] header. It is relative here: the full address is [http://localhost:27110/hello?name=visitor].

Our client stopped there. A web browser, on the other hand, would have automatically requested the new address. That is what our next client will do.

Finally, a request for URL [https] is rejected (the server isn’t even contacted, which allows testing without Internet access):

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet08.Internet08Kt --args="https://kotlinlang.org/docs/ GET"
Incorrect URL [https://kotlinlang.org/docs/]. Syntax: internet08.Internet08Kt http://machine[:port][/document] GET|HEAD

docs.title: 12.6.6. A web client that handles redirects
docs.text:
The previous web client does not handle a possible redirect from the URL it requested. The redirect status codes are as follows:

CodeMeaning301 Moved PermanentlyThe document has permanently changed its address; a browser can save the new address302 FoundThe document is temporarily located at a different address303 See OtherThe response must be requested from another address using the [GET] method (used after submitting a form)307 Temporary Redirect, 308 Permanent RedirectSame as 302 and 301, but the client must resend the request using the same method ([POST] remains [POST])

In all cases, the new address is provided by the [Location] header, in absolute or relative form. Detecting a redirect based on the presence of a word like [moved] in the status line would be unreliable: the message following the code is arbitrary, and we have just seen that the server for JDK responds with [302 Temporary Redirect]. We rely on the status code itself.

The program [Internet09.kt] is as follows:

package internet09

import java.io.IOException
import java.net.Socket
import java.net.URI
import java.net.URISyntaxException

// web client that follows redirections (codes 301, 302, 303, 307, 308)
// call: gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet09.Internet09Kt --args="URL GET|HEAD"

private const val SYNTAX = "Syntax: internet09.Internet09Kt http://machine[:port][/document] GET|HEAD"

// the HTTP status codes that signal a redirection
private val REDIRECTION_CODES = setOf(301, 302, 303, 307, 308)

// maximum number of redirections followed
private const val MAX_REDIRECTIONS = 3

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    if (args.size != 2) {
        println(SYNTAX)
        return
    }
    // uri changes at each redirection: it is a variable, of non-nullable type
    var uri: URI = parse(args[0]) ?: run {
        println("Incorrect URL [${args[0]}]. $SYNTAX")
        return
    }
    val command = args[1].uppercase()
    if (command != "GET" && command != "HEAD") {
        println("The second parameter must be GET or HEAD. $SYNTAX")
        return
    }

    try {
        // one iteration per requested URL
        var nbRedirections = 0
        while (true) {
            // the URL is requested and the possible redirection address is retrieved; null if there is none
            val location = fetch(uri, command) ?: break
            // too many redirections: we give up
            if (nbRedirections == MAX_REDIRECTIONS) {
                println("<-- Giving up: more than $MAX_REDIRECTIONS redirections -->")
                break
            }
            nbRedirections++
            // the new URL: the redirection address can be absolute or relative to the current URL
            uri = uri.resolve(location)
            println("<-- Redirection to $uri -->\n")
        }
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        // IOException (network) or IllegalArgumentException (incorrect redirection address)
        println("The following error occurred: ${e::class.simpleName} (${e.message})")
    }
}

// requests the URL [uri], displays the response of the server
// returns the redirection address, or null if there is no redirection
fun fetch(uri: URI, command: String): String? {
    val port = if (uri.port == -1) 80 else uri.port
    Socket(uri.host, port).use { client ->
        val reader = client.getInputStream().bufferedReader()
        val writer = client.getOutputStream().bufferedWriter()
        // the HTTP request
        val request = listOf(
            "$command ${pathAndQuery(uri)} HTTP/1.1",
            "Host: ${uri.rawAuthority}",
            "User-Agent: web-client-kotlin-course",
            "Connection: close",
        ).joinToString(separator = "\r\n", postfix = "\r\n\r\n")
        writer.write(request)
        writer.flush()

        // the status line, for example: HTTP/1.1 302 Found; "" if the server closed the connection
        val statusLine = reader.readLine() ?: ""
        println(statusLine)
        // the status code is the second field of the line
        val code = statusLine.split(" ").getOrNull(1)?.toIntOrNull()
        val redirection = code in REDIRECTION_CODES

        // the HTTP headers, up to the empty line (or the end of the stream)
        var location: String? = null
        generateSequence { reader.readLine() }
            .takeWhile { header -> header.isNotEmpty() }
            .forEach { header ->
                println(header)
                // the name of an HTTP header is case-insensitive
                if (redirection && header.startsWith("Location:", ignoreCase = true)) {
                    location = header.substringAfter(':').trim()
                }
            }
        println()
        // the possible document
        reader.lineSequence().forEach(::println)
        return location
    }
}

// a correct absolute http URL, or null
fun parse(url: String): URI? {
    val uri = try {
        URI(url)
    } catch (_: URISyntaxException) {
        return null
    }
    return uri.takeIf { it.isAbsolute && it.scheme == "http" && it.host != null }
}

// the path of the document and the possible parameters, for example /hello?name=Serge
fun pathAndQuery(uri: URI): String {
    val path = uri.rawPath.ifEmpty { "/" }
    return if (uri.rawQuery == null) path else "$path?${uri.rawQuery}"
}

Compared to the previous version, the changes are as follows:

  • line 14: the status codes that indicate a redirect, in a read-only set created by [setOf] (Chapter 5);
  • line 17: the maximum number of redirects allowed. Without a limit, a misconfigured server could trap our client in an infinite loop (browsers give up after about twenty redirects);
  • lines 25–27: the URI changes with each redirect; it is a [var]. If it had been declared as in the previous program, its type would have been [URI?], and the smart type conversion following the [uri == null] test would not apply within the loop, where the variable is modified: the compiler would reject [fetch(uri, command)] (“argument type mismatch: actual type is 'URI?', but 'URI' was expected.”). Therefore, we declare the type [URI], which is non-nullable, and the Elvis operator [?:] executes the block [run { … \}]—which displays the error and exits the function—when [parse] evaluates to [null];
  • line 38: the code that was previously executed for a single URL can now be executed successively for multiple URL;
  • line 40: the function [fetch] retrieves the current URL, displays the response, and returns the redirect URL—or [null] if there is no redirect—at which point the Elvis operator exits the loop. Where Java used a *[Optional<String>], Kotlin uses a nullable type, *[String?];
  • lines 42–44: the process aborts if the maximum number of redirects is reached;
  • line 48: the [resolve] method of the [URI] class calculates the new URL. If [location] is an absolute address, it is used as is; if it is relative, it is completed based on the current URL ([uri]). [resolve] throws a [IllegalArgumentException] if the address is incorrect: it is intercepted on line 51, along with the [IOException] from the network. Kotlin does not have a multiple [catch] ([catch (IOException | IllegalArgumentException e)]): here, their common ancestor, [Exception], is intercepted; to distinguish between the two cases, one would write two [catch] blocks, or a single [when (e)] within the block;
  • lines 59–95: the request for a URL:
    • line 75: the status line is read, for example, [HTTP/1.1 302 Temporary Redirect]. The Elvis operator replaces [null] (connection closed by the server before any response) with an empty string;
    • Lines 78–79: The code is extracted—the second field in the line—and checked to see if it is one of the redirect codes. [getOrNull(1)?.toIntOrNull()] returns [null] if the field is missing or is not an integer, and the operator [in] (the [contains] method of the set) returns [false] for [null];
    • Lines 82–89: The headers are read up to the blank line, including the sequence [generateSequence { reader.readLine() \}], which ends at the end of the stream and is terminated by [takeWhile] at the first blank line (which is read but not processed). If there is a redirection, we look for the header [Location], ignoring case since the header names HTTP are case-insensitive: [startsWith("Location:", ignoreCase = true)] replaces Java’s [regionMatches], and [substringAfter(':')] renders what follows the first colon. The lambda in [forEach] modifies the local variable [location]: Kotlin allows this, but Java does not;
    • lines 92–95: the rest of the response is displayed, then the found redirect URL is returned. The [return] placed within the [use] block exits the [fetch] function: the lambda in [use] is “inline,” and a [return] exits the enclosing function (Chapter 7) after the socket is closed.

Let’s look again at URL and [/old]:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet09.Internet09Kt --args="http://localhost:27110/old GET"
HTTP/1.1 302 Temporary Redirect
Date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:55:50 GMT
Content-length: 0
Location: /hello?name=visitor

<-- Redirection to http://localhost:27110/hello?name=visitor -->

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:55:50 GMT
Transfer-encoding: chunked
Content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

e
Hello visitor!
0
  • lines 2–6: the temporary redirection to a relative address;
  • line 7: the new URL, supplemented by [uri.resolve(location)];
  • lines 9–17: the response to the new URL. The document, 0xe = 14 bytes in size, was sent in chunks.

The URL [/moved] is permanently redirected to an absolute address:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet09.Internet09Kt --args="http://localhost:27110/moved GET"
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:55:50 GMT
Content-length: 0
Location: http://localhost:27110/

<-- Redirection to http://localhost:27110/ -->

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:55:50 GMT
Content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-length: 173

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Test server</title></head>
<body><h1>Welcome to the test server of the Kotlin course</h1></body>
</html>

The URL and [/loop] redirect to themselves:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet09.Internet09Kt --args="http://localhost:27110/loop HEAD"
HTTP/1.1 302 Temporary Redirect
Date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:55:50 GMT
Location: /loop

<-- Redirection to http://localhost:27110/loop -->

HTTP/1.1 302 Temporary Redirect
Date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:55:50 GMT
Location: /loop

<-- Redirection to http://localhost:27110/loop -->

HTTP/1.1 302 Temporary Redirect
Date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:55:50 GMT
Location: /loop

<-- Redirection to http://localhost:27110/loop -->

HTTP/1.1 302 Temporary Redirect
Date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:55:50 GMT
Location: /loop

<-- Giving up: more than 3 redirections -->

Our client followed three redirects, then gave up (line 24). With the command [HEAD], no document was sent.

The web server log recorded all requests for the entries [A web client] and [A web client that handles redirects]:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet03.Internet03Kt
Web server started on http://localhost:27110
HEAD / HTTP/1.1 -> 200
GET /hello?name=Serge HTTP/1.1 -> 200
GET /unknown HTTP/1.1 -> 404
GET /old HTTP/1.1 -> 302
GET /old HTTP/1.1 -> 302
GET /hello?name=visitor HTTP/1.1 -> 200
GET /moved HTTP/1.1 -> 301
GET / HTTP/1.1 -> 200
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 -> 302
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 -> 302
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 -> 302
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 -> 302

For each redirection, it shows the request that triggered it, followed by the request to the new address (lines 7–8 and 9–10), and the four requests from the interrupted loop (lines 11–14).

Writing a client HTTP based on TCP helps you understand the protocol, but a real client must handle many other things: TLS encryption, chunked transmission, compression, persistent connections, HTTP/2… The second part of this chapter introduces the [HttpClient] class from JDK, which handles all of this for us and is used directly by Kotlin.

docs.title: 12.7. Classes Specialized for a Protocol
docs.text:
In the previous examples, the HTTP protocol was handled using a TCP client: we had to construct the requests ourselves, parse the status lines and headers, and handle redirects. We could have built a SMTP or POP client in the same way. There are classes specialized for these protocols: they understand the communication protocol between the client and the server and spare the developer from having to manage it. For HTTP, JDK provides the [HttpClient] class, which Kotlin uses directly; for email, we use the Jakarta Mail Java library. We’ll now present them.

The programs in this second part, like those in the first, are packages of the Gradle project [12-internet], numbered consecutively ([internet10] through [internet19]). The project’s [build.gradle.kts] file already declares the two libraries required by some of these programs: Jackson for JSON and Jakarta Mail for email. Whereas the Java course required a separate Maven project for each of these programs, here we only need one additional package. The sample application at the end of the chapter consists of two Gradle subprojects, contained within the [TaxV8] folder. The ports used are in the form 272xx.

docs.title: 12.7.1. The classes URL and HttpURLConnection, now deprecated
docs.text:
Before Java 11, a program in JVM that wanted to communicate with HTTP had two classes, which have been present since the earliest versions of Java:

  • the [URL] class, whose [openStream] method returned, in a single statement, a read stream for the document specified by the URL;
  • the [HttpURLConnection] class, obtained via the [openConnection] method of [URL], which was more flexible: it allowed the user to choose the HTTP method ([GET], [HEAD], [POST]), add headers, and read the status code and response headers.

These classes still exist in Java 25, but they have not aged well: [HttpURLConnection] is entirely synchronous, supports only HTTP/1.1, is used through a sequence of calls with a fixed order (set the headers before writing the document, read the status code before the document…), and report error codes via exceptions. As for the constructors of the [URL] class, which did not correctly parse all URL files, they have been declared obsolete since Java 20: you now create a [URI] object, then convert it if necessary using its [toURL] method. The Kotlin compiler takes into account the [@Deprecated] annotation on Java classes: a small [Old.kt] program containing the [val url = URL("http://localhost:27210/")] statement triggers the following compilation warning:

> kotlinc Old.kt
Old.kt:4:15: warning: 'constructor(p0: String!): URL' is deprecated. Deprecated in Java.
    val url = URL("http://localhost:27210/")
              ^^^

The message indicates that the feature has been marked as deprecated in Java ([Deprecated in Java]); the type [String!] is a “platform type”: Kotlin does not know whether the Java parameter accepts [null]. With the [allWarningsAsErrors = true] option enabled in our projects, this warning would actually prevent compilation.

Java 11 introduced the [HttpClient] class (in the [java.net.http] package), designed from the outset for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, for both synchronous and asynchronous requests, and capable of reusing its connections and being used by multiple threads simultaneously. This is the one to use today, in both Kotlin and Java. We will not discuss [URL] and [HttpURLConnection] further, as the reader may still encounter them in legacy code. Finally, it’s worth noting that the Kotlin ecosystem has its own HTTP clients, such as Ktor Client (JetBrains), which is written using coroutines and can also be used outside of the JVM; Here, we’ll focus on the JDK class, which requires no libraries and, as we’ll see, integrates very well with coroutines.

docs.title: 12.7.2.1. A Test Web Server
docs.text:
To illustrate the capabilities of [HttpClient], we need a more feature-rich web server than the one from Part 1 ([Internet03.kt]): it must accept forms, exchange JSON, and be able to handle delays. So we’ll write a second test server, [Internet10], which is also based on the HTTP server from JDK. To exchange JSON, it uses the Jackson library (Chapter 5), which is declared in the project’s [build.gradle.kts]. Again, it’s not necessary to understand this program in detail—you just need to know what each URL responds with. The [internet10] package contains two files:

12-internet/src/main/kotlin/internet10/
  Internet10.kt      the server
  Person.kt          a person, exchanged in JSON format

The type [Person] is a data class:

package internet10

// a person, exchanged in JSON format
data class Person(val id: Int, val name: String, val age: Int)

As in Chapter 5, Jackson uses the data class’s primary constructor to create objects without any additional modules, using the names of its parameters, which are preserved in the code compiled by the [javaParameters = true] option of [build.gradle.kts].

The file [Internet10.kt] is as follows:

package internet10

import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpExchange
import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer
import java.io.IOException
import java.net.InetAddress
import java.net.InetSocketAddress
import java.net.URLDecoder
import java.util.concurrent.Executors
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper

// a local web server that will be the target of the java.net.http.HttpClient clients
// call: gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet10.Internet10Kt [--args="port"]   (port 27210 by default)
// stop with Ctrl-C

// the home page: an HTML document
private val HOME = """
    <!DOCTYPE html>
    <html lang="en">
    <head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Test server</title></head>
    <body><h1>Welcome to the HttpClient test server</h1></body>
    </html>
""".trimIndent()
// the types of the documents sent
private const val TEXT = "text/plain; charset=utf-8"
private const val JSON = "application/json"
// GET /api/persons/n: a person designated by their number
private val PERSON = Regex("""GET /api/persons/(\d+)""")

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    val port = args.singleOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 27210
    val server = HttpServer.create(InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port), 0)
    server.createContext("/", TestServer()::process)
    // each request is processed by a virtual thread: a slow request does not block the others
    server.executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()
    server.start()
    println("Web server started on http://localhost:$port")
}

class TestServer {
    // a small "database" of persons, exchanged in JSON format, and its lock
    private val persons = mutableListOf(Person(1, "Dupont", 42), Person(2, "Durand", 35))
    private val lock = Any()
    // the objects <-> JSON converter
    private val mapper = JsonMapper.builder().build()

    // processing of a request, then console trace: the request, the client port and the status code
    fun process(exchange: HttpExchange) {
        val start = "${exchange.requestMethod} ${exchange.requestURI} ${exchange.protocol} " +
                "(client port ${exchange.remoteAddress.port})"
        try {
            exchange.use {
                respond(exchange)
                println("$start -> ${exchange.responseCode}")
            }
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            // the connection was cut during the exchange
            println("$start -> error: ${e.message}")
        }
    }

    // the response according to the method and the path of the URL
    private fun respond(exchange: HttpExchange) {
        val route = "${exchange.requestMethod} ${exchange.requestURI.path}"
        // the parameters of the URL
        val urlParameters = parameters(exchange.requestURI.rawQuery)
        when (route) {
            // the home page: an HTML document
            "GET /", "HEAD /" -> send(exchange, 200, HOME, "text/html; charset=utf-8")
            // a text document built from a parameter of the URL
            "GET /hello", "HEAD /hello" ->
                send(exchange, 200, "Hello ${urlParameters["name"] ?: "unknown"}!", TEXT)
            // the HTTP headers received by the server (alphabetical order), sent back as text
            "GET /headers", "HEAD /headers" -> send(exchange, 200,
                exchange.requestHeaders.toSortedMap().entries
                    .joinToString("\n") { (name, values) -> "$name: ${values.joinToString(", ")}" },
                TEXT)
            // temporary redirection (302) to a relative address
            "GET /old", "HEAD /old" -> redirect(exchange, "/hello?name=visitor")
            // a redirection that loops on itself
            "GET /loop", "HEAD /loop" -> redirect(exchange, "/loop")
            // a server error (500 Internal Server Error)
            "GET /error", "HEAD /error" -> exchange.sendResponseHeaders(500, -1)
            // a response that takes its time: the virtual thread is suspended during the wait
            "GET /slow" -> {
                val seconds = urlParameters.getValue("seconds").toInt()
                Thread.sleep(seconds * 1000L)
                send(exchange, 200, "Response obtained after $seconds s", TEXT)
            }
            // a form sent by POST: what was received is described
            "POST /form" -> {
                val fields = parameters(readDocument(exchange))
                val type = exchange.requestHeaders.getFirst("Content-Type")
                val description = fields.entries.joinToString(", ") { (name, value) -> "$name=[$value]" }
                send(exchange, 200, "Content-Type received: $type\nFields received: $description", TEXT)
            }
            // any text sent by POST: it is sent back in upper case
            "POST /text" -> send(exchange, 200,
                "Content-Type received: ${exchange.requestHeaders.getFirst("Content-Type")}" +
                        "\nText received in upper case: ${readDocument(exchange).uppercase()}",
                TEXT)
            // the list of persons
            "GET /api/persons" -> synchronized(lock) {
                send(exchange, 200, mapper.writeValueAsString(persons), JSON)
            }
            // addition of a person: the server gives them a number and responds 201 Created
            "POST /api/persons" -> {
                val newPerson = mapper.readValue(readDocument(exchange), Person::class.java)
                synchronized(lock) {
                    val created = newPerson.copy(id = (persons.maxOfOrNull { it.id } ?: 0) + 1)
                    persons += created
                    exchange.responseHeaders["Location"] = "/api/persons/${created.id}"
                    send(exchange, 201, mapper.writeValueAsString(created), JSON)
                }
            }
            else -> {
                // a person designated by their number, or 404 if they do not exist
                val id = PERSON.matchEntire(route)?.groupValues?.get(1)?.toInt()
                val person = synchronized(lock) { persons.find { it.id == id } }
                if (person != null) {
                    send(exchange, 200, mapper.writeValueAsString(person), JSON)
                } else {
                    // any other URL gives the response 404 Not Found
                    exchange.sendResponseHeaders(404, -1)
                }
            }
        }
    }

    // sending a text document with its status code and its type; no document for HEAD
    private fun send(exchange: HttpExchange, code: Int, text: String, type: String) {
        val bytes = text.toByteArray()
        exchange.responseHeaders["Content-Type"] = type
        if (exchange.requestMethod == "HEAD") {
            exchange.sendResponseHeaders(code, -1)
        } else {
            exchange.sendResponseHeaders(code, bytes.size.toLong())
            exchange.responseBody.write(bytes)
        }
    }

    // temporary redirection (302): Location header, without a document
    private fun redirect(exchange: HttpExchange, address: String) {
        exchange.responseHeaders["Location"] = address
        exchange.sendResponseHeaders(302, -1)
    }

    // the document sent by the client, decoded in UTF-8
    private fun readDocument(exchange: HttpExchange): String = exchange.requestBody.readBytes().decodeToString()

    // the name1=value1&name2=value2 parameters of a URL or of a form, decoded
    private fun parameters(string: String?): Map<String, String> =
        if (string.isNullOrEmpty()) emptyMap()
        else string.split("&").associate { pair ->
            val name = pair.substringBefore("=")
            val value = pair.substringAfter("=", "")
            URLDecoder.decode(name, Charsets.UTF_8) to URLDecoder.decode(value, Charsets.UTF_8)
        }
}

Comments:
