This application demonstrated that [HttpClient] allows us to leverage web resources. The technique is the same every time:

  • determine the URL to query. It is usually preconfigured;
  • query it;
  • find what we’re looking for in the server’s response using regular expressions.

This technique, now known as “web scraping,” is fragile: over time, the URL being queried or the page’s structure may change, and the regular expression that used to find the result may no longer work. It’s a good idea to store this information in a configuration file, but that isn’t always enough; moreover, the terms of use for many sites prohibit it. A robust analysis of a HTML page would, in fact, be better performed using a specialized library—such as the Java jsoup library (which can be used as-is from Kotlin)—rather than with regular expressions. In the next chapter, we’ll see that there are more stable resources on the web, designed for use by programs: web services. Current translation services, for example, all offer an interface of this type, which accepts and returns JSON.

docs.title: 12.7.4. A SMTP client with Jakarta Mail
docs.text:
A SMTP client is a client of a SMTP server—a mail-sending server—whose protocol we introduced in Part 1. Neither JDK nor the Kotlin standard library has a class for email. The de facto standard library for JVM is Jakarta Mail (formerly JavaMail), whose reference implementation is now called Eclipse Angus Mail; a Kotlin program uses it just like any other Java library. It encapsulates the requirements of an email client: the developer does not need to know the details of the SMTP protocol or the MIME message format. Its main classes are [Session] (the configuration), [MimeMessage] (a message), [InternetAddress] (an email address), [MimeMultipart] and [MimeBodyPart] (a multipart message, such as text and attachments), and [Transport], which sends the message. It can also read mail in POP3 and IMAP, and handles the authentication and encryption (TLS) required by real servers.

We cannot send email to a real SMTP server: our test machine does not have Internet access, and, as we mentioned, ISPs block port 25. The email will be sent to a small test server, written in Kotlin and running on the local machine, which will display everything it receives and forward nothing. For real-world use, there are full-featured test servers, such as Mailpit or GreenMail (written in Java), which also provide an interface for viewing received messages.

docs.title: 12.7.4.1. A SMTP test server
docs.text:
Our SMTP server follows the structure of the echo server from Part 1: a loop that waits for clients, one virtual thread per client, and clean termination via Ctrl-C. The service provided to each client is the minimal SMTP dialog presented in Part 1. The [Internet18.kt] program is as follows:

package internet18

import java.io.IOException
import java.net.InetAddress
import java.net.ServerSocket
import java.net.Socket
import java.net.SocketException
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap
import java.util.concurrent.Executors
import kotlin.concurrent.thread

// test SMTP server: it plays the minimal SMTP dialog and displays the messages received,
// without ever delivering them to their recipients
// call: gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet18.Internet18Kt [--args="port"]   (port 27225 by default)
// stop with Ctrl-C

private val connections: MutableSet<Socket> = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()
@Volatile
private var stopping = false

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    val port = args.singleOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 27225
    try {
        // the server only accepts the clients of the local machine (loopback address)
        ServerSocket(port, 50, InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress()).use { listener ->
            Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { services ->
                stopOnCtrlC(listener)
                println("Test SMTP server started on ${listener.localSocketAddress}")
                try {
                    var clientNum = 0
                    while (true) {
                        val client = listener.accept()
                        connections += client
                        val number = clientNum++
                        services.submit { serve(client, number) }
                    }
                } catch (e: SocketException) {
                    if (!stopping) throw e
                    println("Server stop requested")
                    connections.forEach(Socket::close)
                }
            }
        }
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        println("The following error occurred on the server: ${e.message}")
    }
}

// Ctrl-C: closing of the listening service, then wait for the end of the main program
fun stopOnCtrlC(listener: ServerSocket) {
    val main = Thread.currentThread()
    Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(thread(start = false) {
        stopping = true
        try {
            listener.close()
            main.join()
        } catch (_: Exception) {
            // we stop anyway
        }
    })
}

// the SMTP dialog with a client: C: lines received from the client, S: lines sent by the server
fun serve(client: Socket, clientNum: Int) {
    println("--- start of the dialog with client $clientNum (${client.remoteSocketAddress})")
    try {
        client.use {
            val reader = client.getInputStream().bufferedReader()
            val writer = client.getOutputStream().writer()
            // sending a response line, also displayed on the console; SMTP requires \r\n line endings
            fun reply(response: String) {
                println("S: $response")
                writer.write("$response\r\n")
                writer.flush()
            }
            // the envelope of the current message: sender and recipients
            var sender: String? = null
            val recipients = mutableListOf<String>()
            // welcome message
            reply("220 smtp.test ESMTP test server of the Kotlin course")
            while (true) {
                val command = reader.readLine() ?: break
                println("C: $command")
                // the verb: the first four characters, regardless of case
                val verb = command.take(4).uppercase()
                // what follows the ":" character in MAIL FROM:<address> and RCPT TO:<address>
                val address = command.substringAfter(':').trim()
                when (verb) {
                    "EHLO" -> {
                        // response on several lines: 250-... then 250 ...
                        reply("250-smtp.test hello")
                        reply("250-SIZE 10485760")
                        reply("250 8BITMIME")
                    }
                    "HELO" -> reply("250 smtp.test hello")
                    "MAIL" -> {
                        sender = address
                        recipients.clear()
                        reply("250 2.1.0 Ok")
                    }
                    "RCPT" -> {
                        recipients += address
                        reply("250 2.1.5 Ok")
                    }
                    "DATA" -> {
                        // the sender and the recipients are required first
                        if (sender == null || recipients.isEmpty()) {
                            reply("503 5.5.1 Give the sender and the recipients first")
                            continue
                        }
                        reply("354 End data with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>")
                        // the message: all the lines up to a line reduced to a dot
                        var nbLines = 0
                        var line = reader.readLine()
                        while (line != null && line != ".") {
                            println("C: $line")
                            nbLines++
                            line = reader.readLine()
                        }
                        // the client closed the connection before the end of the message
                        if (line == null) {
                            println("[incomplete message: connection closed by the client]")
                            return
                        }
                        println("C: .")
                        val to = recipients.joinToString(", ")
                        println("[message from $sender to $to: $nbLines lines]")
                        reply("250 2.0.0 Ok: message accepted")
                        sender = null
                        recipients.clear()
                    }
                    "RSET" -> {
                        sender = null
                        recipients.clear()
                        reply("250 2.0.0 Ok")
                    }
                    "NOOP" -> reply("250 2.0.0 Ok")
                    "QUIT" -> {
                        reply("221 2.0.0 Bye")
                        return
                    }
                    else -> reply("502 5.5.2 Command not recognized")
                }
            }
        }
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        if (stopping) {
            println("Dialog with client $clientNum interrupted by the server stop")
        } else {
            println("The following error occurred with client $clientNum : ${e.message}")
        }
    } finally {
        connections -= client
        println("--- end of the dialog with client $clientNum")
    }
}

We’ll only comment on what’s new compared to the echo server:

  • line 25: the server listens only on the loopback address; only programs on the same machine can connect to it. The second parameter (50) is the size of the connection queue;
  • Lines 71–74: A local function (Chapter 3), declared within [serve], that sends a response line to the client, terminated by \r\n as required by SMTP, and displays it on the console, preceded by [S:]. Lines received from the client are displayed preceded by [C:], as in the sample dialogs from Part 1. The local function has access to the variable [writer] from the enclosing function. The Java program used a lambda here and had to declare its own functional interface, [Responder], because the functional interfaces of JDK ([Consumer<String>]…) do not allow the controlled exception [IOException] thrown by [write]; in Kotlin, which does not have controlled exceptions, this workaround is unnecessary;
  • lines 68–69: the socket’s read and write streams, in UTF-8 (the default character set for [bufferedReader] and [writer]). They do not need to be closed separately: closing the socket with [use] closes them;
  • lines 77–78: the header of the current message: the sender announced by [MAIL FROM], of type [String?] since it may not have been announced yet, and the recipients announced by [RCPT TO];
  • line 80: the welcome message: in SMTP, the server speaks first;
  • line 82: reading a command; the Elvis operator exits the loop when the client has closed the connection ([readLine] then becomes [null]). Kotlin does not allow assignment within a condition ([while ((command = reader.readLine()) != null)] in Java); this form replaces it;
  • lines 85–87: The command verb is formed from its first four characters ([EHLO], [MAIL], [RCPT]…), capitalized. [take(4)] returns the first four characters, or the entire string if it is shorter. The Kotlin function [uppercase] is independent of the machine language (it uses [Locale.ROOT]): In Turkish, the uppercase version of [i] is not [I], and the Java program had to specify [Locale.ROOT]. [substringAfter(':')] returns the character following the first character of [:] ([MAIL FROM:<address>]), or the entire string if there is none;
  • Lines 89–93: The response to *[EHLO] consists of several lines. In it, the server lists its capabilities: the maximum message size ([SIZE]) and support for 8-bit encoded characters ([8BITMIME]*);
  • lines 107–109: the command [DATA] is rejected if the sender or recipients have not been specified; [continue] proceeds to the next command. Starting with Kotlin 1.4, [break] and [continue] can be used without a label within a [when] placed in a loop;
  • lines 111–128: the message itself. The server prompts the client to send it (code 354), then reads and displays all lines up to a line reduced to a single dot, and acknowledges receipt (code 250). If the client closes the connection before the end of the message, the message is discarded (lines 121–123);
  • lines 138–140: the client has finished; the server responds and closes the connection, exiting the function: [return], defined within the lambda of [use], exits [serve] itself (non-local return, permitted because [use] is a function of [inline]), and [use] closes the socket;
  • line 142: any other command is rejected;
  • lines 50–56: termination via Ctrl-C, as in the echo server: the function [thread] of [kotlin.concurrent] creates the thread that runs when JVM terminates, without starting it ([start = false]), and [addShutdownHook] saves it.

This server doesn't perform many checks and doesn't handle the [STARTTLS] and [AUTH] extensions: all you need to do is look at what Jakarta Mail sends.

docs.title: 12.7.4.2. The SMTP client
docs.text:
The [Internet19] program prompts the user for the email’s details (sender, recipients, subject, attachments, body), then sends it to the SMTP server specified as an argument. It uses the Jakarta Mail library, which is declared in the project’s [build.gradle.kts] file with the following line:

    implementation("org.eclipse.angus:angus-mail:2.0.3")

The [angus-mail] dependency provides the implementation and, via transitive dependency, the API, [jakarta.mail], and [jakarta.activation] libraries that it uses. The code uses only API, found in the [jakarta.mail] and [jakarta.mail.internet] packages. The [Internet19.kt] program is as follows:

package internet19

import jakarta.mail.Message.RecipientType
import jakarta.mail.MessagingException
import jakarta.mail.Session
import jakarta.mail.Transport
import jakarta.mail.internet.InternetAddress
import jakarta.mail.internet.MimeBodyPart
import jakarta.mail.internet.MimeMessage
import jakarta.mail.internet.MimeMultipart
import java.io.File
import java.io.IOException
import java.util.Properties

// sending an e-mail with Jakarta Mail
// call: gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet19.Internet19Kt --args="smtpServer port"
// the attachments are looked for in the current folder

private const val SYNTAX =
    "Syntax: gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet19.Internet19Kt --args=\"smtpServer port\""

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    if (args.size != 2 || !args[1].matches(Regex("""\d{1,5}"""))) {
        println(SYNTAX)
        return
    }
    val (server, port) = args

    // input of the elements of the mail
    val senderAddress = input("Sender")
    val recipients = input("Recipients (separated by commas)")
    val copies = input("Copy to (Cc)")
    val blindCopies = input("Blind copy to (Bcc)")
    val subjectLine = input("Subject")
    val attachments = input("Attachments (separated by commas)")
    // the text: several lines, ended by an empty line
    println("Text of the message (ended by an empty line):")
    val text = generateSequence { readlnOrNull() }
        .takeWhile { it.isNotEmpty() }
        .joinToString("") { "$it\n" }

    try {
        // the mail session: it contains the configuration of the SMTP client
        val properties = Properties().apply {
            this["mail.smtp.host"] = server
            this["mail.smtp.port"] = port
        }
        val session = Session.getInstance(properties)

        // the message
        val message = MimeMessage(session).apply {
            setFrom(InternetAddress(senderAddress, true).also { it.validate() })
            setRecipients(RecipientType.TO, addresses(recipients))
            setRecipients(RecipientType.CC, addresses(copies))
            setRecipients(RecipientType.BCC, addresses(blindCopies))
            setSubject(subjectLine, "UTF-8")
        }
        // a multipart message: first the text, in UTF-8 transported as is (8 bits)
        val textPart = MimeBodyPart().apply {
            setText(text, "UTF-8")
            setHeader("Content-Transfer-Encoding", "8bit")
        }
        val content = MimeMultipart(textPart)
        // then the attachments, designated by their path
        val names = attachments.split(",").filter { it.isNotBlank() }.map { file ->
            val part = MimeBodyPart()
            part.attachFile(File(file.trim()))
            content.addBodyPart(part)
            part.fileName
        }
        message.setContent(content)

        // sending: Transport knows the SMTP protocol; the message knows the MIME format
        Transport.send(message)

        // summary of the sending
        println("Sending successful...")
        println("Subject: ${message.subject}")
        println("Recipients: ${message.list(RecipientType.TO)}")
        println("Cc: ${message.list(RecipientType.CC)}")
        println("Bcc: ${message.list(RecipientType.BCC)}")
        println("Attachments: ${names.joinToString(", ")}")
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        when (e) {
            is MessagingException, is IOException -> {
                println("The following error occurred: ${e.javaClass.simpleName} : ${e.message}")
                e.cause?.let { println("Cause: $it") }
            }
            else -> throw e
        }
    }
}

// a list of addresses separated by commas; each address is checked
fun addresses(list: String): Array<out InternetAddress> =
    InternetAddress.parse(list, true).onEach { it.validate() }

// the addresses of a category of recipients, separated by commas
fun MimeMessage.list(type: RecipientType): String = InternetAddress.toString(getRecipients(type))

// input of a line from the keyboard
fun input(label: String): String {
    print("$label : ")
    return readlnOrNull()?.trim() ?: ""
}

Comments:

  • lines 23–27: The program expects two arguments: the SMTP server and its port (one to five digits, validated by a regular expression). The destructuring assignment on line 27 assigns the first two elements of the array to two variables;
  • lines 30–40: the email content is entered using the [input] function (lines 102–104), which displays the label via [print] (without a line break) and then reads one line at a time via [readlnOrNull], [null] at the end of the data. The message text consists of several lines, ending with a blank line: [generateSequence] produces the sequence of lines read, up to the first [null]; [takeWhile] stops at the first blank line, and [joinToString] combines the lines, each followed by a line break. Since the sequence is lazy, no lines are read beyond the blank line;
  • Lines 44–48: the messaging session. Its configuration is an object [Properties]: here, the machine and port of the SMTP server. The function [apply] executes its block with the object as the receiver ([this]) and then returns the object; [this["key"] = value] calls the [put] method of the dictionary. For a real server, we would add [mail.smtp.auth=true], [mail.smtp.starttls.enable=true] (encryption via [STARTTLS]), and provide the username and password to [Transport.send];
  • lines 51–56: the message, configured in a [apply] block:
    • line 52: the sender, a [InternetAddress] object. The second parameter of the constructor ([true]) requires a strict analysis of the address, and [validate], called by [also] before the address is passed to [setFrom], additionally verifies that it has the form [name@domain]; an incorrect address triggers a [AddressException];
    • lines 53–55: the recipients, those in the “Cc” (Carbon Copy) field, and those in the “Bcc” (Blind Carbon Copy) field. Recipients in the “Bcc” field receive the message, but the other recipients are not aware of this. The function [addresses] (lines 95–96) parses a comma-separated list of addresses using [InternetAddress.parse], and checks each one using [onEach], which applies an action to each element and returns the array itself. Its return type, [Array<out InternetAddress>], is the type that Kotlin assigns to the Java array returned by [parse]: an array from which [InternetAddress] (variance, Chapter 4) can be read, accepted by [setRecipients];
    • line 56: the subject, along with its character set;
  • lines 59–63: the message consists of several parts ([MimeMultipart]). The first is the text, in UTF-8. The header [Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit] specifies that it should be transmitted as-is, in 8-bit mode (the server indicated that it accepts this); without it, Jakarta Mail would choose its own encoding (quoted-printable or base64), which would make the text difficult to read in the server’s display;
  • Lines 65–69: attachments, identified by their file paths. [filter] excludes empty names, and [map] creates a part for each file, which it adds to the message, and returns its name: [names] is the list of attachment names. A relative path is relative to the current folder; in our tests, the file [attachment.txt] is located at the root of the [12-internet] project, which is the current folder for [gradlew run]. [attachFile] creates a section whose content will be read from the file at the time of sending;
  • line 74: Sending the message using the static method [Transport.send], which connects to the server specified by the session, executes the dialog SMTP, and transmits the message in the MIME format;
  • lines 77–82: a summary of the transmission. The extension function [list] of [MimeMessage] (line 99) combines the addresses of a category of recipients into a string using [InternetAddress.toString]; it allows you to write [message.list(RecipientType.TO)]. [message.subject] calls the method [getSubject];
  • Lines 83–89: An invalid address triggers a [AddressException]; a sending error triggers another [MessagingException], and the cause is displayed. A missing attachment is only detected at the time of sending: it triggers a [MessagingException], the cause of which is a [FileNotFoundException]. Since Kotlin does not have multiple [catch] exceptions, all exceptions are caught here; then a [when] exception sorts the two handled categories ([is MessagingException, is IOException]); the others are rethrown by [throw e]. This is an alternative to the two [catch] blocks in [Internet17.kt], which avoids repeating the processing.

The test server SMTP is launched in a command window on port 27225 by [gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet18.Internet18Kt]. In another window, from the [12-internet] folder, a message is sent to two recipients, with one recipient in copy, one in blind copy, and an attachment (keyboard input appears after each label):

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet19.Internet19Kt --args="localhost 27225"
Sender : alice@example.org
Recipients (separated by commas) : bob@example.com, carole@example.com
Copy to (Cc) : david@example.com
Blind copy to (Bcc) : eve@example.com
Subject : Minutes of the meeting at the café
Attachments (separated by commas) : attachment.txt
Text of the message (ended by an empty line):
Hello,
here are the minutes of the meeting at the café.
Best regards,
Alice

Sending successful...
Subject: Minutes of the meeting at the café
Recipients: bob@example.com, carole@example.com
Cc: david@example.com
Bcc: eve@example.com
Attachments: attachment.txt

The file [attachment.txt] contains two lines of text. Here is what the server displayed:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet18.Internet18Kt
Test SMTP server started on localhost/127.0.0.1:27225
--- start of the dialog with client 0 (/127.0.0.1:55324)
S: 220 smtp.test ESMTP test server of the Kotlin course
C: EHLO localhost
S: 250-smtp.test hello
S: 250-SIZE 10485760
S: 250 8BITMIME
C: MAIL FROM:<alice@example.org>
S: 250 2.1.0 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<bob@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<carole@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<david@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<eve@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: DATA
S: 354 End data with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>
C: Date: Sun, 4 Oct 2026 13:04:03 +0200 (CEST)
C: From: alice@example.org
C: To: bob@example.com, carole@example.com
C: Cc: david@example.com
C: Message-ID: <1513712028.1.1791111843048@localhost>
C: Subject: =?UTF-8?Q?Minutes_of_the_meeting_at_the_caf=C3=A9?=
C: MIME-Version: 1.0
C: Content-Type: multipart/mixed;
C:     boundary="----=_Part_0_1603195447.1791111843012"
C:
C: ------=_Part_0_1603195447.1791111843012
C: Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8
C: Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit
C:
C: Hello,
C: here are the minutes of the meeting at the café.
C: Best regards,
C: Alice
C:
C: ------=_Part_0_1603195447.1791111843012
C: Content-Type: text/plain; charset=us-ascii; name=attachment.txt
C: Content-Transfer-Encoding: 7bit
C: Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=attachment.txt
C:
C: This is the attachment of the test mail.
C: It contains two lines.
C:
C: ------=_Part_0_1603195447.1791111843012--
C: .
[message from <alice@example.org> to <bob@example.com>, <carole@example.com>, <david@example.com>, <eve@example.com>: 28 lines]
S: 250 2.0.0 Ok: message accepted
C: QUIT
S: 221 2.0.0 Bye
--- end of the dialog with client 0
Server stop requested

Comments:

  • line 5: Jakarta Mail identifies itself with the local machine name, in this case [localhost];
  • Lines 9–18: the message envelope: the sender, followed by all recipients, including the blind carbon copy recipient ([eve@example.com]). The envelope determines to whom the message is delivered;
  • lines 21–29: the message headers, which make up what the recipients will see: the date, the sender, the recipients [To] and [Cc], a unique message identifier ([Message-ID]), the subject… The blind carbon copy recipient is not listed here: this is how it remains hidden. The subject line contains an accented character; since the headers can only contain ASCII characters, it has been encoded according to RFC 2047: [=?UTF-8?Q?...?=] means “text UTF-8 encoded in quoted-printable,” with each non-ASCII byte written as [=XX] in hexadecimal ([=C3=A9] for the two bytes of [é]) and each space as [_];
  • Lines 28–29: The message is in the format MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, RFC 2045 and following): it consists of several parts ([multipart/mixed]), separated by a boundary line ([boundary]) chosen at random by Jakarta Mail. A header that is too long may be wrapped to the next line, provided that the next line begins with a space or a tab (in this case, a tab);
  • lines 31–39: the first part, the message text, in 8-bit UTF-8: it is readable as is;
  • Lines 40–47: The second part, the attachment. Jakarta Mail recognized a text file ([text/plain]) containing only ASCII characters ([charset=us-ascii]) and transmitted it as is ([7bit]); had it contained other characters, such as [è], it would have encoded it in quoted-printable, which leaves the ASCII characters unencoded and encodes the others ([=C3=A8] for [è]). A binary file (an image, for example) would have been encoded in Base64, which represents arbitrary bytes using 64 characters from the ASCII set. The header [Content-Disposition: attachment] indicates that this is an attachment and provides its name;
  • lines 48–49: the closing delimiter, followed by two dashes, then the line reduced to a single period that ends the message;
  • line 50: our server received a message for four recipients;
  • lines 52–53: Jakarta Mail ends the session;
  • line 55: the server was stopped with Ctrl-C after the tests.

An invalid address is rejected before any message is sent:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet19.Internet19Kt --args="localhost 27225"
Sender : alice@example.org
Recipients (separated by commas) : bob.example.com
Copy to (Cc) :
Blind copy to (Bcc) :
Subject : test
Attachments (separated by commas) :
Text of the message (ended by an empty line):
text

The following error occurred: AddressException : Missing final '@domain'

If the server SMTP is not available, a [MailConnectException]—a variant of [MessagingException]—is launched; this is caused by the [ConnectException] from the socket:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet19.Internet19Kt --args="localhost 27299"
Sender : alice@example.org
Recipients (separated by commas) : bob@example.com
Copy to (Cc) :
Blind copy to (Bcc) :
Subject : test
Attachments (separated by commas) :
Text of the message (ended by an empty line):
text

The following error occurred: MailConnectException : Couldn't connect to host, port: localhost, 27299; timeout -1
Cause: java.net.ConnectException: Connection refused

docs.title: 12.8. Asynchronous Network Programming: From NIO Channels to Virtual Threads
docs.text:
With the exception of the [sendAsync] requests from [HttpClient], the programs in this chapter use blocking network operations, executed by threads (virtual threads for servers). This is not the only way to do it, and the reader will encounter in existing code—whether in Java or Kotlin—the two other models that JDK proposed prior to Java 21.

The first, introduced in Java 1.4, is the non-blocking I/O model from the [java.nio.channels] package. A [SocketChannel] set to non-blocking mode ([channel.configureBlocking(false)]) immediately yields control, regardless of whether there is data to read; a [Selector] object allows a single thread to monitor a large number of channels and be woken up when one of them is ready (a new connection to accept, data to read, space to write to). The program then runs in a single loop that, each time it is woken up, processes the ready channels. Data is read in blocks into byte buffers ([ByteBuffer]): it is up to the program to reconstruct the lines—since a line may be split between two blocks—and to keep track, for each client, of the current state of their dialogue.

The second, introduced in Java 7 (NIO.2), is for asynchronous channels: [AsynchronousSocketChannel] and [AsynchronousServerSocketChannel]. Each operation is initiated with a callback object ([CompletionHandler]), whose method [completed] is executed by a thread from a pool at the end of the operation. A client connection is thus written as [channel.connect(address, null, handler)], and the handler’s [completed] method must initiate the next read, whose [completed] method will initiate the next one, and so on. The code is lengthy, and the dialog logic is scattered across several callback methods.

Both of these models are efficient: they allow a few threads to handle thousands of connections. But they are difficult to program and debug; they are primarily used through libraries such as Netty, on which many servers are based. Java 21’s virtual threads have made these techniques unnecessary for most applications: a virtual thread blocked on a network operation does not block any system threads, and the code reads in the order in which it executes, just like synchronous code. The generic client TCP ([Internet06.kt]) is an example of this: a virtual thread reads from the keyboard while the main thread reads from the network, using simple calls to [readLine].

Keep in mind that asynchrony offers little benefit to a client with only one connection: its thread has nothing else to do but wait for the response. It is, however, essential for a server: a server that serves its clients using blocked platform threads ties up one system thread per client; with virtual threads or non-blocking channels, just a few system threads are enough to serve a large number of clients. This is what the server in the following example application does.

docs.title: 12.8.1. What about coroutines?
docs.text:
Kotlin has its own solution for asynchrony: the coroutines covered in Chapter 9. Can we write the echo server using them? Yes, but you need to understand the benefits. The methods of *[Socket]* and *[ServerSocket]* ([accept]*, [readLine]*…) are blocking, not suspended: a coroutine that calls them blocks the thread executing it. Therefore, like any blocking I/O, they are executed on the [Dispatchers.IO] dispatcher (Chapter 9), whose threads are designed for this purpose. The program [Internet04Coroutines.kt] is the “coroutine” version of the echo server [Internet04.kt]:

package internet04coroutines

import java.io.IOException
import java.io.PrintWriter
import java.net.ServerSocket
import java.net.Socket
import java.net.SocketException
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap
import kotlin.concurrent.thread
import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers
import kotlinx.coroutines.launch
import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking
import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext

// echo server, coroutine version: each client is served by a coroutine
// the blocking socket operations are executed by the threads of the Dispatchers.IO dispatcher
// call: gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet04coroutines.Internet04CoroutinesKt --args="port" ; stop with Ctrl-C

private const val SYNTAX = "Syntax: internet04coroutines.Internet04CoroutinesKt port"

// the service connections in progress, closed when the server stops
private val connections: MutableSet<Socket> = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()

// has the server been asked to stop?
@Volatile
private var stopping = false

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    val port = args.singleOrNull()?.toIntOrNull()
    if (port == null || port !in 1..65535) {
        println(SYNTAX)
        return
    }
    try {
        ServerSocket(port).use { listener ->
            stopOnCtrlC(listener)
            println("Echo server (coroutines) started on ${listener.localSocketAddress}")
            // runBlocking only ends after all the coroutines launched in its block
            runBlocking {
                try {
                    var clientNum = 0
                    while (true) {
                        // wait for a client: the blocking call is handed to a thread of Dispatchers.IO
                        val client = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { listener.accept() }
                        connections.add(client)
                        val number = clientNum++
                        // one coroutine per client, executed on Dispatchers.IO; its end is not awaited
                        launch(Dispatchers.IO) { serve(client, number) }
                    }
                } catch (e: SocketException) {
                    // accept fails when Ctrl-C closes the listening service
                    if (!stopping) throw e
                    println("Server stop requested")
                    // the connections in progress are closed: the service coroutines end
                    connections.forEach { it.close() }
                }
            }
        }
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        println("The following error occurred on the server: ${e.message}")
    }
}

// Ctrl-C: closing of the listening service, then wait for the end of the main program
fun stopOnCtrlC(listener: ServerSocket) {
    val main = Thread.currentThread()
    Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(thread(start = false) {
        stopping = true
        listener.close()
        main.join()
    })
}

// the service provided to a client: the same code as in the virtual-thread version
fun serve(client: Socket, clientNum: Int) {
    println("Start of the service to client $clientNum (${client.remoteSocketAddress}) " +
            "by thread [${Thread.currentThread().name}]")
    try {
        client.use {
            val reader = client.getInputStream().bufferedReader()
            val writer = PrintWriter(client.getOutputStream(), true, Charsets.UTF_8)
            while (true) {
                val request = reader.readLine() ?: break
                println("<--- client $clientNum : $request")
                writer.println("[$request]")
                println("---> client $clientNum : [$request]")
            }
        }
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        if (stopping) {
            println("Service to client $clientNum interrupted by the server stop")
        } else {
            println("The following error occurred while serving client $clientNum : ${e.message}")
        }
    } finally {
        connections.remove(client)
        println("End of the service to client $clientNum")
    }
}

The [build.gradle.kts] in the project declares the [implementation("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-core:1.11.0")] dependency for this purpose (Chapter 9). Essentially, only the [main] function has changed:

  • Line 39: The customer wait loop runs in a coroutine, created by [runBlocking], which blocks the main thread until all coroutines launched within its block have finished: this is structured concurrency as described in Chapter 9. It replaces [ExecutorService] from the previous version, which waited for all services to finish before closing;
  • Line 44: The blocking wait for a client is executed by a thread of [Dispatchers.IO]. The main coroutine is suspended during this time, then resumes with *[Socket]*, returned by [accept]*. If [accept] throws an exception (closing the listening service with Ctrl-C), [withContext]* rethrows it in the main coroutine, where it is intercepted on line 50;
  • line 48: each client is served by a child coroutine, launched on [Dispatchers.IO]. The function [serve] is exactly the same as that of the virtual-thread server: ordinary blocking code;
  • lines 50–55: Upon termination, the current connections are closed, as before. This is essential: coroutine termination is cooperative (Chapter 9), and a coroutine blocked in [readLine] would never see it. Closing the socket causes the read operation to fail, and the coroutine terminates; [runBlocking] then yields control;
  • line 77: the log shows the name of the thread running the service.

The server is running on port 27100; client A sends two lines and then types [bye], client B sends one line, and then the server is stopped with Ctrl-C:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet04coroutines.Internet04CoroutinesKt --args="27100"
Echo server (coroutines) started on 0.0.0.0/0.0.0.0:27100
Start of the service to client 0 (/127.0.0.1:54136) by thread [DefaultDispatcher-worker-1]
<--- client 0 : line1A
---> client 0 : [line1A]
Start of the service to client 1 (/127.0.0.1:54142) by thread [DefaultDispatcher-worker-3]
<--- client 0 : line2A
---> client 0 : [line2A]
<--- client 1 : line1B
---> client 1 : [line1B]
End of the service to client 0
Server stop requested
Service to client 1 interrupted by the server stop
End of the service to client 1

In the window of Client B, who typed their second line after the server stopped:

> gradlew -q run -Pmain=internet05.Internet05Kt --args="localhost 27100"
Connected to the server localhost/127.0.0.1:27100 from /127.0.0.1:54142
Request (bye to stop): line1B
Response: [line1B]
Request (bye to stop): line2B
The server closed the connection

The behavior is that of [Internet04.kt]. Lines 3 and 6 of the log show that both services are executed by threads from the [DefaultDispatcher-worker-N] pool, which [Dispatchers.IO] shares with [Dispatchers.Default]. And that is the main limitation of this version: each connected client ties up a platform thread, which is blocked in [readLine]. [Dispatchers.IO] has only 64 by default: the 65th client (e) would have to wait for one of the first 64 to disconnect. We could increase this limit ([Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1000)]), but that would revert us to the “one system thread per client” model. The solution, as discussed in Chapter 9, is to run blocking coroutines on a dispatcher whose threads are virtual: [Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher()]. This results in exactly the same server as [Internet04.kt], with structured concurrency added.

For a coroutine to be truly suspended—rather than blocked—during a network operation, a library is needed whose I/O operations are [suspend] functions, built on top of the non-blocking channels of NIO. This is what, for example, the Ktor network module (the JetBrains web framework) offers, whose sockets provide line-by-line suspended reads. For a server like ours, which performs blocking I/O, virtual threads remain the simplest solution; coroutines become particularly useful when the application already uses them (a [HttpClient] client with [sendAsync(...).await()], an Android app, a Ktor server, etc.).

docs.title: 12.9. Sample application, version 8: tax calculation server
12.9.1. The architecture of the new version
docs.text:
We’ll revisit the tax calculation application. In version 5 (Chapter 6), it consisted of three layers, each in its own Gradle subproject: [dao] (tax brackets), [business] (the calculation), and [ui] (the console dialog), assembled by Spring’s dependency injection container; versions 6 and 7 replaced the [dao] layer with database access. We’ll start with version 5, which is simpler to run: the new version would work the same way with the [dao] layer from versions 6 and 7.

We will deploy this architecture across two machines:

  • A [server] machine hosts the [business] and [dao] layers from version 5. A layer named [server] is built to allow clients on the network to query the tax calculation service using a text-based protocol named TCP;
  • a machine named [client] hosts the [ui] layer of version 5. A new layer, [business]—which acts as a client to the server’s TCP layer—enables the server to query the tax calculation service.

The architecture is undergoing a major change: Version 5 was a single-user application; Version 8 is becoming a client-server application, and the server will be able to serve multiple clients simultaneously. However, we will write only two new classes, [TaxServer] and [TaxBusinessTcp]—one for option data—and two main programs; everything else is reused without modification.

The [TaxV8] application consists of two Gradle subprojects within the [12-internet] project, which use the subprojects from version 5 via a composite build, just like versions 6 and 7 (Chapters 10 and 11):

12-internet/
  settings.gradle.kts             the subprojects of TaxV8, the composite build ../06-architectures
  build.gradle.kts                the root project (InternetNN programs), which sets the version of the Kotlin plugin
  TaxV8/
    tax-server/
      build.gradle.kts            dependencies: tax-business (V5, which brings tax-dao), Spring
      server.properties           configuration of the [dao] layer and of the server
      TaxData.txt                 the tax brackets
      src/main/kotlin/tax/server/
        Main.kt                   integration of the layers, starting the server
        ServerOptions.kt          the server options
        TaxServer.kt              the [server] layer
    tax-client/
      build.gradle.kts            dependencies: tax-business and tax-ui (V5), Spring
      src/main/kotlin/tax/client/
        TaxBusinessTcp.kt         the [business] layer of the client: a TCP client
        Main.kt                   integration of the layers, dialog

The [settings.gradle.kts] file in the [12-internet] project is as follows:

// Gradle downloads the JDK requested by jvmToolchain(25) itself if it does not find it on the machine
plugins {
    id("org.gradle.toolchains.foojay-resolver-convention") version "1.0.0"
}

rootProject.name = "internet"

// version 8 of the [Tax] application: a TCP server and its client, two subprojects
include("TaxV8:tax-server", "TaxV8:tax-client")

// the layers of version 5 (chapter 6) are reused: composite build
includeBuild("../06-architectures")
  • Lines 1–4: the plugin that allows Gradle to download JDK 25 itself if it cannot find it on the machine (Chapter 2);
  • line 6: the name of the root project, which is the [InternetNN] project;
  • line 9: the two subprojects of version 8, identified by their paths: [TaxV8:tax-server] is the [TaxV8/tax-server] folder. The intermediate folder [TaxV8], which has no build file, is an implicit project;
  • line 12: the composite build. The build from Chapter 6 is included in this one: a dependency declared by its coordinates, such as [examples.tax:tax-business:5.0], is satisfied by the subproject of the included build that has those coordinates ([group], name, [version]), compiled as needed. There is nothing to install beforehand: this is the simpler equivalent of the [mvn install] required by the Maven version of the Java course.

The root project ([12-internet/build.gradle.kts]) applies the plugin [kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.20"]: its version applies to the subprojects, which use the plugin without specifying the version again.

docs.title: 12.9.2. The Communication Protocol
docs.text:
Once the client is connected, the server sends it a welcome message, then accepts the following commands, one per line, case-insensitive:

CommandServer Responsehelpa list of accepted commands, on four linestax married nbChildren annualSalarythe tax for a married person (married is [y]) or an unmarried person ([n]) with [nbChildren] children and an annual salary of [annualSalary] euros, for example, [4282] in response to [tax y 2 60000]; or an error message, on a linegoodbyethe message [Goodbye...]; the server then closes the connection

Any other command receives the response [Command not recognized. Use the help command.]

docs.title: 12.9.3.1. The subproject
docs.text:
The file [build.gradle.kts] from the subproject [tax-server] is as follows:

// TaxV8: the tax-server subproject (the [server] layer and the integration of the layers)
plugins {
    // the version of the Kotlin plugin is that of the root project (12-internet/build.gradle.kts)
    kotlin("jvm")
    application
}

group = "examples.tax"
version = "8.0"

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // the [dao] and [business] layers of version 5, reused as they are
    // (composite build ../06-architectures); tax-business brings tax-dao
    implementation("examples.tax:tax-business:5.0")
    // the Spring dependency injection container
    implementation("org.springframework:spring-context:7.0.9")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
    // gradlew -q :TaxV8:tax-server:run (current folder: that of the subproject)
    mainClass = "tax.server.MainKt"
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}
  • line 4: the Kotlin plugin, without a version—this is provided by the root project;
  • line 5: the applications plugin, which provides the task [run];
  • lines 8–9: the subproject coordinates, for version 8.0 of the application;
  • line 18: the [business] layer of version 5, identified by its coordinates and provided by the composite build. It declares the [dao] layer within its API ([api] configuration, Chapter 6): the server therefore also has access to the classes in [tax-dao] ([ITaxDao], [FileTax]…), without having to declare it;
  • Line 20: Spring’s dependency injection container. The [kotlin("plugin.spring")] plugin is not necessary: as in the [Main.kt] program from version 5, objects are registered in the container via code, without annotations, and Spring does not need to subclass our classes, which can remain final;
  • lines 23–27: the common compiler configuration (JDK 25, warnings treated as errors, parameter names preserved);
  • Line 33: The main class executed by [gradlew -q :TaxV8:tax-server:run]. The task [run] runs the program in the subproject folder: as in version 5, the program reads its configuration and the tax bracket file from the current folder, where the files [server.properties] and [TaxData.txt] are located;
  • Lines 36–39: Programs launched by Gradle write their output to UTF-8 so that accented characters display correctly on Windows (Chapter 2).

The configuration file [server.properties]:

# configuration of the tax calculation server
# the [dao] layer: as in version 5
dao.implementation=FileTax
dao.file=TaxData.txt
# the listening port and the echo of the dialog with the clients in the log
server.port=27200
server.echo=true
  • lines 3–4: the configuration for the [dao] layer, identical to that of version 5: tax brackets are read from the text file [TaxData.txt];
  • lines 6–7: the server’s listening port and the echo of the dialogue with clients in the server log. Rather than an administration console (with commands such as [start], [stop], [echo]…), we opted for a configuration file and termination via Ctrl-C, which are simpler and more in line with how modern servers operate.

docs.title: 12.9.3.2. The Main Program
docs.text:
The server options form a data class:

package tax.server

// the options of the server: listening port and echo of the dialog in the log
data class ServerOptions(val port: Int, val echo: Boolean)

The server’s [Main.kt] file is as follows:

package tax.server

import tax.dao.FileTax
import tax.dao.HardwiredTax
import tax.dao.ITaxDao
import tax.dao.JsonTax
import tax.entities.TaxException
import tax.business.TaxBusiness
import java.util.Properties
import kotlin.concurrent.thread
import kotlin.io.path.Path
import kotlin.io.path.bufferedReader
import kotlin.system.exitProcess
import org.springframework.beans.factory.getBean
import org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext
import org.springframework.context.support.registerBean

// the TCP tax calculation server: configuration, integration of the layers, execution
// call: gradlew -q :TaxV8:tax-server:run ; stop with Ctrl-C
fun main() {
    val server: TaxServer = try {
        // reading the configuration, in the current folder
        val config = Properties()
        Path("server.properties").bufferedReader().use { config.load(it) }
        val implementation = config.getProperty("dao.implementation", "HardwiredTax")
        val file = config.getProperty("dao.file", "")
        val port = config.getProperty("server.port", "27200").toInt()
        val echo = config.getProperty("server.echo", "false").toBoolean()

        // registration of the layers in the Spring container
        val context = GenericApplicationContext()
        // the [dao] layer: the implementation is chosen by the configuration (as in version 5)
        context.registerBean<ITaxDao> {
            when (implementation) {
                "HardwiredTax" -> HardwiredTax()
                "FileTax" -> FileTax(file)
                "JsonTax" -> JsonTax(file)
                else -> throw TaxException("Unknown implementation [$implementation] of the [dao] layer")
            }
        }
        // the [business] layer of version 5
        context.registerBean<TaxBusiness>()
        // the [server] layer: the container will pass to its constructor the [business] layer
        // and the options of the server
        context.registerBean { ServerOptions(port, echo) }
        context.registerBean<TaxServer>()

        // starting the container: creation of the [dao], [business] and [server] layers
        context.refresh()
        context.getBean<TaxServer>()
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        // display of the chain of exceptions and stop
        println("The following error occurred during the initialization of the server:")
        generateSequence<Throwable>(e) { it.cause }.forEach { cause ->
            println("${cause::class.simpleName} : ${cause.message}")
        }
        exitProcess(1)
    }

    // Ctrl-C: the server is asked to stop, then we wait for the end of the main thread
    val mainThread = Thread.currentThread()
    Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(thread(start = false) {
        server.stop()
        mainThread.join()
    })
    // execution of the server until the stop is requested
    server.execute()
}

We can recognize the main program from version 5:

  • lines 23–28: reading the configuration. The values are character strings: the port and echo are converted by [toInt] and [toBoolean], with default values provided;
  • lines 31–42: the [dao] and [business] layers are registered in the container exactly as in version 5, using the [registerBean] extension functions that Spring provides for Kotlin;
  • lines 45–46: the new feature. The server options (port, echo) are registered as a function that constructs them; the bean’s type, [ServerOptions], is inferred from the type returned by the lambda. Next comes the [server] layer itself. The constructor of *[TaxServer] expects a *[ITaxBusiness] and a *[ServerOptions]*: the container will provide them;
  • Line 49: Starting the container creates the server, which triggers the creation of the [business] layer, which in turn triggers the creation of the [dao] layer; this is when the [TaxData.txt] file is read. An error (missing or malformed file) is displayed, and the program terminates (lines 51–57). [try] is an expression whose value—that of its last expression, [context.getBean<TaxServer>()]—initializes [val server]; the [catch] block does not return a value: [exitProcess] is of type [Nothing], and the compiler knows that it never returns. The exception chain is traversed by [generateSequence<Throwable>(e) { it.cause \}]: the type [Throwable] is specified because the sequence starts with a [Exception], but the causes are [Throwable];
  • lines 61–64: Ctrl-C triggers a stop hook that requests the server to stop, then waits for the main thread to finish, as in the echo server;
  • line 67: the server runs until it is told to stop.

docs.title: 12.9.3.3. The [server] layer
docs.text:
The [TaxServer] class is as follows:

package tax.server

import tax.business.ITaxBusiness
import java.io.IOException
import java.io.PrintWriter
import java.net.ServerSocket
import java.net.Socket
import java.net.SocketException
import java.time.LocalTime
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap
import java.util.concurrent.Executors

// the [server] layer: it makes the [business] layer accessible through a TCP protocol of text lines
class TaxServer(private val business: ITaxBusiness, private val options: ServerOptions) {

    // the listening service and the service connections in progress
    @Volatile
    private var listener: ServerSocket? = null
    private val connections: MutableSet<Socket> = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()

    @Volatile
    private var stopping = false

    // execution of the server until [stop] is called
    fun execute() {
        try {
            ServerSocket(options.port).use { listener ->
                // one virtual thread per client; close() waits for the end of all the services
                Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { services ->
                    this.listener = listener
                    log("Tax calculation server started on port ${options.port}")
                    try {
                        var clientNum = 0
                        while (true) {
                            // wait for a client
                            val client = listener.accept()
                            connections.add(client)
                            // it is served by a virtual thread: we immediately go back to wait for the next client
                            val number = clientNum++
                            services.submit { serve(client, number) }
                        }
                    } catch (e: SocketException) {
                        // accept fails when [stop] closes the listening service
                        if (!stopping) throw e
                        log("Server stop requested")
                        // the connections in progress are closed: the services stop
                        connections.forEach { it.close() }
                    }
                }
            }
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            log("The following error occurred on the server: ${e.message}")
        }
        log("Server stopped")
    }

    // request to stop the server (called by another thread)
    fun stop() {
        stopping = true
        // the listening service does not exist yet if the server has not started
        listener?.close()
    }

    // the service provided to a client
    private fun serve(client: Socket, clientNum: Int) {
        log("Start of service to client $clientNum (${client.remoteSocketAddress})")
        try {
            client.use {
                val reader = client.getInputStream().bufferedReader()
                val writer = PrintWriter(client.getOutputStream(), true, Charsets.UTF_8)

                // sending a response to the client, with a possible echo in the log
                fun write(response: String) {
                    if (options.echo) log("---> client $clientNum : $response")
                    writer.println(response)
                }

                // welcome message
                write(WELCOME)
                // loop reading request / writing response, until the goodbye command
                while (true) {
                    val request = reader.readLine() ?: break
                    if (options.echo) log("<--- client $clientNum : $request")
                    // the request split into fields
                    val fields = request.trim().lowercase().split(SPACES)
                    if (fields == listOf("goodbye")) {
                        write(GOODBYE)
                        break
                    }
                    // the response according to the command
                    val response = when (fields[0]) {
                        "help" -> if (fields.size == 1) HELP else INCORRECT_COMMAND
                        "tax" -> calculateTax(fields)
                        else -> INCORRECT_COMMAND
                    }
                    write(response)
                }
            }
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            if (stopping) {
                log("Service to client $clientNum interrupted by the server stop")
            } else {
                log("The following error occurred while serving client $clientNum : ${e.message}")
            }
        } finally {
            connections.remove(client)
            log("End of service to client $clientNum")
        }
    }

    // the command tax married nbChildren annualSalary: returns the tax or an error message
    private fun calculateTax(fields: List<String>): String {
        // 4 fields are required: tax, y or n, two integers
        val nbChildren = fields.getOrNull(2)?.toIntOrNull()
        val salary = fields.getOrNull(3)?.toIntOrNull()
        if (fields.size != 4 || fields[1] !in listOf("y", "n") || nbChildren == null || salary == null) {
            return INCORRECT_CALCULATION
        }
        return try {
            // the calculation is handed to the [business] layer
            business.calculateTax(fields[1] == "y", nbChildren, salary).toString()
        } catch (e: RuntimeException) {
            // the message of the exception, on a single line: the protocol is made of text lines
            (e.message ?: e.toString()).replace(END_OF_LINE, " ")
        }
    }

    private companion object {
        // the fixed responses of the protocol
        const val WELCOME = "Welcome to the tax calculation server"
        val HELP = """
            Accepted commands
            1-help
            2-tax married(Y/N) nbChildren annualSalary
            3-goodbye
            """.trimIndent()
        const val GOODBYE = "Goodbye..."
        const val INCORRECT_COMMAND = "Command not recognized. Use the help command."
        const val INCORRECT_CALCULATION = "Incorrect calculation command. Use the help command."
        val SPACES = Regex("""\s+""")
        val END_OF_LINE = Regex("""\R""")
        val TIME: DateTimeFormatter = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss")

        // the log of the server: each line is time-stamped
        fun log(message: String) = println("${LocalTime.now().format(TIME)} $message")
    }
}
  • line 15: the class receives the [business] layer and its options via its primary constructor, which directly converts them into private properties. It knows only the interface [ITaxBusiness] of the layer [business] and knows nothing about the layer [dao];
  • Lines 19–23: the listening service, which is cached so that the [stop] function can close it ([null] until the server has started), the current connections, and the shutdown flag. [listener] and [stopping] are modified and read by different threads: they are annotated as [@Volatile];
  • lines 26–55: the client wait loop. This is the echo server’s loop: each client is served by a virtual thread that is not waited for (line 41); closing the listening service ends the wait for a client (line 37); we then close the current connections (line 48) and wait for the services to finish before shutting down (closing [ExecutorService] upon exiting its [use] block). No system thread is blocked by a client that is taking its time;
  • line 31: the parameter [listener] of the lambda function [use] masks the property of the same name: [this.listener] refers to the property;
  • Lines 59–62: The function [stop], called by the stop hook in another thread. The safe call to [listener?.close()] does nothing if the listener service does not yet exist; where Java used to test [listener != null] and intercept the controlled [IOException] from [close], a single line is now sufficient;
  • lines 66–108: the service provided to a client:
    • lines 74–76: a local function, defined in the [use] block, which sends a response to the client and also writes it to the log if echo is enabled. It has access to the variables in the surrounding block ([writer], [clientNum]). The Java program used a lambda of type [Consumer<String>], called by [write.accept(...)]; the local function is called just like any other function;
    • line 80: once the client is connected, the server sends it a welcome message;
    • line 83: the command-reading loop, which stops if the client closes the connection ([null]) or if the server is shut down (exception);
    • line 86: the command, stripped of its leading and trailing spaces and converted to lowercase, is parsed into fields. The regular expression [\s+] (one or more spaces) prevents empty fields caused by multiple consecutive spaces;
    • lines 87–89: the command consists solely of the word [goodbye]; the operator [==] compares the contents of the two lists. The server responds and exits the loop: the connection is closed upon exiting the [use] block;
    • lines 92–95: an expression [when] selects the response based on the first field: [help] alone, a command beginning with [tax], or any other command. An empty line, broken down into a single empty field, receives the response [Command not recognized];
  • lines 113–125: tax calculation:
    • lines 115–118: the command must have four fields, with the second field being [o] or [n] and the last two fields being integers. [getOrNull(2)?.toIntOrNull()] returns [null] if the field is missing or is not an integer ([toIntOrNull] also returns [null] if the number is too large for a [Int]): unlike in Java, there is no need to first validate the format with a regular expression to ensure the conversion cannot fail. After the test, [nbChildren] and [salary] are non-nullable [Int] instances (smart type casting);
    • line 122: the calculation is requested from the [business] layer. A single instance of [TaxBusiness] serves all clients—potentially simultaneously—from different threads: this is possible because this class does not modify any data after it is constructed (its list of slices is read-only);
    • Lines 123–125: If the [business] layer throws an exception (for example, a [IllegalArgumentException] from [require] due to a negative number of children), its message is returned to the client. This message may contain line breaks: these are replaced with spaces ([\R] denotes any line break), because the protocol requires a single-line response. An exception message is of type [String?]; otherwise, the exception description is returned;
  • lines 129–146: the class constants, in a private companion object (the [private static final] fields in Java). Strings known at compile time are [const val]. The response to the [help] command, written as a raw string with indentation removed by [trimIndent], contains line breaks: it will be received by the client as four lines. Regular expressions, compiled once and for all, are raw strings, where [\s] and [\R] are written without doubling the backslash;
  • Line 146: the server log on the console: each line is preceded by the time, which allows you to see the sequence of concurrent services. [println] can be called without caution from multiple threads: its writes do not conflict.

docs.title: 12.9.4. The tax calculation server client
docs.text: The client uses the console interface from version 5—the [tax.ui.Dialog] object—without modifying it.

docs.title: 12.9.4.1. The client’s [business] layer
docs.text:
The [ui] layer communicates with a [business] layer, of which it knows only the [ITaxBusiness] interface from version 5, reduced to a single function: [fun calculateTax(married: Boolean, nbChildren: Int, salary: Int): Int].

Therefore, all that is needed is to provide it with another implementation of this interface, which, instead of calculating the tax, requests it from the server. This is the class [TaxBusinessTcp]:

package tax.client

import tax.entities.TaxException
import tax.business.ITaxBusiness
import java.io.IOException
import java.io.PrintWriter
import java.net.Socket

// the [business] layer of the client: it implements ITaxBusiness by delegating the calculation to the TCP server
// the connection to the server (machine, port) is open for the whole lifetime of the object
class TaxBusinessTcp(machine: String, port: Int) : ITaxBusiness, AutoCloseable {

    private val client: Socket = try {
        Socket(machine, port)
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        throw TaxException("Unable to connect to the server ($machine, $port)", e, 21)
    }
    private val reader = client.getInputStream().bufferedReader()
    private val writer = PrintWriter(client.getOutputStream(), true, Charsets.UTF_8)

    init {
        // the server speaks first: its welcome message is read (and ignored)
        try {
            readResponse()
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            client.close()
            throw TaxException("Unable to connect to the server ($machine, $port)", e, 21)
        }
    }

    // tax calculation: one request, one response
    override fun calculateTax(married: Boolean, nbChildren: Int, salary: Int): Int {
        val response = try {
            writer.println("tax ${if (married) "y" else "n"} $nbChildren $salary")
            readResponse()
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            throw TaxException("Error communicating with the server", e, 22)
        }
        // the server returns the tax, or an error message
        return response.toIntOrNull() ?: throw TaxException("The server answered: $response", code = 23)
    }

    // reading a response line; null means that the server has closed the connection
    private fun readResponse(): String =
        reader.readLine() ?: throw TaxException("The server has closed the connection", code = 24)

    // end of the connection: we take leave of the server, if it is still there
    override fun close() {
        try {
            client.use {
                writer.println("goodbye")
                reader.readLine()
            }
        } catch (_: IOException) {
            // the connection is already cut: there is nothing more to do
        }
    }
}
  • Line 11: The class implements [ITaxBusiness]. It also implements [AutoCloseable]: it maintains a network connection, which will need to be closed. The parameters of its primary constructor, [machine] and [port], are not properties (neither are [val] nor [var]): they are used solely for initialization;
  • Lines 13–19: the connection to the server and its read and write streams, initialized in the order they are declared. We open a single connection, used for all calculations in a session, rather than one connection per calculation: this is more efficient, and the server sees one client per user session. A connection error is encapsulated in a [TaxException], the application exception, with code 21;
  • lines 21–27: the [init] block, executed after the preceding properties have been initialized, reads the server’s welcome message. If this read operation fails, the connection is closed and the error is reported as a connection error;
  • lines 32–40: tax calculation. The command [tax y 2 60000] is sent to the server (line 34) and its response is read; [try] is an expression that returns this response. If this is an integer, it is the tax; otherwise, it is an error message from the server, which is passed in a [TaxException]: the Elvis operator throws the exception when [toIntOrNull] evaluates to [null] ([throw] is an expression of type [Nothing]). Code 23 is passed via a named argument, as the exception has no cause;
  • lines 44–45: [readLine] returns [null] when the server has closed the connection: a [TaxException] is then thrown;
  • lines 48–55: the end of the connection. The client logs off from the server with the [goodbye] command, reads its response, and then closes the connection ([client.use] block). If the server has already terminated the connection, the resulting [IOException] is ignored.

This class uses the blocking methods of [Socket], as do all clients in this chapter: the [ITaxBusiness] interface in Version 5 is synchronous ([calculateTax] returns a [Int]; it is not a [suspend] function), and for a console program serving a single user, this is perfectly suitable: the main thread has nothing else to do but wait for the response. If multiple calculations were to be performed in parallel, we would call [calculateTax] from multiple virtual threads, or from coroutines on [Dispatchers.IO] (with one connection per thread or per coroutine, since [TaxBusinessTcp] is not designed to be used by multiple threads at the same time).

docs.title: 12.9.4.2. The client’s main program
docs.text:
The [tax-client] subproject depends on the [business] layer and the [ui] layer from version 5:

// TaxV8: the tax-client subproject (the TCP client [business] layer and the integration of the layers)
plugins {
    // the version of the Kotlin plugin is that of the root project (12-internet/build.gradle.kts)
    kotlin("jvm")
    application
}

group = "examples.tax"
version = "8.0"

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // the interface of the [business] layer and the [ui] layer of version 5 (composite build)
    implementation("examples.tax:tax-business:5.0")
    implementation("examples.tax:tax-ui:5.0")
    // the Spring dependency injection container
    implementation("org.springframework:spring-context:7.0.9")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
    // gradlew -q :TaxV8:tax-client:run [--args="machine port"]
    mainClass = "tax.client.MainKt"
}

tasks.named<JavaExec>("run") {
    // the dialog reads the keyboard
    standardInput = System.`in`
}

// on Windows, the screen output of the program launched by Gradle (run, bootRun...) is encoded in UTF-8,
// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the IntelliJ IDEA console or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}
  • lines 17–18: the interface of the [business] layer and the [ui] layer of version 5, provided by the composite construction;
  • line 20: the Spring container;
  • lines 36–38: the program launched by [gradlew run] must be able to read the keyboard;
  • lines 41–44: The programs launched by Gradle write their output to UTF-8 so that accented characters display correctly on Windows (Chapter 2).

The [tax-ui] subproject in version 5 contains an application (its file [Main.kt]); however, it can be used as a library for its public object [tax.ui.Dialog]. The client’s [Main.kt] file is as follows:

package tax.client

import tax.business.ITaxBusiness
import tax.ui.Dialog
import org.springframework.beans.factory.getBean
import org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext
import org.springframework.context.support.registerBean

// the console client of the tax calculation server
// call: gradlew -q :TaxV8:tax-client:run [--args="machine port"]   (by default: localhost 27200)
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    val machine = args.getOrElse(0) { "localhost" }
    val port = args.getOrNull(1)?.toInt() ?: 27200

    try {
        // the Spring container is closed when leaving use: it then closes the AutoCloseable objects
        // it has created
        GenericApplicationContext().use { context ->
            // the [business] layer is now a TCP client of the tax calculation server
            context.registerBean<ITaxBusiness> { TaxBusinessTcp(machine, port) }
            // starting the container: creation of the [business] layer, hence connection to the server
            context.refresh()
            val business = context.getBean<ITaxBusiness>()
            println("Connected to the tax calculation server ($machine, $port)")
            // the [ui] layer of version 5, unchanged
            Dialog.run(business)
        }
    } catch (e: RuntimeException) {
        // connection or communication error: display of the chain of exceptions
        Dialog.displayError(e)
    }
}
  • lines 12–13: the server’s machine and port, passed as arguments, with default values: [args.getOrElse(0) { "localhost" \}] returns the first argument if it exists, otherwise the value of the lambda;
  • line 18: the Spring container is closed upon exiting the [use] block (it is [AutoCloseable]). When it is closed, at the end of the program, it calls the [close] method on the [AutoCloseable] objects it created: the connection for [TaxBusinessTcp] will be closed properly;
  • line 20: the [business] layer stored in the container is now [TaxBusinessTcp]. Since its constructor expects two parameters that the container does not know, a creation function is provided; the bean’s type is specified explicitly as [ITaxBusiness], because the [ui] layer requests it under this type;
  • line 22: When the container starts up, it creates the [business] layer, thereby connecting to the server;
  • line 26: the Version 5 dialog box, unchanged. The [ui] layer is unaware that the tax is calculated by a remote server;
  • lines 28–30: a connection or communication error is displayed by the Version 5 function [displayError].

docs.title: 12.9.5. Executions
docs.text:
The server is launched in a command window from the [12-internet] folder using [gradlew -q :TaxV8:tax-server:run]; Gradle compiles the Version 5 subprojects as needed, using the composite build. In another window, the client is launched, also from the [12-internet] folder. As before, user input was sent via standard input redirection and then reinserted after the questions:

> gradlew -q :TaxV8:tax-client:run

Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2 60000
Tax=4282 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 3 60000
Tax=2959 euros

Tax=11519 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: x 2 60000

Married: y for married, n for not married
NbChildren: number of children
Salary: annual salary in euros
Incorrect Married argument: type y or n

Married: y for married, n for not married
NbChildren: number of children

Incorrect NbChildren argument: type a positive or zero integer
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2
